Notes - The Secret History of the World

Mark Booth | August 2, 2026

Chapter 1: In The Beginning: God Peers at His Reflection • The Looking-Glass Universe

No Time, No Matter, and the First Happening

Time is only a measure of changing positions of objects in space — a year is earth circling the sun, a day is earth spinning on its axis. Since neither earth nor sun existed "in the beginning," the biblical authors could not have meant that everything was created in seven days in the ordinary sense of "day." Before time, space, and matter existed, something must still have happened to set everything in motion — a first happening that occurred when there was still nothing, meaning it could not obey the physical laws that govern later events. The proposal is that this first happening was more like a mental event than a physical one.

Mental Events as the Model for Creation

This is not as alien as it sounds: mental events generate physical effects constantly in daily life — an idea ("I want to reach out and touch her cheek") triggers a synaptic pulse, an electrical signal down a nerve, and a hand moves. The mysterious transition from no-matter to matter has, throughout history, been explained by many of the world's most brilliant minds as an impulse squeezing out of another dimension into this one — and that other dimension has been conceived of as the mind of God. A childhood sense of wonder at crystals precipitating out of a solution is offered as an intuitive analogy for an impulse squeezing from one dimension into the next.

The Anthropomorphic Objection, Reversed

Materialist scientists such as Richard Dawkins dismiss the idea of a "mind of God" as an anthropomorphic fallacy — the same mistake children and "primitive" tribes make in assuming God resembles them. Their objection is granted as valid on its own terms — there is no reason at all for God's mind to resemble ours — unless the causality runs the other way: if humans were made in God's image, then human minds would necessarily resemble God's mind by design, not by projection. This reversal — "everything is the other way round" — is offered as the master key to the entire history that follows, likened to Alice passing through the looking glass: readers are invited to entertain ideas the intellectual establishment considers heretical, stupid, or mad, not because a formal philosophical argument for them is being made (those exist elsewhere in academic literature) but as an act of imaginative stretching. A warning is given upfront: mainstream thinkers would consider even briefly entertaining these ideas dangerous, fearing a regression into an "aboriginal" or "atavistic" form of consciousness that humanity fought for millennia to leave behind.

God's Reflection: The Primal Myth

The primal mental event, in this account, was God reflecting on Himself — gazing into an imaginary mirror and seeing the future, imagining beings very like Himself: free, creative beings capable of loving so intelligently and thinking so lovingly that they could transform themselves and others in their innermost being, capable of expanding their minds to embrace the whole cosmos while also discerning its subtlest workings in the depths of their hearts. Sometimes the love in these beings was nearly extinguished; at other times they found deeper happiness on the far side of despair, and meaning on the far side of madness. To grasp this, imagine staring at your own reflection in a mirror and willing that image to come alive and take on independent existence — this is, according to the looking-glass history taught by secret societies, exactly what God did: humans are His reflections, gradually and in stages achieving independent life, nurtured, guided, and prompted by Him over immense stretches of time.

An Anthropocentric, Responsive Universe

Modern science offers a universe of blind indifference — in your greatest anguish, crying out to the heavens yields no answering resonance, and the human task is simply to mature and accept this indifference. The universe described in this account is fundamentally different: made with humankind in mind, anthropocentric down to every particle, straining toward humanity, cradling human consciousness through the millennia and guiding individuals toward their life's great moments. When you cry out, the universe turns toward you in sympathy; at life's crossroads, the whole universe holds its breath to see which way you will choose. Scientific rhetoric about "wonder" and interconnectedness (e.g., the fact that everyone's body contains atoms once in Julius Caesar's body, or that "we are stardust") is acknowledged as evocative but ultimately hollow, since underneath the poetic language it remains a universe of blind force where matter precedes mind and mind is merely an accident of matter — "a disease of matter," in one scientist's phrase. André Breton's declaration that "any piece of flotsam or jetsam within our grasp should be considered as a precipitate of our desire" is cited as capturing the alternative view: that the physical world responds to inner desires and fears, an idea ture, notably Duchamp's ready-mades.

Mind-Before-Matter and Its Practical Implications

In the mind-before-matter universe, matter did not just emerge from the mind of God — it was created specifically to provide conditions in which the human mind would be possible, and the human mind remains the focus of the cosmos, nurturing it and responding to its needs. Matter is moved by human minds in the same kind of way — if not to the same degree — that it is moved by the mind of God. This is not offered as a merely poetic claim but as a literal mechanism with real-world consequences.

Schrödinger's Cat and the Observer Effect

Erwin Schrödinger's 1935 thought experiment — a cat in a box with a 50% chance of being radioactive decay, remaining in an indeterminate state of simultaneous life and death until observed — is presented as physics catching up to what secret societies always taught about everyday reality. The childhood question of whether a tree falling in a remote, unwitnessed forest makes a sound is taken seriously: according to this teaching, a tree only falls so that someone, somewhere, at some time is affected by it. Nothing happens anywhere in the cosmos except in intection with the human mind.

Bent Laws of Probability

A key practical claim: a coin flipped under strict laboratory conditions will still land 50/50 according to standard probability — but only because laboratory conditions deliberately exclude human subjectivity. In the normal course of life, when human happinessnd hopes for self-fulfillment depend on the outcome of a roll of the dice, the laws of probability bend, and deeper laws come into play. This extends the familiar, scientifically accepted idea of psychosomatic effects (emotional states causing bodily healing or harm) outward: in this universe, emotional states directly affect matter outside the body too, without the person needing to consciously act — matter can be moved by the way it is looked at.

Bob Dylan and "Power and Dominion Over Spirit

Bob Dylan's memoir Chronicles: Volume One is cited as a literal, non-metaphorical description of this ancient wisdom: to change the times one lives in requires "power and dominion over the spirits," and the capacity to "see into the heart of things... see into metal and making it melt, see it for what it is with hard words and vicious insight." This is presented as evidence that major artists, writers, and thinkers who have shaped culture have been steeped in this tradition. The core belief: the deepest springs of mental life are also the deepest springs of the physical world — "all chemistry is psycho-chemistry" — meaning the physical universe responds to the human psyche according to laws deeper and more powerful than materialence's laws.

Deeper Laws vs. Gamblers' Superstition

An important clarification/warning: these "deeper laws" are not the same as a gambler's belief in "runs of luck" or superstitions about accidents happening in threes. Rather, they are laws woven into the fabric of each individual life at the most intimate level, and into the great providential patterns that have shaped world history. The book's central thesis is introduced here: history has a deeper structure, and events conventionally explained by politics, economics, or natural disaster can be more profitably understood through more spiritual patterns.

The Unavoidable Choice: Matter-First or Mind-First

Almost no evidence exists to settle what actually happened at the beginning of time, yet the choice carries massive implications. Believing matter came first requires explaining how a chance combination of chemicals produces consciousness — a very hard problem. Believing a cosmic mind precipitated matter requires an equally hard problem: providing a working model of how. From the priests of Egyptian temples through Pythagoras to Rudolf Steiner, and in today's secret societies, this model has consistently been conceived as a hierarchy of emanations from the cosmic mind: pure mind first, then increasingly dse thought-emanations, then proto-matter finer than gas, then true gas, then liquid, then solid.

Robots, Tulpas, and Thought-Beings as Analogies for Emanation

Kevin Warwick, Professor of Cybernetics at Reading University, is cited (from a 2001 Royal Institution presentation) as having built robots exhibiting intelligence comparable to bees, with a prediction that within five years robots would match cats and within ten years match humans. His robots' "brains" grow organically, form something like personalities, interact with other robots, and make choices beyond their programming. When criticized for implying his robots were conscious, Warwick argued dogs are conscious "in a doggy way" and his robots are conscious "in a robotic way" — and in some respects (massive instant calculation) robot coniousness exceeds human consciousness. This is offered as a modern analogy for the emanations of the cosmic mind: Tibetan spiritual masters are said to create thought-forms called tulpas through intense concentration and visualization, which attain independent life and go off to perform their master's bidding; similarly, the sixteenth-century Swiss magus Paracelsus described an "aquastor," a being formed by concentrated imagination that can gain its own life and, in special circumstances, become visible or even tangible. At the lowest level of this hierarchy, according to ancient and secret doctrine across cultures, these emanations — Thought-Beings from the cosmic mind — interweave so tightly they create the appearance of solid matter, conceived alchemically as a "net of light and colour" or "the Matrix."

Theulation Hypothesis and Pop Culture Parallels

A February 2005 Sunday Times headline, "Top Scientist Asks: Is Life All Just a Dream?", reported Britain's Astronomer Royal Sir Martin Rees speculating that if computer simulation trends continue, it may become possible to simulate worlds as complex as this one — raising the philosophical possibility that this univee is itself a simulation. This is linked to the growing scientific fascination with the fine-tuning required for life to evolve. Philip K. Dick is credited as the first writer to seed simulation/altered-reality ideas into pop culture (steeped in initiatic wisdom about altered states and parallel dimensions), with his novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? becoming Blade Runner; other films cited include Minority Report, Total Recall, The Truman Show, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, and especially The Matrix. The villains of The Matrix policing a virtual reality for their own purposes is described as, in part, an accurate reflection of Mystery school and secret society teachings — with a warning embedded: although all beings behind the veil of illusion are part of the hierarchy of emanations from the mind of God, some display disturbing moral ambivalence. These are intified as the same beings ancient peoples experienced as their gods, spirits, and demons.

Metaphysics vs. Physics: Different Questions

The renewed scientific openness to these ancient cosmological ideas is framed as encouraging. Ancient cosmology is defended as a "magnificent philosophical machine" rivaling modern science in scale, complexity, and explanatory power. The key distinction drawn: physics has not replaced metaphysics because they explain different things — modern science exains how the universe comes to be as it is; ancient/esoteric philosophy explains how experience of the universe comes to be as it is. For science, the great miracle is the physical universe; for esoteric philosophy, the great miracle is human consciousness itself.

The Fine-Tuning of Consciousness

Just as scientists marvel at the delicate physical balances that make life possible (heat/cold, earth's distance from the sun, the precise strength of gravity and electromagnetism), esoteric philosophy points to an equally extraordinary series of balances required to produce subjective consciousness as we experience it:

  • Memory must be exactly calibrated — strong enough to sustain aontinuous sense of self and follow through on intentions, but weak enough to allow moving forward into the future without being trapped by the past. Italian novelist Italo Calvino is quoted articulating this precise balance.
  • Sensory perception must be balanced so the outside world is perceived without overwhelming all available mental space — otherwise reflection and imagination would be impossible.
  • Attachment and detachment from internal impulses and external perceptions must be balanced to allow the freedom to redirect attention at will (e.g., the freedom to look up from a page and think about something else) — the very possibility of free thought and free will depends on this precise calibration.
  • At the level of "peak experiences" (Abraham Maslow's term), even finer balances operate: at life's great turning points, working with intelligence, a good and whole heart, patience, humility allows a person to just barely discern the right course of action — and executing that choice typically demands the full extent of available willpower.

None of this fine-tuning of consciousness is inevitable unless one believes in Providence — that it was meant to be. Human consciousness is thus framed as a genuine miracle, one the ancients were deeply stirred by even though modern sensibility tends to overlook it.

What Modern Science Suppresses

Modern science is charged witforcing a narrow, reductive view of consciousness, denying the reality of persistent experiential phenomena it cannot explain: the power of prayer, premonitions, the feeling of being stared at, evidence for mind-reading, out-of-body experiences, and meaningful coincidences. More significantly, science in its reductive mode denies the universal human experience that life has meaning — some scientists go so far as to claim the question of life's meaning is not even worth asking. It is claimed that many of history's most intelligent people have beedevotees of esoteric philosophy, and that virtually every intelligent person has, at some point, sought it out.

Coincidence, Providence, and Everyday Signs

Everyday experiences are offered as evidence of a deeper pattern: a seeming wrong turn (failing an exam, losing a job, a failed relationship) leading to one's true calling or true love; someone declining to board a plane that then crashes, producing a sense of guided footsteps; coincidences that feel like more than chance, hinting at hidden patterns of meaning; happiness discovered on the far side of despair, or love found growing inside hatred. Falling in love is singled out as a paradigm case of the feeling that "this was meant to be."

The Crucial Distinction Between "Why" as Cause and "Why" as Intention

Leading scientists' claims that "string theory" will soon explain everything in the universe are used to set up a key philosophical distinction. Illustrated through a scenario: a boy interrogates his girlfriend about why she stood him up, and her early answers ("because I missed my bus," "because I was late leaving work") are causal (essentially answering HOW), while what he actually wants is her final, honest answer revealing INTENTION ("because I don't want to see you anymore"). Similarly, when people ask "why the universe?" or "why life?", they are not really asking for a causal chain of atoms knocking against atoms (an answer to HOW) — they are asking about intention. This means the big WHY questions cannot, as a matter of basic philosophical distinction, be swered by scientists acting in their capacity as scientists. Scientific answers to such questions, however grammatically valid, leave "a twist of disappointment in the pit of the stomach" because they fail to address the intentional level that is deep-seated and perhaps ineradicable in human longing. Scientists who fail to grasp this distinction, however brilliant otherwise, are labeled "philosophical morons."

Meaning Requires a Preceding Mind

Purpose can be locally assigned (kicking a ball into a net "means" a goal because a mind assigned that meaning), but a life as a whole — birth to death — cannot have meaning without a mind existing beforehand to give it meaning; the same logs claimed to apply to the universe as a whole. When scientists describe the universe as "meaningful," "wonderful," or "mysterious," this is characterized as potentially intellectually dishonest, since an atheistic universe can only be meaningful in the same diminished sense that a stage conjuror's trick is called "magic." All scientific equations addressing life's great questions are, in this view, elaborate ways of saying "we don't know."

Closing Framing for the History to Follow

Modern culture encourages setting aside the big questions of life and death as strictly meaningless, which diminishes the sense of how strange it is to be alive. The stance taken is that something valuable is at risk of being extinguished, leaving people "less alive than we used to be" — and that examining the human condition from this different angle reveals science knows less than it claims and fails to address wt is deepest and highest in human experience. The next chapter is framed as an invitation to inhabit the perspective of ancient initiates, under which even the most solid, reliable truths endorsed by modern science become revealed as matters of interpretation — "little more than a trick of the light," illustrated by the ambiguous image that can be seen either as a witch or a young woman in a feathered hat depending on one's predisposition.

Chapter 2: A Short Walk in the Ancient Woods: Imining Ourselves into the Minds of the Ancients

The Table Thought Experiment: Mind Before Matter

Imagining a perfect table and then looking at a real one raises a foundational philosophical question: which is more real, mind or matter? Today most people privilege matter—physical objects are treated as the yardstick of realy. Plato inverted this, calling ideas "the things that really are." Ancient peoples did not arrive at a mind-before-matter worldview through reasoned philosophical debate; they lived and experienced the world that way directly. Their sense impressions of physical objects were comparatively dim and undifferentiated, while their inner, mental images carried the vividness and reality that sense-objects have for us now.

  • Evidence: ancient temple depictions of trees show branches joined incorrectly to trunks—artists were not carefully observing physical nature because it wasn't the primary reality to them.
  • There are two types of history: the conventional kind assuming human nature and consciousness are constant across time, and the kind pursued here, which holds that consciousness itself changes—even between generations. A carving of women washing clothes by a river resembling a similar scene today is only a superficial coincidence; the inner experience behind it was radically different.
  • Ancient artists lavished detail on images of gods in temple inner sanctums (rendered in gold, jewels, fine detail) while giving perfunctory treatment to mundane physical scenes just steps away—revealing where their real attention and belief in "reality" was direc## The Underestimated Complexity of a Thought

Modern reductive thinking treats thoughts as essentially just words, perhaps with minor accompanying feelings or images. This flies in the face of actual experience.

  • Example: the ordinary thought "I mustn't forget to phone my mother this evening," when examined closely, unravels into a cluster of word associations, memories, feelings, and even impulses of will—rooted in complex psychoanalytic material (guilt, desire, anger, loss, betrayal, dendency, nostalgia for unity with the mother).
  • A thought is never static; it shifts and mutates the moment you try to examine it, and can even provoke contradictory reactions.
  • Schopenhauer: "as soon as you try to put a thought into words it ceases to be true." Words cannot capture the full complexity of an image or feeling—hole dimensions lie glistening on the dark side of even the most dull and commonplace thought."
  • Non-obvious parallel: people who have used marijuana or hallucinogens like LSD may recognize this multi-dimensional, constantly mutating quality of thought from direct experience. Professor William Emboden (Biology, California State University) documented that ancient Egyptians used the blue lily along with opium and mandrake root to induce trance states—suggesting deliberate cultivation of this expanded thought-awareness.
  • Thwise men and women of the ancient world (teachers in the Mystery schools) knew how to work with these hidden dimensions of thought and, over millennia, created and refined images to communicate through them. The earliest history of the world, as taught in the Mystery schools, unfolds as a series of such images.

Imaginative Exercise: Walking as an Ancient Initiate

An invitation to imagine oneself as a person roughly 2,500 years ago walking through woodland toward a sacred site (e.g., Newgrange in Ireland, or Eleusis in Greece), en route to Mystery-school initiation. This exercise is explicitly framed as "completely delusional from the point of view of modern science," yet it is argued that many great historical figures deliberately cultivated this ancient state of consciousness, believing it granted superior insight into how the world really works—insight that inspired great art, literature, and scientific discovery.

  • To this person, the wood is alive and watching him. A breeze is the gesture of a god; lightning is an outbreak of cosmic will (prompting him to walk faster).
  • Entering a cave feels like being inside his own skull—private mental space.
  • Climbing a hill makes his consciousness feel like it races to thrizon and merges with the cosmos; at night the sky is experienced as the mind of the cosmos.
  • Walking a woodland path gives a strong sense of following destiny—unlike the modern feeling of "how did I end up in this life that has nothing to do with me." Everyone in the ancient world felt they had a defined place in the cosmos. Every event carried meaning: a mote in a sunbeam, a bee's flight, a falling sparrow—all were punishments, rewards, warnings, or premonitions. Seeing an owl wasn't a symbol of the goddess Athena—it was Athena, her pnce protruding into physical reality and into his consciousness.

Correspondence Between Human Body and Cosmos

The ancients held, quite literally, that nothing inside the human being lacks a correspondence in nature—the visible world is "humanity turned inside out."

  • Worms are shaped like intestines and function similarly (processing matter).
  • Lungs, which give bird-like freedom of movement through space, share the shape of birds.
  • Mystery school teachers noted that viewed from above/outside, the disposition of human internal organs reflects the solar system's arrangement—meaning "all biology is astrobiology."
  • The sun draws life from seeds and unfurls plants upward; the moon, by contrast, was believed to flatten and widen plants—bulbous plants like tubers were considered especially lunar-influenced.
  • The complex symmetric shapes of plants were believed caused by the path-patterns planets and stars trace across the sky. Example: Saturn traces a sharp pattern in the sky, and this was linked tformation of pine needles on conifers. Non-obvious/practical note: modern science shows pine trees contain unusually large traces of lead—the metal the ancients associated with Saturn.
  • Similarly, planetary movement patterns were believed inscribed into the human body: the loop of the ribs and the lemniscate (bootlace/figure-eight shape) of the centripetal nerves reflect planetary orbits.
  • Biorhythms: science recognizes that earth-moon-sun relationships (seasons, day/night) are biochemically built into living things (e.g.sleep patterns). The ancients went further, recognizing more mathematically complex cosmic rhythms: humans breathe on average 25,920 times per day—matching the number of years in a "great Platonic year" (the time for the sun to complete a full cycle of the zodiac). The "ideal" human lifespan of seventy-two years correspondinglhas that same number embedded (in days, per year cycle correspondence noted in text).

Shared and External Consciousness

Interconnectedness extended beyond the body to consciousness itself.

  • A flock of birds turning as one in the sky was believed to be literally moved by a single unifying thought.
  • Sudden panicked, violent group movement of animals in the woods was attributed to being moved by the god Pan.
  • Ancient people commonly experienced great spirits "thinking through" themselves and others simultaneously. At Mystery schools, when a master introduced a new thought, all pupils were believed to experience the identical thought—as if the master held up a physical object for everyone to see. This shared-thought experience felt like closer connection than mere physical proximity.
  • Modern proprietary attitudes toward thought ("my private mental space is inviolate") don't hold up to scrutiny: geniuses like Newton, Kepler, Leonardo, Edison, and Tesla described inspiration arriving as if from outside, sometimes literally in dreams. Everyday language reflects this too—"it strikes me," "it occurs to me." A perfectly timed quip that "just jumps out of your mouth" before conscious phrasing is a small modern echo of this phenomenon.
  • The ancients ustood the "somewhere else" thoughts come from as literally "some-one else"—a god, angel, or spirit. Individuals were not always prompted by the same entity; rather than one unified center of consciousness inside the head (the modern view), ancient people experienced themselves as having multiple centers of consciousness originating outside the head.
  • Gods, angels, and spirits are Thought-Beings, emanations from the great cosmic mind, that express themselves through people. Ancient framin not "people thinking" but "Thoughts peopling."

Spirits, Genius, and the Rise/Fall of Great Figures

Gods, angels, and spirits can bring about major shifts in a nation's fortunes, often channeled through a single individual.

  • Example: Alexander the Great and Napoleon were vehicles for a great spirit—invincible and unstopple for a period, until the spirit left them, at which point everything abruptly began to go wrong.
  • Artists similarly can become vehicles for a god or spirit for a period of their lives, "finding their voice" and producing masterpiece after masterpiece, sometimes transforming a whole generation's consciousness or a culture's direction—until the spirit departs, ter which the artist never creates with the same genius again.
  • The same spirit that wove through an artist to create a work can be present again whenever that work is contemplated by others. Quoted contemporary remark about Bach: "When Bach plays the organ, even God comes to Mass."
  • Contrast with Christian belief: many Christians hold God is present in the Eucharist in an elusive way debated for centuries. By contrast, liturgical records from ancient Egypt (The Book of the Opening of the Mouth) and chronicles from the temple of the Vestal Virgins in Rome recorded regular "epiphanies"—actual appearances of the gods during religious ceremonies—experienced as far more imposing and awe-inspiring than modern equivalents.
  • When a thought came to the man in the woods, he felt "brushed by the wing of an angel or the robe of a god"—sensing presence even without full direct perception. Inside theprecinct itself, he could perceive the angel or god directly, and expected the experience to be visible to others too—what today would be called a "collective hallucination."
  • Non-obvious contrast: today's illumination is experienced as an interior event; the ancients experienced it as impinging from outside. Modern people struggle to know how to encounter a disembodied spirit and often doubt whether they've had a genuine spiritual experience at all; for ancient people, denying the spiritorld would have been as absurd as denying the reality of a table in front of them.
  • Pointed critique: the Church teaches belief is more admirable the more it exceeds available evidence—a notion that would have seemed absurd to ancient peoples, for whom spiritual experience was direct and undeniable.

Warning: The Danger oCommerce with Spirits

Because gods and spirits were believed to control and exercise power over the material world, and because disembodied beings could sometimes break through unbidden—occasionally possessing whole mmunities in convulsions of uncontrollable sexual savagery—commerce with spirits was always considered highly dangerous. Controlled communion with gods and spirits was therefore restricted to the preserve of the Mystery schools, which alone possessed the discipline and structure to manage it safely.

##ncient Scientific Sophistication: The Sirius Example

Robert Temple (Visiting Professor of Humanities, History and Philosophy of Science, University of Louisville; Visiting Professor, Tsinghua University, Beijing) demonstrated that ancient cultures such as the Chinese and Egyptians possessed cosmological understanding in some ways ahead of modern science.

  • The Egyptians knew Sirius was a three-star system—something modern science only confirmed in 1995, when French astronomers using powerful radio telescopes detected the red dwarf later named Sirius C.
  • This overturns the assumption that ancient Egyptians were ignorant or childlike in their cosmology.
  • Correcting a common misconception: the ancients did not worship the physical suns a sentient being. Temple's analysis of Aristotle, Strabo, and other classical texts shows the sun was understood as a lens through which a god's spiritual influence rayed from the spiritual realm into the earthly realm. Other gods rayed their influence through other planets and constellations, and as the positions of these heavenly bodies shifted, the resulting patterns of influence shaped the direction and form of history.

Planetary Influence on the Body: Practical/Scientific Corroboration

Returning to the man in the wood: he experienced the spirits behind the sun, moon, and planets as acting on distinct parts of his mind and body.

  • His limbs moved "like flowing Mercury"; he felt the spirit of Mars raging in his blood, described as a "fierce river of molten iron."
  • His kidney state was governed by Venus's movement. Modern science has begun catching up: early twentieth-century research found the kidney's role in storing testosterone.
  • Notable experimental corroboration: in the 1980s, Swiss pharmaceutical company Weleda conducted tests showing that planetary movements produce chemical changes in metal salt solutions dramatic enough to be seen with the naked eye—ev where the causal influence is too subtle for standard scientific instruments to measure. Crucially, the strongest changes occurred specifically when a metal salt was examined in relation to the planet traditionally associated with that metal—e.g., copper salts (present in the kidney) reacted distinctly in relation to Venus, copper being Venus's traditional metal. This is presented as science verging on confirming the old maxim that "Venus is the planet of desire."
  • Mystery school teaching: beyond head-consciousness, humans have multiple consciousness centers tied to organs/planets—e.g., heart-consciousness emanates from the sun and enters through the heart (the heart as "portal" for the Sun god); kidney-consciousness beams in from Venus via the kidneys. The interplay of these centers produces the full range of human temperament: loving, angry, melancholy, restless, brave, thoughtful, etc. -se planetary/cosmic influences, working through the body's different consciousness-centers, are understood to prepare individuals for the great tests and experiences the cosmos intends for them—meaning the deep structure of a human life is described by the movements of the heavenly bodies (e.g., desire aroused by Venus, severe testing associated with the return of Saturn).

Transition

This chapter's imaginative exercises are framed as an entry point into the esoteric method used througut; the next chapter promises to cross the threshold of the Mystery school itself and begin tracing the ancient history of the cosmos.

Chapter 3: The Garden of Eden: The Genesis Code • Enter the Dark Lord • The Flower People

The First Emanation: The Mother of All Living

At the beginning, before matter existed, a subst finer and more subtle than light precipitated out of the void — an exceptionally fine gas or cosmic mist. This mist was the Mother of All Living, sometimes called the Mother Goddess, carrying within it everything needed for the creation of life. She would metamorphose over the course of history into many forms and names, but in the biblical account she is desibed simply: "the earth was without form and void."

The Second Emanation: The Attack of the Dark Lord

A second emanation then overtook the first — a viole, searing dry wind of cosmic scale, described in Genesis as "darkness upon the face of the earth." To the eye of imagination, this cloud and storm can be seen to cloak two gigantic phantoms locked in combat. The Mother Goddess, though usually remembered as loving and nurturing (comfortingly round and soft), also had a fierce, warlike aspect — among the Phrygians she was worshipped as Cybele, a merciless goddess pulled by lions, whose devotees would work themselves into savage delirium and castrate themselves in her honor.

Her opponent, the Dark Lord, was long, bony, scaly white-skinned, with glowing red eyes, and armed with a scythe — identifying him as Saturn, god of Time and Death. This second emanation from the mind of God would me the god of Saturn, tracing the outer limits of the solar system.

Saturn's Nature and Function

Saturn is the very principle of limitation. His intervention introduced the potential for individual objects to exist — the transition from formlessness to form. Because of Saturn, a law of identity exists in the universe: something exists as itself and nothing else, occupying a specific space at a specific time, and no other object can occupy that same space simultaneously. In Egyptian myology Saturn is Ptah, who molds the earth on a potter's wheel; in many traditions his title is Rex Mundi ("King of the World") or "Prince of this World," reflecting his control over material life.

The dark corollary: if something can exist through time, it can also cease to exist. This is why Saturn is also the god of destruction, sometimes portrayed as Old Father Time or as Death himself, said to "eat his own children." Because of Saturn's influence, everything that lives carries the seeds of its own end — what feeds us also destroys us. Death is woven into everything in the cosmos: the sky, a blade of grass, a baby's pulse, the light in a lover's eye. Every sword is double-edgedevery crown is a crown of thorns. When life feels unbearably hard, it is because Saturn pushes existence to its limits.

A warning for the future: Saturn has returned at different times and in different guises throughout history to pursue his aim of "mummifying" humanity and squeezing the life out of it. His most decisive intervention yet — an event long predicted by secret societies — is expected to take place at the culmination of this history (i.e., in times still to come).

Had Saturn's tyranny not been checked, the potential for life in the cosmos could have been extinguished before it ever began; the universe would have remained eternally a place of dead matter sifting without end.

Decoding Genesis Through Polytheism

Understanding this cosmology requires confronting an uncomfortable truth: the Bible, properly translated, is not strictly monotheistic in the way modern churches prt it. Today's radical Church monotheism is partly a byproduct of scientific pressure, reducing God to a vague, undetectable immanence and spirituality to a fuzzy feeling of "oneness."

But Christianity's roots lie in older, polytheistic, astronomically-oriented religions of its region of origin, and early Christian spirituality meant literal commerce with actual spirits. Evidence of this survives openly:

  • Christian churches — from Chartres and St Peter's in Rome down to small parish church — were built on the sites of older holy wells, sacred caves, temples, and Mystery schools, all understood as portals for spirits, or cracks in the fabric of space-time.
  • Astro-archaeology confirms these portals were astronomically aligned to funnel spiritual influx at propitious times — as at Karnak in Egypt, where a beam onrise light on the summer solstice would travel five hundred yards through the temple to strike the Holy of Holies.
  • All Christian churches remain astronomically aligned (typically due east, oriented to the dedicated saint's day). Cathedrals like Notre Dame and the Sagrada Familia are covered in astronomical and astrological symbolism.
  • The great Christian festivals are themselves astronomically fixed: Easter falls on the first Sunday after the full moon following the vernal equinox; Christmas falls just after the winter solstice, when the sun's path visibly reverses.
  • The Bible itself refers repeatedly to disembodied spiritual beings — gods of rival tribes, angels, archangels, devils, demons, Satan, Lucifer — and a hierarchy of these beings has always been Church doctrine, referenced by St Paul, elaborated by St Dionysus, codified by St Thomas Aquinas, and depicted by Dante.

What has been actively suppressed and reserved for esoteric teaching specifically is that these orders of angels correspond to the gods of the stars and planets. Modern biblical scholarship privately acknowledges many passages describe astronomical deities — Psalm XIX's description of a "bridegroom" sun, for instance, read alongside comparable texts, describes the marriage sun to Venus.

The Four Cherubim and the Zodiac

The four Cherubim — appearing in Ezekiel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Revelation, and prominent throughout Church art — are symbolized by the Ox, Lion, Eagle, and Angel. In esoteric teaching these represent the great spiritual beings behind four constellations of the zodiac: Ox = Taurus, Lion = Leo, Eagle = Scorpio, Angel = Aquarius. This fourfold symbolic pattern recurs across all major world religions.

Elohim: The Plural Gods of Genesienesis 1:26 is commonly translated "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," but the Hebrew word "Elohim" is grammatically plural — the passage properly reads "In the beginning the gods made heaven and earth." Biblical scholars will admit this when pressed, though it is generally glossed over outside esoteric circles.

Thedentity of these gods can be recovered by comparing Genesis with the opening of the Gospel of John: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God and the Word was God ... All things were made by him ... And the light shineth in the darkness and the darkness comprehended it not." John was not inventing this concept — the Greek philosopher Heraclitus had written four hundred years earlier that "the Logos was before the Earth could be." According to ancient tradition, the Word/Logos that "let there be light"efers to the seven great spirits who together constitute the spiritual influence emanating from the sun — called the Seven Spirits of Ra in the Egyptian Book of the Dead, and the Seven Powers of Light in ancient Hebrew tradition. The sun god was conventionally depicted with seven rays representing these seven spirits, and this same imagery was used to depict Christ in the earliest Christian art (e.g., a third-century Vatican mosaic).

The Sun God's Rescue of Earth

The second great act of creation's drama comes when the seven-fold Sun god arrives to rescue Mother Earth from Saturn. In imaginative vision, the Sun is a radiant young man with a leonine mane, riding a chariot, and a musician — known as Krishna in India, Apollo in GreeArising amid the storm, he pushes back Saturn's darkness until Saturn is reduced to a giant dragon or serpent encircling the cosmos.

The Sun then warms Mother Earth into new life, giving out a triumphal roar that reverberates to the cosmos's outer limits. This roar causes cosmic matter to vibrate, dance, and form patterns — called in esoteric circles "the dance of the substances" — eventually coagulating into strange shapes. In essence, the sun sings the world into existence.

The Sun-Liotif recurs throughout ancient art whenever this creative stage is depicted. A modern literary echo of this myth appears, notably, in C.S. Lewis's The Magician's Nephew (prequel to The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe) — Lewis's work is described as steeped in Rosicrucian lore, and his character Aslan singing Narnia into existence directly mirrors this ancient imagery.

The Vegetable Stage of Creation

The victory of the Sun god represents the transition from a purely mineral cosmos to one burgeoning with plant life. In the earliest, mt primitive stage, single germs joined together in vast floating web-like structures filling the universe — described in the Vedas as "the net ofndra," an infinite net of luminous, interweaving living threads.

Over time these threads wove together more permanently into tree-like forms — comparable to the experience of visiting a great hothouse like the one at Kew Gardens (associated with Alice Liddell, inspiration for Alice in Wonderland): humid mists, sunny luminous greenness, tendrils everywhere. The vast vegetable being at the heart of the cosmos, whose soft luminous limbs stretched to all four corners of it, was Adam. This was Paradise.

Because no animal element yet existed in the cosmos, Adam had no desire, and therefore no care or dissatisfaction — needs were satisfied before they could even be felt. Adam lived in endless springtime, nourished by an unending supply of milky sap (similar to that found in dandelions today) — a state memorialized in ancient statues of the many-breasted Mother Goddess. Adam literally occupied thre cosmos, a detail visible in a comparison between a thirteenth-century manuscript depiction and Leonardo's famous drawing (Vitruvian Man), which is often missed.

As time passed, plant forms grew more complex, evolving toward flowering plants recognizable today.

The Vegetable Element Still Within the Human Body

Unlike the purely sequential scientific account of evolution, esoteric teaching holds that the vegetable stage humanity passed through did not simply vanish — it remains an eential, still-functioning part of the human being today.

  • If the sympathetic nervous system were removed from the body and stood upright on its own, it would resemble a tree. As one leading homeopathic healer put it: "The sympathetic nervous system is the gift of the vegetable kingdom to the physical body of man."
  • Esoteric traditions worldwide concern themselves with subtle energies flowing through this vegetable component of the body, and with the "flowers" upon this tree — the chakras — which function as its organs of perception.
  • The great center of this vegetable component, feeding on the sun's light and warmth, is the solar plexus chakra — named "solar" because it formeng the sun-ruled era of creation.
  • Awareness of this vegetable body element survives most strongly in China and Japan. In Chinese medicine, the energetic life force flowing through this network is chi; disease arises when this delicate network becomes blocked. That this energy flow is undetectable by materialist science does not diminish its effectiveness, as attested by generations of patients.
  • In Chinese and Japanese spiritual practice, the solar plexus (the hara, or lower belly) is emphasized as the seat of meditation — a meditating Buddha statue shows someone gathered inward around this center, having withdrawn from the "rigid, deadly mentality of the brain" to connect with all living things.
  • J.B. van Helmont, an important alchemist and scientist, called the stomach "the seat of the soul."

Chakras in Western and Christian Esoteric Tradition

Though popularized in the West via Easrn influence, chakras are equally central to Western esoteric tradition, appearing in Egyptian and Hebrew thought and hidden within Christianity itself.

  • The vegetable body's organs sit in nodes along its trunk, each with differing numbers of petals — the solar plexus chakra has ten petals; the brow chakra has two.
  • The seven major chakras (groin, solar plexus, kidneys, heart, throat, brow, crown) appear in the seventeenth-century writings of Jacob Boehme and, later, in the writings of tholic Saint Teresa of Ávila, where they are called "the eyes of the soul."
  • Coded biblical references to chakras include: the "horns" traditionally depicted on Moses (dismissed by conventional Christians as mistranslation) actually represent the two petals of the brow chakra, or Third Eye; the flowering rod of Aaron refers tothe activation of the chakras — "the opening of the subtle flowers up and down the subtle tree." Revelation's account of the opening of the seven seals is a coded description of the enlivening of the seven chakras and e visions that result.
  • The vesica piscis (the almond shape surrounding depictions of Jesus) derives from the Egyptian hieroglyph Ru, symbolizing both the birth-portal and the Third Eye/brow chakra — as carved by masons on a church at Alpirsbach, Germany, signifying that direct experience of and communication with great spiritual beings is possible by activating the Third Eye. This symbol appears throughout Christian art and architecture worldwide, unrecognized by most Christians today.

The Pineal Gland and the Third Eye

The pineal gland — a small, almond-sized grey gland at the point where the spinal cord meets the brain — is understood in esoteric physiology as the physical seat of the Third Eye.

  • When a person has a hunch, the pineal gland begins to vibrate; spiritual disciplines that increase and prolong this vibration may lead to the opening of the Third Eye, located at the brow.
  • Modern science only "discovered" the pineal gland in 1866 (via near-simultaneous monographs by H.W. de Graaf. Baldwin Spencer). It is large in children, and around puberty — precisely when people naturally become less imaginative — it begins to calcify and shrink. Melatonin, produced mostly by the pineal gland at night, is essential for sleep-wake rhythm and immune function.
  • Ancient peoples knew of the gland's existence and function far earlier, and knew how to manipulate it to achieve altered states: Egyptians depicted it as a uraeus snake; Indian iconography shows it as the Third Eye of Enlightenment (Eye of Shiva); folls of Dionysius carried it symbolically as a pine-cone-topped wand; a fourth-century BC Greek anatomist called it "the sphincter which regulates the flow of thought."
  • It was regarded as an organ of perception into higher worlds — a window onto spiritual hierarchies — openable through meditation and secret practices that gavse to visions.
  • Practical/scientific note: Recent research at the University of Toronto found that meditating on the pineal gland using methods recommended by Indian yogis causes it to release a rush of melatonin âhe secretion responsible for dreams and, in sufficient doses, waking hallucinations.
  • Artists including Peter Breugel, Henri Met de Bles, and Hieronymus Bosch depicted proto-human creatures of pink, waxy bone — imagery whose true esoteric source has gone unrecognized by art critics.

Adam's Transfortion and the Birth of Eve

Returning to the creation narrative: Adam's body was originally soft and amorphous, its skin as delicate as the surface of a pond, but it gradually began to harden. Jacob Boehme, in his commentary on Genesis (Mysterium Magnum), wrote that "what would in time become bone now hardened and became something closer to wax." Warmed by the sun, Adam's green limbs became tinged with pink.

As Adam solidified, he began to divide into two — he had originally been a hermaphrodite reproducing asexually. Genesis 1:27, usually translated "Male and female He created them," properly reads (per biblical Hebrew scholarship, when pressed) "Male and female they [the Elohim] created him [singular]." Eve was thus born out of Adas body by this plant-like method of reproduction, molded from the waxy cartilage that served Adam for bone.

Adam and Eve's progeny likewise reproduced asexually, procreating through sound in a manner analogous to the creative power of the Word. This is connected to Freemasonic lore of "the Word that has been lost" — the esoteric belief that when this Word is one day rediscovered, it will become possible to impregnate using only the sound of the human voice.

Adam, Eve, and their progeny d not die in this era; they merely slept periodically to refresh themselves. But this lotus-eating paradisal state could not continue indefinitely — had it done so, humanity would never have evolved beyond the vegetable stage. It was always intended that the Sun god would separate from the earth for a time.

Historical Evidce: Herodotus at Memphis

Although no physical artefacts survive from the era when gods and proto-humans existed in plant form, a reliable ancient record of such artefacts exists. Herodotus (fifth-century BC Greek writer, "father of history" for his effort to compile coherent, objective historical accounts) visited Memphis, Egypt around 485 BC. There, in vast underground vaults, priests showed him rows of statues of former kings stretching back into almost unimaginably distant times. Walking the rows, he reached a series of 345 colossal wooden carvings depicting beings who reigned before Menes, Egypt's first human king. The priests explained these beings were "born one from the other" — reproduced without a sexual partner, by plant-like parthenogenesis. Each carving bore a plaque recording its name and history, forming a monumental record of a long-lost era of humankind's vegetable life. Mandrake roots — whose shapes often seem to strive toward human form — are cited as a possible visual analogue for what these lost colossi may have resembled.

Chapter 4: Lucifer, The Light of the World: The Apple of Desire • A War in Heaven • The Secrets of the Days of the Week

The Third Act of the Mystery Drama

Creation was re-enacted in Mystery schoolma in three acts. The first act dramatized Saturn's oppression of Mother Earth (the Age of Saturn). The second dramatized the birth of the Sun and his protection of Earth, the paradise time of the flower people (the Age of the Sun). The candidate for initiation experienced these acts in an altered state, half-drugged, guided by priests on a shaman-like journey through spirit worlds — this was closer to a séance than to theatre as understood today.

The third act begins with a momentous cos event: earth and sun separate. The sun's rays now shine down from the sky rather than illuminating the earth from within. As a result the earth cools, becomes denser, less gaseous and more liquid, shrinking until its watery surface is covered by Adam and Eve and their flowery, fluttering progeny.

The Serpent Enters Paradise

At the climax of the drama, the initiation candidate caught a whiff of sulphur and was half-blinded by a lightning-like flash as a glistening, horned alien life-form invaded the peaceful scene — pictured as an endlessly long snake weaving into the cosmos, "a snake with a perverse kind of beauty." Ezekiel 28:13 is cited: "Thou hast been in Eden, the garden ofod... every precious stone was thy covering." The candidate watched in horror as the serpent coiled around Adam's vegetable trunk, understanding this as the image of life's painful transition from vegetable to animal existence — specifically, the entwining of snake and tree is read as a picture of the formation of the spine and central nervous system, retained in the human collective subconscious.

A non-obvious point: since the eighteenth century's shift to a matter-before-mind worldview, the Church's attempts to reconcile Genesis with science have been doomed because they rest on an anachronistic reading. Genesis is not an objective scientific account of evolution but a subjective account of what evolution felt like. The esoteric account is not necessarily inconsistent with the scientific one — it simply views the same facts from a different perspective, like a perspected picture.

The as Lived Ordeal

Vegetable life formed a "seed bed" or cradle into which animal life could be born — this is the beginning of the Fall. Candidates were made to feel the Fall's crisis literally: pitched as if by an earth tremor into a black hole, a snake pit. The esoteric tradition identifies the rough-hewn Chamber of Ordeal beneath the Great Pyramid at Gizah as serving this function. A practical/archaeological detail: recent excavations at Baia in Italy, where a cave system was believed bthe Romans to be the actual entrance to the Underworld, revealed a trap door that would have flung initiation candidates down into a snake pit below.

The candidate experienced how Lucifer and his legions infested the earth with a plague of glistening serpents, and how desire tormented the very ground, making it heave — tracesf this torment supposedly visible in expressive rock formations.

Why the Fall Brought Suffering

Genesis emphasizes torment: "in sorrow shalt thou bring forth children," "cursed is the ground for thy sake," "thorns also and thistles." An explanatory insight bridges ancient language and modern biology: plants reproduce by parthenogenesis — a part of the plantalls off and grows into a new plant, a continuation of the old one that in a sense does not die. The evolution of animal life and its sexual reproduction brought death with it. As soon as hunger and desire were felt, so too were dissatisfaction, frustration, sorrow and fear.

Lucifer Is Not Satan — Identifying the Two Devils

Most people assume Christianity has only one Devil, that Satan and Lucifer are identical — but biblical scholars accept (though it hasn't filtered down to congregations) that this is a distortion caused by the Church covering up its astronomical roots. Satan, the Dark Lord and agent of materialism, is identified with the planet Saturn. Lucifer is a separate entity, identified explicitly in Isaiah 14:12: "How thou art fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning" — the Morning Star being Venus. The Bible therefore identifies Lucifer with the planet Venus.

Thougter-intuitive to equate the seemingly life-enhancing goddess Venus/Aphrodite with an evil tempter, key similarities exist:

  • Both Lucifer and Venus/Aphrodite are bound up with animal desire and sexuality.
  • The correlation appears cross-culturally, e.g., in Mesoamerican mythology as the horned, feathered snake god Quetzalcoatl.
  • The snake coiled round the goddess's body was called "the minister of the goddess" by the Greeks.
  • The apple links both figures: Lucifer tempts Eve with an apple; Paris hands Venus an apple, precipitating the abduction of Helen and the Trojan War. Non-obvious detail: the apple is universally Venus's fruit because slicing an apple in half reveals a five-pointed star at its core — matching the five-pointed star traced by Venus's path across the sky over a forty-year cycle.

Lucifer as Nessary Evil

Lucifer and Venus are ambiguous figures — evil, but necessary. Without Lucifer's intervention, proto-humanity would never have evolved beyond vegetative life. His influence animates humans both physicallymovement) and psychologically (desire). An animal possesses conscious self-awareness denied to plants; Adam and Eve "knowing they were naked" means becoming aware they had bodies. Ancient art shows both beautiful and terrifying representations of Venus — behind the beautiful woman lurked a terrifying serpent woman.

The Emerald, the Third Eye, and Lucifer's Fall

Drawing on medieval German poetry (later adapted by Wolfram von Eschenbach in Parzifal), tradition holds that as Lucifer fell from heaven, Saint Michael struck the crown from his head and a great emerald jumped loose, becoming the Parsifal stone on earth. This signals humanity's increasing loss of vision in the Third Eye (the brow chakra) — a symbolic/practical point about diminished spiritual perception following the Fall.

Venus's Birth and the Nature of Delusion

In Greek myth, Venus is born when Saturn castrates Uranos (the Sky god) with a sickle; Uranos's sperm falls into the sea and Venus springs forth fully formed, floating ashore on a sea shell. Shells were beed to be precipitated out of water just as matter is precipitated out of spirit — hence their symbolism of emanation from cosmic mind, seen also in the iconography of St James of Compostela.

A key distinction: while Satan's influence makes life hard to bear, Venus's influence makes life hard to understand — she brought a paradoxical, tricky quality to the universe. Lucifer endowed matter with a glamour that dazzles humankind and blinds people to higher truths. This explains why the way frd can look like the way backwards, and why the wrong path can seem nearly indistinguishable from the right one. The Luciferic element is infused into human physiology itself, so desire and delusion combine dangerously. Romans 7:19 is cited ("the good that I would do I not; but the evil which I would not, that I do") — Paul, uerstood as an initiate of the Mystery tradition, is describing the part of the self that knows what's right being overruled by the part in thrall to Lucifer.

Delusion, Imagination, and Will as Cosmic Forces

Modern science never asks how delusion, imagination, or willpower came into the world, but to the ancients these were among the greatest forces in the universe — living in three-dimensional space as well as in human minds. Nietzsche's line is invoked: "Unless you have chaos inside you, you cannot give birth to a ncing star" — humans could never become freely creative, brave, or loving without the capacity to err and to see things as other than they are. Because of Lucifer, belief is not proportioned to evidence; people believe what they want to believe (e.g., judging someone's life a failure or a success depending on whether one looks good-heartedly or mean-spiritedly). A warning follows: when "the harsh fire, the primeval sulphur" burns in the stomach, it becomes difficult to choose to be good-hearted.

A New Champion: Disentangling Elohim and Jehovah

Having already witnessed one great battle (Sun god defeating Saturn), the initiation candidate now had to witness a second — against the great snake corrupting Paradise. This requires disegling another deliberately created confusion: in early Genesis, "God" translates "Elohim"; later, "God" translates "Jehovah." Mainstream biblical scholarship treats this as two literary strands woven together by a later redactor. Esoteric scholarship offers a simpler explanation: Elohim and Jehovah are different entities. Elohim is the collective name for the Seven Spirits acting as the god of the Sun; Jehovah came into being when one of these seven broke away specifically to defend Earth against Venus.

The Moon, Reflection, and Human Thought

To find Jehovah's astronomical identity, attention returns to Venus's iconography — specifically the mirror she was traditionally shown holding, not out of vanity but as a symbol of reflection's power to modify desire. Human capacity to resist animal desire (what keeps from becoming mere animals) derives from the capacity for thought and reflection. The god of reflection is the god of the sky's great reflector: the moon.

A striking practical/esoteric claim: initiate priests believed that for human reflection to be possible, sun and moon had to be arranged in the sky so the moon reflects sunlight to earth — and this arrangement had to be reproduced in miniature inside the human head. The pineal gland represents the sun;he pituitary gland, which modifies and reflects on visions received by the pineal gland from spirit worlds, represents the moon. Readers are invited to test this against lived experience — checking whether their own dreams grow more vivid under a full moon. A biological analogy offered: oysters observed in a tray for a month will be seen to wax and wane with the moon, and modern science has confirmed the pituitary gland behaves similarly.

Jehovah/Allah as Moon God and the War in Heaven

The god of the Moon became known to the Hebrews as Jehovah and to Muslims as Allah — "the great god of thou-shalt-not." At the drama's climax, with earth in danger of becoming a living Hell, one of the seven Elohim broke away to become the Moon god and direct operations against Venus/Lucifer, echoing how the El had earlier held Saturn/Satan in check.

This cosmic battle against Venus recurs across world mythologies: Krishna's battle with the snake-demon Kaliya, Apollo's battle with the Python, and Perseus defeating the sexually ravenous dragon threatening Andromeda by using his shield as a mirror (echoing the reflection theme). The Old Testament Jehovah is jealous, angry, and warlike, with Archangel Michael leading his forces — cited from Revelation: "And there was a war in heaven. Michael and hiangels fought against the dragon... and the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent which deceiveth the whole world, he was cast out into the earth."

The Secret of the Days of the Week

The Moon god's victory concludes the third great act of creation. This inaugurates the era of the Moon. The first three epochs of the cosmos — mineral, vegetable, and animal — correspond to Saturn-day, Sun-day, and Moon-day, remembered as the first three days of the week (Saturday, Sunday, Monday). These days are named after these three heavenly bodin this specific order for this reason alone — a direct, non-obvious link between cosmic-mythological history and the everyday calendar.

Chapt 5: The Gods who Loved Women: The Nephilim • The Genetic Engineering of Humankind • The Fish Gods

Berosus and the Fish God Oannes

A Babylonian priest named Berosus, active in the time of Alexander the Great, ranks among the earliest historians, having studied temple king-lists and secret priestly archives, much as Herodotus had done before him. Surviving fragments of his work describe the origins of earth and sky and a race of hermaphrodites — pre-sexual humans who reproduced through parthenogenesis.

Berosus recounts that a primitive human race once inhabited the land until a strange being emerged from the sea: Oannes, described as having the whole body of a fish but with a second head beneath the fish's head, human feet beneath the fish's tail, and an articulate, human voice. Oannes spent daylight hours among people (taking no food) teaching them letters, sciences, and every art âbuild cities, found temples, compile laws, and understand geometry. He taught agriculture, showing people how to distinguish seeds and gather fruit, and generally "humanized" their lives. At sunset he returned to the sea, being amphibious. Berosus notes that after Oannes, other similar fish-beings appeared.

Fish Gods Across Cultures

Parallel fish-god teacher figures recur worldwide:

  • Matsya, the first avatar of Vishnu in Hindu tradition
  • Dagon of the Phoenicians, credited with teaching irrigation
  • Fish gods of the Dagon tribe in West Africa
  • Zeus himself, whose earliest representations (per Plutarch) showed him as a man with a fish tail — an image that survived in Greek myth through his brother Poseidon

A non-obvious point: some modern writers outside esoteric tradition have taken this recurring fish imery as "evidence" of ancient alien invasion or alien genetic engineering of humanity. This is characterized as a materialist misreading that misinterprets esoteric traditions by forcing them into a literal, science-fiction framework rather than understanding their symbolic astronomical meaning.

Genesis 6 and the Sons of God

Genesis 6:1-5 describes "sons of God" seeing that "the daughters of men" were fair, taking wives, and fathering "mighty men... of renown," followed by God's judgment that human wickedness had become great. The phrase "sons of God" elsewhere in the Bible refers to angels/messengers from heaven, and the narrative's framing — angels "coming down" and lowering themselves into the material world — carries moral disapproval, suggesting these beings became too enamored with matter.

The Book of Enoch

These five sparse verses in Genesis become far more comprehensible in light of the Book of Enoch, an ancient Hebrew text that:

  • Disappeared from mainstream (exoteric) history around AD 300–400
  • Was preserved in tradition by Freemasonry despite its physical loss
  • Was rediscovered in 1773 by Scottish explorer James Bruce, who tracked down tattered manuscripts in Ethiopian monasteries — vindicating the old Freemasonic claims abouistence and content
  • Was never canonized in fourth-century Christian scripture but was still quoted approvingly by New Testament writers as an authority akin to sacred scripture
  • Is echoed in Christ's own words: the phrase "This is my Son, the Elect One" at the Transfiguration is meant to identify Jesus as the figure promised in Enoch

Enoch 6:1-4 describes angels ("children of heaven") lusting after human daughters, agreeing amongst themselves to "choose wives from among the children of men," taking them, "defiling" themselves, teaching them "charms and enchantments," and impregnating them.

Later, Enoch tours the Heavens and the rebel angels (called Watchers) ask him to intercede with God on their behalf. God refuses, telling Enoch to inform them: "You should intercede for men, and not men for you." God's rebuke (Enoch 6:15-16) accuses the Watchers of abandoning heaven, defiling themselves with women, fathering giants, and — crucially — despite being spiritual, eternal beings, they "begotten children with the blood of flesh and blood as those also who die and perish." God further states the Watchers revealed "worthless" mysteries to women which caused men and women tork much evil on earth," concluding: "You have no peace."

Additional corroborating fragments:

  • The Epistle of Jude 6:6 says the Watchers "not kept their own appointed habitations"
  • Third-century Christian writer Commodorius wrote that the women who seduced the angels were so lewd that the angels could no longer desire to return to heaven

Decoding the Watchers as Planetary Gods

A key interpretive clue: Jude's description of the Watchers as not keeping "their appointed seasons" implies they function as timekeepers — an astronomical role. The decisive clue to their true identity is their number, given in one version of Enoch as seven — the traditional number of the great gods of the solar system in all ancient traditions. This confirms that the biblical narrative encodes the same astronomical gods found in Greek and Roman mythology: the angels who lusted after human women are identified he gods of Olympus themselves.

Jupiter's Rise and the War with the Titans

Continuing the sequence of planetary gods active in creation (Saturn, earth, sun, Venus, moon), the next age is marked by the arrival of the solar-system gods — Jupiter (Zeus) becomes king of the gods, with Mars and Mercury following.

The infant Jupiter had to be hidden by Mother Earth from his father Saturn, in a cave on Crete, where he was nourished by a goat-nymph's milk and sacred bees' honey. Mother Earth ared Saturn and the Titans (Saturn's elder children) would destroy the infant, since Jupiter's birth signaled the end of Saturn's reign — and the old order always resists yielding to the new.

The Titans, described as Saturn's enforcers and "the consciousness eaters," sought to swallow new life and create what Milton (who unrstood the secret history) called "a universe of Death." They warred against Jupiter throughout his life until he finally defeated and imprisoned them underground, where they became embedded in the earth's structure —heir rumblings explaining volcanic activity.

With the Titans contained, Jupiter ruled Olympus as king of a new age, strong enough alone to wield the thunderbolt. Italian scholar Roberto Calasso (in The Marriage of Cadmus and Harmony) described Olympus as "a rebellion of lightness against precision" — the Olympian gods (Jupiter, Apollo, Mars, Mercury, Diana, Athena) rebelling against Saturn's limitations, flying through the air to perform feats and defeat monsters.

The Moral Ambiguity of the Olympian Age

This era was spectacular but sinister, charged with "a dense fug of testosterone" and animal ferocity. Jupiter raped Callisto (turned into a bear) and Io (turned into a cow), and punished Lycaon for cannibalism by transforming him into a wolf. Apollo's lust for Hyacinth caused the youth's metamorphosis into a flower, and his pursuit of Daphne ended with her becoming a laurel bush.

The non-obvious interpretive point: these myths of transformation are not really about morality in a Mosaic sense but abt the proliferation of natural biological forms — the Olympian gods directing the "galvanizing fecundity" that filled the earth with biodiversity.

The Titans, imprisoned within the earth, became known as Telamones; their offspring were earth-demons or goblins — red-eyed creatures with scaled, grey-fingernail-like skin, still feared in remote rural southern Europe as late as the nineteenth century, said to pursue people even after death.

Fish Gods as Encoded Evolutionary Memory

A striking synthesis: since many mythies recount fish gods arriving to teach humanity, and even Jupiter's earliest form was fish-tailed, and since the Olympian myths encode the proliferation of animal forms, it's proposed that ancient myth anticipated the modern scientific insight that animal life (including that which became human) began as fish — a genuinely sttling claim if true.

Precession of the Equinoxes as the Key to Decoding Evolution

Ancient peoples closely tracked which zodiac constellation the sun rose in each spring, believing that constellation was "vivified" and empowered to shape the world's history that year. Because of a slow wobble in earth's axis, the sun appears to shift backward against the stellar backdrop over roughly 2,160 years per constellation — a phenomenon called precession. Currely, the world is in the Age of Pisces, moving toward the Age of Aquarius. Note that the zodiac in this precessional cycle runs in reverse order to the familiar month-by-month sequence (Gemini followed by Taurus followed by Aries, rather than the other way round).

The 1950s book Hamlet's Mill, by MIT's Giorgio de Santillana and Frankfurt's Hertha von Dechend, first reintroduced this astronomical dimension of myth to modern scholarship outside secret societies, arguing that the widespread mythic motif of a dispossessed son defeating his uncle to reclaim his father's throne (found from Oedipus Rex to Hamlet) encodes the succession of one precessional age to another. However, this work offered only a static model; it did not organize the succession of ages into a full evolutionary chronology, which is undertaken here.

The Zodiac as a Map of Evolutionary Stages

Each precessional age corresponds to a specific evolutionary stage of life on earth, driven by a ruling planetary god:

  • Age of Pisces (ruled by Jupiter): The earliest marine life condensed from the semi-liquid early earth — a jellyfish-like embryonic fish form. In Egyptian tradition this event is remembered as the birth of Horus, whose earliest depictions, like Jupiter's, were half-man, half-fish — evidence that Greek, tian, and Hebrew traditions worship the same underlying gods in different cultural guises.

  • First Age of Aquarius: The era of amphibian evolution — giant, dolphin-like floating creatures with webbed limbs and a lantern-like forehead protuberance. This "lantern" corresponds to the pineal gland, still visible today in some ptiles such as New Zealand's Tuatara lizard, and is recorded in Egyptian tradition as the "Lantern of Osiris." This organ was these proto-humans' primary sense faculty — sensitive to warmth/coolness in other beings bo near and far, allowing intuitive perception of others' inner nature and of which plants were suitable as food or medicine (paralleling instinctive abilities seen in some animals today). Because natural law was not yet fixed, humans could speak to plants and cause a tree to yield fruit or wheat to "grow as tall as the cedars of Lebanon." Their speech resembled a stag's bellow. These lantern-headed beings were later mythologized as unicorns, still directed clairvoyantly by the Earth goddess so that natural law and moral law were identical — a truth depicted in the famous Lady and the Unicorn tapestry at the Musée de Cluny in Paris, where the unicorn rests its head in a virgin's lap. Even then, the unicorn was remembered as a hunted creature: independently existing desires (predating humanity) ran wild and unintegrated, becoming the "dragons" of mythology that terrorized creation.

  • Age of Capricorn: As the marshy earth hardened toward dry land, proto-humans developed calves and limbs to crawl onto land in pursuit of animal desires. Age of (four-footed) Sagittarius, marked by the arrival of Mars: Mars's arrival triggered the evolution of warm-blooded animals during the transition from Capricorn-age lizard-amphibians to land animals. The iron associated with Mars produced red blood and created the conditions for egotism — not merely healthy survival drive, but as earth hardened, dried, and shrank, existence became zero-sum (one being could only prosper at another's expense). Mars is also blamed for the darker aspec of human nature: cruelty, domination, and euphoric exercise of unrestrained willpower over others.

  • Mercury's influence: As proto-humans became fully land-based, Mercury's influence produced the evolution of the thorax and leaner, fitter limbs enabling humans to move toward and cooperate with one another. Mercury (Hermes to the Greeks, Thoth to the Egyptians) was messenger and scribe of the gods — and also, notably, the god of tricks and thieving.

Transmission of This Knowledge Through History

This chapter's interpretive method âding Genesis alongside parallel Egyptian and Greek traditions — originated among Neoplatonists and early Cabalists and was carried forward by gups like the Rosicrucians. Key surviving written expressions include Robert Fludd's seventeenth-century writings (which strongly influenced Milton's Paradise Lost) and Jacob Boehme's Mysterium Magnum commentary on Genesis. Austrian scholar and initiate Rudolf Steiner later elucidated these commentaries and reframed Rosicrucian wisdom for modern audiences; his Anthroposophical Society is presented as perhaps the most legitimate surviving heir of the true Rosicrucian tradition.

Even outside esoteric circles, it's acknowledged that ancient civilizations worldwide showed striking agreement on the imagery associated with the zodiac's sequence — remarkable given how little the actual star patterns resemble these images. The implication drawn is that the constellation sequence encoded a collectively remembered history of the evolution of humanity and the world; for the ancients, history was literallyritten in the stars, since heavenly bodies were understood as the material bodies of spiritual beings with whom people believed they could communicate and whose influence they felt directly. Example: the star Algol, associated with Medusa's severed head in Greek tradition, was independently regarded as malignant across unrelated cultures — Hebrew astrologers named it after the demon Lilith and, earlier, the "Head of Satan," while the Chinese called it a phrase meaning "piled up corpses" —gesting diverse cultures perceived the same spiritual reality in the same patch of sky.

Darwin, Precursors, and the Ancient Priority of Evolutionary Knowledge

The chapter argues that the theory of evolution, generally regarded as a purely modern idea overturning ancient superstition, was itself known to ancient priesthoods thousands of years before Darwin. This knowledge was encoded in the zodiac and preserved by initiates (Boehme, Fludd) and esoteric societies (Freemasons, Rosicrucians), deliberately obscured from outsiders.

In the nineteenth century, the first open publication of Hindu sacred texts in European languages leaked much previously carefully-managed esoteric knowledge into public consciousness, also reviving interest in Cabala and fueling the spiritualist craze. Historical detail: in 1874, Charles Darwin attended séances togetherwith novelist George Eliot. Darwin's contemporary rival Alfred Russel Wallace conducted controlled experiments into spiritualism, believing its phenomena could be scientifically measured like any other. German scholar Friedrich Max Müller, employed by the East India Company in the 1840s to translate the Rig Veda before becoming an Oxford professor, went on to translate fifty volumes of Eastern sacred texts, making Oriental esoteric doctrine widely available for the first time — and maintained a regular correspondence with Darwin. The Origin of Species was published in 1859.

Evolution in the Secret History Was Not Linear

Unlike the smooth progression assumed by mainstream science, secret tradition holds that evolution included deands, false starts, and even deliberate sabotage, with implications for understanding human physiology and psychology today.

  • Snakes, spiders, beetles, and parasitic creatures were shaped under the malignant influence of the Dark Side of the Moon.
  • Familiar animals took their forms under stellar/planetary influence: lions from Leo, bulls from Taurus, etc.
  • Centaurs, mermaids, sirens, fauns, and satyrs were transitional forms representing the impulse toward anatomically modern humans, not separate mythical species.
  • The cosmic plan intended all biological forms to eventually be incorporated into humankind, positioned as the crown of creation. As gods guided humanity toward modern anatomy, they themselves took part-animal, part-human forms (as remembered by Sumerians, Egyptians, Persians, Babylonians) before finally assuming fully human forms as remembered by Greeks and Romans. Examples: cow-headed Hathor (Venus goddess) and dog-headed Anubis (Mercury god) on Egyptian temple walls were later remembered by classical Greeks in more evolved, fully human form.
