Giants and the Antediluvian World

Ancient texts, including the Book of Enoch and Plato, agree that a race of giants arose in the pre-Flood era. Parallel giant traditions appear worldwide: the Danavas and Daityas of India, the Miaotse of China. A fragmentary Dialogue between Midas the Phrygian and Silenus (from Alexander the Great's era) has Silenus stating that people of that earlier age "grew to double the size of the tallest men in his time, and they lived to twice the age."

Notable and non-obvious claim: the Bamyan statues in Afghanistan (destroyed in recent times) were not, in secret tradition, three giant Buddha statues but three life-sized statues of actual giants measuring 173, 120, and 30 feet high, with Buddhist-style plaster drapery added later to disguise them. Nineteenth-century records indicate locals believed them to represent the Miaotse giants of Chinese legend. Similarly, the Easter Island statues are claimed to record the real heights of historical giants.

Freaks, Hybrids, and Monsters

Alongside giants, tradition records "dead-end" evolutionary freaks: one-legged men, bat-men, insect-men, men with tails. Egyptian historian Manetho (third century BC) recorded that the Watchers' progeny included double-winged humans, four-winged two-faced beings, two-headed single-bodied humans, goat-thighed and horned humans, horse-footed man-fronted beings, man-headed bulls, four-headed dogs with fish-tails, and all manner of dragon-like monsters.

This era is preserved in collective memory through fantasy literature — Tolkien's Lord of the Rings and C.S. Lewis's Narnia books are cited as modern expressions of memory of a time when humans coexisted with giants, dragons, mermaids, centaurs, unicorns, fauns, and satyrs, served by dwarves, sylphs, nymphs, and dryads, sometimes fighting these beings and sometim falling in love with them.

Apes as Degeneration, Not Ancestry

According to secret tradition, apes were the last creatures to incarnate before humans, arising because some human spirits rushed into incarnation prematurely, before human anatomical form had been perfected. The key inversion of standard evolutionary thinking: humans are not descended from apes; rather, apes represent a degeneration of humankind.

The chapter closes by noting that none of these fabulous creatures (giants, centaurs, unicorns, etc.) left any trace in the fossil record, posing the open question of why intelligent initiates throughout history believed in them — a question to be addressed going forward.

Chapter 6: The Assassination of the Green King: Isis and Osiris • The Cave of the Skull • The Palladium

The Myth of Osiris

Egyptian tradition preserves the fullest account of the last god-king to rule the earth in human form. Herodotus visited the shrine where Osiris was said to be buried, describing gigantic obelisks and a lake where Egyptians performed the "Black Rite" at night — a secret mystery drama re-enacting the death and resurrection of a being whose name he claimed he dared not speak. A richer account comes from Plutarch, an initiate priest of the Oraelphi.

Osiris was a "Beast Master" — a great hunter and warrior remembered as Orion in Greek myth and Herne the Hunter in Norse myth — who cleared the land of predatory beasts and invading armies. His reign was a golden age of civil and domestic bliss. His name connects to insemination ("ourien" meaning semen), and the belt of Orion was understood in antiquity as an erect penis marking the progress of the new year — a clue that a strong sexual current runs through the entire myth.

trayal and Murder

Osiris's downfall came not from external enemies but from within his own family. His brother Seth invited him to a celebratory feast. Some say Osiris had slept with Nepthys, Seth's wife and Isis's sister, giving Seth a motive — though the deeper clue lies in Seth's name itself, marking him as an envoy of Sata meaning he may not have needed a personal grievance at all.

Seth staged a game: he had crafted an ornate chest of cedar inlaid with gold, silver, ivory, and lapis lazuli, offering it to whoever fit inside perfectly. Guests tried and failed until Osiris lay down and fit exactly. Seth immediately slammed the lid, nailed it shut, and sealed every crack with molten lead — significantly, the metal associated with Satan — then cast the chest into the Nile. As an immortal, Osiris couldn't be killed outright, but Seth intended to dispose of him permanently.

Isis's Search and the First Resurrection

The chest floated to the coast of Syria, where a tamarisk tree grew around it, eventually being cut down and fashioned into a palace pillar. Isis, meanwhile, cut her hair, blackened her face, and wandered the earth searching for her husband, eventually taking work as a servant girl at a foreign court — a story noted as the likely garbled origin of the Cinderella pantomime tale.

Using clairvoyant sight, Isis located Osiris within the pillar in the very palace where she served, revealed her true identity, and had the pillar cut down to retrieve the chest. She fled by boat to the island of Chemmis to revive her husband using m

Dismemberment and the First Mummy

Seth, possessing magical powers of his own, discovered Isis with the body while hunting by moonlight. He attacked again, this time hacking Osiris into fourteen pieces and hiding them across the land. Isis set out once more (a quest Freemasons commemorate by calling themselves "Sons of the Widow"), disguising herself with seven veils and aided by Nepthys, who — despite the earlier suggestion of impropriety — genuinely loved Osiris and turned herself into a dog to help locate the scatteremains.

All pieces were recovered except the penis, eaten by fish in the Nile. At Abydos, Isis and Nepthys bound the pieces together with linen — creating the first mummy. Isis fashioned a golden replacement penis and, unable to fully revive Osiris, instead revived him sexually: hovering as a bird and enveloping the phallus unt he ejaculated, thereby impregnating herself and conceiving Horus, who would grow up to avenge his father by killing Seth. Osiris himself became king and Lord of the Dead in the Underworld, usually depicted with a green face, heavily wrapped, holding the crook and flail — a figure of latent power despite apparent immobility.

Layers of Meaning: Precession and Ferlity

The myth operates on multiple levels. Astronomically, it may represent the succeeding of one constellation by another in the precession of the equinoxes — Hus deposing Seth. Agriculturally, it is a fertility myth: the heliacal rising of Sirius (Isis) after months of invisibility signaled that Osiris (Orion) would rise again and the Nile's inundation was imminent. This pattern — a king wounded in the genitals, land left barren, then a magical spring operation restoring fertility — recurs worldwide in myths of Tammuz, Marduk, and the Fisher King legends tied to Parsifal and King Arthur. Egyptians made corn dollies (linen bags stuffed with corn) that sprouted when watered, demonstrating the god's rebirth; Osiris himself proclaims in the pyramid texts, "I am the plant of life."

This fertility-level reading, while true, has been overemphasized since Frazer's The Golden Bough — to the neof a deeper, historical secret known only to inner-sanctum priests, the same Black Rite Herodotus alluded to.

The Parallel Story of Dionysus

Osiris was equated in antiquity with Dionysus, the last Olympian god. Accounts disagree on his father (Hermes or Zeus), but agree his mother was Mother Earth, who hid the infant in a cave — as with Zeus. Dionysus represented an evolving new form of consciousness that the Titans, again acting as "consciousness eaters," sought to destroy. Disguising emselves with white gypsum to hide their identity as black-faced sons of the crow god, they lured Dionysus from his cave-cradle, tore him to pieces, boiled the pieces in a cauldron of milk, and devoured the flesh. Athena secretly rescued his heart before it was cooked, bringing it to Zeus, who implanted it in his own thigh; Dionysus was later reborn fully grown from Zeus's thigh, paralleling Athena's own birth from Zeus's head.

Decoding the Cave: The Hardening Skull

To understand the historical reality behind both myths, it helps to recall that matter precipitated out of cosmic mind only gradually, and that mythic figures with human-like anatomy are only how they appear to imaginative vision — the physical world looked very different to eyes still evolving at this stage (as recorded in Ovid's Metamorphoses, a world of giants and hybrids). The most anatomically advanced humans were developing two forward-facing eyes, but the "Lantern of Osiris" — a third eye — still protruded from the mid-forehead, where the skull bone had not yet hardened.

As matter progressively hardened, it became more alien to and more of a barrier against the free flow of cosmic mind, producing two parallel dimensions: the spirit world (perceived by the Lantern of Osiris) and the material world (perceived by the two eyes). The Osiris/Dionysus myth marks the decisive stage when portions of universal consciousness became individually parceled into separate bodies — the bony roof of the skull hardening shut, sealing off the Lantern of Osiris and filtering out direct access to cosmic mind.

vious point:** according to ancient wisdom, as long as no barrier separated humans from spirits, gods, and angels above, individual free will and thought were impossible — full exposure to the cosmic mind would completely dazzle and overwhelm human minds. The hardening skull, seemingly a loss, was the necessary precondition for individual thought to exist at all.

Plato's Cave, Read Literally

Plato's Allegory of the Cave — prisoners chained facing a wall, mistaking shadows cast from ode for reality — is usually read as an abstract statement of idealism (that cosmic Mind and its Thought-Beings/ideas are higher reality than physical shadows). But academics miss a surprisingly literal layer: the cave is the bony roof of the skull itself, a dark room covered in flesh. Plato, an initiate, would have understood is occult physiology directly. The brain is described as the most complex and mysterious object in the known universe, created — per secret doctrine — so that the cosmos could think about itself. The idealist framework holds that the universe was created by Mind for minds, and the arrangement of sun, moon, planets, and stars directly shaped the structure of h consciousness; the moon reflecting sunlight down to earth is mirrored in miniature within the human skull.

The Sexualization of the Body

There is a specifically sexual dimension to this developmental turning point. Mystery priests taught that as the Lantern of Osiris withdrew inward to become what we now call the pineal gland, the fleshly penis emerged as one of the last body parts to take solid form — which is why initiate artists like Michelangelo and Signorelli (Leonardo's brother initiate) depicted mythological figures' genitals as plant-like. At this juncture humans lost the older plant-like method of self-propagation (parthenogenesis) and gave themselves over entirely to animal sexuality.

Death as the Price of Thought

Key warning/axiom of the secret doctrine: the beginning of death was the birth of thought. Life processes (digestion, respiration, growth) are largely unconious; conscious thought is only possible through a partial suppression of these processes — the human organism "steals" forces normally used for growth and biological structuring to fuel thought, which is offered as one reason humans are comparatively sickly animals. Thought is described plainly as "a deadly process, restricting both growth and longevity."

As proto-humans transitioned from vegetable to animal characteristics, they first experienced only a foretaste of death resembling dre-filled sleep, from which they would "awake" again. As bones and the earth itself hardened, this sleep deepened until it became indistinguishable from — and finally was — actual death, entangling humanity in cycles of life, death, and rebirth where fathers must die to make way for sons and kings must die to make way for sucors.

Ritual Enactment: The Heb-Sed and Bull Sacrifice

Carvings at the Step Pyramid complex at Saqqara illuminate the "Heb-Sed" rituals, in which a pharaoh underwent a mystery-school death-and-rebirth ceremony in an underground chamber, then emerged to face public trials of strength and potency — including running with a bull — while ritually declaring "I am free to run through the land." Failure meant the pharaoh would suffer the bull's own bloody death. A nineteenth-century British traveler's eyewitness account of a bull-god sacrifice in India is cited as a close parallel: at the beheading, cymbals and tom-toms sound, and the assembly smears itself in blood, dancing with obscene songs and gestures. Herodotus likely witnessed something similar in the Egyptian Black Rite — the ritual death of a great god. In Northern Europe this entangled, nature-bound god survives as the Green Man, a leaf-clad figure who is both fierce like nature and its victim, an image of Osiris that stares down from the walls of countless Christian churches.

The Double Vision of the Third Eye

At this pivotal stage the human skull had largely assumed its present form, but the Third Eye remained far more active than today, not yet vestigperceptions of material and spiritual worlds were equally vivid simultaneously. A person entering a throne room might see an apparent human being, then, looking again with the Third Eye, perceive a god. This double perception is recorded most vividly in the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna reveals his supreme divine form to the doubting charioteer Arjuna before shrinking back into gentle human shape to reassure him. Osiris could plausibly have granted comparable visions in his throne room at Thebes. Jacob Boehme called the ordinary physical world of "cut stone, carved wood, royal robes and flesh and blood" the Outworld, disparagingly, holding that the true, inner world accessible to the Third Eye was the real one — a conviction that sustained followers of Osiris amid a bloody, death-drenched existence.

Consciousness, Not Just Fertility

Ultately the Osiris myth is above all about consciousness: death must be undergone in order to be reborn — but reborn into a higher state of consciousness, not ordinary life. In the Book of the Dead, Osiris proclaims: shall not decay, I shall not rot, I shall not putrefy, I shall not turn into worms, I shall have my being, I shall live, I shall live" — a formula strikingly close to the Christian concept of eternal life.

Sex, Death, and Manipulating Csciousness (Practical Application)

Ancient sages understood that sex, death, and thought became progressively interwoven to produce human consciousness, and — crucially — that because they grasped this historical process, they could use conscious thought to deliberately manipulate sexual and death forces to reach higher states of awareness. These techniques have remained among the best-guarded secrets of Mystery schools and secret societies.

Modern difficulty in understanding this stems from a materialistic view of sexuality that strips it of spiritual meaning — making it hard to correctly "read" erect-phallus imagery on Hindu or Egyptian temple walls. In the ancient understanding, sperm was seen as an expression of cosmic will, containing a particle of the prima materia capable of explodin a whole new macrocosm; adolescents today may faintly echo this ancient intensity in first sexual stirrings.

Warning on desire: desire is inherently open to corruption — what is desired is possessed first in imagination, and desire "hardens," reifying (to borrow Sartre's term) the desired person into an object to be bent to one's will, which is identified as the influence of the Spirit of Opposition. In a mind-before-matter cosmology, this diminishing way of perceiving others is descbed as having literal physiological and chemical effects on them.

For the ancients, sexual attraction was not merely biological but connected to planetary influences and karmic patterns extending across many lifetimes — a man's overwhelming desire for a particular woman was understood as the culmination of forces (the "planeof love" and other celestial powers) at work across millennia and incarnations.

Techniques of Death and Rebirth (Practical Application)

Just as secret societies teach control of sexual forces to reach higher consciousness, parallel teachings exist for channeling death forces. Austin Osman Spare developed a practice of closing off mouth, nostrils, ears, and eyes (referenced via his artwork "The Death Posture," alongside Dürer's "Melancholia I"). In India, adepts including Bhagavan Shri Ramana and Thakur Haranath achieed long death-like trances so convincing they were prepared for burial, before being reborn into higher consciousness.

The ancients also held that when contemplating one's own will, one was looking at something formed long before birth — and that every act of sexual union involved the movement of whole constellations, with consequences echoing through the cosmos for millennia. Rilke's line — "two people coming together in the night summon up the future" — is cited as capturing this magical dimension; making love consciously with this awareness allows participation in a genuinely magical act.

Nepthys, Sophia, and the Dark Redemptive Feminine

A final dark twist concerns Nepthys, Isis's sister, tainted by the suggestion of sexuaopriety with Osiris yet ultimately instrumental — through her own magic — in helping recover and rebind his body. She represents a fallen but redeemable form of wisdom. In Christian mythology this same spiritual impulse reappears as Mary Magdalene.

This connects to a broader point about the Fall: it was not a fall of pre-existing spirits into an already-material world (a common misreading), but a process in which human bodies became progressively denser as the material world itself dened. We live in a genuinely Fallen world where destructive spirits work against us in numbers equal to those that help us evolve. In Christian secret doctrine, the earth's own spirit — often called Sophia — was imprisoned within the underworld as punishment for the Fall, and is reachable only by descending through the earth's (and our own) dark and demonic depths. Practical/spiritual point: it is because of this Nepthys/Sophia principle that people need to touch rock bottom, wrestle with inner demons, push intellect to its limit, and joy to the far side of madness in order to access this wisdom.

The Palladium

Isis was identified in antiquity with Athena. Athena had a beloved dark-skinned half-sister, Pallas, with whom she used to wrestle and play mock battles on the plains of Anatolia. One day, distracted, Athena accidentally speared Pallas to death. In acknowledgment of this dark side of herself — paralleling Nepthys's relationship to Isis — Athena renamed herself Pallas Athena and carved a black wooden statue of her sister, called the Palladium, said to be washed by the goddess's own tears.

This statue was revered in antiquity as an object of world-altering power. While the Trojans possessed it, Troy was the greatest city in the world; once the Greeks captured it, world civilizational leadership passed to them. It was later buried beneath Rome during its imperial glory, then moved by Emperor Constantine to Constantinople, which became the new center of world spirituality. It is said today to be hidden somewhere in Eastern Europe — offered as an explanati why Freemasonic great powers have historically sought to control that region.

The cult of Nepthys, together with its Greek (Pallas Athena) and Christian (Mary Magdalene/Sophia) equivalents, is identified as one of the darkest and most powerful undercurrents in occultism, with forces that continue shaping world history in the present day.

Chapter 7: The Age of Demi-Gods and Heroes: The Ancient Ones • The Amazons • Enoch • Hercules, Theseus and Jason

The Three Dynasties

When Heroquestioned Egyptian priests about wooden statues of kings who reigned before any human king, they told him no one could understand this history without knowing about "the three dynasties." An initiate of the Mystery schools would have recognized these as: first, the oldest generation of creator gods (Saturn, Rhea, Uranos); second, the generation of Zeus, his siblings, and their children (Apollo, Athena); and third, the generation of demi-gods and heroes — the subject of this chapter.

The Gods' Withdrawal and the Rise of Monsters

As matter grew denser, spirit and matter became increasingly incompatible, so the gods became a less constant presence. The higher and more ineffable a g, the harder it became to descend into the tightening net of physical necessity covering the earth. Great gods like Zeus and Pallas Athena intervened only at moments of crisis.

Mystery school teaching held that a decisive shift occurred in 13,000 BC: from that point the higher gods found it difficult to descend further than the moon, and their visits to earth became infrequent and fleeting. On these visits they were believed to have accidentally left behind mistletoe — a plant that cannot grow in earth's soil but grew naturally on the moon.

Without the greater gods present to restrain them, crab-like progeny of Saturn that had been imprisoned in underground caves began creeping back into daylight, infesting the earth's surface and preying on humankind. Sea monsters dragged off tribe members who strayed too close to shore, and giants carried off cattle and sometimes preyed on human flesh.

#Wars Between Humans and Older Epoch's Creatures Full-scale wars broke out between humans and armies of stragglers from the previous cosmic epoch. The war between the Lapiths (a tribe of Neolithic flint-knappers) and the Centaurs is recorded on the Parthenon frieze: the Centaurs, invited to the wedding of the Lapith leader, were inflamed by the sight of the Lapith women's white, hairless bodies. They dragged off the bride and raped her, along with her bridesmaids and page boys. The ensuing fight killed a Lapith king and began a feud lasting generations.

A drawing by nineteenth-century Swiss artist Henry Fuseli depicts a demon sometimes called the Hanon-Tramp. Moon demons inhabit the "Dark Side of the Moon," where they legitimately help tear corruption from human spirits after death. However, if they break through into the earthly realm they appear as malevolent dwarves — about the height of a six- or seven-year-old child, with large hypnotic eyes, sometimes emitting an ear-splitting yell that can freeze a human with fear. They are more powerful when the moon is waning, and may account for some modern "alien" encounters, which have no place in esoteric cosmology in physical form.

Nature Turns Hostile

As bones thickened, the animal world began feeling its own weig; creation grew tired and animals grew vicious as they struggled to survive. As humanity continued its fall, nature fell too — becoming "red in tooth and claw." Lions and wolves began attacking humans. Plants grew thorns to make fruit-gathering difficult, and poisonous plants like wolfsbane evolved.

The Amazons and the Advent of Murder

The Parthenon frieze also records battles against the Amazons, warrior women who were the first to ride horses into battle. An Amazon had to kill a man before she was permitted to marry. Wearing fur armor and carrying half-moon-shaped shields, their cavalry scythed down rows of foot soldiers. They represented a new form of human behavior: hard on the heels of the possibility of death came the possibility of killing and murder. Cut humans and they would bleed; cuthem hard or often enough and they would die — and some humans began to delight in this. The Book of Enoch describes the earth's surface becoming covered with warring armies, stating that "human flesh itself had become perverse."

The Isolation of Consciousness

Because of the encasing bony skull and the enmeshing of the organs of spiritual perception, humans became shut off not only from the gods above them but from each other. It became possible for one center of consciousness to believitself cut off from another. Cain's question "Am I my brother's keeper?" represents this new form of consciousness — a question that would have meant nothing to Adam and Eve, who were like branches on the same tree.

Just as we would be overwhelmed by the spirit worlds without filtering, if there were no filter on empathy we wld feel everyone's pain as our own and be completely overwhelmed by others' suffering. Without a degree of isolation, no human could experience individuality — no one could feel the burning fire in the forehead that drove Cain onward. But this came with pitfalls: history shows humans have a horror of other humans with different forms of consciousness, often findg it intolerable and feeling the need to eradicate it — examples include the European treatment of the Aztecs, the near-genocide of Australian Aborigines, and the Nazi attempt to wipe out gypsies. The Jews have often been at the forefront of forging new forms of consciousness since the time of Moses.

Freedom, Danger, and the Call to Heroism

Humans became free to make mistakes, to choose the bad, and to enjoy it. No longer did humans receive all spiritual nourishment automatically from Mother Earth; natural law and moral law were no longer the same thing. The earth grew colder, harder, and more dangerous. People discovered the road ahead would always carry the danger of death, but that avoiding that road meant dying anyway — from now on they had to risk what they valued most or lose it. Beyond a certain point there is no return, and that point had to be reached.

People discovered they hrown brutalized by this harder world, developing a hard protective carapace of habit. Breaking open this carapace to expose the sensitive, better part of themselves that brought them fully alive was a bloody, painful process few could face. The world became darker — a place of paradox where opposites meet, calling out for heroism.

Typhon and the Rescue of Zeus

The largest and most terrifying of Saturn's monstrous progeny came last: Typhon emerged from the sea heading for Olympus, spittg fire, blotting out the sun with bat-like wings, with the head of an ass and a lower body made of thousands of coiling snakes. Zeus tried thunderbolts, but Typhon shrugged them off. Zeus then snatched the flint scythe Cronos had used to castrate Uranos, but Typhon's snake-limbs wrapped around Zeus, snatched the scythe, pinned him down, and cut out all his sinews. Zeus, immortal, could not be killed but was rendered helpless without his sinews. Typhon retreated to a cave with the sinews to recuperate.

Apollo and Pan hatched a plan, enlisting Cadmus, the dragon-slaying hero who was wandering the earth searching for his sister Europa (carried off by Zeus disguised as a white bull). They promised Cadmus his quest would end if he helped. Pan gave Cadmus his pipes; disguised as a shepherd, Cadmus played for the wounded Typhon, who had never heard music and was entranced. Cadmus claimed this was nothing compared to what he could play on a lyre, but its sinews were broken — so Typhon handed over Zeus's sinews. Cadmus then returned to restring his lyre, Zeus regained his sinews, surprised and overpowered the monster, and buried him under Mount Etna. The key point: Zeus was saved only with a hero's help — the gods now needed humans.

Cadmus Identified as Enoch

Cadmus, Hercules, Theseus, and Jason produced some of the most famous myths in human history, seemingly missing from the biblical account — but according to ancient tradition preserved in secret societies, Cadmus is to be identified with Enoch, the first human in Hebrew tradition to whom ts turn for help.

The Old Testament offers only enigmatic words on Enoch (Genesis 5:21-24): he lived sixty-five years, begat Methuselah, "walked with God" for three hundred years afterward, lived three hundred sixty-five years total, and then "was not: for God took him." Beyond this, a literary tradition about Enoch exists in Hebrew literature, including books widely quoted in the New Testament. In the Book of Jubilees, Enoch is described as discovering "the writings of the Watchers" — a clumsy translation; what is actuallyeant is that he discovered, i.e., invented, language itself.

Enoch's Nature and Practice

Hebrew tradition presents Enoch as a strange figure whose shining countenance was uncomfortable to look at, an uncomfortable presence generally — recalling the Jesus of the Gospels, who captivated crowds yet felt the need to withdraw toe alone with the great spiritual beings revealing themselves to him. In solitude Enoch communed with gods and angels with a clarity humankind was rapidly losing.

Initially Enoch spent one day teaching the multitude and three days alone; over time this shifted to one day a week, then one day a month, then finally one day a year. Crowds yearned for his return, but when he did return his face shone so brightly people had to avert their eyes.

Two Types of Historical Turning Points

Great turning points in history arise from two types of thought: first, when great thinkers (Socrates, Jesus Christ, Dante) think for the first time something nobody has thought before; second, when thoughts are set down and inscribed indelibly because they preserve ancient wisdom in danger of being lost forever. Enoch's solitary vigils belong to the second type.

What Enoch Preserved

The generation of Jared, Enoch's father, was the last to experience uninterrupted vision of the successive waves of gods, angels, and spirits emanating from the mind of God. What Enoch preserved in the first language and the first stone monuments (the oldest stone circles) was this vision of the hierarchies of spiritual beings ranged above. This is why Enoch is a major figure in secret history âe gave a complete account of what we might today call the ecosystem of the spirit worlds. He is remembered as Cadmus in Greek tradition, Idris in Arabian tradition, and Hermes Trismegistus in esoteric Egyptian tradition.

Enoch knew that just as thought processes weaken health, language weakens memory. He also foresaw an approaching catastrophe that would destroy everything made by humankind except what he carried in his head and the sturdiest stone monuments. He memorialized the heavenly hierarchies both in stone monuments and in the invention of language itself, since according to secret doctrine all language originated with the giving of names to heavenly bodies. Likewise, the earliest art — found in the caves at Lascaux (France) and Altamira (Spain) — is really a depiction of these same heavenly bodies, whire the thoughts of the great cosmic mind weaving through everything in the cosmos. Language and art enabled humans to appropriate these cosmic thoughts and make them their own.

Enoch's Final Vision and Ascension

Enoch retreated further into inhospitable, stormy mountains, and fewer followers were able to keep up with him. He described seeing "the secrets of the lightning and of thunder, and the secrets of clouds and the dew," the source of winds, mist, and cloud, and the chambers from which the Sun and Moon come and go. The Book of Enoch relates his final ecstatic vision: a tour of the heavens, the different spheres and orders of angels living there, and the whole history of the cosmos.

Finally, addressing the last ragged band of followers who had kept pace with him on his mountain trek, they looked up to see a horse descend from the sky in a whirlwind; Enoch mounted it and rode into the sky. This ascension reveals that he did not die as humans do, because he was not properly human — like the other demi-gods and heroes of Greek tradition, Enoch/Cadmus was an angel occupying a human body.

Hercules: Everyman Torn Between Cosmic Forces

The stories of Hercules, Theseus, and Jason are too well known to need retelling, but specific aspects carry specl significance for secret history. Hercules's stories reveal just how deeply humankind had fallen into matter — he wanted to be left alone to enjoy worldly pleasures (getting drunk, feasting, brawling) but was repeatedly interrupted by duty to follow his spiritual destiny. A stumbling, bungling, sometimes laughable figure, he was torn between opposing cosmic forces. Ovid shows that as the gods withdrew, Eros began to make mischief — Hercules was hag-ridden by desire as much as by the spirirying to control him.

Beauty, Deception, and Sexual Danger

Today, falling in love with a beautiful person can feel like glimpsing great spiritual wisdom in beautiful eyes — as if finding there the very secret of life. The stories of Hercules's love for Deianira, Ariadne's love for Theseus, and Jason's love for Medea show th the spiritual connection between people was already becoming clouded: it became possible to gaze into a beauty's eyes and be deceived about what one saw there. Sexuality had become tricky. The danger of delusion was compounded by an actual love of delusion — what is best and what is worst, what one most ought to do and most ought not to do, can look remarkably alike. One may know in the heart of hearts which is which, yet a spirit of perversity makes one wt to choose wrongly. Great psychic perturbation always surrounds great beauty — a practical warning about the seductive unreliability of erotic attraction as a guide to truth.

The Twelve Labours as Universal Trial

The twelve labours of Hercules show him moving through trials set by successive spirits ruling the constellations — a series of trials all humans take, mostly unwittingly, as Hercules did. His life illustrates the pain of being human; he is Everyman trapped in a cycle of pain.

Allegory as a Marker of Historical Truth, Not Fiction

Modern sensibility assumes that a story's allegorical form makes it less likely to accurately depict real events, and modern writers try to drain texts of meaning to flatten them into naturalism. Ancients, believing every earthly event was guided by the ons of stars and planets, held the opposite view: the more a narrative brought out "poetic" astronomical patterns, the truer and more realistic the text was considered.

Underworld Journeys as Literal and Symbolic

It may be tempting to view the underworld journeys of Hercules, Theseus, and Orpheus as mere metaphor, and on one level their adventures do represent humanity's early reckoning with the reality of death. But these must not be imagined as purely internal or mental journeys as might be assumed today. When they battled monsters and demons, they confronted forces infesting their own beings — corrupted human flesh, the dark labyrinth of the human brain — but they were also fighting real monsters of flesh and blood.

Theseus, the Minotaur, and Slowing Metamorphosis

Comparing the story of Theseus and theotaur with an earlier myth like Perseus and the Gorgon Medusa reveals that by Theseus's time the rate of metamorphosis had slowed. In the Perseus story, every episode involves supernatural powers or magical transformation; by contrast, the bull-man Minotaur is apparently a rare survivor or straggler from an earlier epoch.

Jason's Quest as Historical Raid and Manual of Initiation

The last adventure the demi-gods and heroes undertook together should also be interpreted as history: wars were fought to steal the "inner sanctum" knowledge of rival tribes, and on one level Jason's quest for the Golden Fleece was such a raid. Isaac Newton revealed part of the secret wisdom of his brotherhood by showing that the quest for the Fleece, like the labours of Hercules, traces the sun's progress through the zodiac signs. What Newton did not reveal — though he undoubtedly knew it — was that the Fleece represents animal spirit totally purified by catharsis, shining like gold.

A snake curled around the tree, intending to prevent Jason from taking the Fleece, is a descendant of the Luciferic serpent that originally worked corruption into human physiology, coiled around the tree in the Garden of Eden. If Jason could wrest the Fleece from the snake, he would win great rs: the ability to send his spirit from his body at will, communicate freely with gods and angels as people of earlier epochs did, control his own physiology, influence others' minds telepathically, and even transform matter. Apollonius's text of Jason's quest should therefore be read as a manual of initiation as well as a true historical account — an insight later acted on by medieval alchemists and Newton himself.

Science Versus Esoteric Memory

Viewed through the eye of science, this riod of Enoch, Hercules, and Jason shows none of the great events described — no heroes or monsters rising from the sea, no phantasmal deities like Zeus, no black magic causing empires' falls. Science shows only wind and rain on a dreary natural landscape with unimpressive dwellings and primitive stone tools.

The neoplatonist ilosopher Porphyry decoded the twelve labours of Hercules to reveal the zodiac signs behind them: Hercules is depicted on a sarcophagus relief journeying through Leo (the Nemean Lion), Scorpio (the Hydra), and Libra (the Erymanthian Boar) — taming the Wild Boar represents Hercules balancing animal spirits with measured intelligence. Modern thinking holds that a narrative's allegorical form is reason to doubt its historical accuracy; but if, as the ancients lieved, all earthly events are governed by the movements of heavenly bodies, the opposite holds true — accounts of real historical events must inevitably mirror astronomical events like the sun's passage through the constellations.

Science may show only the surface; more important things may have been happening underneath. What secret history preserves is a memory of subjective experience — the great experiences that transformed the human psyche during this period. This raises the question of which account is more real and tells us more about the reality of being human in this period: the scientific one, or the esoteric one encoded in ancient myths — and whether there might be levels of truth in today's events missed entirely by the science-oriented common-sense consciousness used to navigate c jams, supermarkets, and e-mails.

Chapter 8: The Sphinx and the Timelock: Orpheus • Daedalus, the First Scientist • Job • Solving the Riddle of the Sphinx

Orpheus, the Transitional Figure

When Jason sailed on the Argo alongside muscle-bound demi-gods like Hercules and Theseus, one crew member possessed entirely different powers: Orpheus, who had travelled from the north bringing the gift of music. His music was so beautiful it could charm not only humans and animals but also trd rocks. On the voyage, when brute strength failed, Orpheus succeeded through song — charming the clashing rocks that threatened to crush the Argo and lulling the dragon guarding the Golden Fleece to sleep.

Orpheus and Eurydice: A New Kind of Death

After the voyage, Orpheus fell in love with Eurydice, who died from a snakeite on their wedding day. Grief-stricken, Orpheus descended into the Underworld — refusing to accept this new order in which death was a painful separation rather than a welcome rest between incarnations. Descending deer, he charmed the ferryman Charon (who initially refused passage), the three-headed guard dog Cerberus, and the demons who tear unregenerate animal lusts from the spirits of the dead.

Reaching the King of the Underworld, Orpheus won conditional release for Eurydice: he could lead her back to the living world only if he never turned to check she was following. At the last moment, as sunlight hit his face — perhaps fearing a trick — he turned around, and watched her pulled back into the Underworld like smoke. Unlike the muscle-bound heroes who succeeded through strength and endurance, Orpheus failed precisely because he tried to do what every good hero did: he tried to make sure. This marks a turning point — brute heroism was no longer sufficient; a new kind of failure, a subtler one, was emerging.

The Death of Orpheus and His Lasting Oracle

His music may also have lost some charm, since it failed to stop maenads (female followers of Dionysus) from tearing him limb from limb. They threw his head into a river, where it floated down still singing, weeping willows crowding the banks. The head was eventually rescued and enshrined on an altar in a cave, where crowds came to consult it as an oracle.

Orpheus as Originator of Mathematics

If Cadmus/Enoch named the planets and stars, Orpheus measured them, and by measuring invented numbers. There are eight notes in an octave, though effectively seven, since the eighth represents elevation to the next octave — these octaves refer to ascent through the seven spheres of the lar system, central to ancient thought. By giving a system of musical notation, Orpheus originated mathematics, enabling concepts to be manipulated and paving the way for scientific understanding of the physical universe. Orpheus embodies an ambiguity seen later in many great scientists: he is simultaneously a magician who moves stones with music and a forerunner of science.

Daedalus, the First Scientist

Daedalus represents the same transitional era (he was a contemporary of Orpheus, as keeper of the Minotaur killed by Theseus). Famous for building wax-and-feather wings to help himself and his son Icarus escape Crete, Daedalus also designed the labyrinth and is credited with inventing the saw and the sail. He was an inventor, engineer, and architect in the modern sense — notabl he did not use magic.

Magic as Applied Science of the Supernatural

Just as science emerged as an innovation of this age, so did magic — understood as the application of a scientific way of thinking to the supernatural realm. Earlier ages had featured effortless shape-shifting; now figures like Medea (Jason's wife) and Circe had to work for supernatural effects using potions, spells, and incantations. The invention of words and numbers gave humans the ability to manipulate not only the natural world but also the spirit world.

  • Medea offered Jason a blood-red potion made from crocus juice to soothe the dragon guarding the Fleece, using chants and sprigs of juniper sprayed on the dragon's eyelids.
  • She dealt in magic elixirs and knew the secrets of snake-charming.

Nature Spirits and Environntal Catastrophe from Black Magic

As the material world grew denser and spirit beings were squeezed out, even nature spirits — sylphs, dryads, naiads, and gnomes — became elusive, seeming to flee into streams, trees, and rocks at first light. These lower spirits remained easiest for magicians to manipulate, then as now. Some magicians attempted to bend great gods to their will, even trying to draw them down from the moon. Myths depicting environmental catastrophe are read as direct conseces of black magic practice:

  • The original werewolf, Lycaon, whose actions prompted the flood of Deucalion.
  • Poseidon's flooding of the Thracian plain, forcing Athena to relocate her city to the site of present-day Athens.
  • The terrible storms that pursued Medea wherever she travelled.

By the end of this period, both humanity and nature were sick.

Orpheus's True Legacy: Art as Healing

Though Orpheus failed by the standard of the conventional hero, his influence on history outlasted that of Hercules, Theseus, and Jason — his music became a balm healing humanity's sick and troubled spirit across millennia. As people grew isolated from gods and from one another, worn down by a rsh environment, and as their imaginations were infected by the perverse and bestial impulses unleashed by magic, this was countered by an aesthetic influence âot just music but literature, painting, and sculpture. Inspiring images of beauty, truth, and love worked on humanity below the level of the conscious mind, proving more powerful than any explicit, abstract moral teaching. Orpheus is regarded as the mythical founder of the Greek mysteries that would illuminate ancient Greece.

Job: The First to Cry "Life Is Unfair"

The most powerful artistic expression of the spiritual crisis at the end of the age of heroes appears in the biblical story of Job — one of the latest-written but oldest-originating texts of the Old Testament. Job was a good man who lost his money, his sons and daughters died, and he was covered in boils while the wicked prospered. His significance lies not in great des but in being the first human to think a deeply true thought: "life is unfair." Hercules had merely been the sport of the gods, but Job cried out to the heavens in defiance — possessing, unlike Hercules, the language to do so.

Language as the Great Achievement Enabling Consciousness

Before language, the mental manoeuvrability to choose what to think about was not possible. Language enables distance from the world, allows withdrawal from what is physically present, and lets experience broken into manipulable pieces, ordered as desired.

  • Warning/non-obvious point: language carries an alienating cost. As well as its advantages, it made the world colder, darker, and trickier — thinking itself is described as a deadening process, and language makes people less vividly alive and less sure-footed in the wor.

Before Job, people felt everything happening to them was meant to happen, governed by divine purpose beyond question. Language enabled Job to step back, notice inconsistencies, and conclude life is unfair — a genuily new form of consciousness.

God's Rebuke and Job's Redemption

God rebuked Job for understanding so little, asking where he was when the foundations of the Earth were laid, when morning stars sang together, when the gates of death opened, and whether he could bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the belt of Orion. What saved Job was his awareness — like waking from a wonderful dream one cannot fully recall — that the range of human experience was diminishing: "Oh that I was as in the times of old, when God watched over me, when his lamp shone on my head" (Job 29:2-4), a reference to the "Lantern of Osiris."

In the apocryphal (meaning hidden or esoteric, not merely "spurious") Testament of Job, he was rewarded for being conscious of what he did not know and had lost. His sons and daughters were restored, his daughters given golden girdles/belts granting three powers: understanding the language of angels, the secrets of creation, and the language of the Cherubim.

Fixing Historical Dates via Astronomy

Music, mathematics, annguage were invented in the age of heroes, and so was astronomy — another achievement attributed to Enoch. The first stone circles marked both the hierarchies of gods and angels and the positions of stars and planets. This is the point in secret history where it becomes possible to begin fixing dates of great events.

The Sphinx and Zep Tepi

Between the Sphinx's paws at Giza, an inscription reads "This is the Splendid Place of the First Time." This mysterious First Time, or Zep Tepi, mark the Egyptian mythological beginning of time, when the primordial mound rose from the waters and the Phoenix alighted on it.

Robert Bauval, standing between the Sphinx's paws, worked to determine the date of Zep Tepi:

  • The Phoenix (Bennu bird) symbolizes the Sothic cycle of 1,460 years — the time for the Egyptian 365-day calendar to resynchronize with the heliacal rising of Sirius.
  • This synchronization occurred in 11,451, 10,081, 7160, 4241, and 2781 BC — dates that coincide with the start of major building projects along the Nile.
  • Ba initially favored 10,081 BC due to esoteric traditions about the Sphinx's construction date.
  • He then discovered that on 11,451 BC, the Milky Way (the "river of souls" in cultures worldwide) lay directly over the course of the Nile, mirroring it.
  • On this same date, the Sothic and yearly cycles coincided meaningfully with the Great Year — the 25,920-year zodiac cycle — because the Sphinx's eastward gaze would have taken in the dawning of the Age of Leo.

The Sphinx as Monument to Matter's Solidification

The Sphinx embodies the four cardinal zodiac constellations — Leo, Taurus, Scorpio, and Aquarius — corresponding to the Four Elements that together constitute the material world. According to secret history, the Sphinx monumentalizes the first moment the Four Elements locked into place and matter became solid.

When Plato in the Timaeus wrote of the World Soul being crucified on the World Body, he was not prophesying Christ's crucifixion (contrary to some Christian apologists) but recalling this crucial moment when conscious finally fixed in solid matter. From this point, the "great clock of the cosmos" was set in its complex orbital pattern, and dates could be firmly fixed because the laws of physics as known today were only then set in motion.

  • Non-obvious/warning implication: if this late solidification of matter is accurate, it would invalidate conventional dating methods like Carbon-14, which assume natural laws held constant across all times and places — an assumption the ancients did not share.

#The Riddle of the Sphinx and the Fixing of Biological Form The Sphinx poses Oedipus its riddle: "What walks on four legs, then two legs, then three legs?" Oedipus correctly interprets it as concerning the ages of man (infant, adult, elder with a cane), but this riddle of "ages" also evokes the evolution of humanity more broadly âhe Sphinx's very form is a monument to this evolution.

Defeated by Oedipus's acumen, the Sphinx casts itself into the abyss — symbolizing how the gods of the elements, the organizing principles of the universe, became successfully absorbed inside the human body at this time. Central to the Oedipal legend is the fate he tried but failed to avoid: killing his faer and becoming his mother's lover — illustrating how, as the laws of nature became fixed and mechanical, humans became trapped within them.

The Sphinx thus also marks the end of the Age of Metamorphosis — the fixing of biological forms as known today — and bars the way back to earlier fluid forms of existence, just as one of the Cherubim bars the way back into Eden in Genesis. The Egyptians, whose Sphinx is composed of four Cherubim, called it "Hu," meaning protector — guarding against any slide back into older modes of procreation.

Correcting the Misconception About Biblical Chronology

It is a common misconception that Bishop Usher's 1650 calculation dating creation to 4004 BC was a vestige of ancient superstition. In fact, this calculation emerged from an era when materialism was gaining ground alongside a narrow, literal biblical interpretation that would have seemed absurd to thts themselves. Ancient belief held that human souls existed for vast, immeasurable eras before 11,451 BC, and only then did the human body as known today fully materialize around the human spirit. Notably, calculations by Manetho (third century BC) place the end of the demi-gods' reign at almost exactly this same time.

The Coming Dissolution of Matter

Esoteric doctrine holds that matter, only precipitated out of mind a relatively short while ago, exists only for a brief interval — it wi dissolve again in just over nine thousand years, when the sun rises again to meet the Sphinx's gaze in the constellation of Leo. In the teachings of secret societies, humanity lives on a small island of matter within a vast ocean of ideas and imagination.

Physical Evidence for an Earlier Sphinx

Eminent Egyptologist R.A. Schwaller de Lubicz (protégé of Henri Matisse) was first to reveal to a wider public that the Sphinx may have been carved before 10,000 BC, pointing to water erosion on the surrounding walls that could not have occurred aer that date. In 11,451 BC, according to this reading, east, west, north, and south were locked in place along with the Four Elements composing the physical world.

Chapter 9: The Neolithic Alexander the Great: Noah and the Myth of Atlantis • Tibet • Rama's Conquest of India

The Platonic Account of Atlantis

Egyptian priests told Solon, a statesman of Plato's great-grandfather's generation, about a great Atlantic island destroyed roughly nine thousand years earlier, around 9600 BC. The civilization was founded by the god Poseidon, who coupled with a beautiful woman named Cleito — a coded account of evolution through a fish-god intervention, as covered regarding animal-headed deities elsewhere. The main island supported lesser islands in the region.

The largest island featured a fertile plain and a large hill where Cleito lived; two streams rose from the earth, one hot, one cold. To keep Cleito for himself, Poseidon dug circular canals around the hill. A sophisticated civilization arose there — taming wild animals, mining met building temples, palaces, racecourses, gymnasiums, public baths, government buildings, harbours, and bridges. Walls were coated with brass, tin, and a red metal unknown today called orichalcum; temples had ivory roofs and pinnacles of silver and gold.

Ten kings ruled the islands, nine subservient to the ruler of the largest island. The central temple to Poseidon held gold statues, including the god in a chariot pulled by six-winged horses, flanked by Nereids riding dolphins. Live bulls roamed the temple's forest of columns, and every five or six years the ten kings were left alone to hunt a bull weaponless, then behead it at the great orichalcum column inscribed with Atlantean law.

Life was so idyllic that people grew restless, decadent, and corrupt, chasing novelty and power. Zeus punished them: the islands were flooded until only small islets remained, then a great earthquake engulfed what was left in a single day and night.

Corroborating Sources Beyond Plato

Aristotle's remark that "Plato alone made Atlantis rise out of the sea, and then he submerged it again" is often taken as proof Plato invented the story. However, classical literature is packed with references to Atlantis — in Proclus, Diodorus, Pliny, Strabo, Plutarch, and Posidinus — containing elements absent from Plato's account and apparently drawn from earlier sources.

Proclus records that three hundred years after Solon, Crantor was shown columns at Sais covered in hieroglyphic history of Atlantis. Pseudo-Aristotle, a near-contemporary of Plato, described a similar island paradise in On Marvellous Things Heard. The historian Marcellus wrote of "seven small islands and three larger ones" in the Outer Ocean, one dedicated to Poseidon — matching Plato's numerical scheme. Theopompus of Chios retold a story from Midas of Phrygia (two hundred years before Plato) describing an unknown continent with giant, long-lived men — consistent with widely recorded traditions of pre-Flood giants.

The Greek myth of Deucalion's flood predates Plato and, like the biblical account, implies the Floodnt to destroy most of humankind because human development had gone wrong. Rudolf Steiner interpreted the eastward journeys of demi-gods and heroes (Cadmus, Theseus, Jason) as symbolic records of migrations away from the deteriorating Atlantean islands before the final catastrophe.

Poseidon, as the original half-fish form of Zeus/Jupiter, was god of the raging sea and of subterranean volcanic depths, his bull-bellowing roar signalling climatic catastrophe — active at both the beginning and d of Atlantis's history.

Cross-Cultural Flood Traditions

The Aztecs claimed descent from "Aztlan," the land in the middle of the water, sometimes called "Aztlan of the Seven Caves" and depicted as a central step pyramid surrounded by six smaller ones. Spanish-collected traditions describe humanity nearly wiped out by flood, saved by a priest and wife who built a hollow-log boat carrying seeds and animals. Sophisticated South American astronomy allowed one modern researcher to date this flood to roughly 11,600 BC — differing from Plato 9600 BC date but agreeing that the Flood coincided with the end of the Ice Age, when melting ice caps sent floods sweeping down from the north.

Underwater archaeologists are finding submerged civilizations worldwide from this period. In April 2002, local fishermen's accounts helped divers locate the lost city of the Seven Pagodas off Mahabalipuram, India — structures far grander than expected for the Neolithic. Graham Hancock noted this vindicated long-dismissed flood myths against academic skepticism.

Personal testimony is offered regarding the Scott stones, artefacts retrieved from the sea bed off the American Atlantic coast, which would reportedly be difficult to reproduce with modern technology, let alone eleven thousand years ago; they resemble Egyptian artefacts in design. Aaron du Val, President of the Miami Museum Egyptological Society, is mentioned as possibly poised to reveal further evidence.

Noah in Near Eastern Traditions

No detailed account of the flood survives in Greek myth, and the biblical version is brief, but merian and other Near Eastern traditions fill gaps — scholars agree these older accounts fed into the biblical story. The ark, doves, and olive branch appear earlier in the Sumerian account (Noah as Ziusudra), the Mesopotamian account (Atrahasis), and the Babylonian account (Upnapishtim). A composite retelling:

Noah, standing in a reed hut, heard a voice through the wall warning of a coming flood, instructing him to tear down the hut and build a boat. He and his family built a vessel of res sealed with bitumen, loading it with plants, birds, cattle, and wild animals. After six days and nights of storm, on the seventh day Noah opened a window to light — the world silent, all humanity "returned to clay."

This deluge is commemorated annually on the Day of the Dead / Halloween; nineteenth-century English villagersressed as the dead and made a closed-lipped "mum-mumming" sound imitating the walking dead — the origin of the word "mummers."

Noah's Drunkenness and Dionysus the Younger

After disembarking, Noah "began to be a husbandman," planted a vineyard, drank wine, became drunk, and lay uncovered in his tent; Ham saw his father's nakedness and told his brothers (Genes 9:20-22). Noah becoming a husbandman fits archaeological evidence that agriculture began in the Neolithic.

To interpret Noah's drunken nakedness, tradition identifies him with Dionysus the Younger — distinct from the earlier Dionysus Zagreus (the Elder Dionysus, dismembered, discussed previously). After the Flood, Dionysus the Younger, often depicted in a boat, travelled from Atlantis via Europe to India to teach agriculture, viticulture, and writing (writing having been earlier taught by Enoch but now endangered by the Flood's devastation).

Dionysus and his followers carried the thyrsus — a pole wrapped in ivy-like snakes topped with a pine cone resembling a pineal gland — symbolizing the secret evolutionary development of the human spine and pineal gland. The fauns and satyrs accompanying Dionysus represent stragglers from Atlantis, remnants of a metamorphosing human form. Noah's sonsering his genitals refers to the petering-out of this transformation process: genitals were the last part of human anatomy to evolve into present form, and the sons wondered whether they descended from a human or a demi-god/angel.

Legend holds the unicorn was the only animal that missed the ark and went extinct — depicting the diminishing power of the Third Eye. As the Flood closed over Atlantis, the era of Imagination ended and the subconscious formed. Dionysus the Younger was educated by e satyr Silenus. His followers, the maenads, tore Orpheus apart in ecstatic, god-possessed drunkenness — both Greek and Hebrew traditions link this figure to grapes and intoxication.

Agriculture as a New Consciousness

Primitive peoples lived closely attuned to plant nature, understanding how different plants affect human ology, physiology, and consciousness. The Greek and Hebrew agricultural-founding myths depict a new, more thoughtful form of consciousness — fields of wheat symbolizing orderly human thought imposed on nature. Humanity's leaders now had to forge this new thought-directed consciousness.

In the Zend-Avesta (Zoroastrian scripture), the Noah/Dionysus figure is called Yima, who instructs people to build a "var" — a fenced stronghold housing men, cattle, dogsrds, and fires — draining water, erecting boundary posts, and building houses from posts, clay, matting, and fences, urging people to "expand the earth by tilling it." He warns against suppression, baseness, dullness, violence, poverty, defeat, deformity, long teeth, giants — anomalous survivals of the previous epoch.

Rama's Conquest of India

The Greek poet Nonnus described Dionysus's migration to India; the Zend-Avesta calls it "the march of the Ram on India"; the fullest account is the Ramayana. These eastward migrations moved into lands still occupied by aboriginal tribes, not empty territory. Dionysus/Rama forbade cannibalism and human sacrifice practiced by native priests, who sometimes kept enormous snakes or pterodactyls — rare antediluvian survivors worshipped as gods and fed captivesh. Rama and his followers stormed these temples with torches, driving out priests and monsters, appearing suddenly among enemies — sometimes armed, sometimes defenceless but able to petrify foes with his pale lotus-blue gaze.

Rama was a dispossessed nomad whose kingdom lay beneath the seas; he camped in the wild with his beloved Sita rather than living as king. When the evil magician Ravana abducted Sita, Rama's journey culminated in conquering India and Ceylon, Ravana's last refuge. Rams army of monkeys — representing hominids, descendants of human spirits who incarnated too early and were doomed to die out — built a bridge over the sea to Ceylon. After a thirteen-day battle, Rama killed Ravana by showering fire upon him.

The Dream of the Crown

Rama, having conquered India, is likened to a Neolithic Ander the Great with the world at his feet. In a dream, walking through moonlit forests, a snow-skinned woman wearing a magnificent crown approached — Sita, offering him the crown to rule the world together. His guardiaangel warned him: placing the crown on his head would mean losing the angel's guidance forever; embracing Sita would kill her instantly with happiness; but refusing her would let her live out a free, happy life on earth while his invisible spirit ruled over her. Rama chose refusal; Sita vanished, and the two never met again, living out their lives apart. Later stories about Sita's subsequent life suggest she was not clearly as happy as promised — an ambiguity felt as strikingly modern.

This story illustrates a core paradox of the human condition: true love requires letting go.

Moral Significance of Rama's Choice

Rama resembles Greek heroes like Hercules in physical prowess (skill with the bow, blue eyes, lion chest), but his story introduces genuine moral surprise. Hercules chose virtue over happiness predictably; Rama's refusal of both the rightful crown and the woman he loves — against the reader's instinct to side with Sita's argument that he deserves the crown — expands the moral imagination and quickens moral intelligence. ic thought consistently seeks to subvert conventional, habitual, mechanical thinking; later storytellers steeped in esoteric tradition (Shakespeare, Cervantes, George Eliot, Tolstoy) would carry forward this capacity to quicken moral imagination, a hallmark of the greatest literature.

The story reinforces that the cosmos exists to create conditions for free thought and free will. Rama could have ruled his people with a rod of iron but instead let them decide for themselves, becoming the archetype of the exiled "Secret King" or "Secret Philosopher" who shapes history not from a throne but incognito among the people. As a demi-god who declines world rulership, Rama marks the point after which gods or demi-gods would no longer sit on thrones in bodies of flesh and bone.

Shambala and Tibet

The emigrants ultimately founded Shambala, a great spiritual fortress in Tibet's mountains — the world's highest, biggest plateau. Some traditions hold the Tibetan population descends directly from Atlantis. Accounts differ on whether Shambala is reached via an underground tunnel or exists in another dimension accessible through a secret portal.

St Augustine, greatest Christian theologian after St Paul and, like Paul, a Mystery school initiate, wrote of a terrestrial paradise soigh the Flood could not reach it, where Enoch and the saints lived. Emmanuel Swedenborg, eighteenth-century theologian, diplomat, inventor, and leading esoteric Freemason, wrote that the "Lost Word" must be sought among the sages of Tibet and Tartary. Anne-Catherine Emmerich, nineteenth-century German Catholic mystic, described a Mount of Prophets housing Enoch, Elijah, and others who "ascended" rather than died, along with surviving unicorns.

From Tibet's mountains flowed streams of spirituality that gathered into a mighty river like the Ganges, feeding the whole of India.

The First Indian Civilization and the Rishis

As the sun entered Cancer in 7227 BC, the earliest and most deeply spiritual post-Flood civilization arose in India. Its founders regarded the newly material world as "maya," illusion obscuring higher spiritual realities, and looked nostalgically toward the pre-material veil era. Ascetic practices — icy baths and self-torture — were efforts to stay awake to the spirit worlds while the veil remained relatively translucent, consciously preserving the lineaments of the spirit world in human consciousness.

This effort succeeded: India remains the world's greatest storehouse of spiritual knowledge, particularly occult physiology — "the air still just crackles with ity," as one high-level initiate reportedly said. Western teachers including Pythagoras, Apollonius of Tyana, and St Germain travelled to India seeking this astrality. The Gospels contain quotations and ideas originating in older Indian sources. Sir John Woodruffe, the Sanskrit scholar who first translated tantric texts, documented how even Sufi tradition drew on Hindu chakra teachings. From the 1960s onward, Western seekers turned to Indian religion for practical spiritual disciplines unavailable in church settings — Western bookshops stilstock more Eastern than Western mystical literature.

The Seven Rishis and Occult Physiology

After Rama's refusal of the crown, no single dominant personality shaped this period; instead came the Seven Wise Ones, or Rishis — still and ictive compared to Rama's action-hero adventures, building nothing but mud dwellings or shelters twisted from roots and tendrils. A Cabala saying — "Everything you have seen... will pass away and turn to dust, but that you have seen them will not pass away" — captures their outlook. Sitting with soles turned upward to resist gravity's downward pull, the Rishis oriented toward the spirit worlds, perceiving spiritual beings assisting seeds' germination, flowers' blossoming, fruiting, and winter preservation — experiencing the ebb and flow of spiritual influence like a giant breath.

A caution is raised: the word "spiritual" is often misappropriated by people to seem good-hearted in a warm, fuzzy, pseudo-mystical way, when its true meaning is the capacity to see, hear, and communicate with spirits se adepts did.

The Rishis communicated occultly, sensing others' inner life by breathing in their air. They poured knowledge into others' souls through unceasing flows of pictures, later transmitted orally for generations before being written down as the Vedas. Their gaze could drive away serpents and calm lions and tigers; nothing could deflect their contemplation. They wandered freely with minimal shelter, ate only fruit and drank flock milk, avoiding meat entirely in the belief that eating meat meant absorbing an animal's death agony.

By immersing in vegetable consciousness — waking, sleeping, breathing, digesting — and mastering the ens vegetalis (etheric body), they gained control over breathing, digestion, heart rate, and blood flow, achieving feats such as stopping the heart by will alone.

Chakra Amy and the Three Arteries

The adepts understood that deep contemplation of the solar plexus chakra enabled clairvoyant perception, and that others could be wrapped in a protective beam of love emanating from the heart chakra. Beyond the heart chakra's sixteen petals, they perceived 101 subtle luminous arteries radiating like spokes, three of which rose to the head: one to the right eye (corresponding to the sun and the future), one to the left eye (corresponding to the moon and the past) — together enabling perception of moving material objects in space and a sense of time. The middle artery ran from the heart through the crown of the head, illuminating the upward spiritual path from below via a radiant heart, and served as the route by which the spirit departs the body at death.

A Neolithic swastika carved on a boulder on Keighley Moor, Yorkshire, symbolizes the revolving two-petalled lotus, matched by a device on a Celtic sun brooch found in Sweden; the Rig Veda invokes "the beautiful splendour of Savitva the Sun-God of the swastika to inspire our visions."

Cosmic Rhythm and the Birth of Yoga

Ancient peoples understood all life as a pulse, rhythm, or breath — human lives breathed temporarily into the world of maya and breathed out again repdly through the ages, with great flocks of souls breathed in and out of material existence together. This early Indian civilization echoed the sun-filled, watery, vegetable world preceding the separation of sun and earth — itself a "lotus-eating" period that had to end for progress to continue.

As higher-hierarchy beings could no longer appear in physical bodies as they had on Atlantis, appearing instead only as semi-material spectres with decreasing frequency (by the age's end, perhaps on or twice in a lifetime), people needed new ways to follow the withdrawing gods — giving rise to yoga.

Kundalini and the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali

At the height of meditation, energy rushing from the base of the spine travelled upward through the middle artery via the heart to the head, sometimes imagined as a serpent bitina point behind the bridge of the nose, releasing an ecstatic lace-like flux of seven hundred thousand lightning flares sounding like millions of bees. Adepts entered another dimension resembling a mighty ocean of giant weaving waves of light and energy — a preliminary mystical experience common across traditions — which, with familiarity, resolved into the outer garments of gods and finally the gods' own faces, the same stellar and planetary deities discussn earlier chapters.

The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, one of the shortest yet most powerful books in the world, was finalized around 400 BC but originated in Rishi teachings. Patanjali instructs concentrating on the strength of an elephant to attain that strength, and states that concentrating on the past reveals past lives. A clear caution is given: such feats remain achievable today only by the most advanced initiates — ordinary people can only hope to attain them in future incarnations. The Rishis taught that the evolution of the whole cosmos is existence's goal, with the seeds of that transformation residing in the human body.

The Shift Westward

In 5067 BC, as the sun entered Gemini, the gods began moving the cosmos toward the next stage of human evolution. Just as the evolutionary impulse hadarlier moved eastward from drowning Atlantis to India, it now began shifting westward — a movement continuing into the present.

Chapter 10: The Way of the Wizard: Zarathustra's Battle Against the Powers of Darkness • The Life and Death of Krishna the Shepherd

Birth of Zarathustra

In 5067 BC, in the region now called Iran, a great leader's birth was foretold. His mother lived in a small agricultural community similar to Çatal Hüyük. During a harsh winter marked by plague, villagused her of witchcraft. In her fifth month of pregnancy she had a nightmare of dragons, wolves and snakes trying to tear her unborn child from her body — but the child spoke from her womb to comfort her. A pyramid of light descended, and down it came a boy carrying a staff and a scroll, whose name was Zarathustra. The rolled roll carried in the right hand is a recurring sign throughout history that a figure is an adherent of secret philosophy — many statues of the great and good in modern cities carry this same symbol.

There is disagreemt about Zarathustra's dates: some ancient writers place him around 5000 BC, others (like Plutarch) around 600 BC, because there was more than one Zarathustra.

His birth provoked hatred. A king, controlled by sorcerers, tried to kill the infant himself but his hand became mysteriously paralyzed. A servant abandoned the baby in a wolf-ridden wilderness, but the wolves saw something in his eyes and fled in terror. The forces of evil knew their greatest enemy had arrived and bided their time.

The Age of Gemini and the Rise of Demonology

The Persian epoch, governed by the Age of Gemini, was an age of division — no longer could people live safely as in Paradise as during the Indian epoch. Where the Indian epoch recapitulated the heavenly time before earth and sun separated, the Persian epoch recapitulated the fiery period when Lucifer's dragons had infected earthly life. Ahriman (Zoroastrian Satan) led hordes of demons that darkened the heavens and thrust themselves between humans and higher spiritual hierarchies. This period is the sourcof demonological knowledge, just as the Indian epoch was the source of the secret physiology of humankind.

Demons are often depicted gnawing at viscera because of the primordial understanding that consciousness and memory are stored not only in the brain but throughout the body — undigested and painful experiences are stored in the viscera.

At this historical turning point, people first began to feel existential insecurity — what Emile Durkheim called anomie, a fear of destructive chaoeeping in at the margins of life, whether from darkness outside the encampment, darkness during sleep, or darkness after death.

Sleep, Dreams and the Spirit World

When falling asleep, humans lose animal consciousness (spirit), which floats out of the body. This has two consequences: first, freed from the agitations of animal consciousness, the vegetable functions of the body renew themselves, so we wake refreshed; second, detached from bodily sensory perception, the spirit enters the sub-lunary spirit world, where in dreams we may be approached by angels, demons, and spirits of the dead.

This was true chiefly in the time of the Rishis. By Zarathustra's era, human nature had become so enmeshed in matter that dreams grew chaotic and difficult to interpret — fantastical, distorted, yet still capable of containing spirit promptings, fragments of past lives, or memories of history. In deepest sleep the Third Eye may open onto the spirit worlds, but we forget upon waking.

Zarathustra's Initiation by the Sun Spirits

After years in exile, the young Zarathustra returned to Iran and, at the border, encountered a gigantic shining spirit that led him — Zarathustra had to take ninety steps for each of the spirit's nine — to a hidden clearing where six similar spirits hovered. This company invited him to leave his physical body and join them. These were the Elohim, the sun spirits of Genesis.

They prepared him for his mission through three ordeals:

  • He had to pass through fire without being burned.
  • Molten lead (the metal of Ahriman) was poured onto his chest, which he endursilence, then calmly returned to them.
  • They opened his torso and showed him the secrets of his inner organs before closing him up again.

Zarathustra returned to court and preached that the sun spirits who created the world were working to transform it into a vast body of light. The new king, like his predecessor, was controlled by evil ministers who had Zarathustra imprisoned, but he escaped repeatedly, surviving numerous assassination attempts. He became the archetype of the wizard — tl hat, cloak of stars, eagle on the shoulder — a dangerous, disconcerting figure willing to fight fire with fire.

Mithraic Initiation and Its Legacy

Zarathustra led followers to hidden grottoes and underground caverns to initiate them, equipping them with supernatural powers to fight evil. This Mystery school survived fiveillennia underground in Persia, resurfacing as Mithraism (popular among Roman soldiers) and later Manichaeism (which counted St Augustine among its initiates).

A marble depiction shows Mithras (archangel of the sun, called St Michael in Hebrew tradition) slaying the cosmic bull of material creation — corn springs from its spine, wine from its blood. Mithras wea the "Phrygian cap," later worn by initiates of secret societies leading the French Revolution. The French Martinist Joseph de Maistre described Mithraic initiation ceremonies: a candidate stood in a pit beneath a metal grille on which a bull was sacrificed, drenching him in its blood; later he lay in a tomb as if dead before the initiator pulled him up by the right hand into "new life." There were seven grades of initiate: Raven, Nymphus, Soldier, Lion, Persian, Courier of the Sun and Father.

Initiation Ordeals and Practical Powers

Zarathustra prepared followers to face Ahriman's demons (Asuras) through terrifying initiation ordeals, teaching that "he who fears death is already dead." The Greek philosopher Menippus (third century BC), initiated by Mithraic successors of Zarathustra, recorded that after fasting, mortification, and solitary mental exercises, candidates were forced to swim across water, pass through fire and ice, be cast into a snake pit, and be cut across the chest with a sword to draw blood. By experiencing the outer limits of fear, the initiate was prepared for the worst in life and after death.

A key part of preparation was inducing conscious experience of the separation between the animal part of one's makeup and the vegetable/material parts — as happens in sleep — and separately, the separation of the animal from the vegetable part, as happens after d: essentially an "after-death experience." By leaving the body, the candidate knew beyond doubt that death was not the end.

Paracelsus said: "It is as necessary to learn evil things as good, for who can know what is good without learning what is evil." Historically significant secret societies such as the Rosicrucians and Freemasons acknowledge the dark side precisely in order to combat it — contrary to the assumption that all secret societies traffic with evil spirits.

Powers Available Through Conscious Dreaming

People who learn to dream consciously — retaining the capacity to think and exercise willpower normally only available in waking life — may develop supernatural abilities:

  • Moving freely about the spirit worlds and communicating with the dead and other disembodiegs.
  • Learning about the future in otherwise blocked ways.
  • Astral travel — viewing distant parts of the material universe without being bodily present.
  • Paracelsus (16th century), a claimed father of both modern experimental medicine and homeopathy, said he could visit others in their dreams.

Many great scientific discoveries have reportedly been revealed to initiates in this alternative state of consciousness.

Mind Influence, Hypnosis and the Evil Eye
