Initiation can also confer supernatural means of influencing minds — genuine mind-reading beyond what skeptical scientists can replicate through "cold reading." Hypnosis, though abused by popular entertainers, is at root an occult practice, explicable only in mind-before-matter terms, originating with the Rishis of India and Egyptian templiest initiation techniques. In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, this power of influencing others' minds is called vibhuti — used originally for benevolent purposes but increasingly needed for both defense and attack as the world grew more dangerous.

Because in a mind-before-matter philosophy the way one looks at someone can affect them at a sub-atomic level, the coiled cobra on the foreheads of Egyptian initiates (representing the Third Eye) symbolizes this power reaching out to strike. Examples: Seventeenth-century scientist and alchemist J.B. von Helmont claimed a man could kill an animal by staring at it for fifteen minutes.

  • From the eighteenth century, European travelers in India reported adepts throwing people into catalepsy merely by looking at them.
  • A nineteenth-century traveler recorded by Gerald Massey (George Eliot's friend, an initiate) was mesmerized by a serpent's gaze and sank into "somnambulic" sleep; when someone shot the snake, breaking its power, he felt a blow to the head as if struck by a bullet himself.
  • Twentieth-century travelers reported wolves able to freeze victims and prevent them from crying out even when unaware of being watched.
  • A local wise man and healer in Crowborough, England, called Pigtail Badger, was feared because villagers said he could stop others in their tracks with a look, and would sometimes do this to farm labourers before eating their lunches in front of them.

Death, Purgatory and the Ascent Through the Spheres

The most crucial initiation teachings concerned how spirit worlds are experienced after death — not because candidates doubted an afterlife (unthinkable at the time), but because they feared what awaited them, particularly demons lying in wait for evasions committed in life. Initiation taught candidates to navigate this journey safely.

In sleep, the animal spirit leaves the vegetable and mineral body behind; in death, the vegetable part (which governs basic life functions and stores memory) leaves along with the animal spirit. As the vegetable part detaches from the material body, both begin to disintegrat and this disintegration causes the spirit to experience a review of the completed life. The vegetable part fully dissipates within days, after which the spirit passes into the sub-lunar sphere, where demons tear away all impure, corrupt and bestial desires and evil impulses of will. This purification process lasts roughly a third of the time spent on earth and is called Purgatory in Christian tradition — the same as the Underworld of Egyptians and Greeks, or the Kamaloca ("region of desir) of Hindus.

Meister Eckhart (13th-century German mystic) said: "If you fight your death, you'll feel the demons tearing away at your life, but if you have the right attitude to death, you will be able to see that the devils are really angels setting your spirit free." An initiate, having the right attitude, recognizes that demons perform an invaluable ecological role in the spirit world — without this purging, the spirit cannot ascend through higher spheres or hear their music, and cannot be reunited with the Father until purified. This knowdge from initiation is existential, not abstract — gained through a shattering out-of-body experience.

The Ascent

From the lunar sphere the spirit rises to Mercury, then Venus, then the sun, at which point it experiences "a lightness which nobody who has not been initiated could either describe or understand" (Greek orator Aristides). This teaching, common across all Mystery schools of the ancient world, has been perpetuated by secret societies and appears from the Egyptian Book of the Dead, through the Christian Cabala's Pistis Sophia, Dante's Commedia, to Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's twentieth-century Le Petit Prince — sometimes hidden in plain view.

Ancient texts record secret names of guardian spirits at the entrance of each sphere, along with secret handshakes and formulae for entry. In the Pistis Sophia, spheres are envisioned as crystal, guarded by archons or demons. In all ancient religions, the god of Mercury guides the human spirit through the underworld past guardian demons.

The Hidole of Lucifer

A secret kept by Mystery school initiates: halfway through the ascent, guidance is taken over by a surprising figure — Lucifer. In the cosmic spiritual ecology, Lucifer is a necessary evil both in life (without him, humans could feel no desire) and in the afterlife (without him, the spirit would be plunged into darkness and fail to understand its own ascent). The second-century Roman writer Apuleius wrote that in initiation the spirit confronts the gods of heaven in their unveiled splendour, all ambiguitiesemoved.

The spirit continues through Jupiter and Saturn, through the sphere of the constellations, finally reuniting with the Cosmic Mind. Plutarch describes the culmination: "a wondrous light shines to greet us, beautiful meadows full of singing and dancing, the solemnity of sacred realms and holy appearances."

The Descent and Reincarnation

The spirit then descends again through the spheres in preparation for its next incarnation, receiving a gift from each sphere it will need upon re-entering the material plane. An account compiled from ancient Iraqi tablets (potentially dating to the third millennium BC) lists seven gates, each restoring an item — a cloak, bracelets, a girdle, breast ornaments, a necklace, earrings, and finally a great crown.

These seven gifts survive day, encoded in the fairy tale of Sleeping Beauty, where six fairies bless the princess and a seventh (representing Saturn/Satan, the spirit of materialism) curses her with death, commuted to sleep. To understand the esoteric content correctly requires inverting the story: the "deathly sleep" actually represents life on earth itself — because of Satan's intervention, humans gradually lose consciousness and memory of their time among the heavenly hierarchies ("Our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting"). The party at the story's beginning takes place in the spirit world; Beauty is truly alive only once she "falls asleep" into material existence, and she effectively dies when she "awakes." A similar paradox appears in the story of Osiris: he is only dead to Isis when alive on the material plane.

Thesstories demonstrate that both earthly life and the afterlife are ruled by planets and stars, and initiation prepares candidates for meetings with the guardians of each sphere on both the ascending and descending journeys. If well imprinted, this teaching ultimately readies the spirit for conscious participation in preparing its next incarnation — the key word being "conscious."

Rosicrucian beliefs about reincarnation are similarly encoded in Snow White and the Seven Dwarves — Snow White "" and is laid in a glass coffin, a legendary Rosicrucian custom. While reincarnation may seem alien to modern Christian culture, the New Testament contains ideas of reincarnation, early Christians believed in it, and senior Christians have secretly believed in it ever since — encoded in art, architecture, and literature such asndrew Lang's Red Fairy Book.

The Purpose of Initiation

Initiation forges a conscious, working relationship with disembodied spirits and existential knowledge of how they operate in waking life, dreams, and death. Histories such as the trials of Hercules are structured according to astronomical cycles — the sun's journey through the year and the precession of the equinoxes — because the same patterns structuring earthly life also structure the spirit worlds. Figures like Hercules and Job who suffered earthly trials musso suffer the same trials in the afterlife unless they become conscious of them; failing that, they must suffer them again in their next incarnation. The entire aim of initiation is to make more experience conscious, rolling back the boundaries of consciousness.

Historical Examples of Initiation Ordeals

A depiction by Renaissance master Andrea Mantegna shows a hooded acolyte threatened and made to feel he has been pushed into a fatal fall, inducing an out-of-body experience that provides personal, existential knowledge of what happens when the spirit leaves the body at death.

The eighteenth-century magus Cagliostro described his own Masonic initiation in a London lodge above a pub in Soho: after swearing an oath of secrecy, he was blindfolded, tied by rope around the waist, and winched to the ceiling by pulleys before suddenly falling to the floor. His blindfold was briefly removed to show him a pistol being loaded with powder and a bullet; blindfolded again, he was handed the pistol and told to prove his obedience by shooting himself in the head. When he hesitated, his initiators accused him of cowardice; he pulled the trigger, heard an explosion, felt a blow to the side of his head, and smelled gunpowder — believi he was about to die, he emerged an initiate.

In ordinary life, both individually and collectively, humans go round and round in circles traced by planets and stars — but becoming conscious of these cyclical influences allows a person to rise above them, moving not in a circle but in an upward spiral.

Zarathustra's Anatomal and Astronomical Legacy

Zarathustra wore a cloak covered with stars and planets to mark the knowledge the sun spirits had taught him, which he passed on through initiation. Candidates who re-entered the body after their out-of-body experience were enabled to explore their bodies' interior workings in ways not rediscovered until autopsies thousands of years later — though the ancients, true to their habit of experiencing life subjectively, knew human anato not conceptually but experientially. This is how the ancients knew of the pineal gland long before its "discovery" by modern science.

At the transition from the sixth to fifth millennium BC, humankind began building the great stone circles that survive today. Just as the withdrawal of the gods during the Indian period forced humankind to seek new ways of following them, the further obscuring of divine guidance in this era made new methods of seeking guidance necessary — drawing humankind further out of itself. As initiator of these stone monuments, Zarathustra can be seen as a post-Flood mirror image of Enoch.

The Megalithic Yard

Megalithic stone circles spreading through the Near East, Northern Europe and Northern Africa were built to measure the movements of heavenly bodies. In the 1950s, Pfessor Alexander Thom of Cambridge University discovered that megalithic monuments worldwide were built according to a common unit of measurement he called the "megalithic yard," later verified by wide-ranging statistical analyses. Dr Robert Lomas of Sheffield University demonstrated how this unit achieved astonishing unanimity and accuracy across different regions: a pendulum swinging 360 times during the time it takes a star to move through one degree of the sky's 360-degree dome produces a length of exactly 16.32 inches — precisely half a "megalithic yard." Because ancients regarded stars and planets as controllers of earthly life, they defined their original mathematical measures by reference to these heavenly (spiritual) bodies — meaning that mathematics in its origins was both holistic (accounting for earthize, shape, and movement relative to heavenly bodies) and an expression of spiritual impulse.

The Death of Zarathustra

Evil powers constantly threatened to destroy Zarathustra, a danger still commemorated in small mountainside Zoroastrian shrines today where a flame is kept alight but perpetually at risk of being snuffed out. At the age of seventy-seven, Zarathustra was murdered on his own altar.

The Birth and Life of Krishna

Shortly before the end of the fourth millennium, in 3228 BC, Krishna was born — a shepherd d prophet who was in some ways a forerunner of Jesus Christ. (Krishna, Osiris and Zarathustra are later shown attending the Nativity in disguise in famous Renaissance paintings.) This Krishna is not to be confused with the earlier, Atlantean war-god Krishna who fought to defeat Luciferic forces of desire and delusion — by this later era, those forces had sunk deeper into human nature, degenerating into desire for gold and for the spilling of blood.

His mother-to-be, the virgin Devaki, experienced increasingly strange visions, including a deep ecstasy in which she heard heavenly music of harps and voices and, amid flashing lights, saw the Sun god appear to her in human form, overshadowing her until she lost consciousness. Krishna was ler born, and an angel warned Devaki that her brother Kansa would try to murder the boy, so she fled to live among shepherds at the foot of Mount Meru.

Kansa's Persecution and Krishna's Powers

Kansa was a child-killer who hunted down the children of the poor, having done so even as a child himself. He sent a giant red-crested snake to kill his nephew, but Krishna killed it by stamping on it. A female demon named Putana, whose breasts were full of poison, tried to kill him by having him suckle her — but Krishna sucked with such force that she crumpled and died.

As Krishna grew to manhood, protected by shepherds who hid him in hills and forests, he preached a gospel of non-violence and universal love — "Return good for evil, forget your own suffering for another's" and "Renounce the fruit of your works — le work be its own reward" — teachings no one had ever spoken before, which further enraged Kansa.

Krishna the Cowherd

Among Krishna's titles are "The Cowherd" and "The Lord of the Milkmaids." He lived a simple count life, preaching while avoiding direct confrontation with Kansa, playing the flute and dancing with the local milkmaids, all of whom were in love with him. In one episode he stole the milkmaids' clothes while they bathed in the Yumana River and climbed a tree so they could not reach him; in another, while dancing with many milkmaids who each wanted to hold his hand, he multiplied himself into many forms so each believed she held the true Krishna's hand. Krishna is depicted as a god of transgression, whose numer (sacred potency) places him beyond conventional morality.

Confrontation and Martyrdom

Krishna and his brother once entered Kansa's city of Mathura disguised as poor country people to attend an athletics festival. They met a deformed girl, Kubja, carrying ointments and perfumes to the palace; when Krishna asked for some, she gave freely despite being unable to afford it, and he cured her deformity, making her beautiful. Kansa, not fooled by their disguise, had primed two giants to kill the brothers during the wrestling competition, with an elephant set to trample them if the giants failed — but Krishna and his brother turned the tables and escaped.

Finally Krishna abandoned all disguise and returned to Mathura, where the populace acclaimed him as saviour, showering him with flowers and garlands. Kansa, waiting with his retinue, declared "You have stolen my kingdom — Kill me!" When Krishna refused, Kansa had his soldiers seize Krishna, tie him to a cedar tree, and martyr him with archers.

The Onset of the Kalia

Krishna's death in 3102 BC marked the beginning of the Kali Yuga, the Dark Age — a yuga being a division of a great year, with eight yugas in a complete precessional cycle. Both Eastern and Western traditions agree this cosmic shift began in 3102 BC and ended in 1899. Freemasons commemorated the approaching end of the Kali Ya by erecting gigantic monuments in the centre of nearly every great Western city — familiar landmarks most people pass by unaware they serve as beacons for this hidden history and philosophy.

As Krishna died, another great personage — a light-bearer — was growing to adulthood and would soon incarnate, just as Jesus Christ would incarnate three thousand yeaer. This incarnated Lucifer's life and times are examined in the following chapter.

Chapter 11: Getting to Grips with Matter: Imhotep and the Age of the Pyramids • Gilgamesh and Enkidu • Abraham and Melchizedek

The Problem of Verifying Altered States

Small groups throughout history have practised secret techniques to enter alternative states of consciousness, believing this grants perception inaccessible to ordinary awareness. Modern commonsense consciousness dismisses such states as delusional. While inspired art, literature and music might be waved away as mere imagination, this chapter asks a harder question: what if these states produced concrete, verifiable results — great feats of engineering and scientific discovery? Examples include the temple of Baalbek in Lebanon (containing a thousand-ton carved granite block no modern crane could lift), the Great Pyramid at Giza, and lesswn pyramids in China.

The Age of Taurus and the Sudden Rise of Civilization

Early in the third millennium BC, the first great civilizations appeared seemingly out of nowhere: Sumerian civilization dominated by the bull-hero Gilgamesh, Egypt's bull cult of Osiris, and bull-running Crete. This is the Age of Taurus. Conventional history has no good explanation for why vast numbers of people suddenly began living in highly organized cities of extraordinary size and technical sophistication.

The Incarnation of Lucifer in China

A shadowy, momentous event took place in China that even great initiates cannot see with full clarity. According to Rudolf Steiner, in the third millennium BC — when Chinese people lived a tribal, nomadic existence — Lucifer incarnated into a human body, just as Christ would later incte as Jesus. This marked the beginning of a specific kind of "wisdom" — the prudential, practical wisdom found in biblical books like Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, which contains no moral or providential dimension, only aice on securing one's own interests.

  • Unlike typical initiations (Cabala initiation traditionally permitted only at age forty; Pythagorean candidates lived in isolation and silence for years before beginning study), Lucifer was raised from birth entirely within a Mystery school, with a circle of magi moulding his soul through the most secret ceremonies.
  • At age forty he had a revelation, becoming the first person able to think about earthly life in an entirely rational way.
  • Consequence: whereas Orpheus (Chapter 8) invented numbers but could not separate them from spiritual meaning, Lucifer's rationalizing influence made it possible to think of numbers as pure quantity, stripped of symbolic or qualitative content — freeing people to measure, calculate, build, and construct.

Imhotep: Builder of the Step Pyramid

Plutarch identifies Orpheus's son Asclepius with Imhotep, who lived around 2500 BC, by which point this revolutionary rationalizing wave had swept from the Far East to Egypt.

  • Imhotep served as vizier to King Djoser and w known as the builder, sculptor, and maker of stone vases; he was also titled Chief of the Observers (later the title of the high priest of Heliopolis).
  • He was depicted wearing a star-covered mantle and holding a rolled scroll, and was famed as architect of the Step Pyramid at Saqqara.
  • Nineteenth-century archaeologists excavating beneath the Step Pyramid found sealed treasures — the "impossible things of Imhotep," some now displayed in New York's Metropolitan Museum. Commentators werespecially struck by giraffe-necked, pot-bellied rock-crystal vases whose hollowed interiors remain difficult to explain even today.

The Great Pyramid: An Incarnation Machine, Not a Tomb

Half an hour's drive from Saqqara stands the Great Pyramid, oriented to the cardinal points with striking accuracy — rebuilding it today uld strain even the world's richest economies and push modern engineering to its limits, especially in astronomical precision.

  • Conventional history assumes Egyptian building progressed from simple mastabas, through the Step Pyramid, to the culminating complexity of the Great Pyramid (dated ~2500 BC) — a narrative built on the absence of carbon-datable organicaterial and the lack of any method for dating cut stone.
  • The esoteric account inverts this: the Great Pyramid was built around 3500 BC — before Egyptian and Sumerian civilizations existed, when only stone circles and cyclopean monuments had been built. Stone Age peoples in animal skins, carrying primitive tools, would have gazed at it in stupefaction. On this view, the Step Pyramid and later pyramids represent a decline, not an ascent.
  • Rejected interpretation: the "excarnation machine" theory, where narrow shafts from the King's and Queen's Chambers pointing at particular stars supposedly aided the pharaoh's spirit's journey to the heavens. This is dismissed as anachronistic — at this time, everyone universally and vividly experienced the reality of spirits journeying through planetary spheres after death; disbelief in that journey would have been as difficult as disbelieving in a table iont of you.
  • The Great Pyramid's true function relates to ancient Egyptian civilization's whole project: getting to grips with matter, seen in its drive to cut and carve stone.

Mummification and Grave Goods Reconsidered

Popular assumption holds that Egyptians believed spirits would literally use grave goods in the afterlife — dismissed here as attributing a stupid belief to the ancients.

  • Non-obvious point: the actual esoteric purpose of mummification and grave goods was to exert magnetic attraction on the ascending spirit to help it achieve speedy reincarnation. Preserving the discarded body kept it as a focus for the departed spirit, pulling it back toward earth.
  • Applying the same logic to the Great Pyramid: since the great gods had retreated as far as the moon (as described in Chapter 7), finding it increasingly difficult to incarnate, the Great Pyramid functioned as a gigantic incarnation machine — designed to draw divine beings back down into matter, not to send human spirits away from it.

Egypt's Spiritl Mission: The Work

Egyptian civilization represented a wholly new evolutionary impulse, contrasting with oriental civilization's teaching that matter is maya (illusion). Egyptians initiated the great spiritual mission of the West — known ialchemy, Sufism, Freemasonry and other secret societies as "the Work": to work on matter, cut it, carve it, imbue it with intention, until every particle of matter in the universe has been worked on and spiritualized. The Great Pyramid was the first manifestation of this mission.

Sumerian Civilization and the God Houses

Sumerian civilization arose around 3250 BC, contemporary with Egypt's rise, between the Tigris and Euphrates.

  • In early Sumerian cities, statues of ancestors and lesser gods stood in family homes; a kept skull could serve as a "house" for a minor spirit to inhabit.
  • The city's greater protective spirit lived in a "god house" at the temple complex center; as cities grew, these became ziggurats — stepped, rectangular mud-brick pyramids housing a central chamber with a jewel-inld, richly dressed divine statue.
  • Practical application/ritual detail: cuneiform texts describe Sumerian gods enjoying eating, drinking, music, dancing, sex and sleep. Food was set before the god, who was left alone to "enjoy" it before priests ate the leftovers; the god's statue was washed, dressed and perfumed for bed. As with Egyptian grave goods, these practices aimed to tempt gods to inhabit the material plane by reminding them of sensual pleasures denied in the spirit worlds.

The Bee Symbol and Bi-Cameral Consciousness

The bee is a key symbol in secret tradition — bee-hives display pre-conscious genius, incorporating exceptionally precise data (e.g., the angle of the earth's rotation is built into hive construction).

  • Sumerian cylinder seals of this era depict figures with human bodies but bees' nest heads, reflecting the belief that an individual's consciousness was a collaboration of multiple centres of consciousness (as described in Chapter 2) — centres that could be shared or transferred between minds like a m moving between hives.
  • Princeton historian Julian Jaynes's 1976 work The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bi-Cameral Mind argued that people of this era had no concept of an interior life as understood today; they had no vocabulary for it, and experienced willing, thinking and feeling as the activity of external spirits or gods rather than internally generated states.
  • This chimes independently with Rudolf Steiner's esoteric account of the evolution of consciousness (Steiner, born Austria 1861, is described as representing a genuine Rosicrucian stream and the modern esoteric teacher with the most detailed account of consciousness's evolution).
  • Illustrative example from the Iliad: when Agamemnon robs Achilles of his mistress, Achilles doesn't decide to restrain himself — a god physically accosts him by the hair; another god rises from the sea to console him; a god whispers homesickness to Helen. Modern scholars read these as poetic metaphors for interior emotion, but Jaynes shows this reads present-day consciousness bkward into a fundamentally different form of mind. Cambridge philosopher John Wisdom is quoted: "The Greeks did not speak of the dangers of repressing instincts but they did think of thwarting Dionysius or of forgetting Poseidon for Athena."
  • Visual example: the Cairo Museum statue of Horus whispering in the ear of pharaoh Kefren depicts this same otherworldly suggestion.

Critiquing Jaynes: The Delusion Problem

Jaynes describes the controlling gods as "aural hallucinations," implying kings and heroes were, in effect, beset by delusions — whereas the ancients understood these beings as independent, living entities, not delusions.

  • Non-obvious counter-argument: since hallucinations are by definition non-consensual, a hallucination-based civilization should produce total chaos and mutual misunderstanding —ching the clinical psychiatric definition of schizophrenia (inability to distinguish externally/internally generated images, with disabling functional impairment).
  • Instead, this era's peoples built the first post-Flood civilizations with organized priestly, military, agricultural, trading and manufacturing orders, canals, ditches, temples, complex economies and disciplined armies — cooperation that would require an implausibly massive, consensual "group hallucination" if Jaynes's framework were taken literally.

Jung's Convergence with the Ancient View

Freud and Jung familiarized the idea that minds contain autonomous psychological complexes independent of ordinary consciousness. Jung described these major complexes as the seven planetary deities of mythology — archetypes of the collective unconscious.

  • Yet when Jung met Steiner (who believed in literal disembodied spirits including planetary gods), Jung dismissed him as schizophrenic.
  • Warning/foreshadowing (developed in Chapter 27): late in life, shortly before his death, Jung went further than mainstream science allows, concluding these psychological complexes were autonomous in the sense of being independent of the human brain altogether — going one step beyond Jaynes by treating the go as hallucinations (individual or collective) but as higher intelligences, effectively embracing the ancient mind-before-matter philosophy.
  • Explicit warning to readers: be on guard against a "momentary lapse of concentration" in which this version of history starts to feel true in some vague poetic or spiritual sense — such a lapse, taken lightly, leads "straight to the lunatic asylum."

Gilgamesh: The Epic of Death-Dread

Gilgamesh, king of Uruk around 2100 BC, is Sumerian civilizatios great hero; his story (reconstructed from nineteenth-century clay tablet excavations, and nearly complete) is full of madness, extreme emotion, anxiety and alienation — poet Rainer Maria Rilke called it "the epic of death-dread."

  • Gilgamesh, called the "butting bull," is depicted as superhumanly strong, beautiful, courageou a great lover — but lonely, longing for an equal.
  • The gods created Enkidu, equally strong but wild, covered in matted hair, living among and eating with beasts. A hunter reports the encounter to Gilgamesh.
  • Gilgame's plan: he sends the most beautiful temple prostitute into the woods to tame Enkidu through lovemaking. Once tamed, wild animals no longer accept Enkidu as one of their own and flee him.
  • Gilgamesh and Enkidu wrestle as champions in the Uruk marketplace before the whole population; Gilgamesh wins by pinning Enkidu while keeping his own foot on the ground, and a great friendship begins.
  • Their adventures include hunting panthers, tracking the monster Hawawa guarding the cedar forest, and slaying the bull of heaven (whose horns Gilgamesh mounts on his bedchamber wall).
  • Enkidu falls fatally ill; Gilgamesh sits by his bed six days and seven nights until a worm falls from Enkidu's nose (marking death). Gilgamesh draws a veil over his friend's face, roars like a grieving lioness, then roams the steppe weeping as fear of his own death gnaws at him.
  • Seeking to escape his dread, Gilgamesh reaches "the tavern at the end of the world" and asks a barmaid the way to Ziusudra — another name for Noah/Dionysus, a demi-god who never truly died.
  • Ggamesh builds a boat with bitumen-topped punting poles (a method still used by marsh Arabs today) to reach Ziusudra, who reveals a secret: a rose-like plant at the bottom of the sea that grants renewed youth if retrieved — esoterically, this represents the lost wisdom submerged with Atlantis at the time of the Flood.
  • Practical detail: Gilgamesh ties stones to his feet like local pearl-divers, descends, plucks the plant, cuts himself free, and surfaces triumphant — but while resting on s, a snake smells the plant and steals it. Gilgamesh is left "as good as dead," having failed the test set by humanity's great leader.

The Tower of Babel and Nimrod

Following Gilgamesh's death comes the era of the greatest ziggurats. The Tower of Babel story — the attempt to build a tower to heaven, resulting in the loss of single unifying human language — represents nations and tribes becoming attached to their own tutelary spirits and guiding angels, thereby losing sight of the higher gods and the great cosmic mind that gives all parts of the universe one shared destiny. Ziggurats represent a misguided attempt to scale the heavens by purely material means.

  • The Tower was built Nimrod the Hunter, called in Genesis "the first potentate on earth." Archaeologist David Rohl identifies Nimrod with the historical Enmer-kar ("Enmer the Hunter"), first king of Uruk, who wrote to a neighboring king demanding tribute — believed to be history's earliest surviving letter.
  • Nimrod was the first man to seek power for its own sake, and from this will-to-power came cruelty and decadence. Hebrew tradition holds that a prophecy of Abraham's imminent birth prompted Nimrod to commit mass infanticide, burying the sacrificed infants' bodies in the foundations of his great buildings.

Abraham's Quest and Egyptian Initiation

Around 2000 BC, Abraham wandered among the skyscrapers of his native Ur (Uruk) and decided to become a desert nomad on a quest to rediscover a fading sense of the divine.

  • In Egypt, the pharaoh gave his daughter Hagar as a servant to Abraham's wife Sarai; Hagar bo Abraham's first son Ishmael, ancestor of the Arab nations. This episode signifies that Abraham received great initiatic knowledge from Egyptian priests.
  • Non-obvious cultural detail: marriages of this era were usually within a tribe or extended family because supernatural powers were believed connected to blood — marriage within the bloodline strengthened these powers (a practice paralleled later in gypsy tradition), while marriage across tribes enabled an exchange of powers and knowledge

The Egyptian Initiation Ceremony

A detailed account of the initiation Abraham likely underwent in Egypt:

  • The candidate lies in a granite tomb, surrounded by initiates who induce a deep, sleep-like trance, during which they raise the candidate's vegetable body (and with it the spirit/animal body) up out of the physical body so it hovers like a phantom over the tomb's mouth.
  • A witness account of a similar ceremony performed on Irish poet W.B. Yeats describes bells rung to mark ceremonial stages, during which Yeats's spirit was seen shining with varying brightness and colour patterns at each stage.
  • Initiates mould the candidate's vegetable body so that once it sinks back into the physical body, the candidate can consciously use its organs of perception. After three days the candidate is "born again" — the hierophant grasps his right hand and pulls him from the coffin.
  • Esoteric significance: the vegetable body controls vital bodily functions and houses the chakras, forming the portal between the physical and spirit worlds. Enlivened chakras can produce supernatural perception, communication with disembodied spirits, and healing powers.
  • Practical/healing application — "temple sleep": still practised by Mystery school initiates two and a half thousand years later, and in some secret societies today. The sick would sleep in the temple for three days while initiates worked on their vegetative bodies similarly to the initiation process.
  • Vision sequence experienced during healing: utter blackness and apparent loss of consciousness/death; a sense of reviving and beied by an animal-headed being through long passages and chambers; being challenged by animal-headed gods and demons, including monstrous crocodiles.
  • Magical formula: in the Egyptian Book of the Dead, the candidate passes threshold guardians by proclaiming "I am the Gnostic, I am the one who knows" — usable both during initiation and after death.
  • Approaching the inner sanctum, the candidate sees bright light through the gates and cries, "Let me come! Let me spiritualize myself, let me beme pure spirit! I have prepared myself by the writings of Thoth!"
  • Culminating vision: the Mother Goddess suckling her child emerges from swirling light — a healing image recalling the paradisaical time (Chapter 3) before earth and sun separated, when earth was illumined from within by the Sun god, free of dissatisfaction, disse or death; it also anticipates a future reunification of earth and sun. Across all ages and places, people have believed meditating on this Mother-and-child image brings healing miracles.

Abraham and Melchizedek

After Egypt, Abraham moved toward Palestine. He armed and trained servants to rescue his brother, captured by bandits, and after a fierce fight met a mysterious figure, Melchizedek, while walking through a valley identified by biblical scholars as the Kidron Valley.

  • As with Enoch, the Bible mentions Melchizedek only briefly but with a strong sense of unspoken significance (Genesis 14:18-20; Hebrews 6:20-7:17, describing him as "without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life," a priest "after the power of an endless life").
  • Melchizedek appears disproportionately often in art and literature relative to his brief biblical mention — for example prominently in France's esoteric ecclesiastical statuary, such as the North Porch of Chartres Cathedral, traditionally shown bearing the chalice or grail.
  • Cabalistic tradition identifies Melchizedek's secret identity as Noah — the great Atlantean leader who taught humankind agriculture, the cultivation of corn and the vine, and who never trulyd but moved to another dimension, later reappearing as Abraham's spiritual teacher to initiate him to a higher level.

The Sacrifice of Isaac as Initiation

Ancient tradition holds Melchizedek was present at a later episode hidden in the biblical account: Isaac, aged twenty-two, was taken by his father up a mountain to be sacrificed on Melchizedek's altar.

  • Key principle of certain initiation forms: at a critical point the candidate must believe, even briefly but with total conviction, that death is imminent. He may realize he has broken solemn oaths, recognize his own moral failures, and understand he lacks the willpower to keep his sworn commitments — effectively condemning himself out of his own mouth, feeling utterly unable to help himself, and only then realizing he needs supernatural help.
  • Comparisona faint echo of these emotions of fear and pity can be felt in great tragedies like Oedipus Rex or King Lear. The candidate is made to feel the tragedy of his own life, an overwhelming need for catharsis, beginning to judge his own life as demons and angels will judge it after death.

Symbolic Meaning of the Ram

As Abraham's knife began to cut Isaac's throat, an angel substituted a ram whose horns were caught in a nearby thicket.

  • The thorns in the thicket represent the two-petalled (two-horned) brow chakra, already entangled in matter. Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac represents this mode of spiritual vision needing to be sacrificed — perception of the spirit worlds had to be put to sleep, for a time, for the sake of Abraham's descendants' mission: developing the brain as an organ of rational thinking.
  • The Jews would be guided by Jehovah, the great spirit of the moon and god of "thou-shalt-not," who helps humanity evolve away from animal and ecstatic tribal-soul experience toward individual free will and free thinking.
  • This sacrifice of the brow chakra, occurring on Melchizedek's altar (high priest of the Sun Mysteries), signifies that Isaac was initiated deeply enough to understand the necessity of this next, lunar stage of human devopment — one that would eventually let humans consciously participate in transforming the world.
  • Isaac remained at Melchizedek's Mystery school for three and a half years learning these teachings.

Sun Temples and Stone Circles

Because Melchizedek is a priest of the Sun Mysteries, his school is pictured as containing a stone circle. This marks the great age of sun temples, examples surviving at Lüneberg (Germany), Carnac (France) and Stonehenge (England).

  • In the fourth century BC, torian Diodorus of Sicily described a spherical sun temple in the north dedicated to Apollo — modern scholars believe this referred to Stonehenge or, more likely, Callanish in northern Scotland. The Apollo association should be understood as anticipating the rebirth of the Sun god from the Mother Goddess's womb.

The Greek Ctribution and the Siege of Troy

The siege of Troy marks the rise of Greek civilization, when the Greeks seized cultural initiative from Chaldean-Egyptian civilization to forge their own ideals — continuing a chronological narrative weaving together cultural heroes worldwide (Adam, Jupiter, Hercules, Osiris, Noah, Zarathustra, Krishna, Gilgamesh), most surviving ly in collective imagination and scattered story fragments.

  • Homer's account of Troy is central; in secret-society usage, calling Homer "blind" may signify he was an initiate whose gaze was directed toward the spiritual rather than material world. Florence and Kenneth Wood have shown the Iliad can be read as an astronomical allegory — without this negating its status as a real historical event, since as an initiate Homer would have been conscious of the great stellar and planetary gods guiding events below.
  • Heinrich Schliemann's 1870s discovery of Troy's ruins remains controversial: the layer he excavated likely dates to 3000 BC (too old for Homer's account), but most scholars now agree a later layer, dated to 1200 BC in the late Bronze Age, is consistent with Homer's narrative.
  • Non-obvious point: ancient wars were fought over possession of sacred, initiatic knowledge, partly for the supeatural powers it conferred — the Greeks fought partly to capture the Palladium, a statue made by Athena's own hand, and the struggle over Helen should be understood the same way.
  • On beauty and altered consciousness: exceptional beauty can seem to hold "the promise of happiness" (Stendhal's phrase) in both a crude and a deeper, mystical sense — as if beauty holds the very secret of life. The presence of exceptional beauty can induce an altered state of consciousness, and male initiates hoften been paired with very beautiful women, partly because their participation intensified the schools' secret sexual techniques. Possession of Helen would enable the Greeks to advance to civilization's next stage.

The Shift Away from Death-Dread

Achilles' famous saying — "Better to be a slave in the land of the living th the king of the shades" — captures the changing consciousness the Troy story represents. Greek and Trojan heroes loved living in the sun, and it was terrible when death sent their spirits to the land of shades, the Weern gloom — an intensification of Gilgamesh's death-dread to an almost modern level.

  • Symbolic parallel: Odysseus blinding the one-eyed giant Polyphemus represents the new mode of thinking destroying the old "Third-Eyed" consciousness. The later story of David slaying Goliath with a pebble aimed at the middle of the forehead (roughly two hundred years afterward) shows that such stragglers from earlier dispensations remained a historical reality at that time.
  • Important distinction: Achilles was not doubting an afterlife's reality, but his conception of it didn't extend beyond the dreary half-life of the sub-lunar sphere — a vision of the higher heavenly spheres had been lost to him.

Odysseus, the Trojan Horse, and the First Lie

The real victor of Troy was not the brave, nearly-invincible demi-god Achilles, but Odysseus "of the nimble wits," who tricked the Trojans into accepting the wooden horse concealing soldiers.

  • To modern sensibility, the Trojan Horse story seems implausible — surely noould be that gullible.
  • Non-obvious historical-consciousness explanation: at the time of the Trojan war, people were only just beginning to emerge from the collective, bi-cameral mind described by Jaynes. Before the Trojan war, everyone shared the same world of thoughts, and others could directly perceive what one was thinking — making deception of this kind previously impossible. People interacted with a "terrible sincerity," sensing that everything they did was part of cosmic events.
  • Concluding point: the date of the sge of Troy is also, in this account, the date of the first trick in history — marking a decisive turning point in the evolution of human consciousness toward individuated, private thought.

Chapter 12: The Descent into Darkness: Moses and the Cabala • Akhenaten and Satan • Solomon, Sheba and Hiram • King Arthur

Reda Exodus: New Chronology

Egyptian civilization is presented as the most successful in recorded history, lasting over three thousand years, compared with roughly two thousand years for European-American Christian civilization. Egypt's exceptionally well-preserved records on temple walls, tablets, and papyri have been essential in placing neighboring civilizations in chronological context.

Traditionally the Exodus has been placed in the reign of Ramasees II, a great builder of Luxor, Abu Simbel, and the obelisk now standing in La Place de la Concorde in Paris — the pharaoh who inspired Shelley's Ozymandias as the archetype of the ruler who believes his works will last forever. However, archaeologists searching for traces of the Hebrews, the fall of Jericho, or the Temple of Solomon in the corresponding archaeological layers of Ramasees II's reign found nothing at all, leading many academics to conclude the biblical origin stories were "just myths" with no historical basis. A pointed question is raised about how much this conclusion was driven by an adolescent glee at overturning nursery certainties rather than by the evidence itself.

In the 1990s a group of younger archaeologists based in Austria and London, led by David Rohl, challenged the conventionalgyptian chronology. They realized that in the Third Intermediate Dynasty, two king lists previously assumed to run sequentially should actually be understood as running concurrently. This "New Chronology" shortens Egyptian chronology by roughly four hundred years and is gradually gaining acceptance even among older Egyptologists.

An important, unintended consequence of this revision (these scholars are said to have no religious motive) is that when archaeologists searched for biblical traces four hundred years earlier than previously assumed, they made striking discoveries:

  • Moses was not a contemporary of Ramasees II around 1250 BC; instead he was born around 1540 BC, with the Exodus occurring around 1447 BC.
  • Using astronomical retro-calculations based on Venus observations recorded in Mesopotamian texts that cross-reference both the Bible and Egyptian records, Rohl argues Moses was raised as an Egyptian prince during the reign of Neferhotep I in the mid-sixteenth century BC.
  • Corroborating evidence comes from Artapanus, a third-century BC Jewish historian who may have drawn on now-lost Egyptian temple records. Artapanus described a "Prince Mousos" who became a popular administrator under Khenephres, Neferhotep I's successor, before being exiled out of the pharaoh's jealousy.
  • Rohl identifies the pharaoh of the Exodus as Khenephres's successor, Dudimose. Excavations at the Dudimose level reveal remains of a foreign settlement of slaves or workers, corroborated by the Brooklyn Papyrus (a royal decree authorizing transfer of such a group at this time), along with death pits and evidence of hasty mass burials that may be traces of the biblical plagues.

A key methodological point: unearthing stone remains grounds historical claims in physical reality, but understanding what was humanly and spiritually significant — the highest and deepest of human experience — requires turning to esoteric tradition rather than archaeology alone.

Moses as Egyptian Initiate

As an Egyptian prince, Moses was initiated into the Egyptian Myster This is recorded by the Egyptian historian Manetho, who identified Heliopolis as the site of the Mystery school, and confirmed in Acts 7:22 ("Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians").

Moses's teachings are steeped in Egyptian wisdom rather than wholly original. Spell 125 in the Book of the Dead — predating the Ten Commandments — has the spirit declare a good life and deny specific immoral acts ("I have not robbed, I have not killed, I have not born false witness") before forty-two judges of the dead. is not a denigration of Moses; his teaching necessarily grew from its historical milieu. What made him historically significant was how he reframed ancient wisdom to advance humankind's evolution of consciousness.

The Burning Bush and Jethro's Initiation

When Moses fled into exile in the desert, he encountered Jethro, an African (Ethiopian) high priest and keeper of a library of stone tablets. Upon marrying Jethro's daughter, Moses was initiated to a higher level — this is the hidden meaning behind the burning bush story. The bush burninwithout being consumed represents a vision of the self that survives the purging fire awaiting beyond the grave. From this vision arose Moses's sense of mission: an impulse to lead humanity toward a land flowing with milk and honey.

The Rod, the Serpent, and Mastery of the Vegetable Cosmos

When Moses hesitated before the scale of his task, he was told, "And thou shalt take this rod in thy hand, wherewith thou shalt do signs." In the pharaoh's throne room, Aaron's rod became a snake and swallowed the pharaoh's court magicians' snakes. Moses then used his rod/wand to bring fire and hail, summon locusts, part the Red Sea, and strike water from rock.

A folk legend holds that this rod was carved from wood originating in the Tree of Eden — pointing to a deeper meaning: the rod is part of the vegetable dimension of the cosmos. By mastering and manipulating it as it ran through his own body, Moses became an adept able to master and manipulate the cosmos around him.

Later, when the Hebrews were punished with a plague of fiery serpents (Nuers 21:9), Moses nailed a bronze serpent to a raised pole to save them. John 3:14 connects this to the crucifixion ("as Moses lifted up the serpent... so must the Son of Man be lifted up"), with "lifted up" carrying a sense of transformation — the bronze serpent, having been smelted, foreshadows the eventual transfiguration of humanity's material body.

The rod used by Moses to smite the Egyptians and discipline his people is read as an image of the Lucifer-serpent of animal consciousnessstraightened and subdued through willpower and a moral discipline that is difficult to sustain.

Morality, Guilt, and the Ban on Images

The great gift Moses gave his people was guilt: morality enters history with him, along with a call to change of heart. The esoteric significance of the Ten Commandments lies particularly in the first two commandments' ban on religious imagery and other gods. Following Abraham, Moses sought a new kind of religion that moved away from older religions' elaborate, overwhelming ceremonies — loud cymbals, blinding smoke, speaking idols — which aimed to diminish consciousness and grant access to spirit worlds in an uncontrolled, riotous way (as with foers of Osiris). Moses instead sought a thoughtful, more conscious communion with the divine. By banning images, he helped create conditions that made abstract thought possible.

The Cabala's Hidden Mathematics

The Ten Commandments and the other laws of Exodus and Deuteronomy constitute Moses's public, exoteric teaching for all people. Esoteric tradition holds that he also secretly taught seventy elders the Cabala, the mystical teachings of Judaism.

Sacred idealism holds the human form as a microcosm of the universe, with divine proportions found in ammonites, nebulae, and the human body. Egyptologist R.A. Schwaller de Lubicz spent fifteen years tracing the divine-mathematical proportions of the Temple of Luxor, showing the temple's foundation ritual was called "Giving the House to its Master." Similarly in Hinduism, temple-building in human form was a magical process — if the overseer erred constructing a particular part of the temple, he would suffer illness or injury in the corresponding part of his own body (a striking practical/warning-type detail about symbolic-physical correspondence).

The Cabala is described as growing out of the older mystical number system of the Egyptians. The eye of Horus (udja eye) encodes hieroglyphic fractions totaling 63/64; reversing this and dividing 64 by 63 yields the "Comma of Pythagoras," called the greatest secret of the Egyptians. Irrational numbers like the Comma of Pythagoras, Pi, and Phi (the Golden Proportion) lie deep in the structure of the physical universe and were seen by Egyptians as principles by which matter is precipitated from cosmic mind — today recognized by science as universal constants describing patterns in astronomy, music, and physics, closely related to the Fibonacci sequence (seen in galaxy spirals, ammonite shells, and leaf arrangements).

Egyptians incorporated these numbers as rhythms and proportions in pyramids and temples — a hall, doorway, or winbuilt with the Golden Proportion would be ineffably pleasing to the human spirit. Egyptian temples burst with vegetable forms (e.g., the bulrush-shaped pillars of the hypostyle hall at Karnak), because it was specifically vegetable life's proportioning of limbs and ribs that temple-builders sought to reproduce. The deeper point: temples were built this way because gods could no longer inhabit bodies of flesh and blood — a temple was literally built to be the body of a god, with divine spirit inhabiting its vegetable and material structure just as the human spirit inhabits its own body.

The Zohar and the Magic of Hebrew Letters

Unlike the Egyptians, the Hebrews left no rich architectural heritage; their number mysticism survives instead encoded in the language of the books of Moses. The great Cabalistic text, The Zohar, is a vast commentary on the first five books of the Old Testament, traditionally ascribed to Moses. According to Cabala, if the world is materialized thought, words and letters are the ans by which this happens — Godreated the world by manipulating patterns of Hebrew letters, giving those letters magical properties and opening hidden layers of meaning in scripture.

Specific examples of encoded numerology:

  • Exodus 14:19–21 each contain 72 letters; stacking these verses in columns and reading column by column reveals the secret 72 Names of God.
  • Each Hebrew letter is also a number (Aleph=1, Beth=2, etc.). The Hebrew word for father = 3, for mother = 41, and for child = 44 (the combination of father anmother).
  • The Hebrew phrase for Garden of Eden = 144; Tree of Knowledge = 233. Dividing 233 by 144 approximates the golden ratio phi to four decimal places.

Modern researchers Witztum, Rips, and Rosenberg searched for transcription codes using equidistant letter sequences in the Torah, finding names of post-biblical historical figures, though no coherent sentences or messages as of the writing. A Cambridge-based statistician is mentioned as having shown results from an extremely complex "skip code" (validated by a Cambridge mathematics professor) producing fragments reminiscent of the Psalms — raising the speculative possibility that entire additional books could be encoded within the isting text, layered with further meanings, an achievement suggested to be beyond ordinary human intelligence.

An occult group's research is cited claiming J.S. Bach composed melodies (such as the famous Chaconne) while simultaneously encoding each note as a letter of the alphabet, spelling out secret Psalm-like messages — again framed as beyond normal human capacity.

This kind of multiply-layered, initiate-encoded language is called the Green Language or Language of the Birds in esoteric circles, said to have been used by Rabelais and Nostradamus (contemporaries at Montpellier University) and by Shakespeare; Wagner alludes to it through Siegfried learning the Language of the Birds by drinking dragon's blood. A speculative closing thought: perhaps everyone speaks the Green Language unconsciously all the time, and great initiates like Shakespeare simply do so consciously.

Akhenaten: A Warng About False Monotheism

Sigmund Freud, deeply interested in the Cabala (a formative influence on his thought), mistakenly argued that pharaoh Akhenaten was the source of Moses's monotheism — it is now understood Moses came first, and Akhenaten's monotheism was subtly but dangerously different.

Akhenaten was born to Amenhotep III and Queen Tiy during the height of the New Kingdom's peace and prosperity, after three daughters — his birth was long-awaited, and he was raised within temple incts with a sense of cosmic mission. He had a chromosomal defect producing a strange, hermaphroditic, almost unearthly appearance — womanly thighs and an elongated, ethereal face — a condition that can also produce mental instability: mania, delusions, paranoia. This combination may have contributed to actions that threatene disrupt the whole progress of human evolution.

Unlike Babylon, where kings acted independently of the priesthood (leading to despotic cruelty), Egyptian pharaohs ruled under the aegis of initiate priests — meaning the popular view of Akhenaten's revolution as radical individualism is mistaken. His reign began at the start of a Sothic cycle (1460 years long), during which Egyptian mythology held that the Bennu bird (Phoenix) would return to herald a new age.khenaten's closing of the great temple at Karnak and founding of a new capital between Karnak and Giza was thus framed as an initiate king enacting cosmic destiny, preparing for the Bennu bird's return in 1321 BC.

His actions, step by step:

  • Built a new temple to Aten (the sun disc god), with an obelisk topped by the Benben stone meant to receive the Phoenix.
  • With his mother Queen Tiy's support, built an entirely new capital city, moving the machinery of government there by barge — an act framed as an attempt to "shift the earth on its axis."
  • Declared all other gods nonexistent and Aten the one true god — monotheism in something very close to the modern sense — banning worship of Isis, Osiris, and Amon-Re, and shutting down and effacing their temples and festivals.

A pointed observation: ten's monotheism, like modern monotheism, is characterized as materialistic — by definition, doing away with other gods tends also to do away with belief in other spirits and disembodied intelligences, denying the very experience that constitutes genuine spirituality. Akhenaten declared the physical sun itself divine. His art abandoned traditional hieratic formalism for a naturalism modern viewers find appealing, and his hymns to Aten strikingly anticipate the Psalms of David (parallel quotions are given: Akhenaten's "How manifold is that which you have made... You created the world according to your desire" versus David's "How countless are your works... you made all of them so wisely").

But behind the poetry lay monomaniacal madness: by banning all other gods and declaring himself the sole channel of Aten's wisdom, Akhenaten effectively made the entire priesthood redundant, replacing them with himself alone. Despite this self-elevation, he withdrew deeper into his palace with wife Nefertiti and their children, composing hymns and refusing to hear bad news about unrest or colonial rebellions threatening Egypt's regional supremacy.

Collapse came from within: fifteen years into his reign his favorite daughter died despite his prayers to Aten; his mother Tiy died soon after; Nefertiti disappears from court records; two years later the priests had Akhenaten killed and installed the boy who would become Tutankhamun. The priests immediately restored Thebes, and Akhenaten's capital became a ghost town, with every monument, depiction, and mention of his name ruthlessly and systematically effaced.

A crucial warning is drawn here: some modern commentators view Akhenaten as prophetic or saintly, but Manetho records that Egyptians remembered his reign as a "Sethian event" — Seth being identical with Satan, the great spirit of materialism that always works to destroy true spirituality. Had Akhenaten, as an envoy of this force, successfully converted humankind to materialism, three thousand years of gentle, gradual spiritual growth and the qualities that evolved with it wld have been lost forever.

Solomon's Temple Redated and Reconsidered

No temple looms larger in collective imagination than Solomon's Temple. Historical corroboration: Saul has been identified in the diplomatic letters of kings subject to Akhenaten, appearing as "Labya," king of the "Habiru." Following these identifications, David ("Tadua") is now understood to have united the tribes of Israel as king of Jerusalem in 1004 BC (during Tutankhamun's reign), laying the temple's foundations before dying, leaving the building to his son, anointed king of Jerusalem in 971 BC.

Before David Rohl's New Chronology, Solomon (if historical at all) was believed to have lived in the Iron Age — a problem because no archaeological evidence from that period matched his legendary wealth and building projects. Relocating him to thlate Bronze Age solves this: Phoenician-style architecture consistent with a builder like Hiram has been excavated in the corresponding strata.

Solomon is remembered in popular imagination as the embodiment of kingly magnificence and wisdom, and in secret tradition as a magical controller of demons. In Freemasonic tradition (per Chevalier Michael Ramsay's 1736 oration), Solomon recorded his magical knowledge in a secret book later laid in the foundations of the second Temple.

Jewish folklore holds Solomon's reign made gold and silver as common as stones in the street. Because the Jews, a formerly nomadic people, had no temple-building tradition, Solomon employed Phoenician architect Hiram Abiff. Though the temple's biblical measurements suggest something no larger than a parish church, it was crammed with unparalleled ornamentation:

  • The Holy of Holies at its center, lined with gold plate and encrusted with jewels, held the Ark of the Covenant containing the tablets of Moses; the protective Cherubim wings represent zodiac constellations.
  • Four horns on the altar's corners represented the moon; a seven-lamped golden candlestick represented the sun, moon, and five visible planets.
  • The Pillars of Jakim and Boaz "measured the pulse of the cosmos," positioned to mark the sun's furthest equinoctial rising points, and according to Josephus and Clement of Alexandria were topped with "orreries" — mechanical models of planetary motion.
  • Decorative pomegranates appear repeatedly in biblical descriptions; priestly robes were decorated with gems representing sun, moon, planets, and constellations, with emeralds specifically named.
  • The temple's most extraordinary feature was a "sea" of molten brass (or, per the Koran, a fountain) — as with M's bronze serpent, this smelting imagery signals hidden practices concerned with transforming human physiology.

Hiram organized his craftsmen into three grades — Apprentices, Companions, and Masters — an early form of fraternal organization that would eventually reshape society at large; the story of his murder serves as a ing about how such structures can go wrong.

The Queen of Sheba, Hiram's Murder, and the Venus Code

An undercurrent of rivalry runs between Solomon and Hiram Abiff in secret tradition. The Queen of Sheba visited Solomon but was equally curious about the temple's designer. When she felt Hiram's gaze, she experienced a sensation "like molten metal inside." Asked how he brought heaven's beauty to earth in the temple's architecture, Hiram held aloft a Tau cross (T-shaped), causing workers to swarm into the temple "like ants." This insect imagery recurs in Talmudic and Koranic traditions describing a mysterious stone-carving insect called the Shameer that aided the temple's construction — paralleling the beehive image as a symbol of commandable spiritual forces.

Three workers, jealous of Hiram's secret powers and wanting to learn the secret of the molten sea, ambushed him after work, and when he repeatedly refused to divulge his secrets, murdered him with fatal blows to the head. Certain secrets are said to have died with him and remain lost forever — the secrets since divulged in Mystery schools and secret societies are considered lesser ones.

The sexual undertone in Sheba's burning sensation and the Tau cross points toward deeper meaning tied to temple's astronomical orientation. Masonic researchers Christopher Knight and Robert Lomas worked out this orientation, beginning with the clue that Hiram came from Phoenicia, whose principal deity was Astarte (Venus) — consistent with the temple's pomegranates (fruit of Venus) and emeralds (stone of Venus).

According to Clement of Alexandria, the curtain sectioning off the Holy of Holies had a five-pointed star cut into it — the enduring symbol of Venus, since Venus traces a five-pointettern around the ecliptic over its eight-year cycle (five morning and five evening appearances), the only planet to draw such a regular figure. This shape recurs as pentagram, five-pointed star, or (in Rosicrucian tradition) five-petalled rose.

The pentagram is also geometrically significant: Leonardo's mathematics teacher Luca Pacioli showed in his treatise on divine proportion that it embodies the Golden Proportion in every part. This sacred geometry extends into time as well as space: five Venus cycles of 584 days occur across exactly eight solar years, meaning a Venus cycle equals 1.6 solar cycles — the same 1.6 ratio at the root of the Golden Proportion, one of the irrational numberdescribing mind's precipitation into matter; in ancient esoteric doctrine, planets and stars govern this process of matter's precipitation.

Venus associations multiply further: one etymology traces "Jerusalem" to "Urshalem" — "ur" (founded by) plus "Shalem," an ancient name for Astarte/Venus in her evening setting. Masonic lodges are modeled on the Jerusalem Temple, with the five-pointed star of Venus displayed above the Grand Master's chair, initiates greeting each other with a fraternal five-pointed embrace, and dormer windows aligned so Venus's light shines through on significant days — a Master Mason is symbolically "raised into rebirth" facing Venus's light at an equinox.

Though Venus is identified with Lucifer, a caution against seeing this negatively: in esoteric history Lucifer is always framed as a necessary evil. The human capacity for thought was forged from a balance between Venud the moon (the moon also featuring prominently in the temple altar's design). Solomon's mission was to lead humankind down into an increasingly material world while keeping the flame of spirituality alive — the same mission Freemasonry would later take up in the seventeenth century at the dawn of the modern age of materialism.

King Arthur and the Crown Chakra

Solomonic legend finds a distant echo in the British Isles. Mainstream modern scholarship, if it accepts any historical basis to thur, places it in the "Dark Ages" following Roman withdrawal from Britain, with a Christian warlord fighting ultimately futile battles against pagan invaders — one candidate being Owain Ddantgwynne, a Welsh warlord who defeated the pagan Saxons at the Battle of Badon in 470, with "Arthur" understood as a title meaning "the bear

An alternative, esoteric account places the original King Arthur at Tintagel around 1100 BC, slightly earlier than Solomon — a period when the peaceful, rural Bronze Age communities of Britain were overrun by the moreilitaristic hill-fort people of the Iron Age. His spiritual mentor Merlin, the wizard of Cellydon Wood, was a survivor from the age of the stone circles who helped Arthur keep the Sun Mysteries alive.

King Arthur is presented as a Sun king surrounded by twelve knights representing the zodiac, married to Venus — Guinevere being understood as the Celtic form of Venere/Venus. His crown is described symbolically as a crown chakra "ablaze," leading his people down through darkness just as Solomon led his own people.

A supporting historical detail: Herodotus recorded that in Iran, the king was believed to emit such intense, unbearable light that he had to remain behind a curtain during audiences with subjects — a crown symbolized that a certain grade of initiation had been achieved, marking the initiate as crowned with buddhic fire.

Chapter 13: Reason - and How to Rise Above it: Elijah and Elisha • Isaiah • Esoteric Buddhism • Pythagoras • Lao Tzu

The Rise of the Prophets

After Solomon, the kingdom of Israel began to disintegand a new institution grew up: the prophets. Unlike the harmonious mentor relationships of Melchizedek and Abraham, or Merlin and Arthur, the relationship between prophets and kings was adversarial and even subversive. Prophets said uncomfortable, unpopular things, ranted and raved, and were sometimes thought mad.

Elijah: Wild Man and Initiate of Fire

Elijah was a wild, solitary figure — almost a tramp — wearing a leather belt and long cloak. Like Zarathustra, he fought fire with fiCommanded by God to hide in the wilderness and drink from a brook, he was fed by ravens; the detail of the raven is significant because "Raven" was one of the grades of initiation in the mysteries of Zarathustra, indicating Elijah was being initiated into that tradition.

When King Ahab married Jezebel and erected altars to Baal (the Canaanite name for Saturn/Satan), Elijah battled and defeated the prophets of Baal by calling down fire from heaven. He later used the same power to kill squads of soldiers sent by Jezebel to capture him. He lived closest to the border of madness among the prophets, and stories credit him with astonishing feats: clairvoyance, turning a poisoned well wholesome, making iron float, healing a leper, and bringing a dead boy back to life by lying on top of him and infusing him with his own spirit.

The Still Small Voice

Fleeing for his life into the wilderness, Elijah found himself on a mountain in a raging storm, raving like a combination of Lear and the Fool. He collapsed under a juniper tree and dreamed of an angel, then set off before dawn to climb Mount Horeb. A great wind shook the mountain and sent boulders bouncing toward him, but he recognized God was not in the wind and took refuge in a cave. Lightning then struck just outside, trapping him in a blaze — but God was not in the fire either. Only when the storm and fire subsided, as the morning star rose in the calm dawn air, did Elijah hear the still small voice of God.

This marks a historic shift: whereas Moses experienced an overwhelming divine presence in the burning bush, Elijah's relation is quieter, almost subliminal. From this point on, people would need to practice mental discipline and directed attention to discern the divine, rather than simply being overwhelmed by it.

Death and Ascension: A Doctrine of the Afterlife

Understanding Elijah's mission requires understanding his death. A parallel is drawn to Indian adepts capable of dematerializing and rematerializing at will — Paramahansa Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi (1946) describes his master Sri Yuktwar materializing in a sunlit window to demonstrate this was possible in flesh and blood, by divine command, as a rare gift to his pupil.

Elijah took this gift further, learning to excarnate and incarnate at will. Contrary to the saying "you can't take it with you," the secret doctrine holds that you can. G.I. Gurdjieff, the great twentieth-century initiate, taught that mastering oneself in this life is exactly what's needed to survive as a conscious being after death — initiation concerns the afterlife as much as earthly life. Plato, in BooVII of The Republic, warned that those unable to apprehend the idea of the good in this life will descend to Hades and fall asleep in its dark abode.

At the end of his life Elijah was carried into the heavens in a fiery chariot, not dying in the ordinary way — joining the ranks of Enoch and Noah, and becoming part of the invisible college of ascended masters who return to earth at times of great change and crisis. In cabalistic thought this chariot is called the Merkabah. Great initiates can work on the vegetable body so it does not dissolve after death, preserving aspects of earthly consciousness into the ascended state through secret techniques for crystallizing fine energies so they are not dispersed. Christian thinkers would later call this same vehicle the Resurrection body.

As Elijah ascended, his mantle fell to Elisha, his chosen successor, mysteriously conferring upon Elisha an increased portion of Elijah's power (a mechanism revisited later in connection with Shakespeare). The succession was not without ambiguity — Elijah tried to send Elisha away, asking "What have I done to you?", as if sensing something uncertain in him. Later, when a gang of boys mocked the bald Elisha, he summoned two bears from the woods to kill them, suggesting the prophetic tradition remained locked in a deadly battle with the forces of Baal.

Isaiah and the Doctrine of Grace

Two hundred years later, a new, more transcendent understanding had developed, and prophecy grew less warlike. In 550 BC Isaiah proclaimed the coming of a child — "Wonderful, Counsellor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace." This is the emergence of the concept of Grace: though kings and peoples failed and their lands were laid waste, a living root emerged from the wasteland purely through divine Grace. Prophets saw this pattern operating both in the immedte rise and fall of their small kingdoms and in the greater cosmic cycles of history they foresaw.

This stood in direct opposition to the followers of Baal, who believed correct sacrifices and magical ceremonies could compel gods to do their bidding. Isaiah repudiated this transactional view entirely: Yahweh's grace could never be demanded, bought, or earned — it was freely given love, shown through choosing, empowering, purging, and forgiving a disobedient people, and promising restoration despite their undeservi. This new understanding of divine love, once grasped, would eventually open a new dimension in human love between individuals.

Isaiah also foresaw Israel's future ("a rod out of the stem of Jesse") and a vision of history's end ("the wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid").

The prophetic tradition died out by roughly 450 BC. Cabalist Rabbi Hayyim Vital wrote at the end of the sixteenth century that after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, prophets could only see into the lowest, most heavily shrouded levels of the heavens. The Old Testament closes with Malachi's prophecy of Elijah's return — still commemorated every Passover with a place set for him at the table, a cup of wine poured, and t door left open.

Esoteric Buddhism: Prince Siddhartha's Awakening

At the same historical moment, a parallel spirit of enlightenment moved through other cultures. Prince Siddhartha was born into a landscape of small warring states in Lumbini, in what is now Nepal, and lived a pampered, sheltered life until age twenty-nine, when he first encountered an old man outside the palace and, further investigating, discovered sickness and death among his people.

He left the palace, his wife, and his child to seek understanding of suffering, living among ascetics for seven years without success in the yoga sutras of Patanjali or the teachings descended from the Rishis. At thirty-five, he sat beneath a Bodhi tree on the banks of the River Neranjara, resolving not to move until he understood. After three days and nights he realized life is suffering, suffering stems from desire for earthly things, and freedom from all desire — and thus from the need to reincarnate — was achievable, making him a Buddha.

The Eightfold Path as Physiolal Practice

The Buddha's path to enlightenment, the Eightfold Path (right belief, conviction, teaching, action, living, intention, thinking, contemplation), can look like abstract moralizing to modern Western sensibility — but esoteric teachi reveals a deeply practical layer beneath it: these eight practices are specific exercises for enlivening eight of the sixteen petals of the throat chakra, using practical techniques to manipulate human physiology for psychological transformation.

This represented a historic shift in initiatic method. Earlier, in rites practiced in the Great Pyramid, a candidate was placed in a death-like trance while five initiates worked externally on his vegetable body, moulding it to perceive higher worlds — the candidate remained unconscious throughout. Buddhist initiation, by contrast, was consciously undertaken: followers worked deliberately on their own chakras, integrating this practice with a more moral way of life grounded in compassion for all living things.

Warning: The Danger of Unearned or Misus Power

As people grew more independent of the spirit worlds, a danger emerged that an individual's powers might outstrip the wisdom or moral will to use them properly — including the risk that evil-minded people could gain the same supernatural powers conferred by initiation. These powers can also arise without any initiation at all: extreme childhood trauma can tear a rent in the psyche through which spirits rush in uncontrolled (some modern mediums report such trauma), or powers can be auired through black magic or practices not attuned to the highest spiritual aims — unlike genuine, venerable secret schools that preserve an authentic tradition. The core danger is that a non-initiate, even a well-intentioned one, may struggle to correctly recognize the nature of the spirits they are communicating with.

Corspondences and the Nature of Loving Attention

In esoteric Buddhism, the Buddha is identified as the spirit of Mercury — notably, the Celts called the planet Mercury "Budh," meaning "wise teaching," and a carving foundn a bucket in Oseberg, Norway proves the lotus position of the Buddha was known to the Celts.

The aim of the Eightfold Path is initiation achieved through controlled, protected moral development — to control the world, one must first control oneself. The throat chakra functions as the organ that formulatespiritual wisdom, connecting the heart chakra to the brow chakra: in an initiate's physiology, currents of love stream upward from the heart through the throat to illuminate the brow chakra, which opens like a flower in sunlight.

A practical, everyday echo of this process is available to everyone: looking at someone with the eyes of love reveals good qualities in them invisible to others, and the mere act of loving attention can help those qualities blossom in the person being observed. People of highly refined spiritual nature tend to be happy, smiling, almost childlike, because they view all of humanity through this same eye of love.

The Buddha achieved his aim at death and was not required to reincarnate — but he remains a presencin this history, resurfacing later in connection with the Italian Renaissance.

Emperor Asoka and the Nine Unknown

The Buddhist Emperor Asoka, grandson of the first man to unify India, ruled from 273 BC. After losing more than a hundred thousand men in battle, he renounced war and thereafter ruled by the example of Buddhist spirituality, erecting some 84,000 stupas (a handful survive). Conventional history remembers him for irrigation, roads, hospitals, botanical gardens, vegetarianism, and banning animal killing. Esoteric history additionally credits him with founding the Nine Unknown, a powerful secret society that many in the twentieth century — including leading Indian scientist D.N. Bose — believed still operated.

Pythagoras: Synthesizer of the Perennial Philosophy

Pythagoras was born on the Greek id of Samos around 575 BC, as the first blocks of marble were being laid on the Athenian Acropolis. No individual has had greater influence on the evolution of Western esoteric thought. Like Jesus, nothing he personally wrote survives — only sayings and accounts recorded by disciples. He was regarded as a demi-god in his lifetime, credited with being in two places simultaneously, stroking a wild white eagle that permitted the contact, and being greeted by name by a river god's voice from the water. He reportedly told fishermen having an unproductive day to cast their nets once more, and their catch nearly burst the nets. He healed the sick, reciting verses from Homer he believed held great power (paralleling later Christian mystics reciting Psalms and John's Gospel), and used music therapeutically. Empedocles said he could heal the sick and rejuvenate the old; like the Buddha, he could recall his own past incarnations, and was said to be able to recall the entire history of the world from its beginning.

Training and Initiations

His wisdom came from decades of study across multiple Mystery schools: twenty-two years learning the secrets of Egyptian initiate priests, further study with the Magi in Babylon, and with theescendants of the Rishis in India, where memory was preserved of a great wonder-worker they called Yaivancharya.
