His mission — as articulated by Leibniz, who would later call this synthesis the Perennial Philosophy — was to gather esoteric knowledge from across the world into one comprehensive cosmo-conception. Historically, this occurred at a turning point when the great ideas emanating from the cosmic mind were becoming increasingly hidden by the very matter they had shaped; Pythagoras's task was to record these ideas ascepts before they vanished entirely, beginning the translation of ancient humanity's picture-consciousness into abstract, conceptual terms.

The Crotona Community

Around 532 BC, exiled from Samos by the despotic ruler Polycrates, Pythagoras founded a community at Crotona in southern Italy (the first of several). Initiation candidates underwent years of training, including an unusual diet (poppy, sesame and cucumber seeds, wild honey, daffodil flowers, and the skin of sea onion with the juice fully extracted), extensive gymnastics intended to harmonize the three human bodies (material, vegetable, animal), and years of enforced silence. Pythagoras granted pupils visions of the spirit worlds and then interpreted them — and from this discursive teaching emerged mathematics, geometry, astronomy, and music.

The Music of the Spheres and the scovery of the Octave

Pythagoras alone was said to hear the Music of the Spheres — a scale of notes produced by the seven planets moving through space. While easy to dismiss, the specific story of his discovery of the musical scale carries an authentic ring: walking through town, he noticed differently sized blacksmith's hammers striking anvils produced different pitches. At home, he hung weights corresponding to the hammer weights from a plank in ascending scale and, through trial and error, found that pleasing musical notes corresponded to weights in mathematically precise proportion. These calculations are the direct origin of the musical octave still used today.

The Rational and the Irrational

As Pythagoras and his followersrticulated the rational element of life, they simultaneously formulated its counterpart — a concept perhaps never before made explicit because it had simply been part of everyone's lived experience: life can be explained rationally only up to a point, and a vast irrational element remains beyond that. The rational teachings of the Mystery schools helped build cities, develop science and technology, and structure the outer world; the irrational teaching, in explicit form, was confined withithe schools themselves — to discuss it openly outside was dangerous and could provoke hostility. Plutarch captured this: "One who knows the higher truths, finds the 'serious' values of society difficult to take seriously. Eternity is a child at play."

It is no accident that figures like Pythagoras, Newton, and Leibniz — who the most to advance humanity's grasp of the physical universe — were also deeply immersed in esoteric thought, because viewing life as subjectively as possible (rather than objectively, as science requires) reveals ve different patterns: life viewed objectively is rational and law-bound, but experienced subjectively it is irrational. By consciously splitting experience this way, Pythagoras enabled clearer thinking about both dimensions.

Pythagoras's pupils lived apart from society, alternating between mystical ecstasy and intellectual analysis. He was the first to call himself "a philosopher" (lover of wisdom), yet — like Socrates and Plato after him — he functioned more as a magus than a modern academic; pupils believed he could make them dream what he willed and could instantly reorient their waking consciousness.

Warning: Murder by the Excluded

Pythagoras attracted murderous rage from those denied entry to his inner circle. He refused to admit a reckless, imperious man named Cyron into his Mystery school. Cyron incited a mob that broke into the building where Pythagoras and his followers were meeting and set it ablaze, killing everyone inside.

Heraclitus and Lao-Tzu: Rational Attempts to Define the Irrnal

In the era of Pythagoras, Heraclitus in Greece and Lao-Tzu in China each briefly surfaced in history, both attempting to rationally define life's irrational dimension. Heraclitus is remembered for observing that we cannot step in the same stream twice.

A likely apocryphal story holds that Confucius sought initiation from Lao-Tzu, who turned him away, mocking his mixture of ingratiating manners and vaulting ambition. Whether true or not, the story illustrates that Confucianism and Taoism represent, respectively, the exoteric and esoteric strands of Chinese thought. Confucius spent years collecting traditional Chinese wisdom, later adopted as manuals of government by Chinese leaders; his sayings are eminently reasonable — a thousand-mile journey begins with a single step, value the task over the prize, adjust your goals if you cannot meet them

Practical Application: Knowing When to Hold On and When to Let Go

Confucius is compared to Rudyard Kipling — both servants of empire whose ethic, exemplified in Kipling's poem "If" (quoted at length, including "Iyou can force your heart and nerve and sinew / To serve your turn long after they are gone... Yours is the earth and everything that is in it"), would be the last word on the conduct of life if scientific materialism explained everything. But this pure force-of-will ethic is incomplete: though there are times when persistence is right, there are other times — as Orpheus discovered to his cost — when it is wiser to give up and go with the flow. Grasping too tightly at what you want can push it further away; sometimes the only way to keep something is to let it go. Lao-Tzu's teaching captures the counterpoint directly: "Because the awakened one puts himself behind, he steps ahead. Because he gives way, he gains. Because he is selfless, he fulfils himself. The still is the lord of the restless."

Political Legacy

Thirty years after Pythagoras's death, Xerxes' Persian army swept over Greece, only to be defeated by the Athenians at Marathon and by the Athenian-Spartan alliance at Mycale. Pythagoras had institutionalized open discussion ptions and collective decision-making on matters concerning the whole community — what is now called politics. Out of this legacy, and within the space created by the Athenian-Spartan alliance, would emerge the unique character of the Greek city-state of Athens.

Chapter 14: The Mysteries of Greece and Rome: The Eleusinian Mysteries • Socrates and his Daemon • Plato as a Magus

Athens, Sparta, and the Flowering of Greek Culture

Athens fostered free, individual thought while Sparta ated individual will, competitive drive, and hero-worship of strong men. This heroic culture created the conditions for fifth-century BC Greece to set lasting standards in beauty and intellectual rigor. This was the era of great initiates — Plato, Aristotle, Pindar, Sophocles, and Euripides. Cicero, himself an initiate, credit the Eleusinian Mysteries as the greatest gift Athens gave to civilization.

The Eleusinian Mysteries

Eleusis derives from "elauno" — "I come," meaning "I come into being." Little survives of the sanctuary beyond scattered stones, but ancient descriptions mention an unmarked grey-blue stone exterior, painted statues and friezes of goddesses, sheaves of graineight-petalled flowers, and a ceiling aperture as the sole light source.

The Lesser Mysteries occurred in spring: rites of purification and dramatizations of divine myths. A myrtle-crowned, torch-bearing statue of a god was led in procession, sacrificed, and "died" for three days before being resurrected, at which point participants shouted "Iachos! Iachos! Iachos!" There was an overtly sexual dimension — Psellus recorded Venus rising from the sea between moving representations of female genitalia, followed by the marriage of Persephone and Hades. Clement of Alexandria recorded the enactment of Persephone's rape, and Athenagoras noted she was portrayed with a horn on her forehead, possibly symbolizing the Third Eye. Ceremonial milk-pouring from a golden breast-shaped vessel connected to Mother Goddess worship but also pointed to a deeper concern with life after death — the Milky Way was cived (per Pythagoras) as a river of spirits, with star-souls ascending through the gate of Capricorn and descending back through Cancer. Pindar: "Happy is he who has seen the Mysteries before being buried beneath the ground, because he knows what happens as life ends." Sophocles: "Thrice happy are those who have seen the Mysteries before they die. They will have life after death. Everyone else will only experience suffering." Plutarch held that the dying merely experience for the first time what initiates already had.

The Greater Mysteries, held near the autumn equinox, involved nine days of fasting followed by a potent drink called kykeon — roasted barley, water, and poley oil, narcotic in sufficient quantity, compounding the visionary effects of extreme hunger. Candidates underwent genuinely terrifying exriences — Plutarch describes terror "as if about to die," because in a sense they were. Proclus's accounts describe candidates assaulted by "rushing forms of troops of earthly demons." By this era it was difficult for gher gods to descend into dense matter, but far easier for lesser spirits — demons and the dead — to do so. Pausanius describes a demon named Euronomos with blue-black, fly-like skin who devoured rotting corpses.

Non-obvious point: Thenitiations were part ritual/drama, part séance. That drugs induced the visions of demons doesn't, from an idealist standpoint, make the visions illusory — comparable to still-current rural Indian ceremonies invoking Pretas, Bhuts, Pisachas, and Gandharvas, which Westerners would call séances. The schools aimed to give candidates a genuine spiritual experience — first of demons and the dead, later of the gods themselves.

Practical magical technique: Priests could summon a god's face to appear within smoke from a sacrificial fire by speaking magic words. Karl von Eckartshausen (18th-century theosophist) recorded the most effective fumigation ingredients for producing apparitions: hemlock, henbane, saffron, aloe, opium, mandrake, salorum, poppy seed, and asafoetida.

Living statues: Greeceously lifelike statues originated in the Mystery schools, continuing the Egyptian/Sumerian practice of statues as physical vessels gods could inhabit and animate. Standing before the statue of Artemis at Ephesus, worshippers felt Mother Earth loom over them like a great tree, sensing absorption into the cosmos's "vegetable matrix." Statues were reported to breathe, move, and sometimes speak.

Successful candidates ascended to the Empyrean, a realm of light, music, and dance, where Dionysus (Bacchus/Iacchos) appeared in radiant vision. The orator Aristedes recalled feeling the god draw near and touching him while "somewhere between waking and sleeping," his spirit unusually light — an out-of-body experience. Initiation thus provided direct, undeniable proof the spirit could exist outside the body; the newly "reborninitiate retained god-like perception and influence afterward.

Esoteric anatomy: The Caduceus (Wand of Hermes) — a pole with two entwined snakes — was echoed in the thyrsus, a hollow fennel-like stalk (recallingmetheus's fire-bearing stalk) representing the Sushumna Nadi of Indian occult physiology, topped with a pine cone symbolizing the pineal gland.

Teaching after initiation: Hierophants explained the initiate's experience using the "Book of Interpretation" (two stone tablets), teaching how the material world and human body were formed and directed by spirit worlds. Symbols included the seven-knotted thyrsus and the "toys of Dionysus" — golden serpent, phallus, egg, and a spinning top sounding "Om." Cicero noted that properly understood, the occult mysteries concern natural science more than religion.

Prophetic symbolism: The final Eleusinian initiation showed candidates a plucked green wheat ear held up in silence — agriculturally about harvest, but esoterically about the harvesting of souls. This wheat represents the star Spica, held by the virgin goddess of Virgo (identified with Isis), pointing toward a cosmic "seed time." This grain becomes the bread of the Last Supper, symbolizing Christ's vegetable body and the altered tative consciousness esoteric Christianity says one must attain to meet him. Spica's importance is confirmed by its being (along with Sirius) one of only two stars depicted on the Dendera planisphere — saved just outside the rim of the great cosmic grinding wheel. In Plato's philosophy, the soul is this vegetative mediator between material body and animal spirit, and must be the focus of spiritual Work.

Socrates and His Daemon

Socrates's surviving busts show a lively, satyr-like face;n secret tradition he was a reincarnation of the spirit that had earlier lived as Silenus. Aeschylus, son of a priest at Eleusis, was threatened with execution for revealing Mystery secrets through his plays; he escaped by claiming he'd never been initiated, but was later killed when an eagle dropped a rock on his bald head — terpreted by many as divine retribution.

Socrates spoke of his daemon — a guiding good spirit. A modern parallel: a pupil of P.D. Ouspensky (influential on T.S. Eliot, Frank Lloyd Wright, Kazimir Malevich, and Georgia O'Keefe) recalled walking away from a lecture full of doubt when an inner voice warned, "If you lose touch with this, you will be doing somethinghat you will regret for the rest of your life." Ouspensky's teaching identified this as the higher self, and a central aim of initiation is to alter consciousness enough to hear this voice continuously.

Socrates carried forward the project — begun with Pythagoras — of converting the lower animal self's instinctive wisdom into concepts; his philosophy, like Pythagoras's, was a philosophy of life, not mere academics. He held that the aim of all philosophy is to teach one how to die. There is dispute even within secret schools whether Socrates was formally initiated. Accused of corrupting Athenian youth and impiety, he drank hemlock and died forgiving his executioners — notable because the oath against suicide was among the most terrible sworn by initiates.

Evolution of conscience: Religion is often blamed for wars, the Inquisition, and suppression of science, yet many glories of human c — sculpture, drama, philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, political and medical ideas — originated in the Mystery schools, which also drove the evolution of consciousness. In Aeschylus's Oresteia (458 BC), wrongdoing brings persecution by external winged demons (Erinyes/Furies). By Euripides's Hippolytus (428 BC), this has been internalized as conscience: "There is only one thing that can survive all life's trials — a quiet conscience." Esoteric tradition holds that conscience did not as a human faculty before this point — it was forged as a new dimension of experience by the Eleusinian Mysteries, not merely named for the first time.

Great drama (tragedy dramatizing Satan's machinations, comedy dramatizing Lucifer's, per Aristophanes's The Frogs satirizing the Mysteries) opens the human condition wider th convention allows, echoing initiation's catharsis: our corrupted animal body forms a hardened carapace we grow reliant on, even though our comfort rests on unacknowledged blood, torture, theft, and injustice, breeding a hidden self-loathing that blocks full living and loving — only the agonizing initiatory process cuts this carapace open. Productions like Oedis Rex or King Lear can evoke an echo of this.

Deceptively simple sayings: Pythagoras's surviving sayings ("Above all things respect yourself"; "Do not yield to temptation except when you agree to be untrue to yourself") and Socrates's "An unconsidered life is not worth living" seem obvious now, but were revolutionary at a time when people lacked the abstract faculty of self-reflection — this was Socrates's great gift to the world.

Plato as a Magus

After Socrates's death, Plato became Greek philosophy's leading figure. Born 428 BC into one of the first generations systematically taught to read, he founded the Academy in the garden of Academus's tomb in Athens. His Dialogues represent the fullest expression of mind-before-matter idealism.

Key insight on idealism's history: Before Plato, everyone experienced the world idealistically without questioning it — instinctively believing s were a higher reality than objects. It only became necessary for a great initiate to conceptualize and systematize idealism once consciousness had evolved enough that people could conceive of the opposing (materialist) view. Plato's pupil Aristotle then made the leaps toward the materialism dominant today.

Warning against a common misreading of idealism: It's tempting to think that if the material world is a precipitate of mental processes, we should be able to manipulate it directly by thought alone, or that reality (as a giant hologram) could simply be "switched off." Bishop Berkeley's version of idealism (most familiar in Anglo-American philosophy departments) holds matter has no existence independent of perception — but this is not the historical mainstream view. Most historical idealists believed matt precipitated out of mind as a gradual process over vast time spans, and that any eventual "switching off" would likewise be gradual over similarly vast periods — not an instantaneous act of will.

Modern students find it hard to equate Platonic ideas with gods and angels, viewing this as crude anthropomorphism — yet historically, believers in idealism as a lphilosophy consistently believed in spirits, gods, and angels. Idealists like Cicero and Newton treated the cosmic "world-weaving" active principles (Newton's "Intelligencers") as neither crudely impersonal nor crudely personal, neither strictly polytheistic nor monotheistic — they experienced life as meaningful and the cosmos as intentional, with something like human consciousness built into its structure. Secret-society initiates, like Mystery-school initiates, encountered these disembodied Intelligencers in altered states of consciousness.

Goethe's testimony: Goethe articulated the modern idealist's felt experience of living, immeasurable interconnection with nature and other people, calling the great universal spirits "the Mothers" (Newton's "Intelligencers"). He described walking with an acquaintance while holding a mental image, only for the companion to spontaneously speak of that vy thing; a man who could silence a room merely by mental power; magnetic attraction especially strong between lovers, even at a distance — recalling instances where his desire for a woman's company drew her to him without prior communication. He described the Mothers as dwelling in eternal obscurity, the creative and sustaining principle behind all earthly life and form; whatever ceases to breathe returns to them as spiritual nature until conditions arise for renewed existence, with all sos and forms — past and future — hovering like clouds in their domain; a magician must enter their dominion to gain power over a being's form.

Alexander the Great's Divine Identity

Athens and Sparta's rivalry gave way to Macedonian dominance under Philip II. Plutarch noted Alexander was born (356 BC) the same day the Temof Ephesus burned. Each Mystery school taught unique wisdom (explaining why Moses and Pythagoras sought initiation into more than one); Ephesus's hierophants taught the mysteries of Mother Earth's shaping powers, and in a sense this school's spirit entered Alexander at birth — his life became a quest to understand this divine element within him. As a boy he alone tamed the fierce horse Bucephalus. Philip secured Aristotle (Plato's greatest pupil) as tuto Alexander and Aristotle recognized each other as kindred spirits.

Just as Plato's formal articulation of idealism made its materialist opposite (Aristotle's classification of physical data via abstraction) inevitable, Alexander's empire — the largest yet seen — became the historical vehicle for spreading Aristotle's philosophy, just as Rome later spread Christianity.

After Philip's assassination (Alexander age 20), Alexander proved a military genius: defeating the Persians at Issus (334 BC, against roughly 10-to-1 odds), sweeping through Syria and Phoenicia, conquering Egypt and founding Alexandria, spreading Greek city-states and philosophy everywhere. His mission (per secret history) was to preserve the newly evolved rational consciousness (forged by Plato and Euripides) from being swamped sia's wealth and by ancient ritualistic clairvoyance/picture-consciousness. He destroyed Persepolis in 331 BC, pushed into Afghanistan and India, and debated Brahmin philosophers (descendants of the Rishis) — his priests were startled at how closely Brahmin initiatory rites resembled their own.

Notable anecdote: Alexander sent a philosopher to summon a Brahmin teacher under threat of decapitation; the Brahmin, found deep in the forest, refused: "The Brahmins neither fear death nor dese gold. We sleep deeply and peacefully on forest leaves... We move freely over the surface of the earth without conflict and all our needs met as by a mother who feeds her baby her milk." This was a rare rebuff for a man who otherwise seemed able to bend the world to his will.

Alexander saw both Perseus and Hercules claimed as ancestors in variant traditions, and memorized Aristotle's gift of Homer's Iliad, sometimes identifying with Achilles. In 332 BC he journeyed to the Temple of Amun at Siwa oasis (500 miles west of Memphis), reportedly nearly dying (possibly a "mystical death"), and was recognized and initiated by the priests there — possibly told he was Amun-Zeus's son, which maexplain his subsequent habit of wearing ceremonial horns; he was remembered as a horned figure in various conquered lands, and appears in the Koran as Dhul-Qarnayn ("the two-horned one"). In secret history, these horns connect to an earlier hunter figure, and Gilgamesh and Enkidu — separated by Enkidu's untimely death — reincarnated as Alexander and Aristotle.

At 33, ignoring Babylonian astrologers' warnings not to enter the city, Alexander died of fever two weeks later; his empire, held together only by his personal magnetism, quickly fragmented.

The Rise of the Magi and Rome's Age of Inauthentic Faith

Buddhism emerged around 200 BC as the first proselytizing, missionary religion — previously religious belief was determined by race or tribe. As the human condition changed, spirit worlds became a fading, uncertain vision for the uninitiated, while deductive and inductive reasoning (in by Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle) developed, enabling people to weigh arguments.

By 140 BC, Rome as world capital offered citizens a marketplace of belief systems: the official planetary-gods cult, neo-Egyptian Serapis worship, Epicureanism, Stoicism, Peripatetic philosophy, Persian Mithraism — with Buddhist monks and Indian Brahmins reaching Alexandria. Virgil, Rome's great initiate poet, expressed reincarnation doctrine in the Aeneid (the spirit's "desire to return to the bodyafter a thousand years).

Non-obvious point: This marked the first era in history when religious choice became a matter of personal decision rather than birth — producing an "age of inauthentic faith," a new cynicism and consciously cultivated sensibility, since people could choose based on evidence or on what they simply wanted to believe. Rome's grandeur mixed with paranoia; imperial ritual pomp (smoke, incense, clashing cymbals) — once used to hypnotize peoples into obedience to Baal — was now redeployed to convince subjects that eacal rulers were literal gods.

Warning example — corrupted power via forced initiation: The Caesars compelled Mystery schools to initiate th, gaining access to ancient Sun-god teachings. Julius Caesar eradicated the Druids for teaching that the Sun god would soon return to earth. Augustus banned astrology not from disbelief but from anxiety that astrologers could read signs undermining his self-presentation as the Sun god. Caligula, initiated by force without proper preparation, could communicate with lunar spirits in dreams but could not properly identify them, leading him to claim Jupiter, Hercules, Dionysus, and Apollo as brother gods and dress as them. Nero's madness peaked when he realized he was not the Sun god after all, preferring to burn the world rather than let a greater individual live — illustrating the dangers of improperly prepared or forced initiation combined with absolute power.

The Golden Asse of Apuleius: This initiatic work's Cupid and Psyche story carries an overt moral warning against curiosity, plus deer esoteric meaning. Psyche, forbidden to see her divine lover Cupid, is provoked by her jealous sister's claim he is a hideous serpent; she illuminates him with an oil lamp while he sleeps, finds him beautiful, but a dropped burning-oil drop wakes him and she is banished forever. Esoteric double meaning: the god truly is also a hideous serpent — this retells, from the human viewpoint, the history of the Nephilim and the entry of serpent-like animal desire into the human condition.

Decayf the Mystery schools: Excavations at Baia's "Underworld entrance" in southern Italy revealed secret passages and trap doors used to fake supernatural experiences for candidates. Robert Temple reconstructed this late, decadent phase as largely scary special effects (even puppets, like a modern ghost train) performed by priests dressed as gods over drugged candidates — but with a lethal difference: those who, on emerging, expressed any doubt about the illusions were killed. The Golden Asse itself, though beautiful and anticipating Rabelais style, marks a shift to consciously literary production — the earlier Mystery schools' monolithic sincerity was gone.

Sincere initiates withdr into more secretive schools outside official cult structures. Stoicism became the era's outward expression of initiatic impulse. Cicero and Seneca, both committed Stoics, tried to temper their rulers' egomania and argued all men were brothers deserving freedom from slavery. Cicero regarded his Eleusinian initiation as his life's formative experience, teaching him "to live joyfully and to die hopefully." Though tolerant of common people's superstitions about venal gods, he held even the most absurd myths could be read allegorically; in The Nature of the Gods he expounds the Stoic idea of a moving cosmic spirit that drives plants to seek nourishment, gives animals sense and near-reasoning instinct, and grants humans reason and higher intelligence — with gods properly imagined not as having human-like bodies but ethereal, beautiful forms, their purposes visible in stellar and planetary movements.icero was ultimately executed, stoically baring his neck to the sword.

Seneca likewise believed in Stoic cosmic sympathy and adepts' ability to manipulate it for personal ends; his play Medea likely quotes real magical formulae of contemporary black magicians, portraying Medea directing concentrated hatred powerfully enough to alter the positions of stars.

Rise of atheism and demon-infested "Age of Disenchantment": For the first time it became conceivable that gods might not exist — t intellectual elite (Epicureans) developed the first materialist, atheist philosophies. What remained was belief in the lowest spirit orders — the dead and demons. New Testament Gospels record an "epidemic of demons" during this period. While elites toyed with atheism, ordinary people practiced atavistic occultism exploiting t fact that demons and low spirits are drawn to fumes from blood sacrifice.

Practical/warning detail: The Jerusalem Temple's high priest wore bells on his robes so lurking goblins could hear him coming and hide; the Temple required a vast drainage system to handle the thousands of gallons of sacrificial blood flowing through it daily. Plutarch wrote against human sacrifice in terms implying it remained common practice, and even in South America a black magician was, in grim parody, being nailed to a cross.

Chapter 15: The Sun God Returns: The Two Jesus Children • The Cosmic Mission • Crucifixion in South America

The Great Turning Point

In Palestine, a decisive threshold in world history was reached. Because gods were no longer experienced as active presences "out there" in the material world, the Sun god, the Word, had to descend to earth directly. His mission was to plant in the human skull the seeds of an interior life — the new arena for spiritual experience, giving rise to the sense every person now has of an "inner space."

The cosmic plan had always been for human spirits to attain individuality: the capacity to think freely, exercise free will, and choose whom to love. To make this possible, matter had steadily become denser unti individual spirit was isolated inside its own skull, no longer wholly controlled by gods, angels, and spirits as it had been a thousand years earlier at the siege of Troy.

This development carried real dangers. Humanity risked becoming cut off not only from the spirit world but from one another. The instinctive, psychic blood-love that had bound tribes and families together like wolf packs was weakening inside newly hardened skulls, in the new towns and cities. This was the great crisis: people no longer felt like spiritual beings because the human spirit itself was in danger of being snuffed out.

Failed Precursors to the New Ethic

Mosaic law (an eye for an eye) enforced communal discipline; the Buddha taught compassion for all living things; the Stoics of Rome gave individuals legal and political status through rights and duties. Yet the irony was that just as individual identity was being formed, the sense that life was worth living was largely lost — the bloodbaths of the Colosseum showed no notion of the sanctity ofndividual life. Jesus ben Pandira, leader of the Essenes, preached purity but as a call to withdraw from the world. The Stoics taught responsibility but as joyless duty — the emperor Marcus Aurelius counseled meeting the future "with the same weapons of reason," words heavy with weariness. Humanity longed for someone to say, "Come with me, ye that are heavy-laden, I will give you rest."

Prophecies and Prefigurations

Candidates at Eleusis were shown the green wheat ear and taught to await the "seed time." In Egyptian temples, initiates saw Isis suckling the infant Horus — a second, coming Horus who would be a new king of the gods, called the Good Shepherd, the Lamb of God, the Book of Life, the Truth and the Life. Isaiah foretold the Messiah and the washing away of sins. The Roman initiate-poet Virgil, in the Fourth Eclogue, predicted a man-god Saviour: "The Golden Age will return as its first-born descends from on high… all the stains of our past wickedness will be washed away."

The life of Christ as handed down resembles a pat of earlier god-figures: born to a carpenter and a virgin like Krishna; born December 25 like Mithras; heralded by an eastern star like Horus; walking on water and multiplying loaves like Buddha; performing healing miracles like Pythagoras; raising the dead like Elisha; executed on a tree like Adonis; ascending to heaven like Hercules, Enoch, and Elijah. A corrosive mind might read this as proof of fiction, but esoterically it represents a universal convergence — the whole cosmos strainingo give birth to the new Sun god.

Decoding the Nativity

Mary carries the presence of Isis; as the sun entered Pisces (Jesus's sign), the opposite horizon held Virgo. Joseph, bearing a crooked staff, is Osiris, his staff symbolizing the Third Eye. The cave of the Nativity is the bony skull in which a new miracle of consciousness is about to be ignited. The infant in the manger has the luminous vegetative body of Krishna. The ox and ass represent the two prior ages — Taurus and Aries — that led into the Age of Pisces. The guiding star of tagi is the spirit of Zarathustra ("the golden star"). One Magus is Pythagoras reincarnated; the Magi were initiated by the prophet Daniel. The angel announcing the birth to shepherds is the spirit of the Buddha.

The Two Jesus Children

The infancy narratives of Luke and Matthew are inconsistent — different genealogies, different birth times and places, shepherds versus Magi — a distinction rigidly preserved in medieval art but since lost. Academic theologians privately concede at least one account must be false. Esoteric tradition resolves this: the two narratives describe two distinct Jesus children, not twins but almost identical, bound by a mysterious kinship.

The Gnostic text Pistis Sophia (contemporary with, and by some scholarly assessments equally authentic to, the New Testament) tells a strange story: Mary encounters a boy who looks exactly like her son but who asks to see "her son, Jesus." Fearing a demon, she ties him to the bed and searches the fields, finding Joseph and Jesus erecting vpoles. Brought together, the two boys gaze at each other in amazement and embrace.

One of the two children carried the spirit of Krishna and needed to sacrifice his individual identity, in a mysterious cosmic transaction, so the surviving boy could later receive the Christ-spirit at the Baptism. As the Pistis Sophia states, "ye became one and the same being." This tradition of two Jesus children was preserved by secret societies and appears in art: the north portal of Chartres, the apse mosaic of San Miniato outside Florence, and paintings by Borgognone, Raphael, Leonardo, and Veronese. The Leonardo Cartoon in London's National Gallery depicts the two children amid swirling, star-spangled light suggesting the world between worlds; in the London Virgin of the Rocks, a later hand added the elongated cross that is John the Baptist's distinctive emblem.

This narrative is a sanctified echo of Romulus and Remus, where one brother is sacrificed as the foundation offering for the Eternal City — great buildings and cities in antiquity were founded on such sacrifices. He, one Jesus child sacrifices himself for the sake of the New Jerusalem.

Creation of the Interior Life

The Gospel of John parallels the creation of the cosmos by the Word with the mission of the incarnated Word — a second creation. As matter had grown too dense for gods to manifest on earth's surface directly, the Sun god descended to plant a seed that would open a new interior space in which gods could manifest. The crucial, often-overlooked point: Jesus Christ created the interior life itself. Earlier intimations existed — Elijah's still, small voice; Jeremiah's "I will put my hand in the inward parts and in their heart I will write it" — but the planting of the sun-seed two thousand years ago was the decisive event producing the inner cosmos each person now experiences.

Without this intervention, individuality (the Ego) would have hardened into something small, self-centered, isolated, and gratification-seeking, with every human at war with every other and no sense of others as independent centers of consciousness. When Jesushe Temple, showed unusual wisdom at the time his kindred spirit disappeared, what passed into him was the ability to read minds, see into souls, perceive people's relation to the spirit worlds, and know how to help them — the gift of empathy, something no one had felt before. New modes of consciousness, once developed by one person or a small group, tend to spread rapidly worldwide.

A New Kind of Love

Jesus introduced gracious love grounded in empathy, allowing individuals to transcendsolated existence and share in another's innermost nature. Before Christ, love was tribal or familial; afterward, individuals could rise above blood ties to choose freely whom to love. This explains his apparent dismissals of family ties (Mark 3:32; Matthew 10:37-8, "He that loveth father and mother more than me is not worthy of me").

Esoteric teaching centers on loving rightly: cooperating with the gracious cosmic forces lets that force flow through a person consciously — a process called thaumaturgy, divine magic. Whether at grand scale or in "little, nameless unremembered acts of kindness" (St Thérèse of Lisieux's "little way"), Christian ethics shifted focus to inner states. Comparing Mosaic law or the Code of Hammurabi to the Sermon on the Mount shows the difference: older s regulated outward behavior (no idols, theft, murder, adultery); the Gospel teaching (Blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the pure in heart) targets inner states.

Non-obvious point: when Jesus said looking at a woman lustfully is adultery "in his heart already," he asserted something unprecedented — that private thoughts are as real as physical objects and directly affect cosmic history. In an idealist universe, intention matters far more than in a materialist one: identical actions performed with different inner states produce different consequences, just as a great painter's elevated soul-state informs the painting itself.

Practical/esoteric application: in Greek myth interpretation, ambrosia (food of the gods) is human love — without it gods fade and lose power to help. In mysthristianity, angels are drawn to us when we ask for help; if we fail to ask, they lapse into a twilit vegetative state and phantoms/demons work on our lower selves instead. We can resist demons and train baser animal selves as one trains a dog, through repetition — esoteric teaching holds that twenty-one days of daily repetition of a meditative exercise is needed to effect deep-seated habit change.

Warning/limitation: a deeper part of the animal self lies entirely below conscious reshold and cannot be transformed by willpower alone, because corruption has seeped down into the vegetable and mineral levels of the self — this requires supernatural help. The Sun god's mission was to sink into the deepest level of matter to introduce transforming spiritual influence, which is why it was written of the crucied Christ, "None of his bones shall be broken."

The Heart Chakra

The twelve-petalled lotus radiating from the heart region envelops those we choose to love and functions as an organ of perception — what is truly ved reveals its secrets. This enveloping is an act of imagination, distinct from fantasy: a true perception of higher reality via the heart chakra (East and West alike). This is referenced on the road to Emmaus: "Did our hearts not burn within us while he talked to us on the road?" When the heart chakra blossoms, one may perceive the Outworld supernaturally and gain conscious experience of the loving intelligence beyond it — "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Love also acts on the will: when we love, we act not wearily like Marcus Aurelius, not coldly or resentfully, but out of devotion.

Son of Man and Initiation

"Son of Man" refers ambiguously to both a state of mind and to Jesus himself — resolved esoterically as the state in which an individual becomes aware of their Higher or divine self, symbolized in iconography by a child carried on the shoulder (e.g., St Christopher) and in the Cabala by the three-pronged letter shin.

Initiation revives older forms of spirit-world contact but adds new elements each erythagoras's initiations enabled the same free communication with spirit worlds familiar to Gilgamesh or Achilles, but with the crucial addition of the ability to think about spiritual experience in a considered, conceptual way. Four hundred years later, Jesus Christ's initiations added a wholly new element: dizzying new dimensions of love.

Jesus and the Mystery Schools

Recent biblical scholarship (drawing on early Christian texts rediscovered in Palestine in the 1950s) suggests some non-canonical sayings of Jesus may be closer to originals than Gospel versions, lending credibility to sayings found nowhere in the Gospels — some bearing on secret teachings. Jesus's warning against casting "pearls before swine" and Mark 4:11 ("The secret of the kingdom of God is given to you, but to those who are outside everythg comes in parables") hint at teachings withheld from the multitude.

A striking account survives in a second-century letter by Clement, Bishop of Alexandria, discovered in 1959 at the Mar Saba Monastery library by Dr. Morton Smith. It describes Mark writing a public Gospel from Peter's teaching in Rome, then, after Peter's martyrdom, composing "a more spiritual gospel" in Alexandria incorporating secret material for "those who were being perfected," guarded carefully by the Alexandrian church. The quoted fragment describes Jesus raising a dead youth at Bethany who then loves him and, six days later, comes to him at night "wearing a linen cloth over his naked body," remaining with Jesus that night while "Jesus taught him the mystery of the kingdom of God." Though this could read to modern sensibility as a homosexual liaison, it in fact depicts a Mystery school initiation.

The raising of Lazarus in John's Gospel is understood as an encoded initiation account: Lazarus "dies" for three days, and Jesus's phrase "Lazarus, come forth" echoes the words used by hierophants in the Great Pyramid, who after three days stretched forth a hand to raise a candidate from the tomb in the King's Chamber. Esoteric doctrine holds that Lazarus later wrote the Revelation of St John the Divine, and that the opening of the seven seals and its visionary events refer to the revivifying of the seven chakras.

Christianity's Occult Core

Core Christian teachings are described as steeped in secret philosophy: "The meek shall inherit the earth," "Faith moves mountains," "Ask and it shall be given" are occult statements about how the supernatural operates in the universe — paradoxical, irrational, statistically improbable, and incompatible with a purely scientific unerse. The meek will not literally inherit the earth and prayers are not answered by forces science describes — unless a supernatural agency intervenes. Modern liberal Christianity, in accommodating science, has downplayed this occult dimension, constituting a kind of deliberate obfuscation by Church leaders.

The New Testament plicitly states John the Baptist is Elijah reincarnated. Scholars including Hugh Schonfield and Morton Smith have shown Jesus's miracles, especially the specific words used, draw on pre-existing magical papyri in Greek, Egyptian, and Aramaic — for instance, using spittle to make a healing paste is not pure unmediated spirit-action but a magical manipulation of matter to influence spirit.

Contemporary parallel: Apollonius of Tyana, a Pythagorean wonder-rker from Cappadocia contemporary with Jesus, grew his hair long, wore only linen and bark shoes, cast out demons, performed healing miracles, and insisted the era of blood sacrifice was over, saying we should approach God "only with the noblest faculty with which we are blessed — namely intelligence." This is not a denigration of Jesus but a reminder that thaumaturgy (divine magic) was, in its historical context, the highest activity a human could aspire to.

Historical Impact

Whatever one's view on the supernatural claims, the effect of the Jesus story on world history is unparalleled — it produced the current civilization of unprecedented freedom, prosperity, cultural richness, and scientific advance. Before Jesus there was little sense of the sanctity of individual life or the transcendentower of freely chosen love, though such ideas were foreshadowed by Krishna, Isaiah, Buddha, Pythagoras, and Lao-Tzu. Christianity's unique "mustard seed" was the interior life itself — giving each person both an infinite inner cosmos and a personal narrative history interwoven with general history: individual falling, doubt, and personal redemption, distinct from the tribal consciousness of earlier Jews or the city-state consciousness of the Greeks.

Crucifixion and Descent

Jesus's mintry lasted three years, from the Baptism to Good Friday, dated 3 April AD 33 (as stated in the text — "AD 3" appears to be a transcription truncation), when at Golgotha, the place of skulls, the Sun god was nailed to the cross of matter. At the Transfiguration, the Sun god began spiritualizing that matter.

Mystery schools froZarathustra to Lazarus involved candidates undergoing a three-day "mystical death" and rebirth — a real spiritual-plane death during which the spirit traveled the spirit worlds and returned with knowledge and power. The crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus mark the first time this initiation process occurred historically, on the material plane itself.

Matthiasrünewald's Isenheim Altarpiece Resurrection depicts Jesus as the Sun god using what Tertullian called the luminous seed, the "augoeides" — planted in earth, it arises as a luminous, star-like body of light rays; this is why the disciples on the road to Emmaus failed to recognize him, encountering instead his augoeidean body. Christ on the cross amid the Four Cherubim (symbolizing the Four Elements) represents him as the Fifth Element, the Sun god come to spiritualize the Four Elements and dissolve matter.

The Harrowing of Hell

Immediately following his death, Christ's descent into Hell — a now largely forgotten story — reflects the loss of the spiritual dimension of the cosmos in modern consciousness. Initiation always concerns the journey after death as much as this life. Before Jesus, humanity's afterlife expectation had shrunk to a dreary half-life of shades in Sheol; the dead lost usness ascending through higher spheres and returned in reincarnation with no memory of that journey. By descending into Hell, Jesus followed Osiris's precedent, lighting a way through the Underworld so the living and dead could walk together to complete the great cosmic Work.

The Cosmic Summary

Esoteric doctrine condenses world history into three stages: a Golden Age when earth and sun were united and the sun gave earth its form; a separation of sun from earth causing materialization and cooling; and the sun god's return to infuse spirit back into earth so the whole cosmos will eventually dematerialize and become spiritualized again. This cosmic vision inspired early Christians, shaped the great medieval churches and Renaissance art, and has since been lost to modern, exoteric Christianity. Andrea Mantegna's Harrowing of Hell illustrates 1 Peter 3:18-19 — "He also went to the spirits in prison… the gospel was also preached to those that are dead" — following St Paul's description of Christ's "descent into the lower parts oEarth," guiding imprisoned spirits.

Historical Causes of the Crucifixion

Beyond cosmological necessity, concrete historical forces drove the crucifixion. Lazarus's initiation was public, not confined to a Mystery school's guarded precincts, and Jesus himself was not a hierophant of any state-sponsored Mystery school. This made him a deadly enemy of the Sadducees, who controlled initiatic knowledge on behalf of the ruling elite — publicly initiating Lazarus signaled the breaking of the bond between initiates and the ruling class, marking the beginning of the end of the Mystery schools and preparing the way for secret societies.

Jesus also threatened Roman power. Soldiers mockingly draped him in a purple cloak — the initiation garment of the Adonis mysteries — and crowned him with thorns, satirizing the wreath given for successful initiation at Eleusis. The Caesars were his great occult enemies.

Crucifixion in South America

A lesser-known enemy operated on the opposite side of the world: a magician who, according to Rudolf Steiuilt supernatural power across multiple incarnations through mass human sacrifice, threatening to pervert history's course. Spanish philosopher José Ortega y Gasset described the release of spirits that spilled blood brings — blood as a frightening mystery that maddens and excites the landscape when spilled. Occultists hold that humans can be ritually killed in ways that harness the victim's spirit; just as great initiates like Elijah shape their own vegetable and animal selves into vehic ("chariots") for traveling the spirit worlds, black magicians can use the souls of sacrificial victims the same way. By sacrificing vast numbers of victims, this magician built an army of controlled spirits beyond the grave.

At the turn of the millennium, a Sun hero, Uitzilopochtli (per the Codex Florentino of Sahagún, one ofthe few surviving Conquistador-era records), was sent to oppose him — born of a virgin mother, his birth prophesied, and the forces of evil attempting to kill him after birth, following the pattern of earlier Sun heroe He survived early assassination attempts and, after many trials, waged a three-year magical war against the black magician, ultimately succeeding in crucifying him.

Key cosmic claim: the crucifixion of Jesus Christ unleashed a huge power to spiritualize the earth; simultaneously, the crucifixion of the great black magician in South America opened a vortex that would draw into itself the great currents of world history — the extremes of both good and evil.

Mary Magdalene and the Mystic Marriage

The Gospel of Philip hints that "Jesus loved her more than all the disciples and used to kiss her often on…" before the text fragments — possibly echoing the Song of Songs ("Let him kiss me with kisses of the mouth") and the theme of "love that is stronger than death." Esoteric thought is fundamentally reincarnational, not primarily concerned with spirits transmitted through genetic bloodlines; Jesus came specifically to abolish bloodlines as a means of transmitting clairvoyance and wisdom, replacing instinctual, tribal love with freosen love. The notion of Jesus marrying Mary Magdalene and fathering children is therefore considered irrelevant to his mission — esoteric literature instead refers to a "Mystic Marriage" (hieros gamos) of sun and moon, a theme to be revisited later.

The Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine, the most popular medieval collection of saints' stories, recounts persecuted Christians in Jerusalem, seven of whom were set adrift in a small boat and washed ashore near what is now Marseilles. A cavin a great cliff above that shore is still shown as the place where Mary Magdalene spent her last thirty years. She is traditionally depicted penitent, naked but for her long red hair; a painting by Fra Bartolomeo near Florence shows her with her jar of anointing oil resting on a stone inscribed: "I HAVE FOUND HIM WHOM MY SOUL LOVES."

Chapter 16: The Tyranny of the Fathers: The Gnostics and the Neoplatonists • The Murder of Hypatia • Attila and Shamanism

The Proliferation of Sects After the Sun God's Death

In secret teachings, the and death of the Sun god (Jesus Christ) marked the halfway point of secret history — the great hinge on which history turns, though unrecognized by official chroniclers at the time. The magnitude of this event was hard to grasp in the momen After a long period of spiritual aridity, many people began having vivid, atavistic experiences of the spirit worlds again, but without the unified institutional authority that the Mystery school hierophants once provided, these experiences were interpreted wildly differently — producing a proliferation of sects in the decades after Jesus Christ's death.

Many Gnostic texts are as old as New Testament books, some with strong claims to authenticity. The Gospel of St Thomas preserves more authentic versions of Jesus's sayings; the Pistis Sophia describes the two Jesus children. The fragmentary Acts of St John gives a rare glimpse into inner-circle practices: a circular dance in which disciples hold hands and whirl around Jesus Christ, accompanied by a paradoxical liturgy:

  • Candidate: "I would be sad" / Christ: "And I would save"
  • Candidate: "I would be pierced" / Christ: "And I would pierce"
  • Candidate: "I would eat" / Christ: "And I would be eaten"

The text uses deliberately absurdist, paradoxical language ("I have no house and I have houses / I have no place and I have places"). After a fragmentary Osirian/Christian death-and-resurrection mystery, Christ says: "What I am now seen to be, that I am not... Know then suffering and thou shalt have the power not to suffer." A parallel Hindu "circular sunwise dance" performed in honor of Krishna — dancers wheeling around the Sun god in imitation of planetary motion — confirms that the Acts of St John reflects a cosmic vision of Jesus Christ as the returned Sun god. The Gospel of St Philip describes five rituals, the greatest being the "ritual of the bridalmber," possibly a ritual-sexual practice akin to those in Egyptian, Greek, and Babylonian temples.

Later Church doctrine would emphasize the uniqueness of Christian revelation and distance Jesus Christ from prior traditions, but early Christians naturally understood Christianity as growing out of — and fulfilling — what came before. Church father Clement of andria may have known people who knew the Apostles; he and his pupil Origen believed in reincarnation and taught advanced students the disciplina arcani — dotional practices that today would be classified as magic.

Neoplatonism as a Living Spiritual Practice

Origen and Clement were part of the intellectual ferment that produced Neoplatonism. Plato had converted a mind-before-matter experience of reality into concepts; in the second century AD, Neoplatonists developed these ideas into a full philosophy of life — even a religion with its own spiritual practices. Neoplatonists saw themselves not as innovators but as commentators clarifying what Plato truly meant; passages now read as dry abstract logic were originally devotional texts used in practice.

  • Plutarch, influenced by Neoplatonism, describes in On the Delay of Divine Justice what spirits look like on their after-death journ: surrounded by flame-like envelopes, some "like the purest full-moon light," others "mottled... dappled with livid spots like adders," others with "faint scratches."
  • Plotinus, the greatest Neoplatonist of the Alexandrian school, was a practicing mystic; his pupil Porphyry reported witnessing Plotinus achieve ecstatic union with "the One" multiple times — Plotinus noted, somewhat dismissively, that Porphyry himself had achieved this only once.
  • Later Neoplatonists Iamblichus and Jamblich emphasized theurgic (godly, magical) practices, with Iamblichus leaving detailed accounts of his own visions.
  • Plotinus elaborated a complex metaphysic of emanations from the cosmic mind, which influenced the Cabala and Hermeticism.

Hermeticism, the Cabala, and the Angelic Hierarchies

Hermeticism and the Cabala are viewed by some scholars as Egyptian- and Hebrew-flavored versions of Neoplatonism, but in secret history they represent the first written, systematized expressions of much older oral traditions.

  • The Hermetica, attributed to the Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus, were collected in forty-two Greek volumes; researcher Yuri Stoyanov of the Warburg Institute confirmed most scholars now accept their genuine Egyptian origins. The Hermetica were tolerant of other traditions, likely because they assumed all traditions addressed the same planetary gods and spirit worlds — parallels can be drawn between Plotinus's numbered emanations, the Hermetica's gods, and the heavenly spheres of the Pistis Sophia.
  • In the Cabala, emanations from the cosmic mind (the sephiroth) form a descending "tree" — the sephirothic tree. Philo of Alexandria's allegorical interpretation of scripture revealed the shared structure underlying all religions.
  • St Paul hinted at orders of angels (Angels, Archangels, Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Mights, Powers, Principalities) assuming his readers understood the system; his pupil Dionysius the Areopagite later set out these nine orders explicitly. These map onto both the sephirothic tree and the gods/spirits of ancient polytheistic anomical religions — for example, St Paul's "Powers" equate to solar-system gods of the Greeks and Romans, with Powers of Light as sun spirits and Powers of Darkness as moon/planetary gods.
  • Jewish scholar Rebecca Kenta compared the cabalistic ascent through the gates of wisdom (Tree of Life) with Sufi teachings, and connected the sephiroth to Hindu chakras.

Non-obvious point: All idealist/religious systems envision creation as emanations descending from a cosmic mind, but what is disnctly esoteric is identifying these emanations with actual stellar/planetary spirits and occult physiology — this link is what generates astrology, alchemy, magic, and practical techniques for altered states. These were not abstractions but lived experience: when St Paul spoke of being "raised to the Third Heaven," he meant dict personal experience of Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones through high initiation.

Manichaeism and St Augustine

Christianity itself was forged from initiatic experiences like these. St Augustine, the greatest Church father, was an initiate of the Persian mystery school Manichaeism.

  • Mani was born in 215 in present-day Iraq. At twelve, a being he called "the Twin" appeared to him and revealed a hidden mystery: the role of evil in human history, including the intertwining of dark forces in the creation of the cosmos, and that in the great cosmic battle between good and evil, evil virtually triumphs.
  • Mani's vision was syncretic, giving exalted roles to Zarathustra, the Buddha, Hebrew prophets, and Jesus Christ.
  • Warning/pattern: the universalism of initiates tends to alarm local tyrants, and an initiate's heightened awareness of evil is easily misinterpreted. Mani was protected by two kings but their successor tortured and crucified him.

Augustine wrote: "I entered my innermost soul and beheld beyond my light and soul, the light." His towering achievement was to frame Church doctrine through Platonism — but this was based on his own direct initiatic experience, not abstract theorizing; he saw with "the mysterious eye of the soul" a light briger than intellect. His Confessions reveal a man tortured by the passage of time ("O Lord make me chaste — but not yet"; "O Beauty so old and so new, too late have I loved thee"). This sense of time carried into his esoteric conception of history, including his prophecy of the founding of the City of God.

Christian Missionaries and the Celts

St Patrick, captured and sold into slavery, later spread the sanctity-of-life ethic Jesus Christ introduced, fighting to abolish slavery and hun sacrifice — but he was also a wizard in the Zarathustra/Merlin tradition, casting snakes out of Ireland with his wand, expelling demons, and raising the dead.

Christianity was readily embraced by the Celts because St Patrick overlaid it onto the Celts' existing cosmic prophecy of the returning Sun god. Celtic Christianity fely intertwined pagan and Christian elements — Celtic art's intertwining motifs represented the interweaving waves of light that mark the first stage of mystical experience across traditions. The fiercely independent Celts insisted on direct personal spiritual experience and developed esoteric traditions independent of Rome, some later branded heretical.

Insht on sectarian conflict: when people share "ultimate concerns" (per theologian Paul Tillich), differences of opinion can breed murderous hatred toward one's own congregation more than toward outside conquerors. Sometimes believers try to ban ideas not because they think them false, but because they believe them true.

Constantine and the Politicization of Christianity

Constantine claimed a dream vision of Jesus Christ before battle telling him to mark his flag with the cross ("In this sign thou shalt conquer") — he won and declared Christianity the Empire's official religion, donating the Lateran Palace to Rome's bishops. This carried clear political benefits: Constantine offered freedom to any slave who converted and twenty gold pieces to free converts, accelerating the spread of the new consciousness.

Rome had made a cult of cruelty, exalting ruthless domination as manly virtue; Chriian meekness and humility inverted this entirely. To Romans, Christian initiates displayed a baffling new inner life — "lit up inside by an enthusiasm and a certainty about spiritual experience," compared to a Papua New Guinea encounter with a European explorer centuries later.

Constantine hoped the new religion would slow Rome's decline but remained anxious about a Sibylline prophecy that Rome would again become "the haunt of wolves and foxes." To thwart it, he transferred Rome's spirit to new capital: he dug up the Palladium (the god-carved statue carried from Troy at Rome's founding) from beneath a porphyry pillar and reburied it in Constantinople, topped now by a statue of the Sun god crowned with nails from the true cross as a nimbus.

Irony noted: even as this symbolism (understood by initiates of all religions) was being enacted, the Church under Constantine began suppressing initiatic teaching and reducing exoteric teaching to rigid dogma. In 325 the Council of Nicea decided which gospels, among many circulating, were canonical. Imperial edicts banned pagan practices; under Constantine's sons, women and children were force-fed consecrated bread through wooden mouth-openers.

Julian the Apostate's Reversal

Constantine's nephew Julian (came to power 361) reversed religious intolerance. Raised as a pupil of Neoplatonist philosopher Iamblichus, he understood the mission of what he called the "Seven-rayed god," granted equal rights regardless of religious belief, and reopened pagan temples. He wrote a famous polemic against the narrow dogmatic Christianity that had developed under Constantine (earning him the label "the Apostate"), believing Christianity denied the reality of gods he had encountered through initiation.

Julian led a military campaign into Persia — paralleling the Greek siege of Troy for its hidden initiation knowledge — seeking the secret knowledge of Persia's Manichaean Mystery school, understanding that its inner mysteries concerned the war between the Sun god and Ahriman/Satan, the spirit of materialism. Before completing his miss Julian was murdered by a follower of Constantine, ushering in a new Saturnine era in which true initiatic spirituality was driven underground.

Theodosius's Suppression and the Murder of Hypatia

Emperor Theodosius ruthlessly suppressed doctrinal disagreement, confiscating "heretic" property and temples. Statues of Isis were rededicated to Mary; the Pantheon in Rome — a temple to all the gods with sublime cosmic beauty (143 feet in diameter, its height to the roof aperture equal to its ameter, containing a vast sphere of air, niches once holding planetary god images) — was converted into a monotheistic church.

In 391 Theodosius besieged the Serapeum in Alexandria, a sacred compound with a temple to Serapis (a statue suspended from the ceiling by a magnet) and libraries holding the era's greatest book collecti. Many books were smuggled out before it was burned and its statues dragged through the streets.

Theodosius then targeted the Alexandrian Neoplatonic school, foremost preserver of Mystery school intellectual legacy. Its leading figure was Hypatia, daughter of a leading philosopher-mathematician:

  • Educated in philosophy, mathematics, geometry, and astronomy; her father devised physical exercises to make her body fit for her brilliant mind — she loved swimming, horse riding, and mountain climbing.
  • Renowned as beautiful and clever, she invented scientific instruments including one to measure liquid specific gravity.
  • Only fragments of her writing survive, but she was known widely as one of the era's most brilliant minds, drawing large lecture crowds.
  • Deeply versed in Plotinus and Iamblichus, she taught how Christianity evolved from Mystery school teachings and argued — like her father — that no single tradition or doctrine held exclusive claim to truth.

In 414, leaving a lecture hall, Hypatia was pulled from her chariot by a gang of black-cowled monks, stripped naked, and dragged through the streets to a church. There, amid incense, they tore her limb from limb, scraped flesh from her bones with oyster shells, and burned her remains. This weliberate attempt to erase Hypatia from history, paralleling how Amun's priests had tried to erase Akhenaten.

A Balanced View of the Church, Gnostics, and Neoplatonists

It is too easy to cast the Church simply as an evil repressor of free thought and romanticize outlawed groups like the Neoplatonists and Gnostics. The Church's history includes black magic practitioners and initiates who abused supernatural powers for selfish ends — but equally, from St Paul and St Augustine onward, itsreatest leaders were high-order initiates guiding humanity according to a divine plan. They understood it was necessary to suppress Western understanding of reincarnation, since the West's cosmic role was to cultivate the developing sense of the value of individual human life.

Conversely, the Neoplatonists, though continuing Pythagoras's and Plato's work of converting spirit-world experience into concepts, seemed unaware of the revolution Jesus Christ had introduced — their writings show no trace of the gospel of universal love. Similarly, Gntic emphasis on direct personal spirit experience (versus passive dogma) aligned with Christ's impulse, but many Gnostics were vehement world-haters, contrary to Christ's mission to transform the material world. Some Gnostic beliefs were fantastical or extreme:

  • Some believed Jesus Christ never inhabited a physical body, living only as a phantom.
  • Bizarre mortification and debauchery practices aimed to disrupt bodily senses and access spirit worlds: some let snakes crawl over their naked bodies; some drank menstrual blood declaring "Here is the blood of Christ"; some practiced sex magic believing it would birth god-like creatures; some castrated themselves, boasting "I am deader than you are."

Attila the Hun

Christian conviction served Constantine and Theodosius by unifying the Empire from within just as barbarian hordes threatened from the East. A domino effect from an expanding Chinese empire pushed Goths, Visigoths, and Vandals into Europe, even reaching Rome before retreating. In the second quarter of the fifth century, nomadic Mongolian tribes united under Attila the Hun, building an empire from Central Asia to northern Gaul, pushing into northern Italy and raiding Constantinople.

Though "scourge of God" Attila is a byword for barbarity, Greek historian Priscus's eyewitness account of visiting Attila's camp paints a different picture:

  • Attila lived in a simple wooden house with a wooden enclosure, woollen-mat carpets, wore plain unadorned linen, drank moderately from a wooden bowl, ate from a wooden plate.
  • He showed little emotion except affection when his youngest son arrived, chucking him under the chin.
  • When Attila conquered Christian Corinth and found a prostitute on every corner, he was outraged and gave them the choice of marrying one of his men or exile.

Nonetheless, had Attila succeeded in overrunning the Roman Empire, this would have been disastrous for the evolution of human consciousness. Romans feared him more than any other enemy: he refused to let his people live in Roman territory or use Roman goods, demolished Roman buildings on conquest (reversing Romanization), and extracted thousands of pounds of gold in tribute. In 452, with Rome in his grip, the Emperor sent Bishop Leo of Rome (the future Pope Leo) to negotiate — securing a deal in which Attila would marry the Eeror's daughter Honoria with a dowry of more gold, at which point Attila believed he had achieved world rule.

Attila and his people practiced shamanism. His shaman-priests guided him wisely in battle. Hun armies advanced with a terror-inducing uproar of howling dogs, clanking weapons, horns and bells — intended to summon the battalions of the dead (ancestral ghosts) to fight alongside them and to shamanistically call on the group souls of wolves and bears to enter warriors and grant supernatural power.

Shamanism Examined

The word "shaman" derives from a Tungus-Mongol noun meaning "one who knows." Shamans across history use "archaic techniques of ecstasy" (Mircea Eliade's term) to reach trance states:

  • Rhythmic drumming and dancing, hyperventilation, frenzied self-mutilation, sensory deprivaon, dehydration, sleep deprivation.
  • Psychoactive plants: ayahuasca, peyote cactus, ergot fungus. Research by Professor William Emboden (California State University) suggests drugs induced trance in Mystery centers too — the kykeon at Eleusis, and blue water lily combined with opium and mandrake root in ancient Egypt.

Scientific/biological detail: scientists have isolated a brain enzyme inducing trance states; about 2% of people naturally have high enough dimethyltryptamine (DMT) leve for spontaneous, involuntary trance. It's likely everyone has higher levels until adolescence, when a crystallization process clads the pineal gland and impedes its function — for everyone else, ancient techniques (or equivalents) become necessary to access these states.

The four-stage shamanic sequence observed across cuures by anthropologists:

  1. Blackout of sensory awareness; sense of journeying through darkness; often great pain, as if the body is being dismembered.
  2. A sea of lights, often forming a shifting geometric net (the "matrix").
  3. Patterns morph into shapes — commonly snakes and half-human, half-animal creatures with pliable, semi-transparent bodies.
  4. Trance fades, leaving a sense of supernatural powers: healing ability, knowledge of enemies, mind-to-mindnimal influence, and prophetic gift.

Gregg Jacobs of Harvard Medical School noted that shamanistic techniques can access "powerful ancestral states of consciousness." However, modern esotericists caution that shamanism only partially illuminates the Mystery schools and secret societies: shamanic trance paintings, though often beautiful, lack the comprehensive panoramic vision of the spirit worlds found on temple ceilings at Edfu or Philae, and the beings shamans encounter are from lower spirit levels rather than the elevated planetary gods communed with by temple priests.

Key reversal in secret history: conventional history holds that religion began with animism/totemism and developed into sophisticated cosmologies. In secret history, the reverse is true — humankind's primordial vision was soisticated and magnificent, and only later degenerated into animism, totemism, and shamanism. Attila's people had genuine spirit-world access many churchmen might envy, but it was atavistic access, running contrary to the evolutionary impulse toward individual intellectual strength developed by Pythagoras and Plato and redirected by Jesus Christ and Paul — the aim being free, powerful, loving movement through both material and spirit worlds while retaining full consciousness.

Warning: mern esoteric teachers forbid drug use as a means of reaching spirit worlds. The goal is to access spirit worlds with intelligence and critical faculties unimpaired — indeed heightened. Entering spirit worlds via drugs, without proper preparation, risks opening "a portal into a demonic dimension which then refuses to close."

##ttila's Death

In 453, as Attila prepared to marry another young bride — already having hundreds of wives — poised to potentially end the Roman Empire, he was found dead the next morning, having suffered a massive nosed. The delicate early growth of a new stage of human consciousness was thus spared being nipped in the bud.

The Birth of Zen and "The Nameless Way"

Tertullian's famous phrase "I believe because it is absurd" influenced thinkers into the twentieth century. A citizen of the declining Roman Empire lived in a disenchanted world where ancient spiritual certainties (Pan, the oracles) had gone silent, replaced by vigorous scientific/technological thought (Lucretius's atomic theories, aqueducts, roads) and harsh political-economic realities. Yet beneath this mechanical "way of the world" ran an opposite undercurrent sometimes called "the nameless way," accessible to anyone willing to listen to inner promptings.

At this juncture, history shifts from the Mystery schools' era to the age of secret societies — from top-down direction by a political elite to something more subversive rising from below. A new mood entered the soul-life of initiates, later traceable in Francis of Assisi ("God's joker"), Shakespeare's fools, Rabelais, Gulliver's Trals, Alice in Wonderland, and Kurt Schwitters's cut-and-paste art.

The Zen fable of the cut finger: A monk raised a finger to answer a question about Zen's meaning. A boy mockingly imitated this whenever the teaching was discussed. The monk grabbed the boy and cut off his finger; as the boy ran off crying, the monk called out, and when the boy turned back, the monk raised his own finger again — and the boy was instantly enlightened.

This fable dates to the era of Attila's death. Abstct thought (via Pythagoras, Confucius, Socrates) had developed for under a thousand years; Buddhism spread from India to China with the twenty-eighth patriarch Bodhidharma, and over the following two centuries Buddhism and Taoism fused into tch'an (Zen), a philosophy of spontaneous, intuitive enlightenment that cautioned against the limits of abstract thought.

Esoteric interpretation: the boy's enlightenment came from suddenly perceiving the world through "vegetable consciousness" centered in the solar plexus rather than the skull — the cociousness that connects every living thing individually across the cosmos, visualized as tendrils of a great cosmic tree with each solar plexus a flower on it. This is the "world between the worlds," the gateway to the spirit worlds, and the "light beyond the light of the intellect" (echoing Augustine). From this consciousness's viewpoint, the monk's finger belongs to the boy as much as to the monk — ordinary head-thought categories cannot capture this. Laughter erupts when one suddenly sees the cosmos "upside down, inside out and the other way round." From this point, great initiates of secret societies, East and West, would always carry "a touch of Zen."

The Rise of Arabian Magic

Under Emperor Justinian, the Byzantine Empire expanded and regained territory from barbarians, but Justinian closed the remaining Greek philosophy schools, causing teachers to flee with texts including Aristotle's now-lost alchemical treatise. Many fled to Persia, where King Khusraw sought to found a great academy rivaling Greek civilization. In the resultg intellectual ferment — blending Neoplatonism, Gnosticism, and Hermeticism with Aristotelian methodology applied to both material and spirit worlds — the golden age of Arabian magic began.

This era produced the childhood-familiar imagery of genies, magic lamps, and "abracadabra," along with rumors of automata, flying machines, self-generating gold, and powerful spells collected into forbidden books. Soon the whole world would fall under Arabia's spell as books of spells — "containing ispers of demons" — spread far and wide.

Chapter 17: The Age of Islam: Mohammed and Gabriel • The Old Man of the Mountains • Haroun al Raschid and the Arabian Nights

Mohammed's Early Life and the Vision of Gabriel

A grimly forbidding spiritual figure watched over these developments from the spirit worlds. Mohammed wn in Mecca in 570. Orphaned at six, he worked as a shepherd's boy before becoming a camel-driver transporting Mecca's specialty spices and perfumes to Syria. At twenty-five he married a wealthy widow and rose to become one of Mecca's richest, most respected citizens — yet remained dissatisfied.

Mecca's religious center was the Kaaba, a large black granite stone at some traditions claim fell to earth from the Sirius star system. Arabia at the time was populated by shamanistic tribes, each worshipping its own gods; a sacred tent beside the Kaaba housed hundreds of idols. Mecca had also grown corrupt through the sale of holy water from a spring Ishmael had caused to spring from the sand. Mohammed saw people obsessed only with money, gambling, horsemanship and drunkenness. Through his caravan travels to Syria and Egypt he learned of Judaism and stories of Jesus Christ — the account of the cleansing of the temple may have struck a particular chord — and became convinced Arabia needed its own prophet to purge superstition and corruption and unite the people in a cosmic purpose.

While brooding in the hills around Mecca, an angel appeared, declaring "I am the angel Gabriel," and showed him a golden tablet, commanding him to read it. Though illiterate, Moha found upon a second command that he could read — beginning the series of angelic conversations that became the Koran. He preached with blazing sincerity, summarizing his creed simply: Allah is the One God, Mohammed is his prophet, give up idolatry, do not steal, lie, slander, or become intoxicated. When challenged to perform a miracle to prove divine inspiration, he refused, pointing instead to the heavens raised without pillars, the earth, rivers, fig, date and olive as miracle enough âtance read as an early whisper of ecstatic materialism heralding the modern age.

The Esoteric Significance of Gabriel and the Moon

During the angelic exchanges, Gabriel offered Mohammed a choice of refreshment; he chose milk — what occultists call "moon juice" — and alcohol was thereafter forbidden in Islam. It is esotally significant that Gabriel, traditionally Archangel of the Moon, dictated the Koran. Allah is the Muslim name for Jehovah, the great god of the moon and of thought, and Gabriel heralds the power of thought to control passion and quell fantasy — his emblem is the crescent moon, the god of "thou-shalt-not." Thought itself is described as a death process that fes on life-giving energies: in the Middle Ages, the sexual impulse had to be suppressed for the human capacity for abstract thought to grow, and religious leaders imposed authority over the people in order to quell excessive Gnostic fantasy.

Conventional Western history frames Europe as besieged by "uncivilized" Muslims through the Dark Ages and Middle Ages; esoteric history holds nearly the mirror opposite — the transformative impulses that would reshape Europe and the whole human race originated in Islam.

An aside on the desert fathers: living in isolation, they practiced extreme techniques to access the spirit worlds, seeding the later monastic movement. St Antony the Great, greatest of the desert fathers, spent long periods in trance in tombs. He once advised a man to cover himself with meat; the man was shredded by wild dogs, learning something of what it is like to be attacked by demons yond the grave. In his own "temptation," Antony entered the sphere of the moon (kamaloca, or purgatory) and was shown a vision of the Devil as a tall black man with his head in the clouds, alongside angels able to guide some spirits beyond the Devil's reach.

Conquest and the Spread of Islamic Learning

Mohammed's marketplace preaching provoked an assassination plot; he fled to Medina with his disciple Abu Behr, then returned to Mecca in 629, establishing control of Arabia before his death four years later. Under his successor (Caliph) Abu Behr, conquest proceeded at an astonishing rate.
