A religion succeeds partly by delivering material benefit in the world: Mohammed's radical monotheism combined with the pre-existing Aristotelian scientific methodology in Arabian thought to spread rapidly from Spain to the borders of China.

While spreading, the Arabs also absorbed ideas — Zoroastrianism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Chinese science including papermaking — and advanced astronomy, medicine, physics and mathematics, replacing clumsman numerals with the numeral system used today.

Sufism: Esoteric Islam

Sufism claims ancient, even primordial roots, some traditions tracing it to the Saramong Brotherhood (Brotherhood of the Bee), founded in the Caucasus during the first post-Atlantean migration, later shaped by Gnosticism and Neoplatonism. Where triumphant Islam tended toward dogmatism and paternalism, Sufism represented the contrary impulse — fascination with the perverse, paradoxical, feminine and feeling side of spiritual life, expressed through a great outpouring of poetry.

A central Sufi teaching concerns the nature of "oneself": what we imagine as our own self is really an independent entity made up of fears, false attachments, dislikes, prejudices, envy, pride, habits, preoccupations and compulsions. Much Sufi practice works to break down this false self. The Koranic verse (50:16) states "God is nearer to a man than his jugular vein," yet distraction by the false self keeps most people from this awareness. The great Sufi writer Ibn Arabi said a Sufi masteis one who "unveils one to oneself." Practices under a master's instruction might involve breathing exercises and music to attain altered states, teaching the sometimes painful process of "waking up" to the cosmic, mystical current running through a person. Because Sufis opened fully to this current, they could appear wild, unpredictable and disconcerting — with a largely unacknowledged but vast later influence on Western culture.

Mohammed's brother-in-law Ali stood to him as John stoodo Jesus Christ, receiving and transmitting secret teachings; Sufis obeyed Islamic law outwardly while regarding it as merely the outer shell of esoteric teaching. Ali and Mohammed's daughter Fatima founded the Fatimid Empire across North Africa and Cairo, establishing the House of Wisdom, a school of esoteric philosophy with seven initiatory grades granting candidates timeless wisdom and secret powers. Sir John Woodruffe, the nineteenth-century translator of key Tantric texts, uncovered a parallel Sufi tradition of occult physiology with centers of power bearing names like Cedar Heart and Lily Heart.

The Old Man of the Mountains

Hassan-i Sabbah, an initiate of the House of Wisdom, founded a sect that in 1090 captured the castle of Alamut south of the Caspian Sea in modern Iran. From this mountain stronghold he directed secret agents worldwide, exerting puppet-master control over distant rulers; his Hashishim ("Assassins") infiltrated courts and armies, and anyone suspected of disloyalty was found dead by morning.

The popular Western image of Hassan is distorted by Marco Polo's account, which claimed the Old Man drugged young followers into three-day sleeps, waking them in a beautiful garden staged as "paradise" filled with beautiful women, before drugging them back to sleep and returning them to Hassan — leaving them convinced he could send them back to paradise at will, making them willing killers in exchange for the promised reward. In reality Hassan banned all intoxicants (even executing his own son for drunkenness) and banned music too; among his people he was rewned as a holy man and alchemist able to control world events by supernatural means — despite leaving his room at Alamut only twice after settling there. This archetype of the seemingly mad figure who secretly controls the world from a single room reappears in the twentieth century as Dr Mabuse in Fritz Lang's esoteric films.

Haroun al Raschid and the Arabian Nights

Haroun al Raschid became Caliph in his early twenties and made Baghdad the world's most splendid city, with a palace seed by hundreds of courtiers, slaves and a harem — glittering materiality where every worldly pleasure could be had and grow tiresome. As the Caliph of the Tales of the Arabian Nights, he drew the era's great writers, artists, thinkers and scientists to his court, and was rumored to slip out disguised through a secret palace dr to eavesdrop on his subjects' true opinions.

One famous tale: a fisherman on the Red Sea nets a large iron pot sealed with the interlocked triangles of Solomon's Seal. Opening it releases a black vapor that spreads across the sky, then condenses into a monstrous Jinn who explains Solomon imprisoned him — after two hundred years he vowed to enrich his liberato after five hundred to reward him with power, but after a thousand years of captivity, to kill whoever freed him. When the fisherman feigns disbelief that the Jinn was truly inside the pot, the Jinn demonstrates by turning back to vapor and re-entering it, whereupon the fisherman claps the lid shut again. Though it reads as a children's story, occultists treat it as packed with esoteric lore: "Jinn" means "to hide," and Arab peoples cultivated a detailed theory and practice for dealing with such entities, said to inhabit ruined houses, wells and bridges. The imprisoning of spirits in amulets, rings and stones via magical sigils like the Seal of Solomon was well established; by the Middle Ages this largely Arabic lore — especially concerning empowering talismans through astrology — was collected into famous grimoires, the greatest being the Picatrix, which fascinated later influential figures iding Trithemius, Ficino and Elias Ashmole.

Rumi and the Whirling Dervishes

Rumi, the great poet of the court, was a disconcerting child who began fasting and seeing visions at age six. In one story, while chasing a cat across rooftops with other children, he protested humans should be more ambitious than animals — then vanished, reappearing behind the frightened group claiming spirits in green cloaks had carried him to other worlds. These green-cloaked figures may relate to El Khidir, e Green One, a Sufi figure able to materialize and dematerialize at will and said to aid those on special missions.

At thirty-seven, a young university professor adored by students, Rumi was accosted while riding by the dervish Shamsi Tabriz, known for insulting sheiks and holy men because he answered to nothing but God, making him unpredictable and overwhelming. The two embraced, lived together meditating for three months, and each found in the other's eyes what he had sought. Rumi's jealous students ambushed and stabbed Shamsi to death. Devastated, Rumi wept and wasted away until, walking past a goldsmith's shop, the rhythmic hammer-beat on gold prompted him to repeat Allah's name and suddenly whirl in ecstasy — the origin of the Mellevi, or whirling dervish order.

Arab Marvels and a Hidden Technology

Medieval Europe was both fascinated a horrified by tales from Arab courts: hundreds of leashed lions, a lake of mercury with a leather bed inflated with air and fastened by silk bands to four silver columns, and — most commonly reported — a miraculous mechanical garden of precious metals with mechanical birds that flew and sang, centered on a golden tree bearing fruit of huge precious stones representing the planets. Such prodigies seemed necromantic, existing on the border between magic and science.

A partial, non-obvious explanation: in 1936 German archaeologist William Koenig, excavating palace drains in Baghdad, discovered what he immediately identified as a primitive electric battery dating to the early Middle Ages. A colleague's replica generated enough current tld-plate a silver figurine in under half an hour — suggesting some "miraculous" Arab technologies may have had a genuine electrochemical basis.

Charlemagne and the Historic Parsifal

In 802 Haroun al Raschid sent Charlemagne a gift of silks, brass candelabras, perfume, ivory chessmen, an elephant, and a water clock marking hours by dropping bronze balls with mechanical knights emerging from little doors — intended to impress upon Charlemagne the superiority and reach of Arabian scienced it not been for three generations of Frankish kings — Charles Martel, Pepin and Charlemagne — Islam might have wiped Christianity from the earth.

Born in 742, Charlemagne inherited the Spear of Longinus (used to pierce the crucified Christ's side); he lived and slept with it, believing it granted him powers to foresee the fe and forge his own destiny. In the early ninth century he won victories against the Muslims, wielding his sacred sword Joyeuse to bar their invasion of northern Spain and protect the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela.

A great impulse of "upside-down, other-way-round" thinking entered the world through Sufism: "The Truth is also seeking the Seeker." P.L. Travers, creator of Mary Poppins, was a disciple of twentieth-century master G.I. Gurdjieff, himself influenced by Sufis and Tibetan Lamas — the literary Mary Poppins (not the sentimentalized film version) embodies a Sufi adept's disconcerting capacity to turn the world inside out and bend natural law.

Charlemagne stood some seven feet tall with blazing blue eyes and simple, moderate habits, yet imposed his will on history — maintaining a Christian "Fortress Europe" identity against Islamic invasion while also protecting his people from corrupt and tyrannical nobles. According to Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim (one of the great Renaissance magi), Charlemagne founded the Holy Vehm — the Secret Tribunal of Free Judges — in 770, using secret ciphers and signs to exclude the uninitiated, also called the Secret Soldiers of Light. Masked men would nail summonses to the gates of castles whose owieved themselves above the law; those who disobeyed, even with bodyguards, would inevitably be found stabbed to death with the Holy Vehm's characteristic cruciform dagger. A noble who obeyed would travel alone at night to a designated spot, sometimes a lonely crossroads, be hooded by masked men and led away for interrogation, and at midnight find himself unhooded before masked, black-robed Free Judges in a vast underground vault to receive sentence — a vault motif echoing legends of Charlemne's own underground initiation.

The Enchiridion of Pope Leo, a book of spells offering protection against poison, fire, storm and wild beasts, only entered exoteric history in the early sixteenth century but was said to have been worn at all times by Charlemagne in a small leather bag; notably, the first chapter of St John's Gospel was included as its most powerful spell — verses still used this way by practicing esotericists today, lending the account a note of authenticity.

More solid evidence of Charlemagne's initiatic worldview survivein the Aachen chapel, the largest building in the world north of the Alps at the time, its octagonal shape anticipating the walls of the New Jerusalem per the Book of Revelation's esoteric numerology. Entry is through the Wolf Door, named for a legendary wolf who tricked the Devil out of possessing the chapel. Inside, a first-floor gallery holds the Holy Roman Emperor's throne of simple white marble slabs; a solid gold casket in the chapel's center contains Charlemagne's bones, above which "the Crown of Lights" — a huge wheel-shaped chandelier — hangs like a blazing crown chakra.

Charlemagne assembled Christendom's great scholars, led by Alcuin of York, to rival Haroun al Raschid's court — a British connection significant to this history, since the spirit of King Arthur lives on in Charlemagne as defender of the faith, wielding a weapon of invincibility and leading a circle of faithful knights (paladins). The original King Arthur belonged to the Iron Age as champion of the Sun god against encroaching darkness; the Grail stories addeegend under Charlemagne are grounded in historical events.

The Historic Parsifal and the Meaning of the Grail

Rather than pure allegory, Parsifal is presented as a man of flesh and blood — a reincarnation of Mani, third-century founder of Manichaeism — unknowingly the nephew of Charlemagne's paladin William of Orange, who fought the Saracens at Carcassonne in 783, a battle so costly it forced Muslim withdrawal from France to Spain. Raised as a forester by his mother far from court andvalry, Parsifal never knew his father or uncle, and unlike the famous knight Roland (whose blazoned deeds were recorded officially), Parsifal's private, local battles would change history's course.

Playing alone in the woods, Parsifal encountered five knights in shining armor and mistook them for a vision of angels (rendered vividly by Chrétien de Troyes) — the sight fired his imagination and he left his heartbroken mother to seek adventure. Despite his ideals he proved a foolish knight, his missions marked by misunderstanding, accident, loneliness and failure. Riding by a river at dusk, he asked two fishermen for shelter and was directed to the castle of the wounded Fisher King, Amfortas, bleeding from the thighs after the evil king Klingsor laid a trap involving sexual temptat. At dinner Parsifal witnessed a procession of page boys bearing a bleeding spear and a shining bowl, then fell into deep sleep; in some versions he faced trials — menacing lions, a tempting demon, and crossing the Bridge Perilous (a giant sword spanning the moat). Waking to find the castle deserted, he discovered the surrounding country reduced to a wasteland from failed crops.

Later accepted at court and knighted, Parsifal was confronted by the ugly Loathly Lady, who explained the land suffered because he had failed, upon seeing the Grail vision, to ask the healing question. On his second visit to the Grail Castle he asked Amfortas what ailed him and succeeded where all other knights — including Sir Launcelot, whose impure heart (his love for Guinevere) disqualified him — had failed. At his s climax Parsifal beholds first the Spear of Longinus (linking back to Charlemagne) and finally the Grail itself.

The visionary elements should be read as an account of an actual initiation ceremony undergone in deep trance — though symbolic or allegorical events can still be literally true. In chivalry, helmet, sword and spurs symbolize initiation; the ceremonial shoulder-tap with a sword recalls an ancient rite of tapping the forehead with the thyrsus rod to make springs of water and wi flow (echoed in some modern initiations by an actual blow to the forehead, said to permit birth of higher thought, as Athena was born from her father's forehead).

What the Grail Really Represents

In the early German version, the Grail is a stone, sharing properties with the alchemists' philosopher's stone: it shines, regenerates, and rejuvenates flesh and bone, offering (per von Eschenbach) "so much of the world's sweetness and delight that it seems like the kingdom of heaven." A stone that fell from Lucifer's forehead, if shaped into a bowl, would still be a worked stone. Functionally, the Grail is a chalice for holding bodily fluids — specifically Christ's blood caught at thcrucifixion and symbolically at the Last Supper. Since blood distinguishes animal consciousness, and in occult physiology the animal nature is carried by (as if in a chalice) the vegetable nature, the Grail's secret is not a bloodline (which would contradict esoteric reincarnation doctrine) but rather symbolizes the vegetable part of human nature as a living receptacle for spirit/consciousness. The quest is for a purified receptacle able to carry a higher form of spirit, and its trials represent esoteric purification techniques for the vegetable body. Rudolf Steiner, called the greatest twentieth-century teacher, held that all serious esoteric work begins with work on the etheric (vegetable) body.

Because of the Fall, the animal self is corrupted by sexual thralldom, and this corruption has seeped into the vegetable and material bodies beyond human power to purify alone — supernatural help andsoteric technique are required. A purified vegetable dimension makes a person naturally more plant-like: saintly individuals can sometimes live on almost nothing but sunlight, as plants do. The twentieth-century German mystic and miracle-worker Therese Neumann reportedly lived for some forty years on nothing but a daily consecrated wafer.

What distinguished the Grail initiation from earlier purification techniques was Parsifal's question to the wounded king — "What ails thee, brother?" âbining selfless compassion with a free, enquiring spirit that was new in the eighth century, marking the start of a new impulse toward freedom of thought that foreshadowed the end of the age of Church authority. The vision of the Grail is thus a vision of the vegetable body/soul transformed by moral feeling and intellectual questioning until fit to carry the Spirit of Jesus Christ. The historical dimension appears in how Amfortas's wound blights the land into wasteland — the private devotions of initiates affect the destinies of nations. Inarlier Mystery schools, gods were called down to inhabit crafted statues; in the Middle Ages, great initiates instead inspired imaginative mental pictures into which the gods would descend and breathe life.

On Charlemagne's death in 814 his empire quickly fractured, but the living idea of a united Europe survived — like King Arthur, he is said never to have truly died, but to wait in reserve for a time of need.

The Church Closes the Door to the Spirit Worlds

As the Church grew in power and wealth, it sought to become the sole keeper of the keys to the Kingdom. It had earlier suppressed teachings on reincarnation to emphasize a single earthly life, and suppressed knowledge of astronomical roots to emphasize one god. Now it moved to emphasize the unity of the disembodied parts of the human being: in 869, at the Eighth Ecumenical Council, the Church abolished the ancient distinction between the vegetable dimension of the soul and the animal dimension of the spirit, declaring soul and spirit identical. e result was that the spirit worlds, formerly directly encountered through the Mass, came to seem an empty abstraction — direct experience of the spirit worlds was replaced by dogma to be accepted on authority alone.

Islamic Influence and Chartres Cathedral

Despite the Church's closure of esoteric experience, a vital Islamic influence — part intellectual, part spiritual — kept flowing into Europe through scholarly centers like Toledo and Sicily. Mathematics, geometry, natural science (inspired partly by the Araeservation and translation of Aristotle), astronomy and astrology spread northward, leading to Europe's first universities, modeled on Islamic institutions, and to the arabesques of Gothic architecture, influenced by the intricate vegetal forms of mosque design.

In the north porch of Chartres Cathedral, founded in 1028, stands Melchizedek bearing the Grail. The astrology Islam reintroduced to Europe (after Rome had driven it out centuries earlier) appears in the west porch's symbolism — the fish of Pisces and the twin Templar Knights of Gemin— and the pediment features a vesica piscis, a "Third Eye" through which the spirit worlds are seen entering the material world. Chartres is a fusion in stone of Islamic mysticism, ancient Celtic spirituality and Neoplatonic Christianity, blt atop a hill honeycombed with ancient tunnels and caves believed sacred to the Mother Goddess; a black virgin in the crypt echoes the kinship between Isis, mother of the Sun god, and Mary, mother of Jesus.

Set into the nave floor is Europe's most famous labyrinth, built in 1200, roughly forty feet across; before its bronze centerpiece depicting Theseus, Ariadne and the Minotaur was melted down for cannon during the French Revolution, walking it required reversing direction seven times without ever repeating a path. Labyrinths and mazes are ancient pagan artifacts found at Knossos, at Hawara in Egypt, and cut into turf across Ireland, Britain and Scandinavia; many Christian churches once had labyrinths destroyed for their pagan associations by the eighteenth century. One Newgrange burial mound in Ireland was still called "the spiral castle" by locals in the 1950s because of a spiral carved at its entrance, and "our king has gone to the spiral castle" was idiomatic for death — a key to the labyrinth's symbolism at Chartres.

Walking the labyrinth's track produces a spiraling motion, curving left then right toward the center, a dance echoing the dance of Jesus described in the Acts of St John; the aim, as in all initiatory activity, is an altered state in which the spirit journeys up tough the spirit worlds, experiencing the after-death journey while still alive. In this Chartrean context, Ariadne — who intercedes to save Theseus — corresponds to Mary, who gave birth to the Sun king and through whose intercession humans may give birth to their own higher selves. The labyrinth functions as a mandala or medion aid, mirrored architecturally by the great rose window.

Medieval stained glass first appeared in Iran/Iraq in the eleventh century; the luminescent glass of Chartres was made by medieval alchemical adepts who had learned Arab secrets now lost to modern reproduction. Egyptologist Schwaller de Lubicz told his biographer André Vanden Broeck that Chartres's brilliat reds and blues used no chemical pigmentation but a separation of the volatile spirit of metals — a technique he tested with alchemist Fulcanelli and also found in glass shards he unearthed in Egypt. The rose window, displaying the zodiac in its outer circle, represents the crown chakra ablaze as it should appear at the labyrinth's center, dancing finally to the Music of the Spheres — Chartres has been called an alchemical crucible for humanity's transformation.

Islam was weaving itself into the fabric of the whole world, esoterically and exoterically, until in 1076 Turkish Muslims took control of Jerusalem.

Chapter 18: The Wise Demon of the Templars: The Prophecies of Joachim • The Loves of Ramón Lull • St Francis and the Buddha

The Founding of the Knights Templar

In 1076 Turkish Muslims took control of Jerusalem and began persecuting Christian pilgrims. The Crusaders freed Jerhen lost it again. In 1119 five knights, led by Hugo de Payens, met at the site of the Crucifixion and, echoing the Grail knights, vowed to make themselves worthy vessels to carry the blood of Christ. They established headquarters on the believed site of the stables attached to the Temple of Solomon, founded between the first and second Crusades. Formally titled the Order of the Poor Soldiers of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, they wore sheepskin breeches beneath their outer clothing as a symbol of chastity, were forbidden to cut their beards, owned nothing but a sword, held property in common, and never asked for mercy from an enemy — only retreating if outnumbered three to one, and even then eventually fighting to the death.

St Bernard of Clairvaux, founder of the Cistercian order and the era's most influentl churchman, wrote the Templars' rule book in 1128, formalizing them as a religious order. He praised them as knowing no fear — "one of them has often put to flight a thousand" — gentler than lambs yet grimmer than lions, combining "the mildness of monks and the valour of knights."

Archaeological evidence suggests an ulterior motive: excavating the Temple sitemplar artefacts have been found in tunnels cut through solid rock, aimed directly toward the supposed site of the Holy of Holies.

Templar Initiation and Rise to Power

Templar initiation ceremonies blended traditions including Sufism and Solomonic wisdom. A lamb was killed and its skin fashioned into a cord placed around the candidate's neck, by which he was led into the initiation chamber. Having sworn on pain of death that his intentions were pure, the candidate wondered whether the Grand Master could see into his soul by occult means, fearing he was about to die. Candidates endured frightening ordeals resembling those used in Zarathustra's initiations, confronting demonic forces to prepare them for death or any horror they might later face. These demonic confrontations would later haunt the order.

For roughly two hundred years the Templars' esprit de corps and tight organization made them extraordinarily influential in world affairs. Wealthy from nobles who joined and surrendered property rights, they invented letters of credit so money could move without risk of theft by robbers — their Paris Temple became the center of French finance, making them forerunners of banks and instrumental in the rise of the merchant classes. They also patronized the first trade guilds independent of Church and nobility, the Compagnons du Devoir, who carried out Templar building projects, ueld ethical codes, and protected members' widows and orphans.

Joachim's Prophecy of Three Ages

By the late twelfth century, other challenges to Church supremacy were emerging. Returning from the third Crusade in 1190–91, Richard the Lionheart (grandson of Guillaume of Poitiers, the first Troubadour) visited a mountain herm gaining fame for prophecy; word came back describing him as harboring "black tidings."

Born around 1135 in a Calabrian village, Joachim lived as a hermit for years before joining an abbey and founding his own Abbey of Fiore. He wrestled with the Book of Revelation and was defeated by it — until one Easter morning he awoke transformed, granted a new faculty of uerstanding. The prophetic commentaries that poured from him afterward influenced medieval mystical thought and, later, the Rosicrucians.

Joachim's writings carry a cabalistic dimension even though the central Cabala texts had not yet been published — likely the fruit of his friendship with Petrus Alphonsi, a Spanish Jewish convert. While the Old Testament already conveys God working through history, what is distinctly cabalistic in Joachim is his interpretation of scripture through complex number symbolism and his vision of a Tree of Life, which he diagrammed two hundred years before a similar Cabalist version appeared — likely drawn from oral tradition transmitted through Alphonsi.

The teaching that most gripped the medieval imagination was his theory of three ages: the Old Testament as the Age of the Father (demanding fear and obedience), the New Testament as the Age of the Son (the age oe Church and faith), and a coming third age of the Holy Spirit, an age of freedom and love in which the Church would no longer be necessary. As an initiate, Joachim's thought carried an astrological dimension usually glossed over by Church commentators: Aries as the Age of the Father, Pisces the Age of the Son, Aquarius the Age of the Holy Spirit.

Joachim prophesied a transitional period between the second and third ages when a new order of spiritual men would educate humanity, and Elijah âs foretold in the last verse of Malachi — would reappear as forerunner of the Messiah to usher in the great inovatio. He also prophesied that the Antichrist would incarnate before the third age began. His prophecies still fascinate secret societies today.

Ramón Lull's Conversion Through Loss

Ramón Lull, called Doctor Iinatus, was a missionary to Muslims whose own thought was nevertheless saturated with Islamic ideas. Born in Palma, Majorca, in 1235 and raised as a royal page, he led a carefree life of pleasure. Lusting after a Genoese lady, he once rode his horse into the church of Eulalia where she was praying; rebuffed at first, she eventually summoned him to a tryst — and without warning exposed her breast to him, revealing it eaten away by malignant disease.

This ock began Lull's conversion and shaped his view of the world as a place of oscillating extremes where appearances mask their opposites. In his most famous work, The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, he asks, "When comes the hour in which water that flows downwards shall change its nature and mount upwards?" He describes the Lover falling among thorns that seem like flowers and a bed of love, and declares that misery is "to get one's desires in this world." A Lover clothed in fine raiment, sated with food and sleep, should be seen as damnation and torment; the scent of flowers reminds the Lover of the stench of riches, meanness, old age, lasciviousness, discontent and pride.

Lull wrote of ascending the ladder of humanity toward the Divine Nature, achieved by working on the soul's powers — feeling, agination, understanding and will — helping forge the deeply personal form of alchemy that would become the great engine of esoteric Europe. In one harsher saying he warned: "If thou speaketh truth, O fool, thou wilt be beaten by men tormented, reproved and killed." While preaching to Muslims in North Africa, he was set upon by a crowd, dragged from the city, and stoned to death.

St Francis and the Encounter with Christ

Francis was born into a world where serfs suffered extreme povertand the deformed, aged, destitute and leprous were treated with contempt, while wealthy clergy profited from the serfs and persecuted dissenters. In 1206 Francis, a rich young man in Assisi, led a carefree, heartless life, holding his nose at the sight of lepers — a life paralleling that of Prince Siddartha.

One day while ridg, his horse reared and he found himself facing a leper. He dismounted, grasped the leper's bloody hand, and kissed his suppurating cheeks and lips. As the leper withdrew his hand and Francis looked up, the leper had vanished — Francis recognized, like Paul on the road to Damascus, that he had encountered the risen Christ.

His life and philosophy were overturnedHe saw that the Gospels called for a life of poverty devoted to helping others, possessing "neither gold nor silver nor money in your purse... nor two coats, nor shoes." Poverty, he said, is to have nothing and wish for nothing, yet to truly possess all things in freedom — experience itself mattered more than things experienced, since possessions hold and threaten to rule us. A voice from a painted crucifix in the Church of San Domenico near Assisi told him, "Go, Francis, and repair my House, which as you can see, is falling into ruin" — an experience he felt was ineffable.

Francis's Transformed Nature and Mission After Death

Francis so transformed his nature across animal, vegetable and material dimensions that animals responded to him remarkably: a cricket sang at his request, birds gathered to hear him preach, and when a fierce wolf terrorized Gubbio, Francis met it, ordered it to hur one, and it lay at his feet before walking tamely beside him — a wolf's skeleton was later found buried beneath the floor of the Church of San Francesco della Pace in Gubbio.

Comparing Lull's mysticism to Francis's reveals a profound shift within a short span: Francis's mysticism is one of simple, natural things, the open air and the everyday. The Little Flowers of St Francis says he discovered nature's hidden things with his sensitive heart, seeing all things as alive — an ecstatic idet vision of the cosmos, everything charged with life by the celestial hierarchies, as expressed in his Canticle of Brother Sun and Sister Moon.

Christianity's spirit had once helped Buddhism evolve, introducing an enthusiasm that helped the Buddha's teaching of universal compassion find fulfilment in the material world. Now, though the Buddha did not incarnate again, his spirit helped reform Christianity by inspiring simple devotion and compassion for all living things through Francis.

Near the end of his life, meditating outside his hermit's cell on Mount La Verna, Francis saw the sky blaze with light as a six-winged Seraph appeared, bearing the same face he had seen on the painted crucifix — he understood Christ was sending him on a new mission. After his death, trouble arose whin the Franciscan order when the Pope required it to take on property and money, which many brothers saw as violating Francis's vision; they formed the breakaway Spiritual Franciscans, or Fraticelli, who were seen — by themselves and others — as the new order of spiritual men Joachim had prophesied, and were consequently hunted down and killed as heretics.

A famous Giotto fresco shows Francis propping up the Church. In esoteric Christianity it is believed the Seraph who gave Francis the stigmata told him his true mission would be fulfilled after death: once a year, on the anniversary of his death, 3 October, he leads the spirits of the dead out of the lunar spheres into the higher hierarchies — a reminder that initiation concerns life after death as much as earthly life.

The Cathars and Thppression

In the same period, new reform impulses grew across Europe — Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Germany, Italy, and above all southern France, where the Cathars attacked Church corruption. Their Gnostic-like central tenet held that they must keep themselves completely pure from an evil world; like the Templars and Francis, they renounced material possessions and kept strict vows of chastity.

The Cathars had no churches of wood or stone and rejected the sacramental system makinghe Church the sole intermediary between God and people. "We value virginity above everything," said one witness. "We do not sleep with our wives but love them as we would our sisters. We never eat meat. We hold our possessions in common." Their only prayer was the Lord's Prayer, and their initiation rite, the consolamentum, was a farewell to an evil world; they welcomed martyrdom.

The Church responded with a Crusade ordered by Pope Innocent III in 1208. At Béziers, when townspeople refused to surrender roughly five hundred Cathars, many thousads were slaughtered indiscriminately — when asked how to distinguish Cathars from others, the papal legate Arnaud-Amaury reportedly said, "Kill them all, God will find his own." At Bram, a hundred hostages had their noses and upper lips cut f and were blinded except one, left to lead a procession to the castle. At Lavaur, ninety captured knights were hanged then stabbed when they took too long to die. An entire army of prisoners was burned alive at Minerve.

In 1244 the last remaining heretics, after a nine-month siege at Montségur, surrendered; two hundred Cathar monks walked down the mountain into waiting fires. Legend holds that four monks escaped a day earlier carrying the Cathars' secret treasure — gold, relics, or secret doctrine remains unknown. It may be too easy to romanticize the Cathars, since their teaching that the world was evil suggests, like the Gnostics before them, a world-hating, death-loving oriental philosophy — yet the true esoteric thought of the age stood closer to it than to the Church's jugular vein.

A rious Child at Monsalvat

In the closing years of the thirteenth century, a weak and sickly child was born and taken in by twelve wise men, living, according to Rudolf Steiner's account, in a former Templar building at Monsalvat on the France–Spain border. Kept entirely hidden from the outside world, his miraculous nature went unseen by locals, though he was filled with such a shining spirit that his body became transparent. The twelve initiated him around 1254; he died shortly after, havi shared his spiritual vision with his caretakers — the thirteen preparing the way for his next incarnation, in which he would change the face of Europe.

Albertus Magnus and the Android

Albertus was born in 1193, apparently a dull, stupid boy until a vision of the Virgin Mary inspired him to pursue study so zealously he qukly became Europe's most famous philosopher, mastering Aristotle's science, physics, medicine, architecture, astrology and alchemy. The Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus — containing the central hermetic axiom "as ove so below" — first surfaced into exoteric history as part of his library. He almost certainly explored occult methods of divining metals deep underground, and reportedly built an automaton called the Android, made of brass and other metals chosen for magical correspondences with heavenly bodies, brought to speech and apparent independent thought and movement through magical incantations and prayer.

The legend that Albertus designed Cologne Cathedral likely derives from his authorship of the Liber Constructionum Alberti, containing secrets of Operative Freemasons, including laying cathedral foundations along astronomical lines.

Underground Initiation: The Legend of Owen in Ireland

Stories of underground journeys to find metals, like those attached to Albertus, often allude to underground initiations, which survived into the Middle Ages — as recorded in three surviving accounts of a soldier named Owen, who served English King Stephen and traveled to the Monastery of St Patrick in Donegal. Owen fa nine days, processing around the monastery and undergoing ritual purification baths. On the ninth day he entered an underground chamber "out of which all who enter do not return," where he was laid in a grave lit only by a single aperture. That night fifteen white-robed men warned him of an impending trial, after which a troop of demons appeared, held him over fire, and showed him scenes of torment resembling those in Virgil. Finally two elders guided him to a vision of Paradise.

Aquinas, Averroës, and the Triumph OverMaterialism

Albertus was spiritual guide to Thomas Aquinas, nearly thirty-three years his junior; Thomas reportedly smashed his master's Android to pieces — some accounts say because he believed it diabolical, others because it would never stop talking.

Aquinas came to the University of Paris to study Aristotle, only to finthat the greatest living Aristotelean was the Muslim philosopher Averroës, who argued that Aristotelean logic showed Christianity to be absurd — raising the question of whether logic would eat up religion and all trupirituality.

Aquinas's life's work culminated in the massive Summa Theologica, arguably the most influential theological work ever written, aiming to show philosophy and Christianity not merely compatible but mutually illuminating. He applied rigorous analysis to categorize the beings of the heavenly hierarchies — the cosmic forces creating both natural forms and subjective experience — and the Summa contains the Church's definitive teaching on the Four Elements, achieved through living, penetrating intellect rather than dead dogma. Aquinas is a key figure in secret history because his intellectual triumph over Averroës prevented Europe from being overtaken by scientific materialism centuries too early — a triumph achieved from a standpoint of direct, personal experience of the spirit worlds. Aquinas, like Albertus, was an alchemist who believed disembodied spirits' power could be harnessed to change the material world; of many alchemical texts attributed to him, scholars accept at least one as genuine.

Transubstantiation as A

Alchemy, seemingly a strange fringe practice today, is in fact familiar to every churchgoing Christian as what occurs at the climax of the Mass. Aquinas first formulated the doctrine of transubstantiation of the bread and wine, describing an essentially alchemical process in which the substance of bread and wine changes while a parallel transubstantiation occurs in the human body — the Mass producing not merely a new frame of mind but a vital physiological change. It is no accident that Aqnas formulated this doctrine just as Grail stories began circulating, describing the same underlying process through different methods.

Roger Bacon: Magic in Thinking

Though enemies — Bacon mocked Aquinas for only reading Aristotle in translation — both men represented the age's impulse to strengthen and refine intellige finding magic in thinking. The capacity for prolonged, abstract, conceptual thought had existed only once before, briefly in the Athens of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, before being extinguished; a new, more lasting tradition arose with Aquinas and Bacon. Both prized experience over dead traditional categories and sought to refine religious belief through experience. "Without experience," said Bacon, "it is impossible to know anything." Bacon was the more practical of the two, invoking entities from the same spiritual hierarchies Aquinas categorized, applying rigorous logic in a mysticism wholly unlike the unthinking, ecstatic mysticism of the Cathars.

A young Oxford scholar in the 1250s, Bacon resolved, like Pythagoras before him, to know everything — gathering into his own mind all the learning once known at the court of Haroun al Raschid. Known as Doctor Mirabilis, he sometimes wandered Oxford's streets in Islamic robes, and worked without rest in college rooms periodically rocked by explosions.

Bacon's Experiments and Prophetic Technology

Bacon conducted practical experiments with metals and magnetism, discovered gunpowder independently of the Chinese, and scared students by shining light onto a crystal to produce a rainbow — a feat previo believed possible only for God. He also possessed a magic looking-glass allowing him to see fifty miles in any direction, owing to his unique understanding of lenses.

Bacon undoubtedly possessed powers beyond modern scientific explanation: he reportedly sent his complete works to Pope Clement IV lodged in the memory of a twelve-year-old boy named John, whom he had taught — using prayers and magic symbols — to memorize all his many books within days. Similarly he taught students Hebrew horoughly that they could read scripture within weeks. All magic is a power of mind over matter, and esoteric philosophy concerns developing mental faculties capable of manipulating natural laws.

In Bacon, intelligence and imagination were both highly developed and worked upon each other. In 1270 he wrote a startlingly prophetic passage envisioning self-navigating ships requiring only one man to steer, cars moving at great speed without animals, and flying machines in which a man could turn an instrument to beat artificial wings — a completeedieval vision of the technological world experimental science would later create. Bacon was a Franciscan who, like his order's founder, longed for a better, cleaner, kinder world for the poor and dispossessed.

Two Kinds of Magic

Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose makes a telling distinction, voiced by William of Baskerville: there are two forms of magic, a Devil's magic seeking to harm others through illicit means, and a holy magic that rediscovers nature's lost secrets, a science known to the ancients. Like the Arab alchemists who influenced him, Bacon worked on the borderline between magic and science — a borderline that is what alchemy essentially represents. Bacon wrote a treatise called The Mirror of Alchemy and liked to quote St Jerome, a great Cabala scholar: "You will find many things quite incredible and beyond the bounds of probability that are true for all that."

In 1273, nearing completion of the Summa Theologica, Aquinas experienced an overwhelming mystical episode while taking Mass in Naples, afterward declaring, "Whahas been revealed to me now, makes all I've written worth no more to me than a stack of straw."

The Training of the Imagination

Idealists hold a more exalted view of imagination than materialists do, treating it as a faculty for grasping higher reality. Training the imagination lies at the center of esoteric practice, secret-society initiation, and magic itself. Imagination is considered the great creative force in the universe — the universe being the creation of God's imagination, itlf the first emanation — and human imagination allows both interpretation of creation and, potentially, its manipulation.

Human creativity, magical or otherwise, results from channelling the imagination's powers; alchemical tracts describe sperm as created by imagination, expressing the idea that imagination not only informs sire but can transform material nature itself. Initiates trained in these creative powers can produce powerful transformations in the material world outside their own bodies — an Indian adept, for example, is trained om an early age to visualize a snake with such concentrated, highly trained imagination that he can eventually make others see it too.

The Danger of Delusion and Systematic Safeguards

There is an inherent danger in this emphasis on imagination bordering on fantasy — workings on the imagination can enin delusion, making magic potentially "a self-deluder's charter." The systematic methods of secret societies were meant to guard against this. St Bernard of Clairvaux, who wrote the Templar rule, recommended systematic imaginative training: by summoning detailed images of Christ's birth, infancy, ministry and death — down to imagined domestic scenes, pots and pans, clothing, facial expressions, and the feeling of being looked at — and then suddenly banishing the visual images, what remained might be the true, real spirit of Christ.

Abraham Abulafia and Words of Power

In thirteenth-century Spain, the Cabalist Abraham Abulafia expanded on God's creative word. Earlier cabalistic texts described the twenty-two Hebrew letters as cree powers, with God combining and recombining them "in the beginning" to unfold all the universe's forms. Abulafia proposed initiates could participate in this creative process themselves by combining and recombining Hebrew letters, recommending retirement to a quiet room, white robes, ritual poses, and pronouncing divine names to achieve ecstatic, visionary trance — and with it, secret powers.

The notion of "words of power" granting dominion over spirit worlds, and thus the material worldis ancient. Solomon reputedly held such dominion; in his Temple, the Tetragrammaton — the most sacred name of God — could be pronounced only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, by the High Priest alone in the Holy of Holies, while trumpets and cymbals outside prevented others from hearing it, since someone who knew how to ounce it could reportedly inspire terror in angels. Even earlier, the Egyptians held that the sun god Ra created the cosmos using words of power, and that knowledge of these words granted power in this life and the afterlife.

Sigils, Grimoires, and Church-Sanctioned Magic

Abulafia also recommended using divine names in diagrammatic form; working with magical signs and sigils, rooted in Hebrew tradition with Egyptian and Arab admixtures, became widespread in the Middle Ages through grimoires such as The Testament of Solomon and The Key of Solomon. Most spells promised fulfilment of selfish desires — sexual, vengeful, or treasure-seeking — requiring preparation of materials like beeswax, animal blood, powdered lodestone, sulphur, and possibly raven's brain, followed by purification and ceremonies involving sickles, wands and swords performed at propitious times. The result might be a ring or scrap of paper inscribed with a sigil, so that its carrier, knowingly or not, would be affected by the disembodied being for good or ill. The mid-fourteenth-century text The Sacred Magic of Abraham the Jew taught how to raise tempests, resurrect the dead, walk on water, and win a woman's love, all through sigils and cabalistic letter-squares.

Today the Church inguishes strictly regulated ceremonies invoking spiritual powers within its own context from all other engagement with disembodied spirits, labelling the latter "occult" — usually meaning black magic in modern parlance. In the Middle Ages, however, no such distinction was practical: Church-sanctioned rituals sought good crops or duel success; consecrated bread was believed to cure sickness and ward off plague; amulets from church candles protected against lightning and drowning; magical fmulae inserted into roofs warded off fire; church bells repelled thunder and demons; formal curses drove away caterpillars; holy water on fields ensured good harvests; holy relics functioned as wonder-working fetishes; baptism reportedly restored sight to blind children; and overnight vigils at saints' shrines produced visionary dreams and cures in the tradition of Asclepius's "temple sleep."

Providence, Magic, and the Universal Medieval Belief

Later Christian apologists tried distinguishing legitimate Church practice — petitioning high-level spiritual beings who might or might not grant a request — from magic as mechanical manipulation of occult forces, but this distinction misustands magic, which is likewise an uncertain process of invoking spirits, including some of very high order. In the Middle Ages, everyone believed in these spiritual hierarchies: repeating a prayer formula or performing a ceremony was universally believed capable of influencing material events for good or ill, communicating with the disembodied beings who controlled the material world. That prayer was efficacious and providence rewarded good and punished evil was the universal belief and universal experience — history seen as a providential process, though not a fatalistic one, since God's plan for humankind, encoded in the Bible and elucidated by prophets, was unfolded by different orders of both disembodied and incarnated beings, and could go wrong at any time.

The Suppression of the Templars and Baphomet

Friday the thirteenth is still remembered as an evil day: on Friday 13 October 1307 e kings of the world finally moved to eradicate esoteric influences they feared were slipping beyond their control. Just before dawn, seneschals of France acting under King Philip the Fair descended on Templar temples and lodgings, arresting some 15,000 people. In the Paris Temple, France's great financial center, they found a secret chamber containing a skull, two thigh bones, and a white burial shroud — the same objects, notably, found today if one breaks into a Freemasonic temple. Only few knights, from La Rochelle on the Atlantic coast, escaped, fleeing to Scotland under the protection of the rebel king Robert the Bruce.

The Inquisition accused captured knights of forcing novices to spit and trample on the cross of Christ, of sodomy, and of worshipping a goat-headed idol called Baphomet, described as bearded, sparkling-eyed, and four-footed. Under pressure from Philip the Fair, Pope Clement issued a Bill of Abolition ending the Knights Templar, with all assets seized by the monarchy. Before a papal commission, knights testified they had been tortured into confessing — one, Bernard de Vardo, produced a wooden box containing charred bones that had fallen from his feet as they were roasted over fire.

Decoding Baphomet's Hidden Wisdom

The truth behind the coessions emerged through Hugh Schonfield, the great Dead Sea Scrolls scholar, who knew of the ATBASH cipher — substituting the first letter of an alphabet for the last, the second for the second-last, and so on — a cipher used to encrypt messages in the Book of Jeremiah and some Dead Sea Scrolls. Applying it to the word Baphomet, Schonfield found encoded within it the word "wisdom."

Yet the personification of wisdom the Templars confessed to communing with was specifically the goat-headed god of worldly wisdom. Since Zarathustra's time, initiation ceremonies had induced altered states in which candidates underwent terrifying ordeals and demonic attacks, preparing them to overcome the worst life and the afterlife could offer. Under torture, the Inquisition's methods induced comparable altered statf consciousness in their victims, in which the demon-king Baphomet reappeared to them — this time in triumph, as they faced the very worst that life and death had to offer.

Chapter 19: Fools for Love: Dante, the Troubadours and Falling in Love for the First Time

Dante's First Sight of Beatrice: An Historical Turning Point

In 1274 in Florence, a youthful Dante saw Beatrice for the first time — a moment held to be not merely his own love at first sight but the very first time anyonll in love at first sight in human history. Conventional history assumes romantic love has always existed as part of human biology, citing the odes of Pindar and Sappho as expressions of it. Esoteric reading of these ancient Greek odes finds them narrowly sexual, lacking the moon-calf pain of separation, the ecstatic delight in a beloved's appearance, and the interlocked gaze that characterize being in love today.

Dante wrote of seeing Beatrice in a crimson robe: the spirit that loves within his heart began to tremble so violently it overtook his whole being, revealing the beginning and end of his life's happiness. He later described believing an angel had materialized on earth. This should not be read as mere poetic convention. In the Commedia he describes being wholly absorbed in her eyes, with the erotic charge from that gaze leading him toward Paradise — an intertwining of the erotic and the mystical entirely new to the West. Dante and Beatrice each married other people, and she died young, yet the mystical yearning and sense-of-destiny quality of modern romantic love traces back to this moment.

Sufi Origins of Romantic Love

What is understood today as romantic love — with mystical yearning and a feeling that a pairing was "meant to be" — derives from the mystic ferment of Islam. Just as Christian love of neighbour grew from Hebrew prophetic concepts of grace, the modern understanding of the sacred was illuminated by altered states of consciousness achieved by Sufi mystics such as Ibn Arabi, whose revolutionary work The Interpretation of Longing expressed sexual n terms of divine love. Sufis expressed a feeling never felt before, thereby creating the conditions for everyone else to feel it afterward.

Sexual Energy Redirected: From Intellect to Sensuality

For over a thousand years, the erotic instinct had been repressed, with sexual energies instead channelled into developing human intellect. This development reached completion by the time of Aquinas and Bacon — Aquinas's Summa Theologica, devised during overnight vigils kneeling at the altar,omprises more than two million words of densely packed syllogisms, a feat of unrelenting intellectual focus that today's greatest philosophers would struggle to match.

An impulse spreading up from Arabia then prompted people to take new delight in the material world — sensual pleasure in light, colour, space, and touch. The pot of evolution of human consciousness moved out of monkish cells and into the pleasure garden, with a scintillating sexual sheen spreading over everything.

The Troubadours of Provence

The Islamic occupation of Europe lasted longest in Spain, and as the brilliant civilization of Mauresque Spain spread northward, this new way of being reached the south of France first. By the twelfth century, Provence and the Languedoc had become the most civilized region in Europe. Provençal poets called Troubadours adapted Arabic-Andalusian poetic forms, inspired by their erotic éclat.

Helen Waddell's The Wandering Scholars (written by a non-esotericist but still regarded as the classic account) relates a story of an abbot riding with a young monk experiencing the outside world for the first time; passing some women, the abbot calls them demons, while the boy monk thinks them the fairest things he ever saw — illustrating the shift in perception underway.

The first Troubadour to surface in conventional history was Guillaume, Count of Poitiers and Duke of Aquitaine, who began composing tender, yearning love songs upon returning from the Crusades. Though this early flowering was courtly, it spread through all classes — Bernart de Ventadorn was a baker's son, Pieral a furrier's son. Poetry filled with vernacular objects: toads, rabbits, farm machinery, pubs, tumbling pigeons, crackling thorns, and a cheek pillowed upon an arm.

The Troubadour poet Arnaud Daniel, whom Dante called "il miglior fabbro," boasted of "hunting hares with an ox, gathering the winds and swimming against the tide" — topsy-turvy language characteristic of esoteric thinkers describing the powers initiation had given him.

The Romance of the Rose and Rose Symbolism

The Roman of the Rose was the most influential literary work of its age, describing a castle surrounded by a sevenfold (and therefore planetary) wall covered with emblematic figures; only those who can explain their meaning are admitted to the garden of roses.

The rose, the most popular Troubadour symbol, was probably derived from Sufism, where it symbolized (among other things) the entrance to the spirit worlds and an obvious allusion to the chakras. In the story of the Nightingale and the Rose, the bird represents the human spirit's longing for the divine, though an undeniable sexual level of meaning connects to the sensual, fleshy qualities of the rose itself. Ezra Pound believed this ubiquity signals the presence of esoteric, perhaps alchemical, techniques of sexual ecstasy. Guillaume of Poitiers wrote of wanting to retain his lady to refresh his heart "so well that I cannot age," claiming a man who succeeds in possessing the joy of his love will live a hundred years.

Love as Social Subversion

The Troubadours crossed class barriers and reversed the traditional subjection of women to men — in their poetry, men enslave themselves to women. Marriage had functioned as an agent of social control, but the Troubadours encouraged a new form of love that was spontaneous rather than arranged, flowing between individuals of different social status. Love became subversive, like the secret societies themselves, and being in love in this new way made people feel more fully alive — a new and intense form of consciousness.

Love as Initiation

In Troubadour poetry, love could be reachely by successfully negotiating trials — passing through hell and high water, finding passage through a labyrinth, combat, slaying wild beasts, solving riddles, choosing the right casket. The lover, pale and tortured by doubt, trembles when finally admitted to the beloved's presence; in consummation he achieves an altered state of consciousness conferring supernatural powers. All true lovers, it is said, know that when they gaze deeply into each other's eyes they really are touching each othe

Thus the experience of falling in love was introduced into human consciousness by initiates, and being in love was given the deep structure of the initiation process itself — full of initiatic symbolism.

The Sexual Root of the Renaissance

At root, the impulse behind the birth of the Renaissance was sexual. The outrageouslaim here is that all of human consciousness transformed and moved to another evolutionary level simply because a few people performed the sexual act in a new way — they made love for the first time. This raises a genne question: when reaching the altered state of orgasm, can one think, or is orgasm inimical to thought? The same question applies to mystical ecstasy. Secret societies and heretical groups such as the Cathars, Templars, and Troubadours taught techniques of mystical ecstasy, raising the concern of whether the hard-won faculty of human thought would be strong enough to survive these ecstasies.

Dante's Commedia: Cosmic Expansion of Love

In the Commedia, Dante took the erotic-spiritual impulse of the Troubadours further, expanding his love for Beatrice to embrace the whole cosmos. At the poem's outset, Dante finds himself lost in a gloomy wood in middle age and is met by Virgil, one of the great initiates of the ancient world, who leads him through a portal inscribed "Abandon All Hope Ye Who Enter Here."

Virgil guides Dante through an underworld resembling that of the Aeneid: crossing the River Acheron, entering the realm of shades, encountering Minos (judge of the dead) and Cerberus, entering the city of Dis, meeting the Furies and the Minotaur, walking the banks of the Lake of Blood (where Attila the Hun is immersed), traversing the Wood of the Harpies and a burning plain of sand, meeting the wizard Michael Scott and Nimrod, and finally seeing what first appears to be a windmill but is really Lucifer's wings.

Dante's Real-Life Initiation

Dante's contemporaries would have understood this first part of the poem as describing a real underground initiation journey, likely involving ordeals and ceremonies similar to those undergone by the knight Owen in Donegal (described in an earlier chapter). "Virgil" may have masked Dante's actual initiator, a scholar named Brunetto Latini, who as an ambassador to Spain met savants from both Hebrew and Arab traditions. Latini's work The Book of Treasure included occult teachings on the planetary qualities of precious stones.

Dante's cosmology is often under-appreciated by the uninitiated: the rungs of hell spiral downward in one direction, and the corresponding rungs are characterized by planetary qualities. The Commedia is written to be read on several levels — astrological, cosmological, moral, and (some say) alchemical. In the ancient world the underworld was coeived as seven-layered or seven-walled, as depicted on Cretan coins showing the labyrinth of Minos, and echoed in Origen's account of the Ophites invoking seven demons guarding seven gates of the underworld. The closest known model for Dante's underworld is now recognized as Sufi master Ibn Arabi's account of Mohammed's journey into other worlds in the Fotuhat. Like the Fotuhat and the earlier Egyptian Book of the Dead, the Commedia functions simultaneously as a guide to the afterlife, a manual of initiation, and an account of how life in the material world — as much as the afterlife — is shaped by stars and planets.

Purgatory and Hell as States Constructed in This Life

The Commedia demonstrates that bad behaviour in this life already constructs a Purgatory or Hell in another dimension intersecting with everyday life — suffering already tormented by demons even if unseen. Failing to aspward through heavenly hierarchies, "making do" with purely earthly successes and pleasures, means one is already in Purgatory.

Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray parallels this: Dorian keeps a painting that decays as he plunges into debauchery while he himself remains unlined, until decay finally afflicts him all at once. Dante's vision is grander because he shows not only that individuals create heaven and hell within, but also what misdeeds do to the very structure and texture of the world — turning the world inside out to reveal the hideous effects of innermost thoughts and secret deeds. According to Dante, everything done or thought materially alters the universe. Umberto Eco called the poem "the apotheosis of the virtual world."

Giordano Bruno's Esoteric Cosmology

Giordano Bruno, executed at the Cao dei Fiori in Rome, is commonly assumed to have been burned for championing the scientific view that the earth revolves around the sun. In fact, his esoteric views were what truly frightened the Church. His experiences of the spirit worlds led him to claim an infinity of interlocking universes and dimensions, invoking the authority of the "Pythagorean poet" Virgil to support his belief that the human spirit could travel between universes but would eventually "desire to return to the body" in accordance with the laws of reincarnation.

Gemistos Plethon and the Florentine Revival

In 1439, a mysterious stranger named Gemistos Plethon slipped into the court of Cosimo de' Medici in Florence, carrying lost Greek texts of Plato along with various neoplatonic texts, Orphic hymns, and esoteric material purporting to date back to the Egypt of the pyramids. Plethon came from Byzantium, where an esoteric neoplatonic tradition survived from early Church fathers such as Clement and Origen — a tradition Rome had repressed.

Plethon fired Cosimo's imagination with the idea of a lineage of universal but secret lore extending back beyond these early Christians to Plato, Orpheus, Hermes, and the Chaldean Oracles, whispering of a perennial philosophy of reincarnation d personal encounters with the gods of the hierarchies achievable through ceremony and the ritual singing of the Hymns of Orpheus. This appeal to vivid, personal experience is what inspired the Renaissance. Cosimo employed scholar Marsilio Ficino to translate Plethon's documents, initially Plato, but upon learning of the Egyptian material, instructed Ficino to set Plato aside and translate the Egyptian texts instead.

Imagination as Magical Technique

The spirit Plethon introduced through his translations of the hermetica spread quickly among the cultural elite. Giordano Bruno captured this fresh, vital relationship with the spirit worlds in his writing on love: "excessive sweat, shrieks which deafen the stars, laments which reverberate in the caves of Hell, tortures which afflict the living spirit with stupor, sighs which make the gods swoon with compassion..." — a new note in literature.

Renaissance literature was lit up by stars and planets, with great writers invoking this energy through active, intelligent use of imaginati. Frances Yates (like Waddell, not an esotericist by her own account, though her meticulous research at the Warburg Institute provides detailed understanding of Renaissance esoteric discoveries) documented how these ideas inspired art and literature. Ficino's translations of hermetic texts described the fashioning of images in esoteric terms: if the spirit is intent upon the work and the stars through imagination and emotion, it joins with the very spirit of the world and the rays of the stars through which the world-spirit acts. In practical terms: imagining as fully and vividly as possible the spirits of planets and stellar gods allows the power of that spirit to flow through the imaginer.

Renaissance Art as Talismanic Practice

Where the Middle Ages was the great age of magic, esoteric thinkers and occultists began constructing mental images which gods and spirits could inhabit and animate, just as ancient temple-builders manufactured statues as bodies for disembodied beings. Renaissance Italian artists with esoteric beliefs recreated these magical mental images in paint and stone.

Whereas grimoire dissemination in the Middle Ages had been wholly underground, the more widely published hermetic literature of the Renaissance gave instructions for constructing talismans designed to draw down influences from the spirit worlds, taken up by artists of the day. Hermetic literature explained that occult influences were more effective when constructed of metals appropriate to the spirit invoked — gold for the sun god, silver forhe moon god — with particular colours, shapes, hieroglyphs, and sigils revealed as sympathetic to particular disembodied beings.

An art critic noted Sandro Botticelli's "predilection for minor tones" and lighter colours, suggesting an ethereal quality as if depicting beings from another realm not yet fully materialized. Ficino'influence appears in Botticelli's Primavera, which illustrates the creation of matter through successive emanations of planetary spheres from the cosmic mind — a painting that has shown a remarkable propensity to live d breathe in viewers' minds ever since.

Neoplatonic Renaissance artists believed they were rediscovering ancient secrets, following Plato's view that all learning is a process of remembering — that human minds are protrusions of a great central cosmic mind into the material world, and everything ever experienced or thought is held in the memory banks of that cosmic mind, or lives in a sort of eternal now.

Genius and Divine Inspiration: Raphael

With the Italian High Renaissance comes the idea of towering genius — Botticelli, Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo — set apart by the magnificence and clarity of their visions, a continuation of the tradition of ecstatic visions of Joachim and St Francis. Like the saints, great artists were sometimes mouthpieces for great spiritual beings; according to esoteric tradition, the painter Raphael was directly inspired by the Archangel Raphael, his hand divinely guided.

A stranger, more mysterious tradition holds that the individuality who incarnated as Raphael had previously incarnated as Johnaptist. According to Steiner, this explains why Raphael painted no major works depicting events after John the Baptist's death — his masterpieces of the Madonna and child, with their uniquely compelling quality, were in effect painted from memory.

Leonardo's Circle: Pacioli and Alberti

Many magi lived in High Renaissance Italy alongside Leonardo, often working within the closed brotherhood of an artist's studio where artistic and spiritual progress were guided together. Mathematician a Hermeticist Luca Pacioli, the first to write openly about the secret formulae behind the Venusian pentangle, was one of Leonardo's teachers regarding "divine proportion."

Architect Leon Battista Alberti, of an older generation, influenced Leonardo (whose notebooks mention him and whose library contained his books). Alberti designed the Rucellai Palace and the façade of Santa Maria Novella in Florence, and authored Hypnerotomachia Poliphili — "the lover of many things in his struggle for love in a dream" — one of the strangest books in Italian literature.

The Hypnerotomachia as Architectural and Alchemical Manifesto

The hero Poliphilo, about to embark on an adventure, instead fanto a dream and pursues his beloved through a landscape of dragons and monsters, through a labyrinthine course into marvellous buildings that are half-stone, half-living organism — a temple's interior appearing as its viscera. Alberti's obsession with nature and natural forms appears similarly in the spiritually expressive landscape forms of Leonardo's two versions of the Virgin of the Rocks, a clear mark of Alberti's influence.

On one level, the Hypnerotomachia is an architectural manifesto: Alberti proposes that Renaissance architecture should have the logic of a dream rather than slavish adherence to precedent, with architects operating in a free state of mind inspired by combinations of forms suggested by altered states of consciousness — a controlled thought-experiment facilitating new ways of thinking generally, not only in architecture.

The channelling of sexual energy becomes explici the story's end, when the hero is united with his beloved in mystic rites in the Temple of Venus. His beloved stirs a cistern with a flaming torch, causing Poliphilo to fall into a trance. A shell-shaped basin of whale sperm, musk, camphor oil, almond oil, and other substances is set alight; doves are sacrificed; nymphs dance around an altar. When the beloved rubs the ground at the altar's base, the building convulses like an earthquake and a tree bursts from the altar's top; the couple taste its fruit and are transported into an even higher state of consciousness. The volcanic power of libido is channelled by the priestess-adept so that all prohibitive rules of behaviour, morality, creativity, and even the laws of nature are inverted.

The Mona Lisa and the Return of Isis

The Mona Lisa may be the most mysterious of Italian Renaissance masterpieces. Nineteenth-century art critic and esotericist Walter Pater wrote of it evocatively: "Hers is the head upon which all 'the ends of the world are come'... She is older than the rocks among whom she sits... she has been dead many times and learned the secrets of the grave and has been a diver in deep seas..." — hinting, perhaps, at deeper knowledge.

Earlier chapters described how the moon separated from earth to reflect sunlight and make human reflection possible, and how in 13,000 BC Isis thdrew from earth to the moon to become mistress of this process of reflection. At the start of the fifteenth century, after aeons of cosmic preparation, this evolutionary step in consciousness finally occurred, and Leonardo's masterpiece is an icon in human history because it captured that exact moment. In the face of the Mona Lisa is seen, for the first time, the deep joy of someone exploring her inner life, free to detach from the world of the senses and roam within — what Tolkien elsewhere called "an unencumbered, mobile, detached inner eye."

In his Treatise on Painting, Leonardo recommends working oneself into a state of receptivity to imaginative imagery, in which cracks and stains on old walls can evoke or invoke gods and monsts. The Mona Lisa thus creates a magical space that the spirit of Isis may inhabit — created, like the Lohan in the British Museum, so that if one communes with it, it will speak.

Joan of Arc: Direct Spirit Guidance in History

Far from the Italian courts, in the unsophisticated north of Europe, a different spirit made itself felt. At twelve or thirteen, a girl in a rustic cottage in France's Loire Valley began hearing voices and seeing visions. The Archangel Michael appeared to Joan antold her she would have spirit guides; she was initially reluctant, preferring to spin by her mother's side, but the voices grew insistent, telling her of her mission — to find the Dauphin at Chinon when an invading English army threatened Orleans, and lead him to be crowned at Rheims Cathedral.

At the Dauphin's court, he teed her by having a courtier pretend to be him on the throne, but Joan saw through the trick and addressed him directly. Convinced, he equipped her with a white horse and armour, which she wore continuously for six days and nights. She saw a vision of a sword hidden in a church, and the sword she described — with three distinctive crosses — was found behind thtar of the Church of St Catherine de Fierbois, exactly as described.

Joan's Military Success and Betrayal

When great spirit-world beings bring power to bear on an individual, that individual becomes seemingly undeniable — nothing could stop Joan even against overwhelming odds. On 28 April 1429, when Joan arrived outside occupied Orleans, English troops retreated before her and her small band; only five hundred supporters defeated an English army of thousands, in a way her own captains called miraculous. At her urging, the Dauphin was crowned King of France at Rheims — her mission accomplished in under three months.

George Bernard Shaw, deeply interested in esoteric philosophy, wrote that behind events "there are evolutionary forces which transcend our ordinary needs and which use individuals for purposes far transcending that of keeping those individuals alive and prosperous and respect and safe and happy."

Betrayed by her own people, Joan was sold to the English and questioned closely on her voices. She stated they were sometimes accompanied by visions and bright lights, that they advised, warned, and gave her detailed instructions several times a day, and that she could ask their advice and receive detailed answers. Such easy, deep familiarity with the spirit worlds outside Church authority was characterized as witchcraft, and on 30 May 1430 Joan was burned at the stake in Rouen. An English soldier turned to another and said, "We have burnt a saint." It was as if the spiritual powers that had made her inviolable suddenly deserted her, allowing the forces of opposition to overwhelm her all at once.

Joan's Historical Legacy

Although the English regarded Joan as the enemy, the secret-history perspective holds that England ultimately benefited most from her divinely inspired actions. France and England had been locked in conflict for centuries; though England had the military upper hand at the time of Joan, it was culturally dominated by France in language and literature. Without Joan's severing of France and England, the distinctly English contributions to world history — the psychological realism of Shakespeare and the detached, tolerant philophy of Francis Bacon — would not have been possible.

Dürer and the Northward Shift of Consciousness

Albrecht Dürer, returning to Germany after a trip to Italy where he was initiated into the esoteric lore of the painters' guilds, would go on to produce Apocalypse-inspired woodcuts and a self-portrait as an initiate holding a flowering thistle sparkling with dew — "the sweat of the stars" — signifying his opening organs of spiritual vision. On his journey he stopped to paint a clump of turf in watercolour — the first still life ever painted, with nothing preceding it in art history; before Dürer, no one had truly looked at a rock and clump of grass the way we take for granted today. His journey signals the evolutionary impulse for human consciousness moving north, as newly powerful nort, at odds with the narrowly Catholic south, became vehicles for new forms of consciousness.

The Iconography of the Fool

In The Zelator by David Ovason, Mark Hedsel gives an analysis of the iconography of the Fool, appearing in the frontispiece of the first edition of Gargantua and Pantagruel (1532) and in the Tarot. The Fool follows "the Nameless Way": the stick across his shoulder represents the vegetable dimension of his being, positioned between the spiritual part above and the animal part below, where a dog clawing at his leg represents unredeemed and corrupted animal elements. The unredeemed part of his vegetable body is represented by the burden in his sack. His three-pointed hat alludes to higher bodies yet to evolve — the transformed animal, vegetable, and mineral bodies — with his upward gaze represeg aspiration toward these; while his beard represents a downward tug, the upward swoop of his hat shows the Third Eye on the point of opening.

Rabelais and the Way of the Fool

François Rabelais, born toward the end of the fifteenth century, walked the streets of Chinon some fifty or sixty years after Joan's footfalls faded, his life and work animated by the pirit of the Troubadours. While Dante wrote with yearning for spiritual heights, Rabelais's delight appears, at first glance, entirely in the material world. His novel Gargantua and Pantagruel tells of giants rampaging around the world with gigantic appetites, giving the Troubadours' joy in everyday objects a humorous new twist — famously including a long, absurd list of objects for wiping one's bottom (a lady's velvet mask, a page's bonnet, a cat, sage, fennel, spinach leaves, sheets, a chicken, a cormorant, an otter).

The long struggle to wake up to the material world, begun with Noah, is completed in Rabelais with sheer delight. Love of light, laughter, food, drink, wrestling, and love-making drives his densely packed, punchy prose. The Church's world-denying philosophy is shown to be unhealthy; Rabelais's advice was to "laugh and face it out boldly whatever it may be," treating laughter, joiness, and good humour as a cure for mind and body alike.

The Fool as Mystic: Initiatic Undercurrents in Rabelais

For Rabelais, love of objects and love of words go hand in hand, with a profusion of things and newly coined words tumbling off the page, yet there is a sly initiatic undercurrent for those who look for it — Rabelais is a mystic, but not in the otherworldly style of the Middle Ages.

Troubadours had written of the madness of being in love, some describing themselves as foo and madmen, meaning they had found new ways into the spirit worlds and, upon returning, saw life upside down and inside out. Rabelais turned this way of seeing into narrative, creating a subversive style of humour that would characterize later initiatic writers such as Jonathan Swift, Voltaire, Lewis Carroll, and André Breton. Unable to take seriously conventional assumptions, conventions, and morality after rampaging through the spirit worlds, his heroes found the Abbey of Thelema, inscribed with "Do what thou wilt" above its gate — a comy of initiates whose transformed consciousness places them beyond good and evil.

The Alchemical Fountain and the Symbolism of Wine
