At the end of Gargantua and Pantagruel, after voyages through many wonders — battling cat-people, armies osausages, windmill-eating giants — the heroes reach a mysterious island. Twentieth-century alchemist Fulcanelli explained this arrival as Rabelais's heroes entering the Matrix. They are led to an initiation chamber in an underground temple — stories of going underground should always alert readers to occult physiology being referenced, since the journey underground is a journey inside the body.

At the temple's deepest centre stands a sacred fountain of life. Fulcanelli noted Rabelais allowed his esoteric, alchemical interests to surface in describing this fountain, with seven columns dedicated to the seven planets, each planetary god carrying appropriate precious stones, metals, and alchemical symbols — Saturn with a scythe and a crane at his feet, Mercury described as "fixed, firm and malleablgnifying semi-solidification in alchemical transmutation.

What flows from the fountain, and what the pilgrims drink, is wine. Rabelais wrote: "Drinking is the distinguishing character of humanity... by wine we become divine, for it is in its power to fill the spirit with truth, learning and philosophy." In oriental occult physiology, wine symbolizes secretions within the brain streaming into consciousness during ecstatic states; some twentieth-century Indian scientists suggested that "wine" in Vedic texts referred to dimethyltryptamine, the enzyme streaming from higher regions of the cerebellum discussed in relation to shamanism. Swami Yogananda similarly spoke of neuro-physiological secretions he called "blissful amrita," the pulsating nectar of immortality bringing moments of heightened consciousness enabling direct perception of the great ideas weaving together the material world. Sufi master Sheikh Abdullah Ansari wrote: "Oh Lord, intoxicate me with the wine of Thy love."

Chapter 20: The Green One behind the Worlds: Columbus • Don Quixote • William Shakespeare, Francis Bacon and the Green One

Columbus and the Templar Legacy

When Christopher Columbus reached mouth of the Orinoco in 1492, he believed he had found the Gihon, one of the four rivers flowing out of Eden, writing home that "there are great indications suggesting the proximity of the earthly Paradise." The same impulse driving the scientific revolution — a hunger to discover everything about the material world — was simultaneously fueling voyages of exploration. Hopes of a New World were bound up with expectations of a new Golden Age, though the gold ultimately found was of the more earthly kind.

Columbus's Templar connections have been exaggerated. He married a daughter of a former Grand Master of the Knights of Christ (a Portuguese order that emerged after the Templars were driven underground), and his ships bore the distinctive red Templar "patte" cross. However, the Knights of Christ did not continue the independent spirit-world commerce that had provoked the Papacy's persecution oe original Templars. Rome, and orders like the Knights of Malta, simply adopted the glamorous Templar mystique for their own purposes rather than its substance.

Columbus wrote to Queen Isabella hoping to find a "barrel of gold" to fund the reconquest of Jerusalem, mirroring her and Ferdinand's recent reconquest of Granada. He did not foresee that this gold would instead fund conflict against a rival much closer to home — one with far stronger claims to being the true spiritual heir of theemplars. The battle for control of the world was being waged not just geopolitically but in the spirit worlds, for the whole spirit of humanity.

Don Quixote as Esoteric Allegory

Cervantes and Shakespeare were near-exact contemporaries, both dying on the same date — 23 April 1616.

Don Quixote, the elderly knight who mistas windmills for giants and a peasant girl (Dulcinea) for an aristocratic maiden, appears at first as knockabout comedy, but the tone deepens into strange magic. On one level he clings to dying chivalric ideals; on another he regresses into a "second childhood" where imaginings feel more real — which, in esoteric philosophy, they genuinely are. Some Spanish scholars argue, based on close textual analysis, that Don Quixote is an allegorical commentary on the calistic Zohar (Book of Splendour).

The Cave of Montesinos episode

At the novel's core is an initiation account marking the shift from simple comedy into something troubling and ambiguous:

  • Sancho Panza lowers Don Quixote on a hundred-fathom rope into the Cave of Montesinos.
  • At the bottom, Don Quixote falls into a deep sleep and awakens in a beautiful meadow where, unlike in an ordinary dream, he can think reasonably.
  • He meets a strange old man in a green satin hood — Montesinos, genius of a crystal palace — who says he has long been expected.
  • Montesinos shows him a knight bewitched by Merlin, prophesied to be revived by Don Quixote himself, who will thereby restore knight errantry.
  • On returning to the surface, Don Quixote insists he spent three days underground and touched and saw ething, though Sancho says barely an hour passed. Sancho dismisses this as foolishness.

The deeper meaning

The whole novel plays on enchantment, illusion, and disillusion at ever-deeper levels, its meaning never explicitly stated. Its real subject is the role of imagination in forming reality: material reality is only one of many layers of illusion, all shaped by our deepest imaginings. The implication — a practical application — is that if we can locate the secret source of our imaggs, we can control the flow of nature. By the novel's end, Don Quixote has subtly changed his surroundings through this power.

This echoes an earlier principle: when in love, we choose to see good qualities in the beloved, and our good-heartedness strengthens those qualities — while the reverse holds for those we despise, whbecome more despicable. Cervantes wrote at a historical turning point when people no longer knew for certain that the world is fundamentally spiritual and good. His message: if, like Don Quixote, we good-heartedly choose to believe in the world's essential goodness — despite fortune's blows and the absurd, slapstick tendency of things that seems to mock such beef — that decision to believe will help transform the world in a genuinely supernatural way. Don Quixote's reckless, extreme, painful commitment to good-heartedss has earned him the title "the Spanish Christ," and his influence on world history has been as great as if he had really lived.

The Shakespeare Authorship Mystery

The documentary record of William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon is sparse: born 1564, educated at the village school, worked as a butcher's apprentice, caught poaching, moved to London to become a bit-part player in a company once under Francis Bacon's patronage, and died leaving his wife his "second best bed." His contemporary Ben Jonson sneered that he knew "small Latin and less Greek" — raising the question of how such a man produced a body of work saturated in the era's erudition.

Candidates proposed as the true author include:

  • The seventeenth Earl of Oxfor(his patron)
  • Christopher Marlowe (on the theory his 1593 death was faked, coinciding with when Shakespeare's plays began appearing)
  • John Donne — American scholar Margaret Demorest noted striking parallels: similar portraits, matching nicknames ("Johannes factotum" / "Johannes Factus"), shared idiosyncratic spellings (both use "cherubin" for "cherubim"), and the fact that Donne's publications begin exactly as Shakespeare's cease

Francis Bacon as leading candidate

Born in 1561 into courtier family, Bacon was an infant prodigy: at age twelve his masque The Birth of Merlin was performed before Queen Elizabeth I, who fondly called him her "little Lord Keeper." A small, sickly child, he was teased with the nickname "Hamlet" ("little ham"). Educated at Oxford, when political ambitions were repeatedly blocked despite the Queen's early favor, he redirected his ambition toward building an "Empire of learning," conquering every branch of human knowledge, earning the title "wonder of the ages." His major works include The Advancement of Learning, the Novum Organon (proposing a radical new scientific method), and The New Atlantis (a vision of a new world order partly inspired by Plato's Atlantis, hugely influential on later esoteric groups). Under James I he finally achieved his ambition, becoming Lord Chancellor — the second most powerful post in the land — with responsibility for distributing land grants in the New World.

Bacon belonged to a secret society called the Order of the Helmet. In The Advancement of Learning he wrote of a tradition of transmitting parables through a chain of succession carrying hidden meanings about the "secrets of the sciences," and admitted fascination with secret codes and numerological ciphers. In the 1623 edition he explained the "Bilateral Cipher," which would later underpin Morse Code.

The cabalistic cipher evidence

Bacon's favored code was the ancient cabalistic cipher, under which the name "Bacon" carries the numerical value thirty-three (recall the significance of 3300 lashes in Don Quixote). Using this ciph- The phrase "Fra Rosi Crosse" can be found encoded on the frontispiece, dedication page, and other key pages of The Advancement of Learning.

  • The same Rosicrucian phrase appears in the dedication of the Shakespeare Folio, on the first page of The Tempest, and on the Shakespeare monument in Stratford-upon-Avon.
  • The rolled scroll on the Shakespeare Memorial in Westminster Abbey bears the phrase together with the number thirty-three — Bacon's number.

Shakespeare's Plays and the Foing of Interior Consciousness

Shakespeare's plays engage with altered states and the madness of love. Hamlet and Ophelia descend from the Troubadours; wise fools like Feste (Twelfth Night) and Lear's Fool — a Christ-like jester who speaks truth when no one else dares — represent the apotheosis of the Troubadour fool tradit

Characters like Gargantua, Don Quixote, and Sancho Panza inhabit the collective imagination and shape human attitudes to life, but as Harold Bloom (Yale Professor of Humanities, author of Shakespeare: The Invention of the Human) has shown, no writer has populated imagination with archetypes as thoroughly as Shakespeare: Falstaff, Hamlet, Ophelia, Lear, Prospero, Caliban, Bottom, Othello, Iago, Malvolio, Macbeth and his Lady, Romeo and Juliet. After Jesus Christ, no individual has done more to develop and expand humanity's sense of interior life — if Christ planted the seed of interior life, Shakespeare made it grow and gave everyone today the sense of containing an inner cosmos as expansive as the outer one. Great writers are architects of consciousness: in Rabelais, Cervantes, and above all Hamlet's soliloquies, we see the origins of our modern sense of personal turning points and vital decisions — before the Renaissance, such inklings could only have come from sermons.

The School of Night and the dangers of esoteric commerce

Sir Walter Raleigh belonged to a secret society called the School of Night, so shadowy that some modern critics doubt it existed, though Raleigh certainly shared esoteric ideas with Christopher Marlowe and George Chap(author of The Shadow of Night). One secret they guarded was "atheism" — though none was atheist in the modern sense of denying spirit worlds or supernatural intervention. Raleigh feared the fate of his friend Thomas Kyd, who suffered prolonged torture, disembowelling, and slow death for professing atheistic views — a stark warning of the real-world danger attached to esoteric heterodoxy in this era.

Marlowe's Faust is described as one of the most learned esoteric works in world liture dealing with the dangers of commerce with the spirit worlds. David Fideler's analysis (in Gnosis magazine) of the frontispiece to Raleigh's History of the World shows it operates on two levels: illustrating Raleigh's view of history as the unfolding of Divine Providence per Cicero's definition, and embodying the cabalistic Tree of Life with planetary correspondences at its nodes.

Alienation as the shadow side of interiority

The new interior richness carries a shadow side, seen most clearly in Hamlet's soliloquies. The new capacity for detachment — withdrawing from the senses to roam one's interior world — is double-edged, risking alienation from the world itself. Hamle"to be or not to be" paralysis exemplifies this alienation, a state far removed from Achilles' fierce desire to live in the light of the sun at all costs. This is a non-obvious warning: the very gift of interior consciousness that Shakespeare helped cultivate carries the built-in risk of existential alienation.

Evidence of Shakespeare as initiate

Shakespeare did more than any other writer in the Anglo-Saxon world to shape ideas of spirit-world beings breaking into the material world — Ariel, Caliban, Puck, Oberon, Titania. Many theatre practitioners still believe Macbeth contains dangerous occult formulae giving it the force of an actual magical ceremony when performed — a practical warning still observed in theatrical superstition today. Prospero in The Tempest is the archetype of the Magus, based on Elizabeth's court astrologer Dr Dee. A spirit spoke to Dee on 24 March 1583 about future course of nature, saying "New Worlds shall spring of these. New manners; strange Men" — closely paralleled by Miranda's line, "O wonder! How beauteous mankind is. O brave new world, that has such people in it."

Initiatic skull-meditation imagery recurs from Hamlet through Zurbarán's brooding monks to Byron's poses. These are not mere memento mori but allude to arcane techniques of invoking dead ancestors' spirits, inherited and nurtured by secret societies such as the Rosicrucians the Jesuits.

The Green Wood and rose symbolism

Entering the Green Wood of A Midsummer Night's Dream and the other comedies means re-entering the ancient animate wood described earlier in the book — an archaic consciousness in which all nature is inhabited by spirits. In art and literature generally, twisted vegetationignals entry into the esoteric, etheric dimension. Shakespeare's writing is dense with flower imagery; while critics have noted the rose as an occult Rosicrucian symbol in Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene (1589), no English writer used the rose symbol more often or more occultly than Shakespeare. Seven roses appear on the Shakespeare memorial in Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon — the number seven signaling, as elsewhere established, the Rosicruciasymbol of the chakras.

A logical-positivist aside is offered: an assertion that no conceivable evidence could disprove asserts essentially nothing (the same argument sometimes used against God's existence). Applied here, the claim "the historical personage Shakespeare wrote the plays bearing his name" asserts very little, since so little is known of the man that it has no real bearing on understanding the plays. Shakespeare, like Jesus Christ, revolutionized human consciousness while leaving almost invisible traces on the historical record.

Hidden Sufi Content in Shakespeare

Sufism was the great historical source of the rose as a mystical symbol, and its influence on Shakespeare's plays has been largely overlooked.

  • The basic plot of The Taming of the Shrew derives from A Thousand and One Nights. The Arabic title, ALF LAYLA WA LAYLA, is a coded phrase meaning "Mother of Records" — alluding to the tradition of a secret library or "Hall of Records" hidden beneath the Sphinx's paws (or in a parallel dimension), storing ancient pre-Flood wisdom. The title itself signals that secrets of human evolution are encoded within.
  • The play's main story derives from "The Sleeper and the Watcher," in which Haroun al Raschid places a gullible young man in deep sleep, dresses him as royalt and instructs servants to treat him as Caliph upon waking — a story about altered states of consciousness, with both tale and play describing methods of achieving higher consciousness.

Decoding Christopher Sly

The framing plot centers on Christopher Sly, whose name and traits are laden with Sufi code:

  • In Sufi lore, a ly" man is an initiate or brotherhood member.
  • Sly is called a "beggar" in the First Folio — a Sufi being "a beggar at the door of love."
  • Sly's line "the Slys are no rogues... We came in with Richard the Conqueror" ferences Sufi influence brought back by Crusaders from the Crusades.
  • Sly's drunkenness is a common Sufi symbol for visionary consciousness.
  • Sly is woken by a Lord — representing instruction by a spiritual master on awakening to higher consciousness.

The taming of shrewish Katharina by Petruchio allegorizes this awakening process. Katharina represents "monkey mind" (Buddhist terminology) — the restless, gibbering part of the mind distracting from spiritual reality. Petruchio uses sly methods to teach her to abandon preconceptions and think "upside down and inside out," illustrated by his vow to reinterpret her railing as song, her frowns as beauty, and her silence as eloquence.

The Green One (Elijah/Elias)

Sufis trace their brotherhood's origins beyond Mohammed, some tracing the chain of transmission back to the prophet Elijah, or "the Green One." This mystical, edgy spirit pervades both A Thousand and One Nights and The Taming of the Shrew.

The parable of the drowning men

A witness be River Oxus saw a man fall in, a dervish drown attempting rescue, and then a figure in a shimmering, luminous green robe leap in after both. On resurfacing, the green man transformed into a log that the other two clung to and floated to safety on. The witness followed the log downstream; it washed ashore and transformed back into the green-robed man, who dried instantly. Compelled to prostrate himself, the witness declared, "You must be the Green One, Master of Saints. Bless me, for I would attain" — noting the robe wamade of green fire, too dangerous to touch. The Green One replied: "You have seen too much. You must understand that I am from another world. Without their knowing it, I protect those who have a service to perform" — then vanished, leaving only rushing wind.

The Green One's presence in Elizabethan England

Robert Burton, aounger Shakespeare contemporary, wrote in The Anatomy of Melancholy that the Rosicrucian fraternity names their head "Elias Artifex," their "theophrastian master," describing him as "the renewer of all arts and sciences, reformer of the world and now living."

The esoteric tradition holds that Elijah reincarnated as John the Baptist, a return prophesied both in the Old Testament's closing words and by the initiate-prophet Joachim (who deeply influenced Rosicrucian views of history), who said Elijah would come to prepare the way for the third age. This raises the possibility that sixteenth- and seventeenth-century secret societies believed Elijah had reincarnated in their own era, protecting and guiding those with a service to perform.

Elijah and Elisha, discussed earlier as separate figures, should instead be understood in secret history as one highly evolved being capable of incarnating, discarnating, and reincarnating at will — even able to parcel out portions of his spirit or "mantle" among multiple people simultaneously, as a flock of birds turns as one under a single guiding thought. Behind the surface glitter of Elizabethan England, speaking through the minds of Marlowe, Shakespeare, Bacon, Donne, and Cervantes, lurks the Green One — spirituaster of the Sufis and architect of the modern age.

Bacon, Arabia, and the Scientific Revolution

Arabia's role extended beyond inspiring literature to inspiring science: at Haroun al Raschid's court and among the Arab peoples generally, mathematics, physics, and astronomy made great leaps forward. A deep mystical connection is drawn between the Arab peoples and the English, since the great Arabian spirit of scientific research is said to have lived again in Francis Bacon — the figure mt closely linked to Shakespeare in occult literature — and it was Bacon who inspired the scientific revolution that shaped the modern world.

Twin revolutions: inner and outer cosmos

As the inner cosmos was opened and illuminated (through Shakespeare), the material cosmos was simultaneously opened and illuminated (through con). Shakespeare revealed a world not of static character types but a crowd of fully realized, passionate, idea-driven individuals; Bacon revealed a world bursting with quiddity — infinitely various, sharply defined psical objects. These parallel worlds expanded into mirror images of one another, with inner and outer realms — previously darkly and indistinctly intermingled — now sharply separated.

Shakespeare's world is one of human values, where human happiness and the shape of human lives are always at stake. Bacoworld strips human values out entirely, focused instead on physical objects and the predictable laws they obey. Bacon devised a new method: discard as many preconceptions as possible, gather maximal data, avoid imposing patterns prematurely, and wait patiently for deeper, richer patterns to emerge — earning him the title "Father of Induction" in the history of the philosophy of science. His key realization — that observing objects as objectively as possible yields very different patterns from those structuring subjective experience — would change the face of the planet.

Chapter 21: The Rosicrucian Age: The German Brotherhoods • Christian Rosenkreuz • Hieronymus Bosch • The Secret Mission of Dr Dee

Meister Eckhart as WeNorthern Consciousness

Meister Eckhart, a shadowy thirteenth-century German mystic born near Gotha in 1260, is described as the seed of the Reformation and a new form of consciousness that would eventually lead Northern Europe to world dominance, much as Dante is regarded as the seed of the Renaissance. He entered a Dominican friary, became a prior, and succeeded Thomas Aquinas teaching theology in Paris. His major work, Opus Tripartitum, was left unfinished; he died while on trial for heresy.

Surviving sermon fragments, transcribed by listeners in Strasbourg, contain startlingly modern paradoxes: "I pray to God to rid me of God," "The eye through which I see God and the eye through which God sees me is the same eye," "God is at home. It is we who have gone out for a walk." Like a Zen master, he uses apparent nonsense to jolt fixed thinking, and he taught an oriental-style meditation involving sustained detachment from the material world and emptiness of mind — withdrawing the powers from bodily form and function so a person "laes into the oblivion of things and of himself." This oblivion, akin to Buddhist emptiness, is a void of infinite, inexhaustible possibility and a place of rebirth and creativity — but also a dangerous place, "the desert of the Godhead where none is at home," entered at one's peril rather than offering easy consolation.

Eckhart reported direct spirit-world experience with unexpected content: "When you're frightened of dying and you're holding on, you'll see demons tearing your life away. If you've made your peace, you'll see that the demons are really angels freeing you from the earth. The only things that burn us is the part you won't let go, your memories, your attachments." He is sometimes counted among "the twelve sublime Masters of Paris," echoing traditions of hidden masters and adepts — the Great White Brotherhood, the Thirty-Six Righteous of Cabalistic tradition, the Brotherhood on the Roof of the World, the Inner Circle of Adepts, the Nine Unknown.

Initiatic Transmission and the Chain of Masters

Ancient tradition holds thatxperiential knowledge of the spirit worlds passes through an initiatic chain from master to pupil — called satsong in the East — a mind-to-mind transmission rather than mere verbal instruction. Plato's notion of mimesis, and the Allegory of the Cave, are read as pointing to something similar: an imaginative image implanted in a pupil's mind that works beyond narrow rationality; Plato regarded the best poetry (citing Hesiod) as casting a hypnotic spell that transmits knowledge directly.

Asonal anecdote illustrates this: an initiate recalled his young Master in New York drawing a circle on a table and asking what he saw. When the pupil answered "a table top," the Master touched him between the eyes, and the pupil experienced a vision of a cold, white moon goddess with six faces, three eyes each, holding a skull and rosary, dancing before the vision faded to a dot — yet remained lodged inside him "like a burning seed" forever.

Secret Societies and the Search for Direct Spiritual Experience

Eckhart's direct spiritual convicti addressed a hunger organized religion could no longer satisfy, as the Church had become pedantically tied to dead letter in both theology and ritual. Loose, shadowy lay associations arose across Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland — the Brethren and Sisters of the Free Spirit, the Brethren and Siste of the Common Life, the Family of Love, the Friends of God — sometimes called "wandering stars," meeting in secret, with rumors even among the poor of mysterious strangers leading people to secret meetings or otherworldly journeys.

A notable, non-obvious point: secret schools reportedly cannot be tracked down by seekers; instead they practice a benevolent occult surveillance, sending a guide to a person only "when the time is right." A related anecdote: at a gathering of esoterically-minded academics, the true teacher present turned out to be the cleaning lady with mop and pail, not any of the professors — paralleling how Rudolf Steiner's own spiritual master was a woodcutter and herb-gatherer, underscoring that true masters may beden in humble guise.

Karl von Eckartshausen, an early theosophist, described these sages as a small number of "children of light," scattered across continents (Europe, Africa) yet bound in soul-harmony and mutual understanding beyond language, a fellowship no evil person could infiltrate without immediate recognition. A comparison is drawn between modern openness about mystical encounters with Indian gurus (e.g., Mother Meera) and modern reluctance to credit Christian mystics with comparable supernatural powers — despite ample evidence of psychic gifts in the lives of great Christian mystics, paralleling Hindu adepts.

John Tauler: The Mysticism of Everyday Life

John Tauler, a pupil of Eckhart (though not in the direct initiatic-master sense), was approached in 1339 by a mysterious layman from the Oberland o told him his preaching lacked true spirituality — a figure some Rosicrucian traditions identify as a reincarnation of Zarathustra. Tauler abandoned his life to follow him and disappeared for two years. On his return, his first attempt to preach left him unable to speak, only weep; his second attempt was inspired, described as the Holy Spirit playing on him "as upon a lute." Tauler said of his initiation: "My prayer is answered. God sent me the man lg sought to teach me wisdom the schoolmen never knew."

Tauler's teaching emphasized spirituality within ordinary labor: told a poor man asking whether to abandon work for church that "one can spin, another make shoes and these are the gifts of the Holy Spirit" — reflecting the practical, sincere character attributed to the German people. Martin Luther later praised him as offering teaching that "more fully agrees with the Gospels" than any other Latin or German source.

Categories of Spiritual Preparation: Avatars, Initiates, and Mediums

Not all initiates are mystics, and not everyone with genuine spirit contact is an initiate. Several distinct categories are described:

  • Avatars (e.g., Melchizedek) — embodiments of great spiritual beings living in constant communion with spirit worlds. Reincarnated initiates** (e.g., Isaiah) — carrying initiatic powers forward from previous incarnations.
  • Specially prepared vessels — Mozart is said to have undergone a series of short incarnations designed to only briefly interrupt his access to the spirit worlds, allowing him to retain hearing of the "Music of the Spheres" in his life as Mozart; Joan of Arc's body was prepared to be finely tuned enough for very high spirits to work through her without her being their incarnation. -ediums** — sometimes created by childhood trauma that tears the membrane between material and spirit worlds. Practical warning: most mediums cannot control or even recognize the spirits they contact; these spirits are often mischievous, feeding reliable trivial information while deliberately misleading on important matters. Unke mediums, initiates aim to communicate altered states of consciousness deliberately, either directly (as with the New York vision) or by teaching techniques for achieving them.

Christian Rosenkreuz and the Founding of the Fraternity of the Rosy Cross

The great being previously incarnated in the thirteenth century as "the boy with luminous skin" reincarnated in 1378 as Christian Rosenkreuz, born to a poor family on the Hesse-Thuringia border, orphaned at five, and raised in a convent where he learned Greek and Latin imperfectly. At sixteen he set out on pilgrimage toward the Holy Sepulchre, traveling through Egypt, Libya, Fez, Cyprus (where a companion died), Damascus, Jerusalem, and finally Damcar, where he studied three years under a Sufi brotherhood, the Ikhwan al-Safa (Brethren of Purity), and translated into Latin The Liber M (Book of the World), said to contain the past and future history of the world.

Returning to Europe, he was mocked in Spain and retreated into seclusion in Germany. Five years later he gathered three old convent friends, founding the Fraternity of the Rosy Cross. Together they wrote a book of "all that man could desire, ask and hope for" and bound themselves to six obligations:

  • Heal the sick for free.
  • Adopt local dress and customs wherever they traveled, to remain inconspicuous.
  • Return annually to the House of the Holy Spirit (Rosenkreuz's house) or send a letter explaining absence.
  • Each brother would choose and initiate a successor before death.
  • The fraternity would remain hidden for one hundred years. Four more brothers joined, bringing the total to eight, who then dispersed to the far corners of the earth to reform and transform it.

Legendary supernatural gifts attributed to the Rosicrucians included great longevity (Rosenkreuz reportedly died in 1485 aged 107), command of disembodied beings and "the secrets of nature," magical will used chiefly for healing miracles, mind-reading, mastery of all languages, projection of living images of themselves across distances, remote communication, and invisibility.

Robert Fludd's Defense and the Loss of Priestly Powers

Cabalist Robert Fludd, reputedly a scholar on the Authorized Version of the Bible under James I and possibly a Rosicrucian himself, publicly defended the Brotherhood against accusations of black magic, arguing their gifts were simply the gifts of the Holy Spirit enumerated by St Paul to the Corinthians — prophecy, miracles, tongues, visions, healing, exorcism. Europe's fascination with the Rosicrucians grew because ordinary parish priests could no longer perform such feats.

A key historical claim: priests of antiquity could once summon gods into the temple's inner sanctum, but after the Church's abolition of the distinction between soul and spirit in 869, understanding of how to reach the spirit worlds gradually eroded; by the eleventh century priests could no longer summon even visions during Mass. By the fifteenth century, the spirit worlds began "flooding back" through the portal opened by the Rosicrucians. Eckhart and Tauler had already gestured toward the material transformation of the body through spiritual practice (Eckhart: "Copper is restless until it becomes Mercury," an alchemical hint), but a more systematic account of this only emerged with Rosicrucianism.

Hronymus Bosch: Alchemy and Esoteric Cosmology in Paint

Bosch, who died in 1516 (overlapping Rosenkreuz's lifetime), is regarded as the first-rank artist whose work carries alchemical ideas closest to the surface. Little is known of his life beyond marriage, horse ownership, and contributions of altarpieces and stained-glass designs for Aachen cathedral.

Professor William Fraenger's mid-twentieth-century study reinterpreted Bosch's baffling imagery through the esoteric thought of his era, showing his paintings are deeply esoteric and actually contrary to Church dogma rather than illustrations of conventional Heaven/Hell/Apocalypse iconography. Notably, Bosch did not believe unrepentant sinners were condemned to eternal Hell; instead he depicted the spirit's post-death journey through the sphere of the moon, ascent through planetary spheres to the highest heavens, then descent again into a new incarnation — a panel of The Garden of Earthly Delights conventionally labeled "Hell" actually depicts a spirit descending from one sphere to another.

Fraenger connects Bos's Table of Wisdom (Prado) to a cross-cultural meditative technique: per Indian teaching, the Purusha (golden lord of cosmic powers) works both in the sun and in the pupil of the eye ("The Purusha in the mirror, on him I meditate" — Upanishs). Practical technique: by staring at one's own reflection mirrored in the right eye of another, consciousness can expand from the limited ego-self to contemplation of the sun-like god-self at the heart of all things. Dutch mystic Jan van Ruysbroek practiced this method, describing how self-forgetting and world-forgetting first produce sensations of vacuity and chaos, then the field of vision becomes charged with cosmic energy, and initially chaotic, dream-like images suddenly cohere meaningfully. This eye-to-eye meditation could also be practiced in a sexual context.

Mystic Mechthild of Magdeburg envisioned a future integration of sensual life into the spiritual order, an impulse she believed would take root specifically in Northern Europe, diverging from the asceticism of Ramón Lull. Esoteric grups such as the Brothers and Sisters of the Free Spirit, active during Bosch's lifetime, envisioned communities bound by love rather than law — wisely controlled love as a path to divine perfection. Fraenger's summary phrase: "Sex... is the knife blade."

Paracelsus: Rough Wisdom, Folk Medicine, and Esoteric Extremes

Paracelsus, most closely tied to the Rosicrucian brotherhood (some of his writings reportedly buried with Rosenkreuz), was born near Zurich in 1493, a strange, aggressive fire who reportedly never grew a beard and retained a youthful appearance into old age. He studied under Trithemius, Abbot of St Jacob at Würzburg, one of the era's greatest adepts (and teacher of Cornelius Agrippa), who claimed he could send his thoughts on the wings of angels over hundreds of miles and reportedly summoned the ghst of Emperor Maximilian I's dead wife at his request, verified by a mole on her neck.

Fellow pupil Cornelius Agrippa became a magic-surrounded itinerant scholar, said to travel with a demonic black dog named Monsieur that kept him informed of events within a hundred-mile radius; his De Occulta Philosophia attempted an encyclopedic account of practical Christianized Cabala, including a grimoire of spells still used by occultists today.

Paracelsus, unimpressed by library learning, sought direct experience — living among miners to learn minerals firsthand and traveling from Ireland to African crocodile swamps gathering folk remedies. Non-obvious insight: he understood that as human intellect developed, humanity would lose the instinctive knowledge of healing herbs it had once shared with animals, and he tried to systematically record this vanishing knowledge before it was lost — paralleling the later Brothers Grimm's folklore preservation.

Setting up as a doctor in Basle in 1527, he became famous (and made enemies) for miraculous cures, scorning conventional medicine and mocking Galen crudely ("sticky in Hell... they would make the sign of the cross upon themselves with a fox's tail"). He carried a swordstick rumored to contain his most potent alchemicalicine (the "azoth") in its pommel — a name for the alchemists' secret liberating fire, contained in a seed, paralleling Indian alchemy's notion of Mercury as the semen of Shiva; the swordstick is interpreted as forged from sexual desire, since semen was believed to be a net in which a spirit might land and incarnate. Paracelsus reportedly also knew secret sexual techniques performed before sleep that could loosen the "vegetable body" from the material body and invite other kinds of spirits tappear in dreams.

Cured a wealthy canon who then refused payment; when local magistrates ruled against him, friends urged him to flee, and he spent years wandering, declaring nature his true teacher: "I desire neither to live comfortably, nor do I wish to become rich... He who wants to study the book of nature must wander with his feet over its leaves."

Alongside this practical, empirical bent (which some credit as founding "modern experimental medicine"), Paracelsus's writings include markedly strange material: the Monstra, an invisible being arising from putrefying sperm; Mangonaria, a magical power allowing heavy objects to be levitated; localities inhabited by Elementals wearing human clothing and manners; teachings that during sleep the sidereal body (animal spirit) becomes free and may rise to converse with ancestors and stars, that spirits act on sleepers through dreams, that people can visit others in dreams, and that incubi and succubae feed on nocturnal emissions. In later years he prophesied the return of Elijah to "restore all things." This paradox — rigorous empirical medicine alongside wild occult claims — is presented as key to understanding the deeper character of the age.

Dr Dee: The Magus Who Sought Systematic Access to the Spirit Worlds

John Dee, born to a Welsh family in London, was a brilliant young scholar teaching Euclid in Paris in his twenties and a friend of Tycho Brahe. In the late 1570s he formed a circle called the Dionisii Areopagites with Sir Philip Sidney and Edmund Spenser (whose Faerie Queene is saturated with Rosicrucian and esoteric imagera memoir described Sidney as "seeking out the mysteries of chemistry led by Dee." Dee built a magnificent library said second only to French historian de Thou's, with Cabala central to his studies; he believed in a mathematical foundation underlying all things, encoded in his complex glyph, the Monas Hieroglyphica (esoteric scholar Fred Gettings reportedly deciphered a layer of meaning in it relating to two parallel evolutionary universes, the "Baconian" and "Shakespearean").

Dee's public standing was immense: the young Princess Elizabeth invited him to choose the astrologically auspicious date for her coronation as Elizabeth I; he helped shape Elizabethan foreign policy and the settlement of America; he owned a charter granting him ownership of the entire landmass of Canada, and coined the phrase "British Empire," helping inspire the nation's voyages of discovery.

The Descent Into Séance and the Kelley Partnership

Craving more direct spiritual experience, in 1580 Dee began working with mediums. After disturbed dreams and mysterous knockings in his house, he employed medium Barnabus Saul, who claimed to see angels in a magic crystal but was dismissed after six months. In 1582 Dee met Edward Kelley, who wore a skull cap reportedly to hide ears cut off as punishment for coining (counterfeiting), and who claimed to see the Archangel Uriel in Dee's shewstone. Hundreds of séances followed, through which Dee learned to decipher what he called the Enochian language, the speech of angels.

Warning embedded in the narrative: Dee's decline is traced directly to this partnership with Kelley. On a trip to Prague, Dee told Emperor Rudolf II he had spent forty years seeking answers no book could give, so he turned to calling on angels to intercede with God for the secrets of creation, insisting he always ensured the spirits he dealt with were good, not demonic — but Kelley's own scrupulousness is called into question: the pair boasted to Rudolf they could transmute base metal into gold, then had to flee when they failed. Kelley reportedly abused the aging Dee, forcing him inhumiliating wife-swapping, and many suspected Kelley of fraudulently inventing the angelic responses.

In 1590 Kelley received an Enochian message so terrifying he ceased the practice and severed ties with Dee. Translated, it reads in part: "The Lion knoweth not where I walk... I am deflowered, yet a virgin... I am a harlot for such as ravish me, and a virgin with such as know me not. Purge your streets, O ye sons of men..." — possibly read by Kelley as the Scarlet Harlot of Revelation, forelling the world's imminent end.

Dee ended his life in Lear-like poverty, unable to support his family, given to paranoid ranting about conspiracies. After his death a cult formed around him, with figures including diarist John Aubrey and Freemason Elias Ashmole believing he had been a Rosicrucian.

Dee's Deeper Mission: Systematizing Access to the Spirit Worlds

Beneath the popular legend lies Dee's real ambition, tied to the era's broader crisis: the Church could no longer provide direct spiritual experience, and only secret societies retained the knowledge to satisfy public demand for wonders. Dee told the Holy Roman Emperor that if his ceremonial-magic techniques were adopted, every church in Christendom could produce apparitions daily, restoring the spiritual fervor of the early Church of Clement and Origen, when cabalistic and hermetic elements were not excluded — turning the world Church back into a "magic Church." This was Dee's great evangelical vision.

Though this seems outrageous by modern standards, it must be read in context: the line between priestcraft and witchcraft was already blurred in Church practice, and to Dee the magical practices of parish priests seemed unsophisticated superstition lacking intellectual rigor and system. A neoplatonic drive toward systematic spiritual thinking had spread up from Southern Europe, influencing Trithemius, Agrippa, and Dee; Johannes Reuchlin formulated a Christianized Cabala and used cabalistic argument to "prove" Christ's divinity by showing Jesus's name encoded in the Tetragrammaton.

Des distinguishing contribution was experimental rigor combined with systematic theory: he proposed a reasoned application of specific techniques to produce spiritual phenomena on a controlled, regular, predictable basis — essentially an early scientific method applied to spirit contact. Practical detail: Dee told Rudolf II that a prescribed regimen — fasting for a set duration, specific breathing exercises repeated a set number of times at set intervals, a specific sexual practice, and pronouncing a formula at an astrologic predetermined time — would reliably produce an altered state enabling free, reasoned communication with spirit-world denizens, validated by repeatable experiment and thousands of years of precedent. In Dee, as in Bacon, early stirrings of the scientific spirit are visible — the mental faculties needed for modern science partvolved within an occult context.

Rosicrucian "Laws of Evolution" and Dee's Historical Role

Rosicrucian activity is said to be guided by knowledge of the "laws of evolution of the human race," per contemporary insider commentator Michael Maier. These deeper, paradoxical laws — echoed in Paramahansa Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi as "subtler laws that rule the hidden spiritual planes... knowable through the science of yoga" — are formulated in Rosicrn literature as: "Heaven is never where we believe it to be"; "If you cease to limit a thing within yourself... and if you withdraw from it, it will come to you"; "That which kills produces life. That which causes death leads to resurrection." These conceptions would soon surface in mainstream history and transform Western culture.

Dee's career is notable for running unusually close to the surface of exoteric history: he was openly Elizabeth I's resident "Merlin," attempted to introduce ceremonial magic into the Church via the Holy Roman Emperor, and was famous enough that playwrights depicted him expecting audience recognition — in Ben Jonson's The Alchemist and Shakespeare's The Tempest. He is framed as the first of several strange, tragic figures who would attempt to introduce esoteric doctrine to public life.

Chapter 22: Occult Catholicism: Jacob Boehme • The Conquistadors and the Counter-Reformation • Teresa, John of the Cross and Ignatius

Luther's Reformation and Its Hidden Currents

In 1517 the Pope revived the selling of indulgences to fund a lavish new basilica of St Peter in Rome. Martin Luther, a teacher at Wittenberg, nailed his objections to the door of the local church, which served as a community notice board. When Luther received a papal bull of excommunicatioe burned it before an admiring crowd, declaring "Here I stand." A groundswell in Northern Europe, especially Germany, resented demands for unthinking obedience and yearned for spiritual freedom; Luther, protected by a local lord, became the hero of that movement and Protestantism was born. Some believed Luther to be the reincarnation of Elijah, whose return had been prophesied by Malachi and later Joachim.

Luther was deeply steeped in mystical thought, particularly the teachings of Eckhart and Tauler. His closest friend and collaborator was the occultist Philip Melanchthon, nephew of the Cabalist Reuchlin, an advocate of astrology who wrote a biography of Faust. Luther himself communicated with spirit worlds on familiar terms, heard guiding voices, and once famously hurled an inkpot at a demon that had mocked him.

There are intriguing hints that Luther may have been an initiate of secret societies: he once called himself a "passed master," a phrase used by Freemasonic initiates of a certain grade, and he spoke approvingly of alchemy for its "allegory and secret meaning," recognizing its role in humanity's resurrection. He also adopted the rose as a personal symbol — though his white five-petalled rose containing a small cross is distinct from the mystic red rose of the Rosicrucians, and there is no reason to think Luther attached the same occult-physiological meaning to his emblem.

Paracelsus, an early supporter of Luther, grew disillusioned when Luther promulgated predestination, which struck Paracelsus as old Roman elitism in new clothing. As a pacifist, Paracelsus was also troled that Luther, though not directly responsible for massacres of Catholics carried out once he gained political power, did nothing to stop them — becoming morbid and paranoid, fearing the very mystical fervour that had swept him to power as a threat to his authority.

Jacob Boehme: Rosicrucianism's Radical Wing Turned On

The Rosicrucians represented the extreme radical left wing of the Reformation, and the way the Lutheran establishment turned against this wing is illustrated by the percution of Jacob Boehme.

Boehme's Mysterium Magnum, a commentary on Genesis, opened vistas of cabalistic meaning that captured the popular imagination of the Protestant age, notably influencing John Milton's Paradise Lost. His detailed descriptions of the body's occult physiology stand as the clearest evidence of an independent Western chakra tradition predating the eighteenth-century influx of oriental teachings. He also produced a near-comprehensive account of correspondences between heavenly bodies, minerals, and plants — building on sketchier earlier work by Agrippa and Paracelsus. This achievement is remarkable given that Boehme was almost completely uneducated. His biblical interetation, reading creation as a series of alchemical separations, is anticipated by Fludd, though no evidence suggests Boehme ever read him.

Born in 1575 to illiterate parents, Boehme was apprenticed to a cobbler. A stranger once entered the shop, bought boots, then called Boehme by name and prophesied to him in the street: "Jacob, thou art yet but little, but the time will come when thou shalt be great and the world shall be moved at thee... thou must endure much misery and poverty and suffer persecution. But be courageous and persevere, for God loves thee." The stranger vanished and was never seen again, but the encounter left a deep impression. Boehme became noticeably more serious, was thrown out by his master, worked as a journeyman, and eventually opened his own shop.

His first illumination came while sitting in his kitchen: sunlight reflecting off a pewter plate blinded him temporarily, and then everything — the table, his hands, the walls — became transparent. He realized ordinary air, though thought of as transparent, is actually cloudy; now it cleared entirely and whole spirit worlds opened before him in every direction. He saw his own body become transparent and realized his center of consciousness had floated free, moving into the spirit worlds — making him, like St Paul, Mohammed, and Dante before him, someone who journeyed through spiritual hierarchies while slive.

Boehme was physically unimpressive — short, with a low forehead — but his blue eyes began to shine with special luminosity. People who met him were struck by his ability to see into their past and future, and he could sometimes speak languages from different parts of the world and different eras. A second illuminationurred while walking through fields, giving him direct experiential access to the mystery of creation; he later wrote, "In one quarter of an hour I saw and knew more than if I had been at university for many years." This did not contradict his Lutheran, Bible-based beliefs but clarified and illuminated them with new dimensions of meaning.

What distinguishes Boehme's writing is its description of these teachings as urgent, personal experience. He originally wrote Aurora merely as an aide-mémoire for one of his mystical experiences, but a local nobleman had copies made, one of which reached the local pastor of Goelitz. Apparently jealous of someone who evidently knew far more of the spirit worlds than he did, the pastor accused Boehme of heresy, threatened him with prison, and eventually drove him from town under threat of being burned alive.

Shortly after his expulsion, Boehme called his son Tobias to his bedside, asked if he could hear beautiful music, and asked that the window be opened so they could hear it better. He then said, "Now I go hence to Paradise," sighed deeply, and died. When once asked where the spirit goes after death, Boehme answered with something of Eckhart's Teutonic Zen: "It has no need to go anywere. The spirit has heaven and hell within itself. Heaven and hell are within one another and are to one another as nothing."

The Conquistadors: Two Forms of Consciousness in Collision

The mutual incomprehension between Boehme and the pastor of Goelitz — two radically different forms of consciousness eyeing each other across the village green — played out on a vastly greater and more tragic scale on the other side of the world.

Less idealistic men followed in Columbus's wake. In 1519 Hernando Cortés, sailing thetan coast, established a base called Veracruz. He and his fellow Spaniards had heard rumors of fabulous Aztec wealth, and were astonished when an ambassador of the ruler Moctezuma arrived bearing gifts: a gold image of the sun as large as a cartwheel, an even larger silver moon, a helmet overflowing with gold grains, and a great headdress of quetzal feathers. The ambassador explained these were offerings meant for the god Quetzalcoatl, who had long ago left earth to dwell on the moon. The Conquistadors realized that bearded, helmeted, fair-skinned Cortés resembled prophetic depictions of this god, and — coincidentally, as they saw it — had arrived at precisely the moment Aztec astrologad prophesied his return.

Some of the intricate Aztec objects were shipped to Europe, where Albrecht Dürer saw them and said their subtlety and ingenuity "made his heart sing." But Cortés's followers had baser interests. Arriving at the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan (now Mexico City), built in the middle of a lake and accessible only via easily defended artificial bridges, they were greeted by Moctezuma, who bowed before Cortés and invited them in. Cortés's plan was to kidnap Moctezuma for ransom, but when his men saw the gold throughout the palace, they impatiently killed the king — a blunder that meant they escaped only after a long battle. This marked the start of one of history's bloodiest episodes.

The Conquistadors heard rumors of a secret gold source and a gilded king, El Dorado, who bathed in liquid gold each morning; Walter Raleigh wrote of "Imperial El Dorado, roofed with gold." Co rival Francisco Pizarro sailed to Peru intending to rob an entire country protected by tens of thousands with an army of only two hundred. Like Cortés, he kidnapped the king after offering to meet unarmed, then demanded a room filled to the ceiling with gold as ransom. Natives spent weeks bringing plates, goblets, and artifacts, but when the room was nearly full the Spaniards claimed the deal had specified gold ingots and began melting down artifacts to make room. Eventually Pizarro's men, ike Cortés's, grew impatient and killed the king, sparking open war. Pushing into the capital, they found palaces with golden walls and furniture, statues of gods and animals in gold, an artificial garden where trees, flowers, and animals were made of gold, and a field three hundred by six hundred feet where every stalk of maize as silver with ears of gold.

An estimated 100,000 Aztecs died at the battle for Tenochtitlan against a mere handful of Conquistador losses; roughly two million natives died over the course of the Conquest overall. Natives eventually adopted the Europeans' treacherous fighting mentality, and Conquistador casualties rose. Despite the plunder, the Conquistadors never found El Dorado or any mine source for the abundant gold — yet the gold extracted from South America was sufficient to fund the Counter-Reformation.

The Counter-Reformation's Occult Machinery

Centered in Spain and enforced largely through the Spanish Inquisition, the Counter-Reformation made Mass attendance compulsory. Occult forces and initiatic brotherhoods operated in its service as well. The world's greatest library of occult literature is housed in the Vatican; the Church has never believed occult sciences fail to work — it has only sought to keep exclusive control over them. Sociologists attribute religion's power over people to its capacity to explain life's unknown, numinous dimensions and thereby keep dread at bay; religion must appear able to manage the dark, volcanic power of spirits that sometimes erupts into the material world.

In seventeenth-century Catholicism, esotericchings rose close to the surface — the visions of Marie des Vallées and Mary Alacoque led directly to popular Church teachings on the mysteries of the sacred heart. In present-day London, the most genuinely occult bookshop — meaning one emphasizing supernatural phenomena such as levitation, apparitions, and bodily transmogrification — is not an overtly labeled esoteric shop but the Padre Pio Bookshop in the shadow of Westminster Cathedral.

Teresa of Ávila: Direct Mystical Experiein the Church

While many in Northern Europe pursued spiritual paths outside Roman Catholicism, Spain was galvanized by a mysticism equally dark and dangerous but operating from within the Church. Teresa was born at Ávila near Madrid in 1515, probably to a family of Jewish converts. She ran away from home to join a nunnery, and hile ill drifted into a mystical state that kept recurring; she used manuals of medieval mystics and texts by Ramón Lull as guides to develop a working knowledge of mystical experience.

Teresa's mystical ecstasy upon encountering a Seraph was famously sculpted by Bernini, the great initiate-artist of the Counter-Reformation. She described the angel: "He was not tal but short, marvellously beautiful. In his hands was a long golden spear and at the point of the iron there seemed to be a little fire... that he thrust several times into my heart... he drew out the spear, leaving me all on fire with a wondering love of God... so exciting sweet is this greatest of pains." This account carries an irrepressible suggestion of sexual ecstasy, inviting comparison to the sex-magical practices of mystical societies of the same era — among the most closely guarded secrets of esoteric lore (examined further in Chapter 25).

Teresa's spiritual journals describe an ascent of the soul paralleling cabalistic accounts of ascent up the sephirothic Tree, along with out-of-body experiences and the soul's organs of spiritual vision — the chakras, which she called "the eyes of the soul." While her writing may be informed by knowledge of the Cabala, what comes through most stly is an immediate, authentic account of direct personal experience of how the spirit worlds work — a rarity outside of India, with no trace of literary artifice.

Other levitating saints include Thomas Aquinas, Catherine of Siena, Francis of Assisi, Joseph of Cupertino, and, in the twentieth century, Padre Pio and Gemma Galgani. Teresa's extreme spiritual states induced frequent levitations witnessed by many, with nuns struggling to hold her down. Importantly, bodily levitation is not necsarily a blissful experience — Teresa described being "suspended between heaven and earth and receiving no comfort from either," echoing the loneliness and spiritual aridity Eckhart had predicted, which would receive its finest expression in the work of her pupil, St John of the Cross.

St John of the Cross and the Dark Nighof the Soul

Because contemporary experience of the spirit worlds is rare, there is a danger of reading Teresa or John of the Cross as mere allegory — an idealized account of finer feelings, or even trivial mood changeframed aspirationally. But John of the Cross's account of his dark night of the soul, written after a period of solitary confinement in prison, describes not altered moods but an altered state of consciousness — as radical an alteration of mental faculties as that produced by hallucinogenic drugs.

Spaniardcharacteristically throw themselves at death: the work of their mystics, writers, and artists reflects an existential, not merely theoretical, awareness of death's immanence. They see it weaving through them, are ready to wrestle with it, and risk defeat by it to snatch what is most valuable from its jaws. This spirit finds electrifying expression in The Dark Night of the Soul, which describes the Mystic Death — a stage of initiation the candidate must pass through. After the first comforting, illuminating manifestations of spirit, the candidate is pitched into profound misery: convinced he is about to die, convinced God has abandoned him and the whole cosmos finds him despicable, no longer even wanting more than the shadowy half-exience he is shown.

John's account carries a prophetic dimension too — he was anticipating an era in which incarnated humanity as a whole would have to pass through its own collective Dark Night of the Soul. His writing helped formulate the very language later used to describe the spirit's journey through Purgatory, the sphere of the moon.

Ignatius Loyola and the Jesuits

Perhaps the most characteristic form of occultism within the Counter-Reformation was the Jesuit order. Ignatius Loyolaa professional soldier, was invalided out of the Spanish army after his right leg was shattered at the siege of Pamplona. During convalescence, reading a book on the lives of the saints, he realized his religious vocation. In 1534, while studying in Paris, he gathered seven fellow students into a brotherhood intended as highly disciplined soldiers of the Church. In 1540 the Pope recognized the order as the Society of Jesus.

The Jesuits became the Church's intellectual elite and military intelligence — servants unto death dedicated to searchinout heresy and unlawful entry into the spirit worlds. They also became the Pope's educators and missionaries, instituting a rigorous system oriented toward Rome and instilling obedience, with remarkable missionary success in Central and South America and India.

Loyola devised trials and techniques for achieving altered states, including breathing exercises, sleep deprivation, meditation on skulls, training in lucid dreaming, and active imagination — constructing an elaborate, sensual mental image a disembodied spirit might inhabit, a technique the Rosicrucians called "building a hut by the palace of wisdom." However, there is a crucial and non-obvious difference: while Rosicrucian techniques aimed at a free-willed, free-thinking exchange with beings from higher hierarchies, Loyola's spiritual exercises were designed to still the will and induce unquestioning, soldier-like obedience — captured in the prayer, "Take, Lord, and receive all my memory, my understanding and my whole will, everything I have." Despite the current dominance ondu, Buddhist, and other oriental esoteric literature in Western esoteric bookshops, Loyola's Spiritual Exercises remain the most readily available and widely published esoteric techniques from the Western tradition.

El Greco and Occult Painting

El Greco's stretched figures, with half-closed eyes contemplating inner mystery, stand within convulsive landscapes and stormy skyscapes. He portrayed not just people in altered, mystical states but conveyed a sense of what it feels like to be in that state. French art critic René Huyghe analyzed the light in El Greco's panoramic view of Toledo: while the real city is bathed in fierce, clear Mediterranean light, El Greco's vision swallows ordinary daylight in a fantastic, supernatural light. As an initiate, El Greco painted what John of the Cross described as "the dark nght of the fire of love... without a guiding light other than that which was burning in my heart."

Valentine Tomberg and Meditations on the Tarot

In 1985 an anonymously published book, Meditations on the Tarot, created a stir in esoteric circles by demonstrating, with great erudition, that tarot symbolism points to a unified set of beliefs underlying Hermeticism, the Cabala, oriental philosophies, and Catholic Christianity. It later emerged the author was Valentine Tomberg, who had been initiated by Rudolf Steiner but then left Anthroposophy to become a Catholic convert. Its underlying purpose — drawing esotericists back into the Church — becomes apparent once this history is known. Like Loyola before him, Tomberg was working to ensure the initiative in esoteric matters would not be entirely taken from Rome.

Evidence of a Secret Network

Northern European figures such as Eckhart, Paracelsus, Dee, and Boehme are often examined more or less in isolation, raising the question of whether documentary evidence supports rumors of an organized secret brotherhood like the Rosicrucians. In 1596 a man named Beaumont was convicted of magical practices by a court at Angoulême, France. The historian de Thou recorded his confession: he "held commerce witial and Heavenly Spirites," and that "Schools and Professors of this noble Art had been frequent in all Parts of the World, and still were so in Spain at Toledo, Cordova, Grenada," having formerly flourished in Germany "but for the most part had failed since Luther had sown the seeds of his Heresy." In France and England it was preserved secretly by tradition in certain gentlemen's families, with only the initiated admitted to the sacred rites.

Less than thirty years later, a series of anonymous pamphlets published in Kassel, Germany (1614–1616) purported to reveal the inside story. The first, the Fama Fraternitatis ("Rumour of the Brotherhood"), called for spiritual revolution. The second, the Confessio Fraternitatis, told the story of Christian Rosenkreuz (CRC), founder of the brotherhood, gave his rules, a revealed that his tomb had been discovered in 1604 — a door under an altar inscribed "After one hundred and twenty years I shall be opened," leading to a seven-sided mausoleum with an artificial sun above a circular table, beneath which lay CRC's uncorrupted body surrounded by books (including a Paracelsus text), clutching a scroll reading "Out of God we are born, We die in Jesus, We will be reborn through the Holy Spirit." Notably, the title page of this mphlet's first folio featured Dr Dee's occult emblem, the Monas Hieroglyphica — a detail an observant literary detective might have caught. The third pamphlet, The Chemical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreuz, was an allegorical account of initiation as a sex-magical Chemical Marriage in the tradition of the Hypnerotomachia.

These publications caused a sensation across Europe. It gradually emerged the author was a young Lutheran pastor, John Valentine Andreae, whose spiritual mentor was the famous mystic Jean Arndt, himself a disciple of John Tauler, who was in turn a disciple of Meister Eckhart.

The Dichotomy of Esoteric History

Esoteric history is frustrated by inherently sparse evidence, since successful secret societies leave scant traces almost by definition — yet the claims made for them grand: that they represent an ancient, universal, and coherent philosophy explaining the universe more adequately than any other, and that many of history's great figures were guided by it. This raises the natural question of whether such societies represent a genuine secret coalition of history's greatest geniuses, or merely the fantasy of a few marginal, none-too-bright individuals. Two seemingly parallel traditions — a largely exoteric line of great mystics (Eckhart, Tauler, Arndt) and largely esoteric network of magicians and occultists (Rosenkreuz, Paracelsus, Dee) — finally become inextricably intertwined in the single person of Valentine Andreae in 1614.

The Battle of White Mountain and the Rosicrucian Collapse

The hidden hand of secret societies rarely reveals itself, and as with Dr Dee's Lear-like sgrace, exposure to daylight changes its very nature and puts it at risk. Following publication of the Fama, the Rosicrucians emerged from the shadows to the sound of cannon and musket, fighting a bloody, hopeless battle against the Jesuits for the spirit of Europe. Conventional histories treat the manifestoes' publication as the beginning of the Rosicrucian phenomenon; in this account, they instead mark the beginning of the end of the true Rosicrucians.

The same period also saw the founding of another secret society that would dominate world affairs into the present. The institution of Holy Roman Emperor, founded by Charlemagne in 800 to hold Christendom together with the Pope's blessing, had dimmed by the early seventeenth century — no emperor had been crowned between 1530 and Rudolf II's coronation in 1576, and many German principalities had turned Protestant, undermining the notion of a united Roman Europe. Following Rudolf's death (the tolerant, occult-minded emperor whom Dee had failed to impress), a succession dispute drew the Rosicrucian brotherhood into a plot: if Frederick V, a Rhineland prince and Rosicrucian sympathizer, could be placed on the Bohemian throne, Europe might be won for Protestantism.

The Rosicrucians had cultivated James I ofngland — Michael Maier sent him a Rosicrucian greeting card, and in 1617 Robert Fludd dedicated his cosmology Utriusque cosmi historia to James, saluting him with an epithet sacred to Hermes Trismegistus. In 1612 James's daughter Elizabeth married Frederick, and The Tempest was given a special court performance with the masque scene newly inserted for the wedding. The plan was that when Frederick traveled from Heidelberg to Prague for coronation in 1619, James would defend his son-in-lawnd daughter from Catholic attack.

James did nothing when Frederick's forces were decisively defeated at the Battle of White Mountain. Frederick and Elizabeth fled Prague after so brief a reign that they became known forever as the Winter King and Queen. The ensuing Thirty Years War, waged by Ferdinand of the Catholic Hapsburg dynasty whose intellectual outriders were the Jesuits, aimed to re-establish Catholic supremacy in Europe. Five out of six German towns and villages were destroyed and the population fell from roughly nine million to four million — the Rosicrucian dream was extinguished in a carnival of bigotry, torture, and mass slaughter, leaving Central Europe a desert. Yet the urch's victory proved pyrrhic: if it truly believed itself at war with the secret societies over black magic, it may have been making the mistake of believing its own propaganda — the real enemy being the oldest enemy of all, wearing a new disguise.

Chapter 23: The Occult Roots of Science: Isaac Newton • The Secret Mission of Freemasonry • Elias Ashmole

The Hidden Continuity Between Ancient Wisdom and Modern Science

Copernicus's heliocentric thesis (1543), Galileo's falling-body experiments (1590), Kepler's laws of planetary motion (1609), and Newton's unifying mechanical theory (1670s) are conventionally presented as humanity's triumphant escape from superstition into reason. But Egyptian initiate-priests already knew Sirius was a three-star system and understood millennia earlier that the earth orbits the sun. The scientific revolution's heroes were themselves deeply immersed in anwisdom rather than opposed to it.

Copernicus acknowledged his ideas came from ancient texts. Kepler was explicit about channeling ancient wisdom, writing in Harmonices Mundi (1619): "Yes, I have stolen the golden vessels of the Egyptians to build a shrine to my God." Kepler was also a lifelong friend of Richard Beshold, a close collaborator of Valentine Andrae on the Rosicrucian Manifestoes — tying the founding of modern astronomy directly to Rosicrucian circles.

Isaac Newton's HiddeAlchemical Life

Newton, born in Woolsthorpe, Lincolnshire, never grew above five feet and was strange, eccentric, sexually confused, and lonely. As a schoolboy he lodged with an apothecary who turned out to be an alchemical adept, setting his life's path. Like Cornelius Agrippa, Newton sought to discover the complete system of the world.

  • Newton believed the secrets of life are encoded numerically in the fabric of nature, with clues hidden in numerical and linguistic codes in ancient wisdom books and ancient structures like the Great Pyramid and the Temple of Solomon.
  • He believed this was a divine test: only when humanity developed sufficient intelligence would it be able to recognize and decode these patterns — and he believed that time had arrived in his own era.
  • In Newton'cosmology, every part of the universe is intelligent, even a stone — not merely evidencing design, but possessing actual intelligence. Animal, vegetable, and mineral are not fixed separate categories but overlap and can morph into one another.
  • His cabalistic contemporary Lady Conway described this chain: "There are transformations from one species to another, as from stone to earth, from earth to grass, from grass to sheep, from sheep to human flesh, from human flesh to the lowest species of man, and from these to noblest spirits."
  • Everything in the universe strains toward greater intelligence: inanimate matter toward vegetable life, vegetable life toward animal sensitivity, higher animals toward near-human reason, and humans wait to evolve into super-intelligent beings.

Ptolemy's Spiritualosmos and the Living Seed

Ptolemy's map of the spheres, though superseded materially by Copernicus and Galileo, remains an accurate map of the cosmos's spiritual dimension — a dimension that felt more real to the ancients than the physical cosmos.

Isaac Luria, the sixteenth-century Cabalist, wrote: "There is nothing in the world, not even among silent things such as dust and stones, that does not possess a certain life, spiritual nature, a particular planet and its perfect form in the heans." This described the intelligence within a seed responding to the intelligent intention in sunlight — growth was understood as a process of the seed's intelligence interacting with the intelligence of the surrounding cosmos, not merely information contained within the seed itself.

Drawing on John Maynard Keynes's investigatn into Newton's occult worldview, Newton pondered whether distinct intelligences or centers of consciousness lay behind the material surface of things — not naive anthropomorphic angels, nor purely impersonal abstractis, but what he called "Intelligencers," a term implying volition.

The Vegetable Dimension as Gateway Between Mind and Matter

Esotericists are especially interested in the interface between animal and vegetable, and between vegetable and mineral — this interface is considered the key to understanding and manipulating nature's secrets. The vegetable dimension is the intermediary between thought and matter, the "gateway between the worlds."

  • If the world is formed by mind, there must be an explanation for how the immaterial forms the material. Traditional cultures explained this through emanations of mind — initially too ethereal for sensory perception, finer than light — from which matter eventually precipitated.
  • This ethereal dimension sits between mind (the animal dimension) and matter, producing the gradation: animal, vegetable, mineral.
  • Mind cannot order matter directly, only through the vegetative medium. Paracelsus called this malleable substance the ens vegetalis — because the mineral dimension grows out of it, minercise power over matter through this medium. This is a practical application for occultists: the vegetable dimension is the actual lever by which thought reshapes physical reality.
  • Newton's name for this medium was the sal nitrum. His alchemical notes describe real experiments testing how sal nitrum could bring metals to life — he described metal compounds coming alive in nitrate solutions and "growing" like plants, a phenomenon he called "vegetation of metals." This confirmed his lief that the universe is alive, and he privately used the sal nitrum concept to help explain gravity.

Scientists Who Were Secretly Occultists (and Occultists Who Were Practical Inventors)

Examining the hidden lives of science's heroes reveals many were deeply immersed in esoteric thought, particularly alchemy — while manfamous occultists were also practical inventors. There is no clean line between scientist and occultist, but rather a spectrum.

  • Paracelsus — revolutionized medicine with the experimental method, first isolated a named zinc, advanced medical hygiene, and formulated principles underlying homeopathy.
  • Giordano Bruno — burned at the stake in 1600 for iisting on heliocentrism, which he believed fervently because the ancient Egyptian initiate priests had held the same view.
  • Robert Fludd — occult author and Rosicrucian defender who also invented the barometer.
  • Jan Baptiste van Helmont — Flemish alchemist who reintroduced reincarnation ideas ("the revolution of humane souls") into Western esotericism, separated gases in his alchemical experiments, coined the word "gas," and coined "electricity" while studying magnets' healing powers.
  • Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz — Newton's rival in devising calculus, whose discoveries arose from cabalistic number mysticism shared with his close friend Athanasius Kircher, a Jesuit occult scholar. In 1687 Kircher reportedly resurrected a rose from its ashes before the Queen of Sweden. Leibniz provided the most detailed and credible historical account of alchemical transmutation of base metals ind.
  • Sir Robert Moray — published the world's first scientific journal (Philosophical Transactions) and was a fervent Rosicrucian researcher.
  • Robert Boyle — his law paved the way for the internal combustion engine; he was a practicing alchemist who wrote of being initiated into an "invisible college" in his youth.
  • Robert Hooke (inventor of the microscope) and William Harvey (discoverer of blood circulation) — both practicing alchemists.
  • Descartes — fathered ism yet spent considerable time tracking down and researching the Rosicrucians; he rediscovered the ancient esoteric idea of the pineal gland as the gateway to consciousness (the inner eye), and his philosophical breakthrough came to him whole in a visionary state. His famous "I think therefore I am" can be read as a recasting of Rosicrucian teaching meant to foster an independent intellectual faculty.
  • Blaise Pascal — after his death, a note sewn into his cloak recorded a precise mystical illumination experience ("FIRE") on the night of3 November 1654 — comparable to the illumination sought by monks of Mount Athos.
  • Jonathan Swift — in Gulliver's Travels (1726) predicted the existence and orbital periods of Mars's two moons, not discovered by telescope until 1877; the discovering astronomer, awed by the accuracy, named them Phobnd Deimos ("fear" and "terror").
  • Emmanuel Swedenborg — eighteenth-century Swedish visionary whose detailed accounts of journeys into spirit worlds inspired esoteric Freemasonry; he also discovered the cerebral cortex and ductless glands, and engineered what remains the world's largest dry dock.
  • Charles Darwin — attended séances and may have learned the esoteric doctrine of evolution (fish to amphibian to land animal to human) through his close association with Max Müller, translator of sacred Sanskrit texts.
  • Nikola Tesla — dismissed by one historian as "the ultimate visionary crank," patented some seven hundred inventions (fluorescent lights, the Tesla coil); like Newton, his breakthroughs arose from belief in ac dimension between mental and physical planes.
  • Thomas Edison and Alexander Graham Bell — both believed psychic phenomena were legitimate scientific research areas and were involved in esoteric Freemasonry and theosophy. Edison tried to build a radio that would tune into the spirit worlds. Even the television reportedly originated from attempts to capture psychic influences on gases fluctuating before a cathode ray tube.

Francis Bacon's Mysterious Method

Bacon's supposed great diovery — viewing sense experience objectively, stripped of preconceptions, to reveal new patterns usable for prediction and manipulation — is credited by historians as the birth of inductive reasoning and the entire scientific-industrial revolution. But Bacon's own account of discovery is stranger than this tidy narrative.

-on said: "Nature is a labyrinth, in which the very haste you move with will make you lose your way," describing the scientist as playing chess with nature, needing to trick her into giving up her secrets because nature is inherently deceptive.

  • Despite being cast as a pure materialist by modern historians, Bacon believed in "astrologica sana" — receiving magil celestial influences into the spirit, as recommended by Renaissance magus Pico della Mirandola.
  • Bacon believed in the same ethereal intermediary between spirit and matter as Newton, calling it the "Aetheric body," existing in humans "inclosed in a thicker body, as Ayrein Snow or Froath."
  • Bacon wrote that entering the "kingdom of knowledge" requires becoming "first as a little child" — implying a child-like altered state of mind is prerequisite to higher knowledge. Paracelsus expressed something similar using biblical phrasing about desiring "with his whole heart" and knocking "vehemently."
