  • Van Helmont: "There is a book inside us, written by the finger of God, through which we may read all things." Michael Maier: "To drink the interior life in a long draft is to see the higher life. He who discovers the interior, discovers what is in space." These sayings imply scientific discovery's k lies within, accessed through altered consciousness.
  • Non-obvious implication: genius may not be "next to madness" but rather next to altered states deliberately induced through esoteric training — the great founders of modern science were fascinated by ancient wisdom and altered states as a matter of practice, not coincidence.

Rosslyn Chapel and the Scottish Roots of Freemasonry

Rosslyn Chapel, near Edinburgh, built in the fifteenth century by William Sinclair, first Earl of Cahness, incorporated replicas of Solomon's Temple's twin pillars (Jakim and Boaz), anticipating every Masonic lodge in the world. A carving in its south-west corner window appears to depict a Freemasonic First Degree. Scottish lodges predate recorded English ones by at least a century. The Scottish roots of Freemasonry were deliberately covered up in the eighteenth century because they had become entangled with the Stuart dynasty's throne claims.

Freemasonry's Secret Roots and Purpose

Freemasonry presents a straight, respectable face to the world — Anglo-Saxon lodges in particular have been coy about their esoteric origins. It may seem implausible even to many Freemasons that atufficiently high initiation levels, members are taught the secret doctrine and history of the world.

Masonic lore traces the society's roots to:

  • The building of Solomon's Temple by Hiram Abiff
  • The suppression of the Knights Templar
  • Secretive craftsmen's guilds: the Compagnons Du Devoir, the Children of Father Soubise, and the Children of Father Jacques

An often-overlooked influence is the Co-fraternities, founded in the fifteenth century as lay brotherhoods affiliated with monasteries. Members pursued spiritual life while working in the community — organizing charities, commissioning art, leading holy day processions. Their secrecy was originally meant to keep charitable works anonymous, but it generated rumors of robes, secret rituals, and initiates. In France these Co-fraternities absorbed ideas from Joachim and the Cathars before being driven underground.

Modern "speculative"reemasonry is officially dated to the seventeenth century.

Elias Ashmole and the Chain of Transmission

The first recorded initiation into Freemasonry is sometimes claimed to be that of Elias Ashmole in 1646 — celebrated antiquary, collector, and founder member of the Royal Society, and one of the earliest and most influential English Freemasons.

  • Born in 1617, son of a sadler, Ashmole qualified as a lawyer and became a soldier and civil servant, as well as a restless collector of rios. The Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, built around his collection, was the first public museum.
  • In 1651 Ashmole met William Backhouse, an older man who owned a manor called Swallowfield containing an extraordinary long gallery — a treasure house of "Inventions and Rarities" including rare alchemical manuscripts.
  • Backhousenvited Ashmole to become his "son," meaning he intended to adopt him as successor and heir, promising to pass on before his death the ultimate secret of alchemy — the true matter of the Philosopher's Stone — so Ash could carry forward a tradition dating back to Hermes Trismegistus.
  • Backhouse's teaching over the next two years was slow and hesitant, but in May 1653, lying sick and unsure whether he would live, Backhouse told Ashmole "in Sillables the true Matter of the Philosophers Stone which he bequeathed to me as a Legacy" — an unusually clear, documented account of secret knowledge transmission.
  • John Théophile Desaguliers, second grand master of the London Lodge and a follower of Newton, likewise spent years studying alchemical manuscripts, reinforcing the alchemical current running through early institutional Freemasonry.
  • Freemasonic symbolism from this period is saturated with alchemical motifs — from the central notion of "the Work," to the cornerstone/philosopher's stone (ASHLAR), to the compasses and l'equerre (square).

Nostradamus's Coded Prophecy

As an aside illustrating the era's occult sophistication: Michel de Nostradamus predicted the execution of Charles I with striking accuracy in 1555. His line "CHera pAR LorS, Le is cabalistic code for "Charls Le Roy" — encoding the king's name within an apparently bland prophecy that he would be "kept in a fortress by the Thames" and "seen in his shirt." Charles wore two shirts to his execution so he would not shiver and appear afraid.

What Alchemy Actually Is

Alchemy is ancient — Egyptian texts describe distillation and metallurgy as mystical processes; Greek myths like the quest for the Golden Fleece carry alchemical meaning; Fludd and Boehme interpretedesis in alchemical terms.

  • Alchemy, like the Cabala, is a broad tradition approached through varied codes: Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt in some systems; roses, stars, the philosopher's stone, salamanders, toads, crows, nets, the marriage bed, and astrological symbols (fish, lion) in others.
  • Geographic and historical variation exists: Chinese alchemy focuses less on gold and more on the elixir of life and immortality. Third-century alchemist Zozimos wrote that gold "comes forth from creation for those who rescue and purify the divine soul chained in the elements." Early Arab texts manipulate the Four Elements; European alchemy (medieval through seventeenth century) introduces a mysterious fifth element, the Quintessence.
  • Interpretive lens: prescribed durations and repetitions in alchemical operations (distilling, applying gentle heat) parallel meditative practice, suggesting these are descriptions of subjective states of consciousness rather than literal laboratory chemistry.
  • Rosicrucian sources repeatedly suggest these operations act during sleep and the border between sleeping and waking — possibly related to lucid dreaming or carrying dream consciousness into waking life.
  • Sexual symbolism is pervasive: the "Chemical Wedding" motif, Paracelsus's references to the azoth. The Codex Veritatis (commentary on the Song of Solomon) instructs: "Place the red man with his white woman in a red chamber, warmed to a constant temperature." Tantric texts equate alchemical Mercury with sperm.
  • One interpretive school reads alchemical texts as manuals for raising the kundali serpent from the base of the spine through the chakras to activate the Third Eye.
  • A Jungian school treats alchemy as a precursor to psychology — Jung's study of alchemist Gerard Dorn supports this; Dorn wrote: "First transmute the earth of your body into water... your heart that is as hard as stone, material and lazy, must become subtle and vigilant." This combines individual faculty work (as with Ramón Lull) with moral development (as in esoteric Buddhism and Cabala).
  • A stated posin: alchemical-sexual practices genuinely exist (addressed further in Chapter 25), and some texts likely do deal with kundalini rising — but this is not considered central to the golden age of alchemy that peaked with the Rosicrucians and Freemasons. Jung's purely psychological reading, while interesting, is considered "totalluninteresting" from an esoteric perspective because it disregards journeys into spirit worlds and communication with disembodied beings.

The True Nature of the Alchemical "Work"

Bacon, Newton, and other Rosicrucian/Freemasonic adepts pursued both direct personal experience and scientific experiment. As idealists, they were fascinated by what connects matter to mind, conceiving of this connection as Paracelsus's ens vegetalis, or vegetable dimension.

  • What sustained their exploration despite the vegetable dimension being immeasurable by instruments was the belief that it had been experienced across all times and places, with an authentic ancient tradition of manipulating it that many historical geniuses had joined.
  • Bacon, Newton, and Roger Bacon developed scientific/experimental procedure to find universal laws viewing the world as objectively as possible — then applied the same methodology to life viewed as subjectively as possible.
  • Core claim: the result was a genuine science of spiritual experience — this is what alchemy actually is. The "gold" achieved at experiment's end was spiritual gold: an evolved state of consciousness that made mere metallic, worldly wealth uninteresting by comparison.

The Three Alchemical Principles Mappo the Body

In the golden age of alchemy:

  • Sulphur = animal dimension, centered in the sex organs, governing will and sexuality (intertwined in esoteric philosophy)
  • Mercury = vegetable dimension, centered in the solar plexus, the realm of feeling, and the mediator between Sulphur and Salt
  • Salt = material dimension, centered in the head, the precipitate of thinking

The Two-Stage Practical Process

Stage One: work on the vegetable dimension (Mercury) to achieve initial mystical experience — entering the Matrix, the "sea of light" that is the world between worlds.

Stage Two: the "Chemical Wedding," when soft, female Mercury makes love to hard, rigid, red Sulphur.

Practical application/technique: By meditating repeatedly over long periods on images that inspire loving feeling, a candate brings about change that sinks into the obstinate Will. It takes twenty-one days for any exercise to produce a material change in human physiology.

  • If selfish sexual desires are transmuted into living spiritual desires, the "bird of resurrection," the Phoenix, rises. A heart overtaken by these transformed energies becomes a center of power — anyone o has met a truly holy person has felt this radiating power.
  • The heart is described as an organ of perception: when we love someone, we perceive things others cannot. The alchemically transformed initiate makes a conscious, willed decision to see the entire world this way, gaining perception of how the world really works, denied to others.
  • Persisting with these exercises and purifying the barrier between self and spirit worlds (per French mystic St Martin) improves powers of perception — first the spirit worlds shine into dreams more coherently, then spiritual promptings (hunches, intuition) begin invading waking life, allowing detection of deeper laws beneath the everyday surface.
  • In specifically Christian alchemy (Ramón Lull, St Martin), the Sun-spirit transforming the body into a radiant body of light is identified with Jesus Christ. Other traditions describe the same process withouhis identification — Indian sage Ramalinga Swamigal wrote: "O God! You have shown me eternal love by bestowing on me the golden body. By merging with my heart, you have alchemized my body." These parallel reports across cultures indicate the opening of the Third Eye.

Alchemy Confers Supernatural Intelligence

The alchemical acronym VITRIOL stands for Visita Interiora Terrae Rectificando Invenies Occultum Lapidem — "Visit the interior of the earth to find the secret stone." This iuction to visit the earth's interior is really an instruction to sink down into one's own body: alchemy is fundamentally concerned with occult physiology.

  • By gaining working knowledge of his own body's physiology, an alchemist could gain a degree of control over it. Great alchemists like St Germain were said to be able to live as long as they wished.
  • On a practical level, altered states allowed figures like Paracelsus and van Helmont to solve medical problems and devise treatments beyond their era's medical understanding, by "going inside" to see the outer world with supernatural clarity.
  • In cabalistic terms, man is the synthesis of all the Holy Names — all knowledge is contained whin, if one learns to read it.
  • The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali describe powers (siddhis) including traveling the heavens and shrinking perception to the size of the smallest particle, granted to practitioners of its arcane techniques. Indian adepts still claim the ability to travel to the cosmos's far reaches and concentrate perception down to the atomic level. These same "excellencies" are proposed as what enabled ancient initiate priests to perceive the third star of Sirius, understand species evolution, and grasp the pineal gland's form and function.

A Modern Counter-Example: Francis Crick and DNA

Addressing skepticism about whether altered states can genuinely produce valid knowledge (rather than delusion or diminished intelligence):

  • Each human cell contains a double-stranded ribbon (DNA) only ten molecules wide but roughly six feet long, encoding all genetic information for that person — the most complex version of this molecule found in any living cell, carrying a coded message of roughly three billion characters that organize cells into individual human patterning.
  • Scientists detected complex relational patterns in these characters suggestive of human language, later confirmed by statistical analysis — but it was Cambridge biologist Francis Crick who cracked the code, discovering the double helix structure (with James Watson), winning the Nobel Prize and launchingern genetic medicine.
  • Key point: although Crick had no known connection to secret societies, he achieved his moment of inspiration and unlocked DNA's structure while in an altered state induced by taking LSD — paralleling the historical use of hallucinogens for higher consciousness and grasping higher realities since the Mtery schools.
  • Later in life, Crick published Life Itself: Its Origin and Nature, arguing DNA's complex structure could not have arisen by chance — echoing Newton's belief (as a fellow Cambridge figure) that the coss had encoded deep messages about our and its origins, placed there to be decoded once humanity evolved sufficient intelligence.

Closing Moral

What lies outside the collective consensus is the realm of the demonic — but this same realm is also the realm of the innovative, the evolutionary, and that which addresses the deep, unquenchable human need for the infinite. History demonstrates that those who have worked at the very boundaries of human intelligence have reached that frontier through altered states of consciousness.

Chapter 24: The Age of Freemasonry: Christopher Wren • John Evelyn and the Alphabet of Desire • The Triumph of Materialism

From Rosicrucians to Freemasons

Alchemy formed the core practice linking Rosicrucians and early Freemasons, but the outward character of the two movements differed sharply. Only eight brothers made up the original Rosicrucian brotherhood, and their "House of the Holy Spirit" was thought by many to exist on another plane entirely — later generations remained similarly elusive, hintimembership always stayed tiny. Freemasonry, by contrast, spread rapidly worldwide, recruiting thousands and then hundreds of thousands. Today a Freemasonic Lodge exists in most large towns, and although it doesn't advertise itself, outsiders generally know its location even without knowing what happens inside.

After the Rosicrucians' catastrophic attempt at direct political action ended in the Battle of White Mountain, Freemasons shifted strategy: rather than imposing reform from above, they reverted to influencing society from below, operating behind the scenes. Their aim was to help foster social conditions — tolerance, prosperity, social and economic freedom — that would bring people to a developmental stage where they'd be ready for initiation and better able to explore both outer and inner cosmos. This evoon of free will was meant to help realize the changes foreseen in Francis Bacon's New Atlantis, his vision of the perfect Rosicrucian state. Bacon had prompted people to see inner and outer cosmos as distinct, and this separation enabled an understanding of the material world that would not otherwise have been possible — an understanding that within a few decas threw a "metallic embrace" around the world through railways and mass manufacturing.

Christopher Wren, John Evelyn, and the Rebuilding of London

St Paul's Cathedral in London stands as a landmark achievement of Freemasonic collaboration. Diarist John Evelyn helped his fellow Freemason Christopher Wren with plans for St Paul's and the reconstruction of London following the Great Fire of 1666. Evelyn and Wren submitted a new street plan to Charles II that would replace the old chaotic streets with one mapped according to the pattern of the cabalistic Tree of Life — a striking practical application of esoteric geometry to civic planning. In this scheme St Paul's occupies the position of Tiferet, the "heart" of the Tree, associated with Jesus Christ in Christianized Cabala.

John Evelyn's Secret Life and the Alphabet of Desire

Beneath his respectable public image as a diarist and Royal Socty member, Evelyn concealed an esoteric double life. What he kept out of diaries written for eventual publication was that he had a "seraphic," or cabalistic, girlfriend thirty years his junior — Margaret Blagge — whom he taught secret meditation techniques. Evelyn initiated her into cabalistic exercises derived from Abraham Abulafia's imaginative manipulations of the Hebrew alphabet. The distinctive twist in Evelyn's version was that the exercises involved imagining naked bodies eroticalontorted into the shapes of Hebrew letters; through this practice Margaret began experiencing ecstatic trance states. This anticipates the twentieth-century artist Austin Osman Spare, whose "Alphabet of Desire" was built on correspondences between inner sexual impulses and outer form, manifesting as erotic, magically charged sigils or fetishes. William Blake, another Freemason, similarly depicted naked bodies shaped as Hebrew letters in his pictures. The pattern that emerges: respectable Freemasons — Wren, Evelyn, Blake — known publicly for gworks kept their esoteric interests carefully hidden.

The Triumph of Materialism

Science's great appeal was that it worked — producing testable, reliable results and tangible benefits, in sharp contrast to religion, where the Church no lonr functioned as a reliable source of spiritual experience. Scottish philosopher David Hume asked sarcastically why miracles always seemed to happen only in remote times and places. The consequence was that physical objects became the yardstick of reality, and the inner world came to seem like a mere shadow or reflection of the outer one.

In philosophy's central debate between idealism and materialism, idealism had dominated since philosophy's beginnings — not because people had weighed arguments and rationally chosen idealism, but because they had actually experienced the world through an idealistic form of consciousness. Now a decisive shift toward materialism took hold.

Dr Johnson, compiler of the first English dictionary, is presented as a transitional figure: a church-going Christian who acpted the existence of ghosts and once reported hearing his mother crying out to him from over a hundred miles away, yet who became one of the apostles of the common-sense, materialist view of life that dominates today. Challenged to refute Bishop Berkeley's idealism, he famously kicked a stone and declared, "I refute it thus!" This new outlook was corrosive to religion: if nature obeyed fixed, predictable, universal laws, it followed that nature was indifferent to human fate. Thomas Hobbes summed up the resulting view of life as a "war of all against all." Rembrandt's series of self-portraits — though containing little explicit esoteric content — captures this shift more powerfully than any other medium, showing the human spirit conscious of being trapped in an aging body of flesh.

Freemasonry's Response te Spiritual Wasteland

The devastation of central Europe following the Thirty Years' War became, in effect, the spiritual wasteland of the Western world. The gradual withdrawal of the spirit worlds has generally been experienced as an increasing sense of alienation — without the living presence of gods and angels, people were left to confront their own demons ale. Humanity was entering a new Dark Age, and Neo-Solomonic temples sprang up worldwide in response. The esoteric aim of Freemasonry was precisely to help lead humanity through this age of materialism while keeping the flame of true spirituality alive.

Freemasonry is often dismissed as atheistic, particularly by Church enemies, but a Freemason has traditionally sworn an oath to "study the hidden secrets of Nature and Science in Order the better to know his Maker." Freemasons wanted to discard unthinking religion, false piety, and centuries of Church dogma — particularly the crude image of a vindictive father-god — but the higher orders always sought direct personal experience of the spirit worlds and worked as philosophers to define what could reasonably be said about life's spiritual dimension. Many famous eighteenth-century Freemasons usually regarded as sceptics or atheists were in fact prsing alchemists, and some participated in ceremonial magic. Notably, some great Freemasons of this period were held to be reincarnations of great personages from the distant past, returning to fight in the greatest battle against evil since the first War in Heaven.

Freemasonry and the American Revolution

While Scottish and English Freemasons supported constitutional monarchy paired with democratic parliament, the situation in the American colonies was very different. George Washington was initiated as a Freemason in 1752. On 16 December 1773, men disguised as native Indians dumped British tea into Boston Harbour before hurrying back inside St Andrews Masonic Lodge — an event that helped inspire the American Revolution. In 1774 Benjamin Franklin met Thomas Paine in a London Lodge and urged him to emigrate to Arica; Paine, fond of quoting Isaiah, became the great prophet of Revolution, coining the phrase "The United States of America," proposing a federation of states, and arguing for the abolition of slavery and state-funded education for the poor.

A striking, non-obvious episode: in 1775, members of the Colonial Congress staying in a Cambridge, Massachusetts house met to design the American flag. Washington and Franklin were present, along with an old professor apparently staying there by coincidence. To the surprise of others, Washington and Franklin deferred to this stranger immediately and unreservedly, adopting all his design suggestions — after which he vanished and was never seen again, raising the question of whether he was one of the Hidden Masters said to direct world history. The five-pointed stars on the flag, in both their individual shape and arrangement, echo symbols on the ceiling of a chamber in the Egyptian pyramid of Unas, where they represented spirit powers raying down guidance on human history. Understanding Freemasonry's leaders requires recognizing that they felt themselves prompted by mysterious powers — some incarnated, like the old professor, others the disembodied spirits of the stars. This architecture of invoking disembodieirits traces back to an occult, magical tradition rooted in ancient Egypt, encapsulated in the saying: "When the materials are all prepared and ready, the architect shall appear."

Astrology and the Founding of Washington, DC

On the doors of the Capitol building in Washington, DC, a depiction commemorates the Masonic ceremony of 1793 when Washington laid its cornerstone. The key to understanding Freemasonry's secret plans for the age — perhaps shockingly for those who see Washington as model of Christian piety — is astrology. This interest had deep roots in the Royal Society: when challenged on the subject, Newton reportedly replied, "Sir, I have studied the subject. You have not." Elias Ashmole cast horoscopes both for the founding of the Royal Exchange in London (soon to become the centre of world finance)nd for St Paul's Cathedral. When Washington had a horoscope cast for the Capitol's founding, he was following this solemn Freemasonic tradition of charting humanity's history by the movements of stars and planets.

For esoteric Freemasons like Wren and Washington, consecrating a cornerstone at an astrologically propitious moment meant actively inviting heavenly hierarchies to participate in the ceremony. Significantly, at the exact moment Washington laid the Capitol's foundation stone, Jupiter was rising in the East. The phrase "Annuit Coeptis" on the dollar bill's pyramid is adapted from Virgil's Aeneid ("Jupiter, favour us in our undertaking"). The phrase "Novus Ordo Seclorum," which troubles conspiracy theorists, is also adapted from Virgil — from the Eclogues, where he anticipates a new age when people will be reunited with the gods, making religion unnecessary. The dollar bill thus looks forward to the end of Catholic world domination and the dawn of a new spiritual era; it was designed under President Roosevelt, a 33rd-degree Freemason, advised on occult symbolism by Vice President Henry Wallace, a fellow Freemason and disciple of theosophist-artist Nicholas Roerich.

Researcher David Ovason, granted access to Masonic archives, documented how Wasngton DC's astrological orientation involves a complex pattern linking Jupiter, the sun, the moon, Sirius, and the constellation Virgo. A great triangle of streets with Pennsylvania Avenue as hypotenuse was designed by Washington and Latrobe to mirror the constellation Virgo. In an achievement rivaling Egyptian astronomical architecture, the city is laid out so that on 3 August each year the sun streams down Pennsylvania Avenue and strikes the pyramidion atop the Post Office tower. The city, in short, was laid out to welcome Isis, the goddess associated with Virgo — Washington built his capital under the sign of Virgo, inviting the Mother Goddess to participate in the destiny of the United States.

Prophecy, the Coming of Michael, and the Age of Obelisks

Secret societies teach techniques for achieving altered stes through graded levels of initiation, with higher levels granting the gift of prophecy; great initiates possess such comprehensive knowledge of higher spirits' plans that they can work consciously to help fulfil them. Initiates across traditions predicted the dawn of a new age: Joachim, Dee, and Paracelsus prophesied the return of Elijah, working behind the scenes to help humankind grow strong enough for coming trials. By inviting the Mother Goddess into America's destiny, Washington was likewise looking toward a new dispensation in which the United States would dominate the world — contingent on his "great prayers in stone" being answered and ancient prophecies fulfilled.

Abbot Trithemius, influenced by Joachim and himself influencing both Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus, predicted that the epoch of Gabriel, Archangel of the Moon, would be succeeded by the epoch of Michael, Archangel of the Sun — an event he dated to 1881. Michael was foreseen (as established earlier regarding his war against evil forces) as returning to fight corrupted angels and demons predicted to assault earth in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; his defeat of these forces, with human help, was to end the Kali Yuga, the Hindu Dark Age begun in 3102 BC with murder of Krishna (the Yugas being astronomically determined across eight divisions of the Great Year). Freemason initiate-astrologers determined that Trithemius had made a small calculation error and that the Michaelic age actually began in 1878 — prompting Freemasons worldwide to plan monuments, above all obelisks, as this date approached.

Practically, obelisks served as more than decoration: Egyptians regarded the obelisk as a sacred structure on which the Phoenix would alight to mark t end of one civilization and the birth of another, and as a kind of gigantic lightning conductor drawing down the spiritual influence of the sun. Constantine the Great had converted an Alexandrian temple sacred to Thoth/Hermes into a church, reconsecrating its flanking obelisks to Archangel Michael. In 1877 transatlantic Freemasons arranged to transport these two obelisks by sea: one to London, raised on the Victoria Embankment (popularly "Cleopatra's Needle") on 13 September 1878 when the sun was at its zenith; its twin was raised in New York's Central Park by Freemasons led by members of the Vanderbilt family.

The Secret of Thirty-Three

The Masonic star with thirty-three rays appears prominently on public monuments in city centres worldwide. The number thirty-three recurs throughout this history — encoded in the works of Bacon and Shakespeare, in the Rosicrucian Manifestoes, and on the tombs of Shakespeare and Fludd (translator of the Authorized Bible); Jesus Christ lived thirty-three years. This number's significance is one of the oldest and most closely guarded secrets of esoteric philosophy: thirty-three is the rhythm of the vegetative realm of the cosmos, the dimension controlling interactions between spirit worlds and the material world. The closest explicit literary reference comes in Ovid's Metamorphoses, where the murdered Caesar's spirit is described exiting through his thirty-three wounds. The secret of thirty-three refers to the number of gateways through which the human spirit may travel between material and spirit worlds — practical knowledge restricted to highest initiates, since it enables them to slip unobtrusively in and out of the material realm.

War in the Heavens and the Role of Public Monuments

Because what happens on earth always echoes events already unfolded in the spirit worlds, the transition between celestial orders is always marked by battles — a great war fought first in the heavens before being fought on earth. In erecting the Central Park obelisk, Freemasons were invoking St Michael and all his angels for help in establhing American leadership among nations for the war-torn age soon to dawn.

Obelisks were placed with equally prominent ecclesiastical significance, exemplified by the one erected by initiate artist Gianlorenzo Bernini in the square before St Peter's in Rome — a pointed warning that upper Church hierarchy deliberately withholds om its flock conscious knowledge of the astral roots of their own religion. Such monuments operate on multiple levels simultaneously: they attract disembodied beings from spiritual hierarchies and work on people below the conscious level, where great disembodied beings weave in and out of mental space. Initiates both inside and outside the Church have created great works of art and architecture specifically to help condition humanity for its future evolution — and these works also carry enough encoded clues for those inclined to decode them.

Chapter 25: The Mystical-Sexual Revolution: Cardinal Richelieu • Cagliostro • The Secret Identity of the Comte de St Germain

France Ascendant: Cartesian Rationalism and the Death of Sincerity

In the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, France displaced other nations as the most powerful and culturally influential force in Europe, with fate decided in the corridors of the Louvre and Versailles. Descartes spent years researching the Rosicrucians, even travelling to Germany to track them down, but never succeeded — unlike Newton, he lacked adeptness in alchemical techniques that might grant repeated or controlled access to the spirit worlds. In collaboration with mathematician-theologian Marin Mersenn patron was Richelieu), Descartes developed a rationalist philosophy: a closed system of reasoning that dispensed with reference to the senses. This philosophy fostered a new cynicism, enabling French diplomats and politicians to outmanoeuvre their counterparts abroad — a difference in consciousness likened to that between the Conquistadors and the Aztecs.

The French court became the most materially and culturally sophisticated in history, but also heartless: La Rochefoucauld's maxims witti reduced all human action to vanity ("When we dwell on the good qualities of others, we are expressing esteem for our own finer feelings"; "No matter how well we are spoken of, we learn nothing we do not already know"). In the vacuum left by departed sincerity, a tyranny of taste and style arose.

Poussin's Hidden Message

Nicholas Poussin's painting Et in Arcadia Ego has been linked to the Rennes-le-Château mystery, leading many to suspect Rosicrucian influence — a misdirection. Poussin's actual spiritual mentor was the Jesuit Athanasiuircher, arguably the greatest scholar of esoterica of the seventeenth century and the era's foremost Egyptologist, who sought to verify a perennial philosophy and universal secret history encoded across Egyptian texts, the Bible, and classical tradition. The painting's crouching shepherd points to an inscription on a tomb (since destroyed) that confirms this secret history: "Even I was in Arcadia" refers to the turning point when humanity's idyllic vegetative life was invaded by animal desire and death — the Fall of the Mother Goddess. Since Mary Magdalene, in esoteric Christianity, was the incarnation of the goddess redeemed by her Beloved, and Church tradition places her final years in the south of France, what Poussin was literally indicating was the tomb of Mary Magdalene.

As spirituality split from sexuality, libertine figures became cultural icons: Choderlos de Laclos (author of Les Liaisons Dangereuses, reputedly a spider at the centre of a web of sexual and political intrigue), Cbillon fils (author of Les Egarements du Coeur et de l'Esprit), Casanova, and de Sade — all admired for the cleverness and complexity of their power plays. All sex contains an element of striving; in this era that striving became an end in itself, so that even among sensitive and intelligent people, sex was reduced to an exercise of power.

The Dark Side of the Sun King's Court

Following Cardinal Richelieu's unprincipled machinations under Louis XIII, Louis XIV assumed the title of Suning, but concealed a dark underside: haute cuisine was devised to keep nobles content while peasants were taxed to starvation, and Richelieu massacred religious dissenters. Marie Antoinette was later shielded from any sight of the sick, old, or poor, while Louis XVI obsessively reread accounts of the beheading of Charles I — dring to himself the very fate he most feared (an early illustration of a recurring warning: fixation attracts what is feared).

Rumours of esoteric power circulated at court. The Elixir Experiment

One of Louis XIV's doctors, Lesebren, recorded an account of a friend who believed he had concocted the elixir of life. Taking a few drops each sunrise in wine, the man's hair and nails began falling out after fourteen days, and he st his nerve. He passed the potion to an elderly servant, who also became frightened and stopped. He finally tested it on an old hen by soaking its corn with the substance: after six days its feathers fell out entirely, but two weeks later new feathers grew back brighter and more beautiful than in its youth, and the hen resumed laying eggs — an ambiguous parable about the dangers and potential of alchemical experimentation, and the cost of losing nerve before completing a dangerous process.## Initiates as Tricksters: Cagliostro

Amid rampant cynicism and gullibility, with quacks and frauds everywhere, genuine initiates learned to disguise themselves — presenting as tricksters and scoundrels rather than sages, since esoteric wisdom had always looked foolish to the uninitiated. Count Cagliostro reinvented himselfrom a poor Sicilian backstreet boy into a European sensation through mesmeric charm, his beautiful wife Seraphita used as bait, and his rumoured possession of the philosopher's stone. To the poor of Paris he performed healing miracles they could not otherwise afford, making him a popular hero — some eight thousand people cheered his release from the Bastille after imprisonment. Challenged to a public debate by Court de Gébelin (a friend of Benjamin Frankls and renowned esoteric expert), Cagliostro's opponent quickly admitted defeat against superior erudition. Cagliostro also displayed prophetic powers: in a letter dated 20 June 1786 he predicted the Bastille's total destruction, and reportedly even inscribed the exact date — 14 July — as graffiti in the prison cell where he later died.

The Temptation of Supernatural Power: Warnings from Gurdjieff and Sai Baba

Anyone possessing supernatural power faces temptation. G.I. Gurdjieff, perhaps the most charismatic and disconcerting initiate of the twentieth century, deliberately packaged his teaching in absurd terms — inventing an organ at the base of the spine called the "Kunderbuffer" (a deliberately laughable disguise for the kundalini serpent, the reserve of unredeemed energy central to Tantrctice), and writing of gods in giant spaceships and a cool solar surface. Those who dismissed this proved themselves unworthy by his design; those who persisted found his spiritual disciplines genuinely effective. A friend's account of visiting the miracle-worker Sai Baba in India illustrates a similar warning. He then rang a copper bell engraved with Tantric sigils, seemingly conjured a golden chain and crucifix from mid-air, and offered it to the girl as "real magic" — the object appearedo glow with a dark aura. Evidence That Magic Persists Today

A cache of letters found in a secondhand bookshop in Tunbridge Wells detailed occult advice, including a spell involving secretly introducing menstrual blood into food to awaken a man's sexual desire. As a modern parallel demonstrating that such thinking persists institutionally, in 2006 the British government announced grants for "biodynamic" farming developed by Rudolf Steiner, which relies on correspondences between plants and stellar spirits as described by Parelsus and Boehme — Steiner recommended dealing with field mouse infestations by burying the ashes of a field mouse prepared while Venus is in Scorpio.

The Comte de St Germain: Encounter with Cagliostro

If Cagliostro remains enigmatic, the figure he revered — the Comte de St Germain — is an even greater mystery. Cagliostro's own account describes meeting St Germain at a German castle in 1785: arriving at 2 a.m. with his wife, they crossed a lowered drawbridge into a darkened room bereat doors opened onto a vast temple ablaze with thousands of candles. St Germain sat centrally, adorned with fabulous diamond rings and a bejewelled device on his chest reflecting candlelight onto his visitors; two acolytes held incense bowls beside him. A disembodied voice — St Germain's, though his lips did not move — askeWho are you? Where did you come from? What do you want?" — questioning not Cagliostro's identity in the mundane sense (the visit had been pre-arranged) but his previous incarnations, his daemon, his deeper motives. Caglstro prostrated himself, declaring he came "to invoke the God of the Faithful, the Son of Nature, the Father of Truth... to ask one of the fourteen thousand and seven secrets he bears in his bosom... to give myself up as his slave, his apostle, his martyr." St Germain then initiated Cagliostro into Templar mysteries via an out-of-body journey above a molten sea of bronze, exploring heavenly hierarchies.

St Germain's Public Persona and Longevity

St Germain appeared suddenly in European society in 1710, apparently from Hungary and around fifty years old — small, dark-skinned, always dressed in black with extraordinary diamonds, with hypnotic eyes as his most arresting feature. He commanded attention through accomplishments: fluency in many languages, violin playing, painting, and an apparent ability to read minds. He was believed to practise secret breathing techniques from Hindu fakirs and adopted yoga positions unknown in the West at the time; though he attended banquets, he was never observed eating in public and drank only a self-coocted herbal tea.

The greatest mystery was his longevity: having appeared in public life in 1710 in apparent late middle age (meeting composer Rameau in Venice), he remained active without visibly ageing until at least 1782, with sightings continuing as late as 1822. This would be easy to dismiss as romantic legend were the witnesses — Rameau, Voltaire, Horace Walpole, Clive of India, and Casanova — not of such consistently high standing across such a long span. He was a prominent figur Louis XV's court, intimate with both Madame de Pompadour and the king, undertaking diplomatic missions to Moscow, Constantinople, and London. In London in 1761 he negotiated the Family Compact, paving the way for the Treaty of Paris and ending Franco-British colonial wars. Unlike Cagliostro, St Germain's efforts always seemed devoted to peace, and he was never caught in any act of dishonesty. Though nobody knew the source of his wealth (some claimed alchemy), he was evidently independently wealthy and no desperate adventurer.

St Germain's Secret Identity

A key to St Germain's true identity lies in Freemasonic history: he is credited with coining the Masonic motto Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, and may be regarded as the living spirit of esoteric Freemasonry. More significantly, in the secret history, St Germain is identified as Christian Rosenkreuz reincarnated for the age of Enlightenment, imperial expansion, and international diplomacy — borrowing Philip K. Dick's phrase, he had learned to "reconstitute his body after death."

This points to an even deeper layer of identity: in an earlier incarnation, Rosenkreuz/Germain had been Hiram Abiff, the Master Builder of Solomon's Temple, whose murder caused the loss of the Word — on one level, a power of supernatural procreation wielded by humankind before the Fall into matter. Part of St Germain's mission through esoteric Freemasonry was reintroducing knowledge of the Word into history's stream.

La Très Sainte Trinsophie: An Initiation Text

A booklet often attributed to St Germain, La Très Sainte Trinsophie, oris from the same school of occult Freemasonry and gives an initiation account: the candidate descends into the earth's volcanic depths, spends the night there, then climbs out at dawn following a star. Enoch and the Deepest Layer of Identity

The deepest mystery of this individuality concerns an even earlier incarnation, from when human bodies stood at the borderline of becoming solid flesh: Enoch, earliest prophet of the Sun god, whose face shone with sun-like radiance. The motto Liberty, Equality, Fraternity looked forward to a time when humanity would reach out to the Sun god with freedom of thought and will — succeeding where it had failed thfirst time He came. The secret history from the late sixteenth to nineteenth centuries is dominated by the hidden work of the great ascended masters Enoch and Elijah, preparing for the descent of the Archangel of the Sun and, beyond that, an even greater being — these men were preparing the way for the Second Coming.

Freemasonry as Incubator of a New Optimism

As sightings of St Germain grew rarer through the eighteenth century, optimism filled the secret society lodges. In France, "the Unknown Philosopher" St Martin taught that "every man is a king." Chevalier Ramsay, the Scottish laird who founded a Grand Lodge in Paris in 1730, told new initiates in 1737 that the world is "nothing but a great republic," striving for reunion of enlightened minds through virtue, science, and religion, so thatthe subjects of all kingdoms can learn to love each other." Freemasonry offered a protected space for tolerant discussion, free scientific inquiry, and investigation of the spirit worlds.

The Order of Elus Coens and Ritual Practice

The great Freemasonic event of the 1760s was the founding of the Order of Elus Coens ("chosen priests") by Portuguese magus Martines de Pasqually. His rituals could last up to six hours and involved incense blending hallucinogens with fly agaric mushroom spores. In later rituals devised by Stanislas de Guaita (heavily influenced by de Pasqually), a blindfolded candidate might have it removed to find himself facing men in Egyptian masks and headdresses silently pointing swords at his chest. As Dr Dee had once worked to restore genuine spiritual experience to the Church through ceremonial magic, de Pasqually and Cagliostro did the same within Freemasonry — Cagliostro founded Egyptian Rite Freemasonry in 1782, which proved highly influential in both France and America.

De Pasqually's pupil and succsor, St Martin, shifted emphasis away from ceremony toward internal, esoteric disciplines, influenced by his reading of Boehme; his Martinist philosophy remains influential in French Freemasonry to this day. Living in Paris during the Terror, St Martin initiated men and women in his own apartment through mystical laying on of hands — participants were in such danger that they wore masks even during meetings, concealing their identities from one another.

Voltaire's Initiation and the Alchemical Undercurrent

Voltaire, often mischaracterized as a God-hater, was in reality opposed only to organized religion. When initiated by Benjamin Franklin, he was given the apron of Helvetius — the famous Swiss scientist whose account of alchemical transmutation is the second-most highly authenticated such account after Leibniz's — to kiss. Masonic historian A.E. Waite described Masonry's "dreams of antique science" and called Voltaire the man "who held the keys... which opened up the door to this reality," suggesting that "condemned practices,dden arts might lead through some clouds of mystery into the light of knowledge." The initiates of the secret societies were filled with genuine wonder at these new vistas — enough faith and optimism to share Wordsworth's sense that it was bliss to be alive at that dawn.

The Birth of Romanticism from Secret-Society Idealism

The wealth of enthusiasm among artists, writers, and composers connected to secret societies gave rise to the Romantic movement. As a general principle, whenever a eat flowering of imaginative art and literature occurs (as in the Renaissance and Romanticism), one should suspect the hidden presence of sacred idealism as a life philosophy, cultivated by secret societies. Idealism, in the philosophical sense of ideas being more real than objects, underlies this entire secret history; idealism in the common sense of living by high ideals was, as George Steiner noted, actually a nineteenth-century invention.

The Enlightenment-era lodges of England, America, and France worked to build societies less cruel, superstitious, ignorant, repressive, and prejudiced — and more tolerant, though also more insincere and frivolous. Even before the Terror, disquiet grew that a society run along rationally straight lines could not adequately address human nature odarker forces operating outside natural law. Romanticism arose partly as a reckoning with an intense, galvanic feeling rising from what we would now call the unconscious, producing intense music and poetry impatient of convention and encouraging spontaneity and self-abandon. German writers in Eckhart's tradition characterized France as full of "soulless little dancing masters who did not understand the inner life of man." Lessing, Schlegel, and Schiller made philosophical idealism a life philosophy again, exalting imagination as a higher mode of perception than the senses — trainable to grasp higher realities beyond the materialism of common-sense apostles. In conventional history, Romanticism reacted against the polite, ordered eighteenth century; in secret history, it was demonic forces — not me subconscious ones — driving the reaction. The roots of this reaction were sexual.

Swedenborg's Breakdown and Its Sexual-Occult Origins

In July 1744, London watchmaker John Paul Brockmer grew alarmed by his lodger, the previously quiet and respectable Swedish engineer Emmanuel Swedenborg (a regular at the local Moravian chapel). Swedenborg's hair stood on end; he foamed at the mouth, chased Brockmer down the street claiming to be the Messiah, was turned away from the Swedish embassy, tn stripped and rolled in a drainage ditch, throwing money at onlookers. Marsha Keith Suchard's research reveals Swedenborg had been experimenting with sexual techniques for achieving extreme altered states of consciousness, taught at the outwardly respectable Moravian chapel — and that William Blake, raised in this same church, absorbed these practices as inspiration for his poetry. These sexual techniques represent the most closely guarded secrets of the secret societies, more potent than breathing exercises, dancing, or meditation alone.

#Swedenborg's Documented Practice: Breath Control to Trance States

Even as a boy, Swedenborg experimented with breath control, discovering that holding his breath for long periods induced trance, deepened further by synchronizing breath to pulse. He recorded being "reduced into a state of insensibility as to the body senses, thus almost unto the state of dying persons," while retaining "interior life unimpaired" and "the power of thinking." Persistence brought rewards: "a certain cheering light and joyful, confirmatory brightness... a kind of mysterious radiation... that darts through some temple in the brain... the soul is called into a more inward communion... the golden age of its intellectual perfections," with the mind despising "all merely corporeal pleasures" in comparison. Modern neurological research corroborates that meditation raises DHEAS and melatonin levels — secretions from the pineal and pituitary glands which occultists say together create the Third Eye.

Cabalistic Sexual Cosmology

At fifteen, Swedenborg moved in withis brother-in-law, who mentored him for seven years, during which his research turned markedly cabalistic. In Cabala (as in all esoteric traditions), creation is conceived as emanations (sephiroth) from the cosmic mind, understood as gendered — male and female — spirits. The unattainable En Sof emanates these spirits, which intertwine sexually as creation's impulse spirals downward; just as erotic mental images generate sperm, the En Sof's loving imagination generates physical effects, makthe sexually-fired imagination the root principle of creativity. On this account, the Fall resulted from an imbalance between male and female sephiroth, and an adept who imagines balanced, harmonious love-making between the sephiroth helps correct this primordial cosmic wrong.

The Cherubim arching their wings above the Ark of the Covenant in the Holy of Holies represented the harmonious love-making of male and female sephiroth. When the second Temple was sacked by Antiochus in 168 BC, these erotic images were paraded through the streets to mock the Jews; the Temple's destruction in AD 70 created a deep collective need to rebuild it, with sacred imagery of sephirotic love-making central to righting this historical wrong.

Practical Technique: Sex Magic and Its Dangers

While living with his brother-in-law, Swedenborg practised breath-control exercises combined with imagining naked human bodies contorted erotically into the shapes of Hebrew letters — believed to be powerful magical sigils. Similar techniques for channeling sexual energy toward spiritual ends are used by some Hasidic groups today; Bob Dylan, heir in some sense to Blake's poetic tradition, has explored comparable practices.

Control is the crucial element in these disciplines, echoed in Tantric traditions whose rumours filtered back to Europe as empires expanded eastward. Swedenborg studied sexual tantra in detail: psychological discipline enabled prolonged arousal, redirecting sexual energy to the brain to achieve breakthrough into the spirit worlds — a visionary ecstasy rather than a narrowly sexual climax also mastered an extremely difficult muscle-control technique known to Indian adepts, whereby at the moment of ejaculation sperm is diverted to the bladder rather than expelled. These techniques are explicitly dangerous — a key reason for their secrecy — risking nervous breakdown (as witnessed by Swedenborg's landlord), as well as madness and death.

The Moravian Sacramental Sex Cult

Swedenborg's specific admixture came from the Moravian church in New Fetter Lane, London, then under sway of charismatic Count Zizendorf, who is presented as a Christian adaptation of the arcana of love. Congregants were encouraged to visualize, smell, and imaginatively touch the side wound in Christ's body, envisioned in Zizendorf's teaching as a "sweet, luscious vagina oozing a magical juice," into which the spear of Longinus was to be thrust "repeatedly and ecstatically." Zizendorf promoted sex as a sacramental act, urging followers to perceive divine spiritual emanations in each other at the moment of climax; a joint mental prayer at that moment carried particular magical force. Swedenborg described it: "partner sees partner in mind... each partner has the other in himself" so they "cohabit in their innermost" — in visionary trance, partners could meet, communicate, and even me love in dismembered spiritual forms.

Blake's Inheritance and Censorship

Blake's parents belonged to this Moravian congregation, and Blake absorbed these ideas through wide reading of Swedenborg. Suchard documents how prudish Victorians erased explicit sexual imagery from Blake's drawings — including painting pairs of underpants over genitals — obscuring the specific sex-magic techniques underlying his imaginative vision, beyond the popularly acknowledged general influence of Swedenborgian esotericism.

Blake experienced visions from early childhood: at age four he saw God looking through a window; at four or five, walking in the countryside, he saw a tree filled with angels "bespangling every bough like stars." The secret techniques of Zizendorf and Swedenborg gave him a systematic, cabalisframework for these phenomena, reflected in lines like: "In Beulah the Female lets down her beautiful Tabernacle Which the Male enters magnificent between her Cherubim And becomes One with her mingling... There's a place where Contraries are equally true, This place is called Beulah."

Romanticism as Cosmic, Symphonic Love

In Romanticism, individual interior life expanded into a vast cosmos of infinite variety, with love conceived as one cosmos loving another — moving into a new, symphoc mode. The broader historical significance: the secret meditative and prayerful practices of a small number of initiates generated a popular surge of feeling against materialism. A new way of making love — re-enacting the creation of the cosmos — asserted that right is not simply might, that higher ideals exist beyond expedi or enlightened self-interest, and that cultivating the right frame of mind allows the world to be experienced as meaningful: "If the people make love so that they become illumined, the world will become a world of shadows. When they awake again, meaning will have settled on the world like dew."

The Musical and Literary Flowering

Romanticism's roots were both sexual and esoteric. German poet Novalis spoke of "magical idealism," a volcanic spirit that produced the music of Beethoven and Schubert. Beethoven, hearing an unprecedented musical language, became obsessed (like Alexander the Great) with identifying the divine influx behind his genius, reading and rereading Egyptian and Indian esoteric texts; his Sonata in D Minor and the Appassionata are presented as his equivalents to Shakespeare's The Tempest — his most explicit expressions of occult ideas.

In France, Martinist writer Charles Nodier wrote of secret-society conspiracies within Napoleon's armies working to bring him down, and later introduced young French Romantics — Victor Hugo, Honoré de Balzac, Dumas fils, Delacroix, and Gérard de Nerval — to esoteric philosophy. Owen Barfield described a persistent current of Platonic ideas that fine intellects like Shakespeare and Keats could; Keats termed this capacity "Negative Capability" — being "capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries and doubts without any irritable searching after fact and reason," paralleling Francis Bacon's scientific advocacy of deliberately withholding imposed patterns to let richer ones emerge.

Coleridge, immersed in Boehme and Swedenborg, carried an aura of the supernatural ("Weave a circle around him thrice... For he on honey-dew hath fed, and drunk the milk of Paradise"). His friend Wordswor wrote the purest expression of idealism as a life philosophy, describing feeling "a presence that disturbs me with the joy of elevated thoughts... a motion and a spirit, that impels, all thinking things, all objects of all thought, and rolls through all things" — a still-resonant articulation, even for readers who consciously ny the higher reality it describes; something in them recognizes it, or the poem would be wholly meaningless. In Wordsworth's era, people did not need to struggle to access such feelings — Goethe, Byron, and Beethoven led a genuinely popular movement.

The Turn Toward Catastrophe

A closing question is posed: why did this impulse toward freedom eventually collse into the abuse of power? Understanding this requires tracing the infiltration of the secret societies by proponents of materialism. Chevalier Ramsay had explicitly forbidden political discussion in the lodges he founded in 1730, but Freemasonry's hold over Europe's political leaders made it an irresistible temptation to anyone seeking political influence — setting up the trajectory explored in the following chapter.

Chapter 26: The Illuminati and the Rise of Unreason: The Illuminati and the Battle for the Soul of Freemasonry

Founding of the Illuminati

In 1776 a Bavarian professor of law, Adam Weishaupt, founded a secret organization called the Illuminati, recruiting his first members from among his own students. Modeled on military lines like the Jesuits, the order demanded that members surrender their individual judgement and will. As with older secret societies, initiates were prised an ancient wisdom and ever more powerful secrets as they climbed a ladder of initiation. Members worked in isolated cells and knowledge was shared on a strict "need to know" basis, mirroring modern intelligence tradecraft, justified by the supposed danger of the knowledge involved.

Weishaupt joined the Freemasons in 1777, and Illuminati members quickly followed him into the lodges, rapidly infiltrating them and rising to positions of seniority.

Exposure of the Fraud

In 1785 a member named Jacob Lanz was struck by lightning while traveling to Silesia. When his body was found, Bavarian authorities discovered papers on him revealing the Illuminati's secret plans. Combined with documents in Weishaupt's own hand seized in subsequent raids, a complete picture of the order emerged.

The seized writings exposed that the "ancient secret wisdom" and supernatural powers promised to initiates were a cynical fabrication. Candidates who progressed through the grades eventually discovered the spiritual teachings were a smokescreen — srituality itself was derided within the inner circle. Jesus Christ's teachings were reinterpreted as purely political, calling for abolition of property, marriage, family, and religion. Weishaupt's real goal was a purely materialistic revolutionary society, and France was chosen as the testing ground. At the final stage, a candidate was told the ultimate secret was that there was no secret — inducting him into a nihilistic, anarchistic philosophy that appealed to his worst instincts. Weishaupt anticipated tearing down civilization not to liberate people but for the pleasure of dominating others.

Weishaupt's own words reveal his cynicism and intent:

  • "In concealment lies a great part of our strength… The lodges that are under Freemasonry are the most suitable cloak for our high purpose."
  • On recruiting the young: "Watch them, and if one of them pleases you, lay your hand on him."
  • On the goal of secret rule: "The final aim of our Society is nothing less than to win power and riches… and to obtain mastery of the world."

The order wicially suppressed following these revelations — but too late to stop what had already been set in motion.

Infiltration and the French Revolution

By 1789 France had roughly three hundred Masonic lodges, sixty-five in Paris alone, with claims of more than seventy thousand French Freemasons. Though lodges were originally meant to instill hope and will for reform, Illuminati infiltration was so thorough that it has been claimed the program enacted by the French Constitutional Assembly in789 had actually been drafted by German Illuminati in 1776. Revolutionary leaders — Danton, Desmoulins, Mirabeau, Marat, Robespierre, and Guillotin — had all been "illuminated." A diagram by Weishaupt captured his ambition directly: "One must show how easy it would be for one clear mind to direct hundreds and thousands of me When Louis XVI stalled on reform and called troops to Versailles in June 1789, mass desertions followed, and on 14 July an angry mob stormed the Bastille. The king was guillotined in January 1793; cut off by a drumroll as he tried to address the crowd, he was heard saying, "People of France, I am innocent, I forgive those who are responsible for my death. I pray to God that the blood spilled here never falls on France or on you, my unfortunate people…" Tt such an act occurred in the heart of the most civilized nation on earth opened the door to the unthinkable. It is said a man leapt onto the scaffold afterward shouting, "Jacques de Moloy, you are avenged!" — a stark contrast to the king's grace.

Robespierre and the Terror

In the ensuing chaos, leaders of the Masonic lodges took control, and many of their own were soon denounced as traitors to the Revolution, launching the Terror. Maximilian Robespierre, an austere and personally incorruptible lawyer and the most "principled" of Freemasons, drove the killing as head of the Committee of Public Safety, sending hundreds to the guillotine daily — roughly 2,750 executions total, of which only 650 were aristocrats, the rest ordinary working people. He even had Danton executed: Saturn eating his ohildren.

A key insight offered here is that in an idealistic philosophy the ends never justify the means, because motives shape outcomes even when deeply hidden. Robespierre believed he shed blood as a grim duty for the common good and the protection of citizens' rights and property — a purely "rational" justification — yet this yearning to be completely reasonable appears to have driven him mad.

On 8 July 1794, Robespierre staged an elaborate ceremony before the Louvre: members of theional Convention sat in a makeshift amphitheatre each holding an ear of wheat symbolizing the goddess Isis, while Robespierre, in a light blue coat with powdered white hair, proclaimed before an altar, "The whole Universe is assembled here!" He invoked a Supreme Being in a speech lasting hours, closing with a vow to continue fighting "vice and tyrants." He then set fire to a veiled effigy, designed by the Illuminated Freemason Jean-Jacques David, revealing a statue of the goddess Sophia rising from the flames like a phoenix — later claimed byoet Gérard de Nerval to represent Isis. A pointed distinction is drawn: the ruling spirit of this moment was not the true Isis (whose unveiling leds to the spirit worlds) nor the gentle, nurturing Mother Nature, but "Mother Nature red in tooth and claw."

Robespierre was accused of trying to have himself declared a god by an elderly prophetess, Catherine Théot. Public revulsion at the bloodletting finally reached a breaking point; a crowd laid siege to the Hôtel de Ville and cornered him. He attempted suicide by gunshot but only blew away half his jaw, and when finally guillotined — still in his light blue costume — he could only manage a strangulated cry instead of the speech he intended.

Napoleon's Star and Egyptian Connections

Napoleon famously spoke of following his star, usually read as poetic shorthand for a sense of destiny, but treated here as something more literal — a visible star in the sky that, so long as no one else could see it, he would not let anyone distract him from following.

Goethe described Napoleon as a anently "illuminated," always clear-headed and decisive, moving "from battle to battle, and from victory to victory" like a demi-god — a state of continual illumination that, in Goethe's words, eventually forsook him along with his fortune and his good star. Napoleon's astonishing run of success made him identify himself with Alexander the Great, uniting East and West through conquest.

His Egyptian campaign, though not militarily glorious, mattered to him personally. According to Fouché, h of the French secret police, Napoleon met a man purporting to be St Germain inside the Great Pyramid. It is documented that Napoleon chose the esotericist and astrologer Fabre d'Olivet as an adviser and arranged to spend a night alone inside the Great Pyramid — leaving open whether he met St Germain in the flesh or in spirit. apoleon commissioned Description de l'Egypt, a catalogue of Egyptian antiquities dedicated to "Napoleon le Grand," inviting comparison to Alexander, and had himself portrayed on its cover as Sol Invictus, the Sun god. As his empire expanded across Italy, Egypt, Germany, Austria, and Spain, he had Charlemagne's crown and sceptre brought to him in 1804 and, forcing Pope Pius VII to attend, snatched the crown from the Pope's hands and crowned himself Emperor — the first such coronation since Charlemagne.

Isis, Josephin and Cosmic Symbolism

Napoleon commissioned scholars to conclude that Isis was the ancient goddess of Paris, then decreed that the goddess and her star be added to the city's coat of arms; on the Arc de Triomphe, Josephine is depicted kneeling at his feet bearing the laurel of Isis. The inference drawn is that Napoleon did not identify himself with Sirius but followed it, just as Orion follows Sirius across the sky. In Masonic initiation, candidates are symbolically reborn as Osiris was reborn, gazing up at a five-pointed star representing Isis — Osiris/Orion the Hunter embodying the masculine impulse toward power, action, and impregnation, pursuing Isis as gatekeeper to life's mysteries.

This is presented as the template for Napoleos relationship with Josephine, who came from a family steeped in esoteric Freemasonry and was herself already a Freemason when they met. Napoleon could conquer mainland Europe but never fully conquer her; his longing for her is likened to Dante's longing for Beatrice, and this longing made him aspire higher. Osiris and Isis are linked to sun and moon, tied to the cosmos's arrangement to make human thought possible; in ancient Egypt, the heliacal rising of Sirius in mid-June presaged the Nile's flooding, and in some esoteric traditions Sirius is regarded as the central sun around which our own sun rotates. This entire nexus of esoteric symbolism, combined with his love for Josephine, is presented as having shaped Napoleon's sense of destiny.

The Warning of Withdrawn Inspiration

In 1813 the guiding powers that had empowered Napoleon left him suddenly — as they always eventually leave everyone — and, as Goethe described, the forces of reaction rushed in from all sides to destroy him. A parallel warning is drawn with artistsey struggle to find their voice, reach an inspired period where they cannot make a wrong mark, perhaps redefining an entire era — then the spirit suddenly departs and cannot be recaptured no matter how hard they try. This functions as a broar caution about the impermanence of "illumination" or inspired states, whether in political, military, or creative life.

Humanity's Collective Initiation and the Global Spread of Freemasonry

Drawing on the earlier concept of kama loca (purgatory), where soul and spirit are still united and attacked by demons as part of individual initiation, it is proposed that the whole of humanity was to undergo something like a collective initiation, and that secret societies were preparing humanity for this ordeal by cultivating a stronger sense of self.

In the mid-eighteenth century, Freemasonry spread worldwide — to Austria, Spain, India, Italy, Sweden, Germany, Poland, Russia, Denmark, Norway, and China — inspiring republican revolutions globally following the American and French examples. Madame Blsky wrote that among the Carbonari, revolutionary precursors of Garibaldi, more than one member was deeply versed in occult science and Rosicrucianism; Garibaldi himself was a 33rd-degree Freemason and Grand Master of Italian Freemasonry. Other freedom fighters identified as Freemasons include Louis Kossuth in Hungary, and in South America Simon Bolivar, Francisco de Miranda, Venustiano Carranza, Benito Juarez, and Fidel Castro. By 2001 there were an estimated seven million Freemasons worldwide, including some 13,000 lodges in the USA alone.

The Novel as Vehicle for Interior Life

Jesus Christ is credited with planting the seed of interior life, later expanded and populated by Shakespeare and Cervantes. In the eighteenth and especially nineteenth centuries, initiate-novelists forged the modern sense that this interior world has its own history — a meaningful narrative with highs, lows, reversals of fortune, and turning points. Novelists such as the Brontës and Dickens conveyed that just as human consciousness evolved througistory, so too does consciousness evolve across an individual life.

John Comenius, who grew up in Prague under Rudolf II and attended the coronation of the Winter King, knew John Valentine Andrae in Heidelberg and was later invited to London by the occultist Samuel Hartlib "to help complete the Work." Through his educational reforms, Comenius introduced into mainstream culture the now-familiar idea that childhood represents a fundamentally different state of mind from adulthood — an idea visible in novels such as Jane Eyre and David Copperfield, though it was radically new at the time.

The area of esoteric thought with the greatest influence on the novel, however, was that of "deeper laws" — universal patterns governing meaning and fate that novelists steeped in esoteric philosophy dramatized through individual characters' lives.

The Problem of the Deeper Laws

A split in consciousness between objective Baconian thought and subjective Shakespearean consciousness (attributed earlier to Elijah's hidden historical influence) allowee laws of physics to come into focus by viewing the world objectively. But this left subjective experience — the structure of meaning itself — unaddressed. Psychology, when it later arose, made the materialistic assumption that matter influences mind but never the reverse, and so overlooked the universal human experience of meaning.

Rosicrucians had begun formulating laws paralleling the Eastern esoteric concept of "the nameless way," bound up with human wellbeing, corresponding to yang yin — concepts with a long tradition in the East but which remained elusive in the West, falling between the cracks of physics and psychology.

Deeper Laws Illustrated Through Literature

While the deeper laws are hard to grasp abstractly, they can be seen clearly in action. Several nineteenth-century novelists wrote explicitly occult fiction: Dickens's A Christmas Carol; Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights, in which a spirit pursues its beloved beyond the grave; George Eliot's Lifting the Veil, born of her passionate investigation of the occ but suppressed by her publisher; and Dostoyevsky (discussed further elsewhere). Beyond explicit occultism, an implicit vision of deeper laws working through irrational, non-scientific patterns pervades the greatest novels — Jane Eyre, Bleak House, Moby Dick, Middlemarch, and War and Peace — each holdinga mirror to universal patterns of order and meaning that persist even when science denies the evidence of our own hearts and minds.

Novels are described as inherently reducing egotism, since reading one requires seeing the world through another's eyes, and character flaws in fiction are often rooted in self-interest or failure to empathize. But the deeper contribution of the novel is cultivating the sense of an inner narrative — that an individual life, seen from within, has a meaningful shape and story.

Mother Goose, in an eighteenth-century engraving, is identified as secretly Isis, the Moon goddess — evidenced by her name (the goose being a traditional Egyptian attribute of Isis) and by the crescent shape of her profile, illustrg how fairy tales remain saturated with the numinous, paradoxical qualities of ancient secret philosophy.

Life as a Testing Labyrinth

What gives novels their shape is life's paradoxical quality — that it does not run in a straight, predictable line, that appearances deceive, and fortunes reverse. This connects directly to the idea of the deeper laws and life's meaning.

Why the Deeper Laws Go Unnamed

It is noted as surprising that the West lacks even a name for these laws, despiteheir supposed importance to human happiness. Ordinary proverbs and cautionary childhood wisdom only address the basics of avoiding physical harm and securing necessities, while deeper laws concern destiny, good and evil, and the highest levels of fulfillment.

A contrast is drawn between the caution "look before you leap" and this parable by proto-Surrealist Guillaume Apollinaire: "Come to the edge, he said. / They said, We are afraid. / Come to the edge, he said. / They came. He pushed them. / They flew."

Like Paracelsus, the Brothers Grimm collected esoteric folklore before it disappeared. A non-obvious example given: Dopey, Happy, Bashful, Sleepy, Grumpy, Sneezy, and Doc are literal translations of seven earth demons from Scandinavian esoteric lore — Toki, Skavaerr, Varr, Dun, Orinn, Grerr, and Radsvid — showing that even Disney's cozy imagery carries esoteric roots closer to the surface than expected.

The Surrealists and Irrational Law

Inspired by secret-society teachings, the Surrealists sought to destroy entrenched scientific materialism partly through promoting irrational acts. Apollinaire's parable suggests that acting irrationally invites reward from the irrational forces of the universe — proposed here as one of the deeper laws, a form of cause and effect operating outside ordinary probability.

Though Surrealists were unusually open about this philosophy's roots in secret societies, the same irrational logic runs through mainstream culture — notably It's a Wonderful Life and its literary forebear A Christmas Carol (Dickens being an initiate of the secret whose philosophy the story embodies). In both stories, a central figure (Scrooge; George Bailey) is shown visions of how his actions have caused misery and what would happen if he continued or if he had never existed. Both are then made to pass again through the same door they faced earlier in the story — but this time choosing rightly. This is read as evidence that life has a circular, testing quality: we are directed toward crucial decisions and may be looped back to face them again if wfail the first time.

Deeper Laws Across the Literary Canon

The same irrational patterning is identified in Oedipus Rex, Hamlet, Don Quixote, Doctor Faustus, and War and Peace:

  • Oedipus draws to himself the very thing he fears most, killing his father and marrying his mother.
  • Hamlet repeatedly avoids his life's central challenge (avenging his father), which returns to confront him in ever more dire forms.
  • Don Quixote's stubbornly good-hearted vision of the world is so strong that it mysteriously transforms his material surroundings by the novel's end.
  • Faust knows what he should do but fails to do it, and a providential order in the universe punishes him.
  • Tolstoy's Pierre is tortured by his love for Natasha and only wins her once he releases his attachment to the outcome.

A thought experiment proposes feeding all of world literature into a computer and asking what laws determine a happy, fulfilled life; the resulting body of laws would include:

  • If you duck out of a challenge, it will return in a different form.
  • We always draw toward us what we fear most.
  • Choosing the immoral path means ultimately paying for it.
  • A good-hearted belief will eventually transform what is believed in.
  • To hold onto what you love, you must let it go.

By contrast, feeding the same question to scientific data alone would yield entirely different, and mutually contradictory, "laws":

  • The best way to keep something is to try hardest and never give up.
  • You cannot transform the world by wishful thinking — you must act.
  • If you avoid detection and pishment by other people, there is no reason to expect a providential order will punish you.

The clear implication is that the structure of the external, scientifically measurable world and the structure of inner, meaningful experience yield genuinely different sets of laws.

Subjectivity as the Key to Perceiving Deeper Laws

Tolstoy addressed this same distinction in his essay On Life — that the same underlying laws operate in both the outer world of phenomena and inner life, yet appear very different when considered parately. Abraham Isaac Kook, a leading twentieth-century Cabalist and first Chief Rabbi of Palestine, is quoted: "God is revealed in the deep feelings of sensitive souls." The deeper laws, it is argued, can only be discerned by viewing external events with the deepest subjectivity, as an artist or mystic would — raising the qstion of whether their inherent subjectivity, operating so close to the center of consciousness, is precisely what makes them so hard to keep in focus.

Rainer Maria Rilke, in a letter to a young poet, is quoted as coming close to describing these laws explicitly: "Only the individual who is truly solitary is brought under the deep laws, and when a man steps out into the morning that is just beginning, or looks into the evening that is full of happenings, and when he feels what is coming to pass there, then all rank drops from him as from a dead man, although he is standing in the midst of sheer life." This is read as confirming that the deeper laws can only be perceived through prolonged, solitary, subtle concentration, shutting out all else.

Contemporary Mystical Testimony

A personal encounter is recounted with young Irish mystic Lorna Byrne, who had not read any of the esoteric literature underlying this account nor met anyone who had transmitted its ideas to her — her knowledge coming instead from direct personal experience. She reports meeting Michael, Archangel of the Sun, and encountering the Archangel Gabriel manifesting as the Moon, split in half yet joined, moving like pages turning in a book. She has described seeing the group-spirit the fox in local fields, appearing foxlike but with human elements, and meeting Elijah — once human, now bearing the spirit of an angel — walking on water like the Green One of Sufi tradition. Her perception is presented as an alternative, parallel mode of accessing a dimension that interacts with and moves things within our own.

Closing Warning

The chapter ends on an ominous note: in the late nineteenth century, ancient creatures are said to have begun stirring in the depths of the h, moving toward "the appointed place." Described as "consciousness-eaters" imprisoned since the first War in Heaven, they were said to be on the move again — a foreboding transition into the book's subsequent material.
