Chapter 27: The Mystic Death of Humanity: Swedenborg and Dostoyevsky • Wagner • Freud, Jung and the Mlizing of Esoteric Thought

The Darkening After Romanticism

Early Romanticism's joy in self-expression and animal aliveness in nature gave way to disquiet in the second half of the nineteenth century. Hegel recognized this force operating through history: "The spirit cheats us, the spirit intrigues, the spirit lies, the spirit triumphs." Materialist history explains the era's crisis as "alienation"; esoteric history sees it as a spiritual crisis caused by demons.

Swedenborg's Vision of the Demonic

Swedenborg — a man described as rolling around in the mud rather than a revered academic like Hegel or Schopenhauer — became the great exponent of demonic forces rising from the depths. He prophesied humanity would have to come to terms with the demonic both in the world and within itself. Today the Swedenborg Church is the only esoteric movement admitted to Sweden's National Council of Churches, and his teachings influenced communal-living groups such as American Shakers. In his own time he was more dangerous: his exceptionally detailed and accurate clairvoyance made him world-famous, though he repudiated spiritualists who tried to claim him, insisting his gifts were unique and heralded a new age.

Swedenborg's Heaven and Hell directly shaped Ge's sense of intruding supernatural evil in Faust, Baudelaire's notion of correspondences, and Balzac's supernatural themes in Seraphita. His most far-reaching influence, however, was on Dostoyevsky, darkening the mood of an entire era.

Dostoyevsky's Confrontation with Evil

Dostoyevsky's heroes are poised over an abyss, heightened by awareness that choices matter and arrive disguised. A paradoxical notion runs through his work: those who confront the evil, supernatural dimension — en thieves, prostitutes, murderers — stand closer to heaven than those whose cosy worldview shuts evil out and denies its existence.

Eastern Orthodox Christianity, less dogmatic than the Western Church and more respectful of individual spiritual experience, gave Dostoyevsky freedom to explore the outer limits of spiritual experience — describing battles between darkness and light occurring in realms most people are barely conscious of. His journey through Hell, like Dante's, is both a spiritual journey and a journey through the Hell on Earth hity has created. He originated a new impulse that would characterize art in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries: the desire to know the worst that can happen.

His library at death was well stocked with Swedenborg, including accounts of the many different hells that people with different capacities for evil fashion for themselves. Swedenborg insisted these hells were not fictional — they elude conventional assumptions of what is real. Hell may look identical to ordinary life until anomalies show themselves: a group of genial, amusing libertines who love to deflower virgins turn to reveal themselves as "like apes with a fierce face … a horrible countenance."

Non-esoteric literary criticism has missed how directly passages in Crime and Punishment draw on Swedenborg — such as Svidrigailov's vision of eternity as "one little room, like a bathhouse in the country, black and grimy and spiders in every corner." Similarly, in The Brothers Karamazov, when Ivan is visited by the Devil in a nightmare, neither Ivan nor the readmeant to believe it mere delusion — devils can squeeze through into the material dimension. Dostoyevsky conveys a sense of vital contact with other, sometimes hellish, worlds, alongside a spiritual extremism: there is no middle way — if one does not run to embrace the most spiritual, the demonic fills the vacuum, and those who try to follow a middle path end up nowhere. Like Swedenborg, he looked forward to a new age, though his version grew from a distinctly Russian sense of history.

Russian Esoteric Undercurrent

The poet Nikolai Kliuev captured the Russian perspective, decrying Western Christianity's gifts of "rationalism, materialism, a technology that enslaves, an absence of spirit." Orthodox Christianity preserved esoteric doctrines, some pre-Christian, that Rome discarded or declared heretical. Dionysius the Areopagite's mystical vision emphasized direct, personal experience of spirit worlds. In the seventh century, Maximus the Confessor urged disciplined introspection, writing "Illumination must be sought … and in treme cases the whole body will be illumined too" — a phenomenon reported by monks of Mount Athos, whose caves would suddenly illuminate during ep prayer (the hesychast vision), achievable through rhythmic breathing, repetitive prayer, and meditation on icons.

In the seventeenth century, Patriarch Nikon reformed and centralized the Russian Orthodox Church, leaving the Old Believers (Raskolniki) to preserve the spiritual disciplines of early Christianity underground as outlawed, driven communities. Dostoyevsky stayed in contact with them throughout his life.

Wagner and Esoteric Destiny

No esoteric artist conveys the sense of impending, overwhelming destiny like Wagner. He aimed to bring a non-existent world into being; Baudelaire described how watching Lohengrin induced an altered state dissolving the ordinary sensory world. The occultist Theodor Reuss claimed personal acquaintance with Wagner gave him special insight into a secret doctrine concealed in Parsifal — reading the closing scene, where Parsifal stands holding his lae erect, as a glorious deification of the sex drive.

Old Believer Offshoots: Stranniki, Khlysty, and Rasputin

The Old Believer tradition produced the Stranniki (Wanderers) — solitary individuals renouncing money, marriage, passports, and official documents, promising ecstatic visions, healing, and prophecy; if caught, they were tortured, sometimes beheaded.

A later movement, the Khlysty (People of God), was a persecuted underground society known for extreme asceticism and world-rejecon. They reportedly met at night in forest clearings lit by candles, dancing naked under white robes in two circles — men moving with the sun, women against it (widdershins) — aiming for liberation from the material world and ascent into spirit realms. Participants would collapse, speak in tongues, heal the sick, and cast out demons. Rumors of orgies likely misrepresent what were more probably sexual ascetic practices, akin to the Cathars, sublimating sexual energy for spiritual purposes.

The young Rasputin stayed at the Verkhoturye monay, where he encountered Khlysty members, and developed his own radical doctrine: spiritual ecstasy through sexual exhaustion, in which the flesh is crucified and orgasm's "little death" becomes the mystic death of initiation. After a vision of Mary instructing him to become a wanderer, Rasputin walked two thousand miles to Mount Athos, returning two years later exuding powerful magnetism and displaying miraculous healing powers.

Arriving in St Petersburg in 1903, Rasputin was introduced to the royal family's confessor, who declared, "It is the voice of the Russian soil which speaks through him," and thence to a court already fascinated with esoteric ideas. Martinism was already discussed in Russia's Masonic lodges; Maître Philippe and Papus visited the Russian court in 1901, with Papus making Nicholas II head of a Martinist lodge and acting as the Tsar's healer, reportedly conjuring the spirit of Alexander III, who prophesied Nicholas II's death at revolutionaries' hands. Papus also warned the Tsar against Rasputin's evil influence. Raspuin would later be slandered and murdered by Freemasons, but in 1916 the initiate Rudolf Steiner said of him, "the Russian Folk-Spirit can now work through him alone and through no-one else."

Occult Themes in Popular Literature and Art

Below the very highest rung of art and literature, an explicit occult literature emerged that would dominate twentieth-century popular culture. Oscar Wilde, steeped in Order of the Golden Dawn lore, brought the occult doppelgänger into public consciousnes through The Picture of Dorian Gray, as did Robert Louis Stevenson's Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. M.R. James — Cambridge don and father of the ghost story — translated Apocryphal gospels, lectured on occult sciences at Eton, and wrote Count Magnus, featuring a pilgrimage to Chorazin, birthplace of the Antichrist; Chorozon iso the name of a demon that conversed at length with Dee and Kelley, suggesting James's genuine occult knowledge.

Frankenstein's monster fictionalized Paracelsus's homunculus. Polidori (present at the same house party where Mary Shelley conceived her novel) wrote an early vampire story, but Bram Stoker's Dracula is most famous — its preserved tomb-body a demic version of Christian Rosenkreuz. Stoker himself belonged to the OTO (Ordo Templi Orientis), a ceremonial magic society. Gustav Meyrink explored similar themes in The Golem, which influenced German expressionist cinema. Huysmans was rumored to have broken his oath of secrecy by describing real black magic rituals in Là-Bas; Aleister Crowley noted with approval that Huysmans later died of tongue cancer as a result.

Explicit occult themes appear in the symbolism of Gustave Moreau, Arnold Böcklin, and Franz von Stuck; Max Klinger's waking dreams; Felicien Rops's weird erotic-occult art (dubbed "a sarcastic Satan" by a contemporary critic); and Odilon Redon's writing of "surrendering himself to secret laws."

Materialism's Capture of Esoteric Ideas: Darwin, Marx, Freud, Jung

Throughout this period materialism worked to devise materialistic versions of esoteric philosophy: esoteric ide of species evolution appeared in materialistic form in Darwin's theories; the manipulative methodology of the Illuminati fed revolutionary movements; and Marx's dialectical materialism translated St Germain's spiritual ideals onto a purely economic plane.

Occultism shaped Freud's ideas as well. His mentor Charcot had himself been taught by the occultist and mesmerism inventor Anton Mesmer. The young Freud studied Cabala and wrote approvingly of telepathy, speculating it might be an archaic form of communication predating language. Freud introduced into mainstream thought an essentially cabalistic idea — that consciousness has a structure — with his super ego/ego/id model representing a materialized version of the tripartite cabalistic model. Even more fundamentally, his notion of impulses independent of consciawareness that can impinge on it from outside is a secularized version of esoteric accounts of consciousness, though Freud reinterpreted these hidden forces as sexual rather than spiritual, and later reacted against his ideas' esoteric roots, stigmatizing as mad the ancient form of consciousness from which they grew.

The esoteric influences on Jung are even clearer: he interpreted alchemical processes as descriptions of psychological healing and identified seven archetypes of the collective unconscious with the symbolism of seven planetary gods. However, by treating alchemy as purely psychological, he denied the level of meaning alchemical writers intended — that such mental exercises can influence matter supernaturally. Though Jung saw the seven archetypes as acting independently of the conscious mind, he stopped short of viewing them as disembodied centres of consciousness fully independent of the human mind; he even dismissed Rudolf Steiner as a schizophrenic upon meeting him.

Late in life, though, Jung's collaboration with physicist Wolfgang Pauli pushed him further: they came to believe that besides the purely physical mechanism of atoms interacting, there exists a network of non-physical, causal connections binding events together, brought about mind. Contemporaneously, French anthropologist Henri Corbin, researching Sufi spiritual practices, concluded that Sufi adepts worked in concert and communicated in a realm of "objective imagination" — Jung coined the identical phrase independently.

Freud's Uncanny Experiences

Late in life, the materialistic explanations Freud had imposed on spiritual experience sprang back at him, plaguing him with what he called "the uncanny." He wrote his essay on this subject at age sixty-two, appently trying to forestall a feared death by thinking about it — a few years earlier the number sixty-two had come at him insistently via a hat-check ticket, a hotel room number, and a train seat number, making him wonder if the cosmos was trying to tell him something.

In the same essay he described repeatedly, no matter which rection he took, finding himself back in an Italian town's red-light district while trying to walk the most direct route out — an experience recalling Francis Bacon, as if the maze itself were changing shape to thwart t wanderer. These experiences led Freud to suspect some complicity between his psyche and the cosmos, or that the cosmos might be manufacturing meanings independently of human agency and beaming them at him. Had he been forced to admit either possibility even once, his entire materialistic worldview would have been shattered — so he anxiously worked to block these promptings, which left him disturbed.

Reverse Colonization of Esoteric Ideas

European colonization prompted a flow of esoteric ideas back into Europe. British rule in India led to English publication of esoteric Hindu texts, meaning oriental esotericism remains better represented in Western bookshops than its occidental counterpart. French colonies in North Africa lent French-speaking esotericism a strong Sufi coloring. The partition of Poland spread that country's alchemical traditions across Europe. A genuine Rosicrucian impulse survived in central Europe via Rudolf Steiner's Anthroposophy. The Russian Revolution caused court occultists to flee, introducing a stream of Orthox esotericism to the West, and the Sufi- and Orthodox-influenced philosophy of Gurdjieff and Ouspensky became influential in Europe and America. In the 1950s, China's invasion of Tibet dispersed Tibetan esotericism worldwide.

As organized state religion risks becoming mere sterile formalism, intelligent individuals reaching a point in life of confronting the great questions of life, death, and meaning find esoteric philosophy the richest, deepest, and most fascinating body of thought addressing them.

Modernism as Esoteric Revolt

The greatest art at the turn of the twentieth century expressed the cry of hurt and puzzled humanity. Some artists, including great ones, concluded existence was meaningless — human life an accident of chemical combination, as Sartre concluded at the end of La Nausée, meaning attable only if one chooses to devise personal goals. Other artists embraced the material age's shiny surfaces, and Modernism was undoubtedly iconoclastic, but by century's end the tyranny of kings, clerical superstition, and stodgy bourgeois morality were soft targets.

For most great modern artists, the real icon they wanted to smash was the mechanical model of the universe. Modernism is popularly thought of as atheistic, but in the radical modern sense it is not — if esotericism is dismissed as ancient superstition, then Modernism itself is exactly that. The unifying spirit connecting Picasso, Joyce, Malevich, Gaudí, Beuys, Borges, and Calvino is a desire to undermine and subvert prevailing scientific materialism; probing their lives reveals deep occult involvement, with esotericism providing their core philosophy and guiding aesthetic.

Baudelaire and Rimbaud's recommended "derangement of the senses" is easily misread as an end in itself, but they believed that dissolving the material world would reveal the spirit worlds' lineaments. Rimbaud: "The poet makes himself clairvoyant by turning all meaning upside down in a long and reasoned manner."

Painters and the Occult

Gauguin, Munch, Klee, and Mondrian were theosophs. Mondrian's theosophy taught him to discern a spiritual reality structuring material appearances. Gauguin saw his sculptures as Golem-like objects enlivened by disembodied spirits. Kandinsky, like Franz Marc, was a disciple of Rudolf Steiner, but the formative influence on his path into abstraction was the "thought forms" perceived in trance and recorded by theosophists Annie Besant and C.W. Leadbeater. Klee depicted himself meditating on the Third Eye. Malevich was in thrall to Ouspensky. Matisse said he would look at an object he intended to paint for weeks or months until its spirit urged him to give it expression. Gaudí's Arab-influenced, surging arabesque architecture invites visitors into an altered state of consciousness.

Picasso, described as the great artist-magus of Modernism, always had a strong feeling for spirit-world intrusions; as aboy some friends believed he had supernatural abilities like mind-reading and prophecy. In France, Max Jacob, Erik Satie, Apollinaire, Georges Bataille, and Jean Cocteau initiated him into a sophisticated occult tradition. Picasso often painted himself as Harlequin, a figure associated with Hermes and the Underworld, particularly in his native Barcelona where Harlequin's victory over death is re-enacted in annual street carnivals; Apollinaire called him "Harlequin Trismegistus." He also portrayed himself via Tarot imagery, suspended between material and spirit worlds.

A long-overlooked 1934 Picasso bullfight drawing, analyzed by Mark Harris, highlights a Parsifal theme — Picasso had in youth founded a group called Valhalla to study Wagner's mystical aspects, and the drawing depicts the black magician hurling the spear of Longinus at an initiated Parsifal, where it merely hovers over his head. Bataille researched Mithraism, and in 1901 Picasso painted women wearing the Mithraic cap, a traditional initiation symbol; Harris shows the 1934 drawing portrays an underworld initiation, echoing Dante and Dostoyevsky in showing that the hell a candidate must traverse begins with the hell of his own desires — hell lies beyond the grave, but life itself is helliscording to the temper of the times. The drawing depicts Picasso's grand theme: the world being shattered by an eruption of evil, subterranean forces, with the initiatic artist able to remake the world as a reborn fertility god — not through conventional canons of beauty but by recombining the discarded, shattered, and ugly into beautiful new forms.

Abstract painter Yves Klein discovered esoteric thought through a book by Max Heindel, a modern Rosicrucian who had been initiated by Rudolf Stner before founding his own movement. Klein intended his unbroken ultramarine canvases to inaugurate a new Age of Space in which human spirit, freed of matter's restrictions, would levitate and float.

Writers and the Occult

Inspired by rumors about William Blake's sexual religion, W.B. Yeats and his wife Georgie explored the direct link between sexual and spiritual union found in the Zohar, then Tantric yoga. Yeats even had a vasectomy hoping to stem semen flow and build energies for visionary trance. Their experiments produced over four thousand pages of spirit-inspired automatic writing, and Yeats remained sexually rejuvenated into old age, writing some of his most magnificent poetry then, describing "the love that moves the Sun." He belonged to both the Order of the Golden Dawn and the Theosophical Society, studied the Hermetica, wrote openly about magic, and introduced a popular edition of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

Joyce's Ulysses and Finnegans Wake show familiarity with Hindu and Hermetic doctrine, including direct quotes from Swedenborg, Madame Blavatsky, and Eliphas Levi. T.S. Eliot used occult references eclectically, attending Theosophist meetings and the breakaway Quest group alongside Ezra Pound, Wyndham Lewis, and Gershom Scholem (the great scholar of Jewish mysticism). The formative influence on Eliot's poetic sensibility, however, was the Sufi-inspired philosophy of Ouspensky, whose lectures he attended — the famous opening lines of Four Quartets, on time past and future contained in time present, paraphrase Ouspensky's philosophy directly.

Fernando Pesa may be the most occult writer of the twentieth century, best living up to Rimbaud's dictum of becoming a medium. He wrote of holding within himself all the dreams of the world and awaiting the return of the Hidden One, who has himself been waiting since the beginning of time. Pessoa emptied himself like a medium, allowing himself to be taken over by a series of personae under whose names he wrote poems with very different voices — echoing an ancient Taoist text ("I am the cleverness in theice") and the Gnostic Hymn of the Pearl ("I am the active in the deeds"). To move things in space and time and make the world better, it is not enough to push as hard as possible — spirits must work through us, requiring some of that spirit of cleverness.

Later twentieth-century writers Borges, Calvino, Salinger, and Singer de openly with esoteric themes, in accord with Karlheinz Stockhausen's assertion that all genuine creation makes conscious something from the esoteric realm not previously conscious. Rudolf Steiner's Anthroposophy influenced Kandinsky, Marc, and Beuys, as well as William Golding and Doris Lessing, both of whom lived in Anthroposophical communities. Strikingly, C.S. Lewis and Saul Bellow — very different writers — were both instructed in esoteric philosophy by same spiritual master, the Anthroposophist Owen Barfield. Bellow and John Updike, leading turn-of-century novelists, both show esoteric influence; Updike's overtly occult novel is The Witches of Eastwick, and a passage from his later novel Villages describes sex as "a programmed delirium that rolls back death with death's own substance."

This tension reaches to the heart of the divide between exoteric and esoteric worldviews: according to esoteric thinkers, life in a mechanized, industrialized, digitalized environment deadens mental processes — concrete, plastic, metal, and electrical screen impulses become internalized, producing a sterile wasteland that does not regenerate itself. A conscious shift in consciousness is needed to reopen the free-flowing, revivifying influence of the spirit worl.

Occult Roots of Revolution: Bolshevism and Nazism

In 1789 the armies of angels led by St Michael won a victory in heaven, but for that victory to become decisive it needed to be fought again on earth. On 28 June 1914 — the very day Rasputin was overtaken by a plot to kill him — Archduke Ferdinand of Austria was assassinated, and hell broke loose.

Much has been written about evil occult influences on early twentieth-century Germany; less known is the occult story behind the Russian lution's revolutionary communists, the enemies of Rasputin and the Martinists already discussed. Marxism can be seen as a materialistic reframing of Freemasonry's fraternal ideals; the revolutionary cell structure instigated by Lenin and Trotsky was closely modeled on Weishaupt's working methods. Marx, Engels, and Trotsky were Freemasons; Lenin was a 31st-degree Freemason belonging to several lodges, including the Lodge of the Nine Sisters — the most important lodge infiltrated by the followers and nihilistic philosophy of the Illuminati. Lenin d Trotsky waged war on God.

Like Augustus and James I, Hitler persecuted occultists because he believed in them, not because he disbelieved. One of the era's most learned occultists, Franz Bardon, was arrested with a disciple by the SS; the disciple reportedly lost control under torture and shouted a cabalistic formula that froze his torturers, though once the spell broke he was shot. Bardon worked professionally as a stage magician — the archetype of the stage magician who is secretly a real occultist appears in Thomas Mann's story Mario and the Magician and the film The Cabinet of Dr Caligari.

The Deeper Mystery of Lenin's Power

A deeper mystery remains: how did a man like Lenin bend millions to his will, seemingly beyond the sinister strategies of a Weishaupt? US military research into occult means of gaining advantage over the Soviet Union has been well documented, with testimony from key personnel appearing authentic, though results were limited. Only now is the far more extreme — and successful — use of occultism by Soovernment agencies emerging. Reluctant surviving initiates speak of "the red initiation," secret-agent training conducted in former monasteries, employing occult techniques to strengthen the will to a supernatural degree by exploiting the psychic energies of torture victims and sacrificial victims; only someone who had killed in the cause could become a red initiate.

This form of black magic recalls the pyramid culture of South America. In secret history, Lenin is understood as the reincarnation of a high priest, born again to oppose the second coming of the Sun god; when Trotsky fled to Mexico City, he was, in this reading, returning home. The image of the mummified Lenin as pyramid-initiate reincarnation is both resonant and slightly absurd to modern sensibility — yet it encapsulates Modernism's very spirit, mixinthe iconic and the offbeat, the cheap and tackily up to date with ancient occult wisdom.

Gandhi: The Evolved Consciousness

Occult circles have long debated how much esoteric wisdom should be made public — how much aids the war against materialism, and how much is dangerous.

Returning to India, where post-Atlantean history began: by this point in history, hunity can be seen to have evolved far from the communally minded creature of earlier times who had little awareness of the surrounding world or an interior life. In Gandhi appears individual free thought, free will, and free love — someone who so expanded his sense of self that turning points in his own personal, interior narrative became turning points in world history. Gandhi stands as a great embodiment of the new form of consciousness that secret societies have worked throughout history to help evolve.

It is a small irony, marking the global reach of secret societies, that Gandhi — from the land of the Rishis — first learned esoteric ideas from the Russian/English/Egyptian/American hybrid Theosophy taught by Madame Blavatsky.

Gandhi's Spiritual Discipline and Soul Force

As a young man Gandhi described himself as "in love" with the British Empire, seeing the best in its upright, fairng administrators. As he matured he perceived a deeper reality beneath the fair play: the unfairness of taxation and India's lack of freedom to determine its own destiny. Influenced partly by American Transcendentalist Henry Thoreau's philosophy of civil disobedience and by art and social critic John Ruskin, Gandhi set about turning the world upside down and inside out.

In 1906, at age thirty-six, Gandhi renounced sex with his wife. His spiritual discipline involved daily work on a hand-spun spinning wheel — partly to provide employment for the poor through cloth-weaving, but also because he believed working on the cloth was simultaneously working on his own vegetable body; mastering the body in its different dimensions would develop what he called soul force. He believed the cosmos is governed by truth and the ls of truth, and that acting in accordance with these laws would yield Satyagraha, the force of truth and love.

Practical Application: Non-Violent Resistance as Occult Technique

Gandhi taught that trusting an opponent without fail would eventually influence him toward trustworthy behavior — both through psychological influence and, crucially, through a supeatural one. Similarly, if attacked, one should remain free from all thoughts of anger and hatred toward the assailant. Following this philosophy, Gandhi taught, would make a person "free of fear of kings, people, robbers, tigers, even death."

In the upside-down thinking typical of secret societies, Gandhi blamed Indians, not Britons, for India's occupation, pointing out that 100,000 Britons could not control three hundred million Indians without their compliance. Indian cotton was exported to Britain's Lancashire mills, then sold back to India at profit to Britain and loss to India. At his spinning wheel he said, "It's my certain conviction that with every thread I draw, I am spinning the destiny of India."

On 26 January 1929 Gandhi called for observance of Independence Day nationwide, urging boycotts of law courts, elections, and schools. He also challenged the British monopoly on salt manufacture, which forced Indians to pay for salt lying in open abundance around their own coasts. In March 1930, at age sixty, Gandhi set off on a twenty-four-day walk to the sea, joined by thousands; he waded into the sea for ritual purification, then scooped up a handful of salt, and the crowd acclaimed him "Deliverer!"

Gandhi's soul power was such that armed soldiers would lower their weapons when they met him, and Hindus and Muslims forgave each other in his presence. His imprisonment and hunger strikes sapped the moral will of the British government, leading to Indian independence in 1947 — the largest empire the world had ever seen melting away with unprecedented lack of bloodshed.

Gandhi's Place Among History's Great Figures

Compared to great leaders such as Alexander the Great and Napoleon covered earlier in this history, Gandhi in a sense surpassed them all. He believed soul force could deflect the greatest military power, because the intention behind an action could have greater and more widespread effects than the actn itself. Though a devout Hindu, Gandhi lived by the deeper laws laid out in the Sermon on the Mount, teaching hostile Hindu and Muslim factions that self-sacrifice confined to one's own community eventually becomes selfishness that makes the whole community selfish — the spirit of self-sacrifice should embrace the whole world. Like St Francis, he loved the whole world.

Chapter 28: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday: The Anti-Christ • Re-entering the Ancient Wood • The Maitreya Buddha

The Peculiarity of Materialist Belief

Matter-before-mind beliefs are historically anomalous — held only in this "obscure suburb of history," an age of declining educational standards. At every other time and place, people believed mind preceded matter, and would have found current beliefs incomprehensible. This shift is explained as a change in consciousness rather than a rational conclusion reached by weighing arguments: people a few generations ago believed in idealism not because they argued their way there but because they experienced the world ically.

Generational Shifts in Consciousness

Consciousness changes rapidly between generations — evidence used to argue that esoteric claims about radical shifts in perception across centuries are plausible. Compared with parents' generation, current consciousness tends to be:

  • More liberal and sympathetic to different races, classes, genders, and sexual orientations
  • More self-aware, particularly regarding underlying sexual motivations (due to the spread of Freud's ideas) and commeral motivations (due to Marx)
  • Less repressed, less fearful of authority, more questioning, with weaker family ties
  • More prone to lying, with weaker concentration and less determination for boring, long-term tasks
  • Less committed to lifelong romantic/sexual partnership despite lip service paid to romantic love — echoing Ril's observation in The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge that part of a person wants to flee the responsibility of being loved

Projecting this rate of change backward implies that only a few generations ago, everyday waking consciousness might have resembled dream consciousness. This raises the central question of the chapter: how will consciousness change going forward?

Mirrored History: Jesus Christ as the Midpoint

Esoteric Christianity holds that the life of Jesus Christ occurred at the midpoint of cosmic history, and everything since mirrors everything before it in reverse order — future development revisits earlier stages backward. Practical example: around AD 2000, life mirrors Abraham's experience in 2000 BC walking among the idolatrous skyscrapers of Uruk. Today's literal skyscrapers represent modern fundamentalism, understood as having two faces:

  • Right-wing Christian and crude forms of Islamic fundamentalism, which repress individual free will and intelligence and lure people into unenlightening ecstasy — the influence of Lucifer
  • Militant scientific materialism, which mechanizes humanity and seeks to snuff out spirit altogether, reducing people to mere matter — the influence of Satan

The Coming Incarnation of Satan (the Anti-)

Just as Lucifer once incarnated, Satan will incarnate in turn — as a writer. His mission will be to destroy spirituality by "explaining it away": he will have genuine ability to create supernatural events, then supply reductive scientific explanations for them.

Non-obvious warning: he will not begin as an obvious villain. At first he will appear a great benefactor and genius, dismantling dangerous superstition and working to unite the world's religions — and he himself may initially bee he acts purely out of love for humanity, unaware of his true identity. Only later, in a moment of pride upon realizing he has achieved things Jesus Christ apparently could not, will he become conscious of his identity and mission.

Practical Warning Signs: Recognizing False Prophets and False Teaching

Concrete diagnostic criteria are offered for spotting Satan, any false prophet, or any spurious spiritual teaching:

  • False teaching has little or no moral dimension — for instance, recommending chakra reawakening purely for selfish "personalrowth" rather than for the sake of others. Genuine spiritual teaching centers on intelligent, freely given love of others and of humanity.
  • Be wary of any teaching that forbids questioning or cannot tolerate mockery — such a stance is effectily telling adherents that God wants them to be stupid.

The Purpose of Secret Societies

Throughout history, highly intelligent individuals immersed themselves in esoteric philosophy, using secret techniques to enter altered states granting access to abnormally elevated intelligence. These groups worked deliberately to forge new, more highly intelligent forms of human consciousness — an influence on human development now almost entirely overlooked by conventional history.

The Thinning Veil Between Worlds

Humans once had unhindered access to spirit worlds; this access became obscured as matter hardened, but the barrier is now thinning again as the material world "frays" and becomes threadbare. Anticipated developments as this progresses:

  • Greater awareness of the deeper laws suggested by "coindences" and synchronicities
  • Less certainty that one's own intuitions and brilliant ideas originate purely from oneself, and more openness to their being otherworldly promptings
  • Recognition that people are connected to one another more directly through thinking than through speech or physical observation
  • A heightened sense that interpersonal interaction is far more mysterious than routinely assumed
  • Learning to interpret relationships through reincarnation — understanding "subconsciousfeelings of instant liking or disliking toward strangers as residue from previous incarnations

The Limits of Scientific Materialism

Scientific-materialist belief is itself a choice made from a psychological predisposition, not a neutral conclusion from evidence. When contemplating vast questions like the origin of the universe, enormous speculation is mapped onto vanishingly small amounts of actual evidence — leading physicists' and cosmologists' theories about infinite dimensions, parallel universes, and "soap bubble universes" involves much imagination as Aquinas's musings on angels on a pinhead. The world resembles an ambiguous "perspected" picture (readable as either a witch or a young girl): people gravitate toward whichever worldview they deep down want to believe.

Practical application: becoming conscious of this underlying predisposition allows a genuinely free choice, based on knowledge rather than unexamined bias. The part of oneself that wants to believe in a mechanical-materialist universe may not be the part that should be allowed to determine one's fate.

The Fourfold Work on the Four Elements

Drawing on "Know Thyself" and techniques from ancient Mystery schools and modern groups like the Rosicrucians, becoming aware of the rhythms of one's breath, heartbeat, sexual cycles, and the cycle of waking/dreaming/dreamless sleep allows conscious attunement of individual rhythms to cosmic rhythms (symbolized by the pillars Jachin and Boaz) — potentially joining individual evolution with cosmic evolution, described as life's highest meaning.

A secret preserveby figures as diverse as Plato, St Paul, Leonardo, Shakespeare, and Newton is laid out as a fourfold sequence, tied to St Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 13 ("For now we see through a glass darkly... faith, hope, love"):

  1. Thinking deeply enough to rediscover the spiritual roots of thought — recognizing thoughts as living spiritual beings
  2. Developing individuality strong enough to become aware of interaction with these Thought-Beings without being overwhelmed
  3. Recreating ancient wonder tawaken dormant willpower in one's deep recesses
  4. Allowing the fire of love for fellow humans to rise from the heart into tears of compassion

Undertaking this process constitutes "work on the Four Elements" and their transformation:

  • Intuition = transformed intellect perceiving spiritual beings as real (Paul's "faith")
  • Wonder = transformed feeling, aware of spiritual workings without being overwhelmed (Paul's "hope")
  • Conscience = transformed will, once thought, imagination, faith, and hope have worked on subconscious willpower (Paul's "charity"/love)

By applying faith to hope and both to love, a human being can be transformed into an angel: symbolically, the Scorpion becomes an Eagle, the Eagle works on the Bull so it grows wings, the winged Bull works on the Lion so it too grows wings, and the winged Lion works on Man to transform him into an Angel. This fourfold mystery was taught in ancient Mystery centers and became the central mystery of esoteric Christianity. Leonardo's painting Allegory is cited as depicting this exercise — noting the creature usually catalogued as a wolf (in the Queen's collection) is actually a bull.

Cosmic scope of the practice: the Four Elements are crucial to the formation of the physical universe, so working on them as they weave through a person transforms not just that individual but the whole universe to its outer limits. If a person weeps tears of compassion, their own animal nature is transformed, but so too are the Cherubim interwoven throughout the cosmos — changes in human physiology become seeds for transfiguring the entire rial universe. Cabalist Isaac Luria is cited for the claim that eventually there will be no single atom left untouched by this human work.

Reversal of Creation's Order

Creation proceeded: mineral, then vegetable, then animal, then human — each stage nurturing conditions for the next. Later history reverses this order, transforming human, then animal, then vegetable, then finally mineral. At the end of time, even the atoms of material nature will be transformed, as in Christ's Transfigution.

Humanity is only briefly "dipped into matter" — the hardening of the earth and of human skulls enabled a proper sense of self and thus the capacity for free thought, will, and love. Before this brief material sojourn, human experience consisted of ideas — Imagination's objects (conceived as coming from spirits, angels, gods) were as real as, or more real than, physical objects, and remained so for most of human history even after matter had formed. The lesson drawn from modern history is that matter is currently being transformed andpersed, foreshadowing a future re-entry into the realm of Imagination.

The Seven "Days" of the Great Week and What Comes Next

History divides into seven cosmic "days": Saturday (rule of Saturn), Sunday (earth united with the sun), Monday (age before the moon departed), and Tuesday (beginning with the material world locking into fixed place in 11,145 BC, with Christ's death marking its halfway point). Projected future stages:

Philadelphia (from AD 3574): Following past evolutionary impulses from India, Persia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, and Northern Europe, the next great impulse will emerge from Eastern Europe and Russia — explaining why Freemasonic-influenced American and British governments have taken particular interest in that region. Extremes are already visible there, both of spirituality and of evil (e.g., Russian organized crime).

Great historical personalities who once led humanity out of the spirit worlds will be reborn to lead humanity back into them — a new Shakespeare, a new Moses, a new Zarathustra, a new Hercules.ard the end of the Philadelphian era, Jesus Pandira (Teacher of the Essenes) will reincarnate as "the Fifth Rider who rides a horse called Faithful and True" from Revelation — known in oriental tradition as the Maitreya Buddha. He will open "the eyes of the soul" (the chakras), a phrase attributed to St Teresa of Avila.

Re-entering the sacred wood: Humanity will re-enter the primordial sacred wood, becoming aware once more of spirits, angels, and gods alive in everything, but without bng controlled by them. People will again perceive the spiritual beings ranged on either side whenever making a decision. As communication with good and evil spirits becomes universal, organized religion will no longer be needed ("Imagine no religion"). Abilities once possessed by Adam — controlling animals and plants through thght — will partly return, alongside the ability to remember past lives and foresee the future. Waking consciousness will develop such that it relates to present-day waking consciousness the way present waking consciousss relates to dreaming — revealing that what feels like wakefulness today is actually a kind of sleep.

Warning — the cost of this progress: These developments will be hard-won. The Philadelphian era ends in a catastrophic world war, afthich the earth's surface becomes a spiritual wasteland except for America, which preserves the flame of spirituality — a mirror image of the era of the first Zarathustra.

Laodicea (AD 5734–7894): As matter becomes less dense, bodies increasingly respond to spiritual impulses — goodness will visibly shine from good people, while evil people's faces and bodies will be molded by the animal passions dominating them. Good people will find happiness increasingly difficult while others remain miserable, until eventually no one is happy unless everyone is happy. As the material world's brevity implies death's brevity too, people will stop dying and instead sleep ever more lightly, and eventually not at all — death "swallowed up," per St Paul. Biological generation itself will become unnecessary Word that has been lost" of the Freemasons is rediscovered — the ability to create by the power of the voice.

Thursday: Time as currently understood will cease to exist; thoughts will take on independent life, working on a person's behalf but autonomously. As history nears its end, evil reasserts itself through Sorath, the Sun demon — the third being in a trinity of evil, described in Revelation as the beast with two lamb-like horns — who will lead the forces of evil in the Last Batventually the sun will rise differently, as predicted by St John Chrysostom, and ultimately a sun will rise up inside each individual.

Thought as the Engine of History

All of this is accomplished by the power of thought. Historically, the individuals who most changed the course of events have generally been artists and thinkers rather than generals or politicians — a single person alone in a room giving birth to an idea can shift history more than a general commanding armies or a politician commanding millions. In a mind-before-matter univee, thinking carries not just romance and excitement but literal magic: what one thinks, not merely what one does or says, affects fellow humans and the entire course of history.

Closing Argument Against Scientific Certainty

Plato held that philosophy begins in wonder; modern science is charged with killing off both wonder and philosophy by claiming to already know everything and discouraging the asking of fundamental "Why" questions as strictly meaningless. Scientists are portrayed as treating the known as a vast continent covering nearly all reality, whereas the esoteric-minded historical figures profiled throughout this account treat the known as a tiny island floating on a vast, strange sea.

Recommended stance: sow seeds of doubt, follow Francis Bacon's advice against rushing to impose a pattern on the world, and wait — as Keats advised — for a deeper pattern to emerge. Science itself is characterized as a myth like any other, reflecting what people in their depths want to believe. Rudolf Steiner is cited for the claim that peowho lack the courage to be outright cruel often develop cruel beliefs instead — and asserting that the universe is not reciprocal is labeled a needlessly cruel position. Accepting such cruel views means deferring to specialist experts over personal experience, and denying truths that Shakespeare, Cervantes, and Dostoyevsky convey.

The overall aim has been to show that fundamental assumptions about existence may be seen in a radically different, nearly opposite light from conventional upbrging — genuine philosophy's proper function. Remnants of ancient wisdom persist all around in the names of weekdays and months, the arrangement of pips in an apple, the strangeness of mistletoe, music, children's stories, and the design of public buildings, statues, art, and literature — invisible only because of conditionin materialism.

Science treats idealism as having dominated until the seventeenth century, when its discrediting began, and assumes materialism will remain dominant until time's end; in the view represented here, materialism will eventually be seen as a mere historical blip.

Final Reflection: Imagination as the Key

This account is framed as a "night history" â visionary history retained in the human psyche, preserved by adepts capable of slipping from the material dimension into another, potentially true in other dimensions even where incompatible with conventional taught history. Physicist Niels Bohr is quoted: "The opposite of a correct statement is a false statement, but the opposite of a profound truth may well be another profound truth."

Beyond roughly 11,451 BC in the past, or 11,451 AD equivalent distance into the future, hard scientific evidence gives out almost entirely, with vast interpretive structures balanced on tiny data points in both directions — meaning imagination becomes unavoidable once one leaves "this little island of matter" in either temporal direction. Materialists distrust imagination, associating it with fantasy and illusion, but secret societies hold an exalted view of it: each individual mind is regarded as a protrusiointo the material world of one vast cosmic mind, and imagination is the faculty used to reach back into and engage with that cosmic mind. This use of imagination is what made Leonardo, Shakespeare, and Mozart god-like. Imagination is identified as the key.
